- Sentence, Feb 12 1599: men over 25, one foot cut off + 20 years' servitude; males 12-25 and females over 12, 20 years; children under 12 taken from parents; ~70 girls sent to convents in Mexico ("in all probability, none ever returned home" - NPS); two Hopi captives each lost a right hand.
- Mutilation's execution disputed (Simmons recanted; Kessell doubts) - but the ORDER is in the record and Onate was convicted for Acoma: 30 charges, convicted on 12, banished for life, exiled, fined.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="native-nations" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Nations still held nearly the whole continent; the newcomers were a coastal fringe that survived on Native food, Native trade, and Native permission. The century's pattern from the nations' side: first accommodation and alliance-building on their own terms, then war when the newcomers stopped needing permission — and, in the Southwest, the most successful Native rising against a European power in North America.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tsenacommacah" -->
In eastern Virginia the mamanatowick Wahunsenacawh ("the Powhatan") built a tribute state of more than 30 nations — about 15,000 people across some 10,000 square miles, each town under its own weroance paying tribute upward. Jamestown (1607) was planted inside it and spent its first years dealing with him as the power in the land.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Wampum diplomacy and the Covenant Chain" -->
Diplomacy ran on wampum — agreements recorded in beadwork and memory. The Two Row Wampum (Guswenta) holds the Haudenosaunee's first agreement with the Dutch (their tradition dates it 1613): two vessels on the same river, side by side, neither steering the other. With the English the alliance became the Covenant Chain (first recorded 1677, Albany) — a chain of silver, because silver tarnishes and must be polished: the alliance had to be renewed, council after council, and was.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The coastal wars" -->
- **Pequot War (1636–38):** at Mystic on May 26, 1637, an English-led force burned the Pequot town and killed hundreds, mostly elders, women, and children, in under an hour. The Treaty of Hartford (1638) declared the nation dissolved and outlawed its very name — and failed: the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation exists in Connecticut today.
- **King Philip's War (1675–76):** Metacom's coalition against the New England colonies; about 9,000 dead — by share of population the bloodiest war in American history, killing roughly half the Native people of New England.
- The Beaver Wars — Haudenosaunee campaigns over the fur trade — remade the eastern interior.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Pueblo Revolt" -->
August 10, 1680: the Pueblo nations of the Rio Grande rose together — coordinated across many towns and languages by Po'pay of Ohkay Owingeh — took Santa Fe, and drove Spain out of New Mexico. 401 settlers and 21 friars were killed; most Spaniards were allowed to flee. The Pueblos governed themselves for 12 years, through drought and famine, until the reconquest began in 1692. Horses: the traditional account has the revolt's captured herds (1,500+) spreading horses west and north along Native trade routes; a 2023 study in *Science*, working with Lakota, Comanche, and Pawnee partners, dated horses among Plains nations to the early 1600s — matching oral histories. The timing is unsettled; both accounts go in.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="pope" name="Po'pay (Popé)" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Po'pay (Popé)
> **Who:** Tewa religious leader from Ohkay Owingeh who organized dozens of towns speaking different languages into one rising — by Pueblo accounts, knotted cords carried the countdown from town to town. · **When and where:** New Mexico, August 1680.
His statue stands in the U.S. Capitol today — a leader of the one revolt that pushed an empire off Native land for a decade.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="pope" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="metacom-native-nations" name="Metacom (King Philip)" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Metacom (King Philip)
> **Who:** Wampanoag sachem, son of Massasoit who had made the peace with Plymouth; led the coalition war of 1675–76 when the peace had been eaten away. · **When and where:** southern New England; killed at Mount Hope, August 12, 1676.
His wife and nine-year-old son were sold into slavery (Bermuda per most sources); his head was displayed at Plymouth; hundreds of captives were sold to pay the war's bills. Told plainly. Topic doc for the era (not about him alone): *We Shall Remain: After the Mayflower* (PBS, 2009).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="metacom-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="native-nations" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The age of play-off diplomacy: nations held the balance of power between the French and British empires and traded on their own terms — while dependence on trade goods quietly grew. Confederacies expanded, adopted whole nations, and ran a foreign policy the empires had to respect.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Neutrality as strategy" -->
At the Great Peace of Montreal (August 4, 1701) about 1,300 delegates from more than 30 nations made peace with New France, and the Haudenosaunee committed to neutrality between France and Britain — a position they worked for half a century, selling their weight to neither side cheaply.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Tuscarora move north" -->
After defeat in the Tuscarora War in North Carolina (1711–13), about 1,500 surviving Tuscarora walked north and asked the Five Nations for sponsorship; the Oneida took them in, and in 1722 the Tuscarora became the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee — a nation that lost its homeland and was adopted whole by a confederacy hundreds of miles away.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Comanche power" -->
On the southern Plains the Comanche built the dominant power of the century — Comanchería eventually covered about 240,000 square miles. They bred and traded horses, controlled the horse trade south-to-north, and in the 1740s traded robes and horses to the French for guns better than Spanish equipment. Horses, trade, raiding, and diplomacy — an economy and a foreign policy, not just fighting.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Treaty councils" -->
Treaty councils were working diplomacy with their own protocol — wampum, condolence, speakers. At Lancaster, Pennsylvania (June–July 1744), the Onondaga speaker Canasatego closed the council on July 4, 1744 by advising the colonies to unite as the Haudenosaunee had: "We heartily recommend Union and a good Agreement between you our Brethren." Benjamin Franklin printed the minutes.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="canasatego" name="Canasatego" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Canasatego
> **Who:** Onondaga leader, the Haudenosaunee's speaker at the great treaty councils — his printed speeches are among the best-documented Native diplomacy of the century. · **When and where:** Lancaster, Pennsylvania, 1744.
The diplomat-in-the-treaty-minutes target, filled: a man whose July 4 advice about union was set in type by Benjamin Franklin thirty-two years before another July 4.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="canasatego" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="native-nations" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
War between empires became war on Native land. The French defeat (1763) broke the play-off system; the Revolution split the oldest confederacy on the continent; and a new republic began signing treaties — 374 of them, eventually, now held at the National Archives — while a Native confederacy handed its new army the worst defeat it would ever take.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pontiac and the Line" -->
With France gone, Great Lakes and Ohio nations under the Odawa leader Pontiac took or besieged British forts across the west (1763–66). Britain answered with the Royal Proclamation of October 7, 1763: no colonial settlement west of the Appalachians — the land beyond reserved to the nations. Settlers crossed it anyway, but the Line became a root of treaty law.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Revolution splits the Haudenosaunee" -->
The Revolution broke the Confederacy's unity for the first time in centuries: Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the Americans; Mohawk, Seneca, Cayuga, and Onondaga fought with the British, many under Joseph Brant (Thayendanegea). At Oriskany (August 6, 1777) Haudenosaunee men fought each other. In 1779 Washington ordered "the total destruction and devastation of their settlements": Sullivan's army burned more than 40 Seneca and Cayuga towns and their crops; refugees starved at Fort Niagara that winter. Seneca chiefs to Washington, 1790: "we called you the Town-destroyer; and to this day, when that name is heard, our women look behind them and turn pale."
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The treaty system begins" -->
The first U.S.–Native treaty was signed with the Lenape (Delaware) at Fort Pitt, September 17, 1778 — it recognized Delaware sovereignty and even floated a Native fourteenth state with a seat in Congress (never acted on). Nation-to-nation treaties became the legal spine of everything after — including everything later broken.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Northwest Confederacy" -->
Ohio Country nations — Little Turtle (Miami), Blue Jacket (Shawnee), Buckongahelas (Delaware) — confederated to hold the Ohio River line. On November 4, 1791, they destroyed Gen. Arthur St. Clair's army: over 650 U.S. soldiers killed of about 1,000 — the largest defeat of a U.S. army by Native forces ever, bigger than Little Bighorn, and the trigger of Congress's first-ever investigation. Defeat came at Fallen Timbers (1794); at Greenville (August 3, 1795) the confederacy ceded most of Ohio.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="little-turtle" name="Little Turtle (Mishikinaakwa)" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Little Turtle (Mishikinaakwa)
> **Who:** Miami war leader who co-led the confederacy that beat St. Clair in 1791 — then judged the fight unwinnable, signed at Greenville, and spent his last years arguing for peace. · **When and where:** the Wabash and Maumee country (present Indiana and Ohio), 1780s–1790s.
Both halves matter: the general who won the biggest victory, and the statesman who decided when to stop.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="little-turtle" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="native-nations" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Nations organized to hold their land two different ways — a fighting confederacy in the north, a national rebuilding in the south with a written alphabet, a newspaper, a constitution, and a Supreme Court win. The United States answered both with removal. Removal is told here from the nations' side: governments broken and rebuilt; the journeys themselves are `migration`'s.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa" -->
Tenskwatawa's movement to return to Native ways (from about 1805) and Tecumseh's diplomacy built Prophetstown on the Wabash (1808) as the capital of a many-nations confederacy — the idea that no single nation could sell land all held in common. While Tecumseh was away recruiting, Harrison attacked (Tippecanoe, November 7, 1811) and burned the town. Tecumseh fought on with the British and died at the Thames, October 5, 1813; the confederacy died with him.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Cherokee renaissance" -->
Sequoyah demonstrated his 86-character Cherokee syllabary in 1821; within a few years most of the nation could read and write it. The Cherokee Phoenix (1828) became the first Native American newspaper, printed in Cherokee and English; a written constitution (1827) set up three branches of government at New Echota. The Cherokee answer to "civilization" policy was to out-build it — and it did not save the land.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Removal" -->
The Indian Removal Act (1830) authorized removal treaties. In *Worcester v. Georgia* (1832) Chief Justice Marshall ruled Georgia law had no force in the Cherokee Nation — a foundation of tribal sovereignty law to this day — and Georgia simply ignored the ruling. The Cherokee removal of 1838–39 (the Trail of Tears): more than 16,000 removed, over 4,000 dead — the traditional estimate; some scholars argue higher. All five southeastern nations — Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole — were removed to Indian Territory, where they rebuilt governments, courts, newspapers, and schools within a generation.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Seminole resistance" -->
The Second Seminole War (1835–42) became the longest and costliest Indian war in the East. Osceola was seized under a white flag of truce (October 21, 1837) — a ploy condemned even then — and died a prisoner. But a few hundred Seminoles withdrew deep into the Everglades and never surrendered; their descendants, the Seminole Tribe of Florida and the Miccosukee Tribe, note that the Seminole were never conquered.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="tecumseh" name="Tecumseh" movie="We Shall Remain: Tecumseh's Vision (2009)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Tecumseh
> **Who:** Shawnee leader who traveled thousands of miles arguing that Native land was held in common and could only be defended in common. · **When and where:** the Ohio country and the South, 1805–1813; died at the Thames, October 5, 1813. · **Movie:** *We Shall Remain: Tecumseh's Vision* (PBS, 2009) — a documentary about him and his brother.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="tecumseh" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sequoyah-native-nations" name="Sequoyah" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Sequoyah
> **Who:** Cherokee silversmith who could not read or write any language — and worked about twelve years to build one, the only person in recorded history known to have created a writing system alone without first being literate. · **When and where:** Cherokee Nation (born Tennessee about 1770; syllabary demonstrated 1821; died 1843 in Mexico).
Within a few years his 86 characters made the Cherokee Nation a reading and writing nation — newspaper, constitution, laws, letters between removed families.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sequoyah-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="osceola-native-nations" name="Osceola" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Osceola
> **Who:** Seminole war leader in the fight against removal from Florida. · **When and where:** Florida; seized under a truce flag October 21, 1837; died a prisoner at Fort Moultrie, South Carolina, January 30, 1838.
The capture-under-a-white-flag is told plainly — it was condemned by the public even in 1837.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="osceola-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rebecca-neugin-native-nations" name="Rebecca Neugin" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Rebecca Neugin
> **Who:** a Cherokee woman who was about three when soldiers took her family from Georgia in 1838 — she rode in the wagon while her mother, father, and older brother walked — and who told her memory of it in 1932, at about 97, to historian Grant Foreman. · **When and where:** Georgia to Indian Territory, 1838–39; interviewed in Oklahoma, 1932.
Our angle: what removal did to a nation and a family. The journey itself is `migration`'s (their story slug: rebecca-neugin-mig). Topic doc: *We Shall Remain: Trail of Tears* (PBS, 2009).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rebecca-neugin-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="native-nations" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The hardest half-century: the wars that filled the reservations, the killing of the bison economy, the end of treaty-making, allotment that took two-thirds of the remaining land, and schools built to take the children. Told from the nations' side, it is also a record of decisions — when to fight, when to run, when to sign, how to survive. By 1900 the census counted about 250,000 Native people — the low point. The chapter does not end here.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The wars, from the nations' side" -->
- **Dakota, 1862 (Minnesota):** war after promised food and payments never came; 392 five-minute trials without lawyers; Lincoln cut the death list to 39; 38 Dakota men hanged at Mankato December 26, 1862 — the largest mass execution in U.S. history; two were hanged by mistake.
- **Sand Creek, November 29, 1864 (Colorado):** Chivington's volunteers attacked Black Kettle's Cheyenne and Arapaho camp — flying a U.S. flag and a white flag — and killed about 230 people, mostly women, children, and elders.
- **Red Cloud's War → Fort Laramie Treaty (1868):** the Bozeman Trail closed; the Great Sioux Reservation, including the Black Hills, promised "for the absolute and undisturbed use" of the Lakota. Custer announced gold in the Black Hills (1874); the government ignored its own treaty; an ultimatum ordered the winter camps in by January 31, 1876, then the army came.
- **Little Bighorn (the Greasy Grass), June 25, 1876:** the allied camp — Sitting Bull its center, Crazy Horse a battle leader — destroyed Custer's command within about an hour.
- **After:** Crazy Horse surrendered in May 1877 and was bayoneted to death at Fort Robinson that September; the Nez Perce fled about 1,170 miles (NPS trail figure; some accounts longer) and surrendered 40 miles from Canada; Sitting Bull came back from Canada in 1881; Geronimo's surrender (September 4, 1886) was the last — his people were held as prisoners of war for 27 years. The Navajo, marched to Bosque Redondo in 1863–64, negotiated the 1868 treaty that took them home — nearly unique among removed nations.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The bison, and the end of treaties" -->
Roughly 30 million bison in the early 1800s; fewer than 1,000 by 1900 (one 1884 count: 325). Railroads, industrial hide-hunting — and army encouragement, because the herds were the Plains nations' food, economy, and religion. In 1871 Congress quietly ended treaty-making with Native nations (existing treaties stayed in force). The two facts together are the mechanism of the reservation era: the economy destroyed, the diplomacy closed.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Allotment" -->
The Dawes Act (1887) cut communal land into individual parcels and sold the "surplus": Native landholdings fell from about 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934 — about 90 million acres, two-thirds of what was left, gone. Ended only by the Indian Reorganization Act (1934).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The boarding schools — this chapter leads" -->
Carlisle opened November 1, 1879 (founder: Army officer Richard Henry Pratt). His stated purpose, in an 1892 speech to a national charities conference — the exact words, often misquoted: "all the Indian there is in the race should be dead. Kill the Indian in him, and save the man." How the taking worked: an 1891 law let the government compel attendance; an 1893 law let it withhold rations, clothing, and annuity payments from parents who refused; some agents sent reservation police for the children. On arrival: hair cut, uniforms, an English name, home language forbidden — punishments documented by the later federal investigation include beatings, solitary confinement, withheld food, mouths washed with soap. Half the day was unpaid labor that ran the school; Pratt's "outing system" placed children with white families to work. The federal count (2024): 417 federal schools in 37 states and territories, 1819–1969; at least 973 children died at them; at least 74 burial sites beside them — and the report itself says the count is low. The other half of the truth, told in the same breath: children kept their languages in secret, made friendships across nations that seeded the next century's organizing, and some came home and turned the schooling against the policy.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee" -->
On January 1, 1889, during an eclipse, a Northern Paiute man named Wovoka had a vision: live rightly, dance the dance, and the dead would return and the world be made whole. The Ghost Dance spread across hungry reservations; agents and newspapers called it an uprising. Sitting Bull was killed December 15, 1890 during an arrest attempt. On December 29, 1890, at Wounded Knee Creek, the 7th Cavalry — disarming Spotted Elk's band — opened fire with carbines and Hotchkiss guns: between 250 and 300 Lakota killed, most of them women and children. Wounded Knee is where the wars end, and where this book refuses to end the story: the next era opens with Native doctors, lawyers, and athletes organizing.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sitting-bull-native-nations" name="Sitting Bull" movie="Sitting Bull: A Stone in My Heart (2006)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Sitting Bull
> **Who:** Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man; the resistance camp on the Greasy Grass formed around him. · **When and where:** the northern Plains; Canada 1877–81; killed at Standing Rock, December 15, 1890. · **Movie:** *Sitting Bull: A Stone in My Heart* (2006) — a documentary built from his own recorded words.
Refused the reservation until hunger left no choice; toured one season with Buffalo Bill (1885, $50 a week) and went home; died in the Ghost Dance panic at the hands of Indian police sent to arrest him. Also portrayed in HBO's *Bury My Heart at Wounded Knee* (2007).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sitting-bull-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="chief-joseph" name="Chief Joseph" movie="I Will Fight No More Forever (1975)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Chief Joseph
> **Who:** Nez Perce leader in the 1877 flight — about 750 people, only some 200 of them fighters, moving roughly 1,170 miles with the army behind them. · **When and where:** Oregon to Montana, June–October 1877; surrendered October 5, 1877, 40 miles from Canada. · **Movie:** *I Will Fight No More Forever* (1975, TV film).
"From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever" (as recorded at the surrender). The promised return home was overruled: exile to Kansas and Indian Territory, then the Colville reservation, where he died in 1904 — never allowed back to the Wallowa Valley.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="chief-joseph" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="sarah-winnemucca-native-nations" name="Sarah Winnemucca" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Sarah Winnemucca
> **Who:** Northern Paiute writer, interpreter, and lecturer who argued her people's case across the East. · **When and where:** Nevada and the lecture halls of the East, 1870s–80s.
*Life Among the Piutes* (1883) — the first known autobiography written by a Native American woman (and she was the first Native woman known to hold a U.S. copyright). In the mid-1880s (sources give 1884 or 1885) she opened her own school for Paiute children near Lovelock, Nevada, teaching in Paiute and English — her own answer, before the government's schools swallowed the era.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sarah-winnemucca-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="zitkala-sa-native-nations" name="Zitkala-Ša" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Zitkala-Ša
> **Who:** Yankton Dakota writer, musician, and organizer, taken as a child (at eight, by her own account) to a mission boarding school in Indiana. · **When and where:** Yankton reservation, South Dakota, and Washington, D.C.; born February 22, 1876, died January 26, 1938.
Published the boarding schools from the inside — autobiographical essays in the *Atlantic Monthly* (1900, including "The School Days of an Indian Girl"), collected in *American Indian Stories* (1921); co-founded the National Council of American Indians (1926). The strongest first-person school account in the chapter; her story bridges into the next era's organizing.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="zitkala-sa-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="native-nations" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The frontier "closes" and the nations do not. This is the half-century the rest of the book most easily drops Native people; this chapter carries them straight through it: the first national Native-run organizations, Osage oil wealth and the murders that followed it, citizenship, the Indian New Deal, two world wars won partly in Native languages — and the boarding schools still running the whole time.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Organizing" -->
The Society of American Indians (founded October 12, 1911, Columbus, Ohio) was the first national rights organization run by Native people themselves — doctors, lawyers, writers, many of them boarding-school alumni using the schools' English against the schools' purpose; Zitkala-Ša edited its journal. In Alaska, the Alaska Native Brotherhood (1912, Sitka) and Sisterhood (1915) fought for citizenship for half a century. The National Congress of American Indians followed (November 16, 1944, Denver — 80 delegates from 50+ tribes), and it is still the major intertribal body today.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Osage and the Reign of Terror" -->
Keeping their mineral rights collective (1906 act) made the Osage, when the oil came in, among the richest people per capita in the world. Then the law put many Osage adults' money under court-appointed white "guardians," and from about 1920 to 1925 more than 60 Osage headright holders died in murders and suspicious deaths — the Reign of Terror. Our angle: a nation's wealth and the legal machinery built to take it; the investigation is `crime-justice`'s. Film: *Killers of the Flower Moon* (2023).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Citizenship and the Indian New Deal" -->
The Indian Citizenship Act (June 2, 1924) made every Native person born in the U.S. a citizen — but voting was state law, and some states barred Native voters until 1957. The Meriam Report (1928) documented allotment's failure (tribal land down from 137 to 47 million acres) and the schools' grim conditions in federal print. The Indian Reorganization Act (June 18, 1934, under Commissioner John Collier) ended allotment and let nations adopt constitutions and charter their own governments — the first turn of federal policy back toward nationhood.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The schools continue" -->
The boarding schools did not stop in 1900 — the federal count of the system runs to 1969, and enrollment kept growing for decades (it peaked around 60,000 in 1973, next era). Collier's 1930s reforms shifted toward day schools and allowed some Native-language teaching, and some schools closed — but tens of thousands of children were still taken from home each year. The plainest documented irony, by name: Chester Nez had his mouth washed with soap at the Fort Defiance boarding school for speaking Navajo — the language the Marine Corps then built its unbreakable code from.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The code talkers" -->
First, Choctaw soldiers in World War I: with German intelligence tapping the lines in the Meuse-Argonne, Choctaw men of the 36th Division began passing orders in Choctaw (first secure messages October 26, 1918; "little gun shoot fast" = machine gun). In World War II, 29 Navajo recruits (May 1942) built a code from Navajo; 350–420 Navajo code talkers served in every Marine division in the Pacific. The 5th Division's signal officer at Iwo Jima: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima." The code was never broken, stayed classified until 1968, and earned Congressional Gold Medals in 2001.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jim-thorpe-native-nations" name="Jim Thorpe" movie="Jim Thorpe – All-American (1951)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Jim Thorpe
> **Who:** Sac and Fox athlete, Carlisle student, first Native American to win Olympic gold. · **When and where:** Stockholm Olympics, 1912 — pentathlon and decathlon, the decathlon world record standing to 1927. · **Movie:** *Jim Thorpe – All-American* (1951).
Medals stripped in 1913 over $2-a-game summer baseball; restored as co-champion 1982; restored as sole champion July 15, 2022 — 110 years to the day. Our angle: a boarding-school student beating the world in the decade the country called his people vanishing (the athletic career itself is `sports-play`'s).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jim-thorpe-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ira-hayes" name="Ira Hayes" movie="The Outsider (1961)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Ira Hayes
> **Who:** Akimel O'odham (Pima) Marine from the Gila River community, one of the six who raised the second flag on Mount Suribachi. · **When and where:** Iwo Jima, February 23, 1945; died at home in Arizona, January 24, 1955, at 32. · **Movie:** *The Outsider* (1961); also portrayed in *Flags of Our Fathers* (2006).
The country celebrated the photograph and did little for the man: paraded, toasted, and left to struggle, he died of exposure after a night of drinking. Told plainly, because leaving it out would be the dishonest telling.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ira-hayes" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="chester-nez-native-nations" name="Chester Nez" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Chester Nez
> **Who:** Navajo Marine, one of the original 29 who built the code — and a boarding-school boy punished for speaking the language the code was made of. · **When and where:** Fort Defiance school, then the Pacific war, 1942–45; the last of the original 29, died June 4, 2014.
His memoir *Code Talker* (2011, with Judith Schiess Avila) is the only one by an original code talker — the documented life that carries both of this era's threads at once.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="chester-nez-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="native-nations" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Federal policy swung from trying to end the tribes altogether to recognizing their right to govern themselves — and the swing was forced, case by case and law by law, by Native people: fishermen who would not stop fishing, students who took an island, nations that sued, and a terminated tribe that won itself back.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Termination and Relocation" -->
House Concurrent Resolution 108 (August 1, 1953) declared the policy of ending federal recognition; by 1970 about 60 termination proceedings had hit more than 100 tribes and bands and moved over 3 million acres out of trust. The Menominee of Wisconsin — terminated 1954, pushed into poverty — organized (the DRUMS movement, with Ada Deer) and won the Menominee Restoration Act (December 22, 1973): the tide turning in law. Meanwhile relocation moved about 30,000 people to cities in the 1950s and over 100,000 by the 1970s (the movement itself is `migration`'s); poverty followed many, and so did urban Indian communities — Minneapolis, Chicago, Oakland, Los Angeles — where the next movement was born.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Red Power" -->
The American Indian Movement was founded in Minneapolis (July 1968) to patrol police abuse in the city relocation built. "Indians of All Tribes" — Richard Oakes among the leaders — held Alcatraz Island for 19 months (November 20, 1969 – June 11, 1971), offering to buy it for "$24 in glass beads and red cloth"; the occupation made the nations national news and helped end termination: Blue Lake and its 48,000 sacred acres went home to Taos Pueblo (December 15, 1970), and the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act (December 18, 1971) settled 44 million acres and $962.5 million through Native-owned corporations. In 1973, about 200 Oglala Lakota and AIM members held the village of Wounded Knee for 71 days (February 27 – May 8) — the site chosen because of 1890.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The fish-ins and the Boldt decision" -->
Nisqually, Puyallup, and other Northwest nations fished in open defiance of state arrests — "fish-ins," centered on Frank's Landing on the Nisqually — to force the 1850s treaties into court. United States v. Washington (the Boldt decision, February 12, 1974): the treaties entitle the tribes to half the harvestable salmon, and the tribes became co-managers of the fishery; the Supreme Court affirmed it in 1979. Treaty words a century old, made to mean what they said.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Self-determination in statute" -->
The Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act (January 1975) let nations contract to run federal programs themselves — schools, clinics, police ("Education" is in the title because the schools were the heart of it). The Indian Child Welfare Act (1978) set federal standards to keep Native children with Native families. The Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (October 17, 1988) framed tribal gaming — a major revenue source for some nations, small for others; say so. NAGPRA (November 16, 1990): remains and sacred objects in museums belong to their nations, and must go home.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Nations take the schools back" -->
The Navajo Nation founded the first tribally controlled college in 1968 (Navajo Community College, today Diné College); dozens of tribal colleges followed. The Kennedy Report (Senate, November 1969 — *Indian Education: A National Tragedy — A National Challenge*) found federal Indian education was "coercive assimilation" with "disastrous effects" and recommended Native control. Boarding-school enrollment peaked about 60,000 in 1973, then fell as nations took the schools over or closed them; survivors began publishing their accounts.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="wilma-mankiller" name="Wilma Mankiller" movie="Mankiller (2017)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Wilma Mankiller
> **Who:** first woman Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. · **When and where:** Cherokee Nation, Oklahoma — chief December 1985 to August 1995; elected 1987, re-elected 1991 with 83% of the vote. · **Movie:** *Mankiller* (2017, documentary).
Her family was moved to San Francisco under the relocation program when she was a child; Alcatraz drew her into the movement; she came home and led ~140,000 citizens, building water lines and clinics community by community. Presidential Medal of Freedom, 1998; died 2010. Her life is the era's arc in one person: relocation → Red Power → self-government.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="wilma-mankiller" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="billy-frank-jr-native-nations" name="Billy Frank Jr." movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Billy Frank Jr.
> **Who:** Nisqually fisherman arrested more than 50 times — the first time at 14 — for fishing under his nation's treaty. · **When and where:** Frank's Landing, Nisqually River, Washington, 1940s–1974 and after.
The fish-ins he led ended in the Boldt decision; he chaired the Northwest fisheries commission for decades after. Died 2014; Presidential Medal of Freedom 2015; Washington is placing his statue in the U.S. Capitol (slated 2026). The fish-in-participant target, filled — with the man the movement centered on.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="billy-frank-jr-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="adam-fortunate-eagle" name="Adam Fortunate Eagle" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Adam Fortunate Eagle
> **Who:** Ojibwe writer and artist — a Pipestone Indian Boarding School student (Minnesota, 1935–1945) who, three decades later, was a lead organizer of the Alcatraz occupation. · **When and where:** Pipestone, Minnesota, then the San Francisco Bay Area, 1969–71.
His memoir *Pipestone: My Life in an Indian Boarding School* (2010) is a first-person account published in his own lifetime — and it complicates the picture: he calls his Collier-era school days "a little bit of heaven" while recognizing the system's harm. The boarding-school-survivor target, filled with a named account published by the survivor himself; paired with Zitkala-Ša and Nez it keeps the chapter honest about the range of experience.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="adam-fortunate-eagle" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="native-nations" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
574 federally recognized nations governing themselves — courts, police, schools, clinics, businesses — plus state-recognized nations, nations still seeking recognition, more than 200 Alaska Native villages and their corporations, and Native Hawaiians (territories thread, shared with america-world). 9.7 million people identified as American Indian or Alaska Native in the 2020 census — from about 250,000 counted in 1900. The Navajo Nation's land is larger than 10 states (27,000+ square miles); the Cherokee Nation passed 450,000 citizens. In 2004 the National Museum of the American Indian opened on the National Mall with some 25,000 Native people in the opening procession. Current through 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Sovereignty in court and in office" -->
*McGirt v. Oklahoma* (July 9, 2020) held that the Muscogee (Creek) reservation — 3.25 million acres of eastern Oklahoma, including much of Tulsa — was never disestablished; the opinion opens: "On the far end of the Trail of Tears was a promise." *Haaland v. Brackeen* (June 15, 2023) upheld the Indian Child Welfare Act, 7–2. In 2018 Deb Haaland and Sharice Davids became the first Native American women elected to Congress; on March 15, 2021 Haaland was confirmed Secretary of the Interior — the first Native American cabinet secretary, heading the department that once ran the boarding schools.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Standing Rock and land back" -->
Standing Rock, 2016: the Standing Rock Sioux opposed the Dakota Access Pipeline's crossing under Lake Oahe, their water supply. Youth carried the message on foot — 500 miles to the Army Corps in Omaha, then 2,000 miles to Washington; thousands of people from hundreds of nations camped at Oceti Sakowin — widely called the largest gathering of Native nations in more than a century; over 2,000 veterans arrived in December 2016 to stand with them. The Army Corps halted the easement December 4, 2016; the next administration approved it and oil moved in 2017 — both truths stated plainly. Land back in concrete cases: the National Bison Range (18,800 acres taken in 1908) was restored to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes by law in December 2020. Film: *Awake, a Dream from Standing Rock* (2017).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The boarding-school reckoning" -->
Secretary Haaland ordered the Federal Indian Boarding School Initiative in 2021 — the government counting its own record. Final report (July 30, 2024): 417 federal schools in 37 states and territories; at least 973 documented child deaths; at least 74 burial sites at 65 schools; and the report says the true toll is higher. October 25, 2024: at the Gila River Indian Community — Ira Hayes's home — the president issued the first formal apology for the system. The children are coming home: the Army returned Little Chief and Horse to the Northern Arapaho from the Carlisle cemetery in 2017, and nine Rosebud Sioux children home to South Dakota in July 2021, escorted by Rosebud youth.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Languages come home — the school thread ends here" -->
The direct answer to the boarding schools is the immersion school. Hawaiian: Pūnana Leo preschools from 1984, the ban on teaching in Hawaiian lifted in 1986, Hawaiian-medium schooling now running preschool through graduate school. Wôpanâak (Wampanoag): silent since the mid-1800s, reconstructed from written records by Jessie Little Doe Baird's project (founded 1993) — the first American language with no living speakers brought back to living use, now taught to Wampanoag children. Cherokee, Lakota, Diné, and many others run immersion schools. The languages the schools punished helped win a world war, and are now taught to children on purpose — end the thread on that sentence's facts.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="deb-haaland-native-nations" name="Deb Haaland" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Deb Haaland
> **Who:** Laguna Pueblo; one of the first two Native women elected to Congress (2018); first Native American cabinet secretary (Interior, confirmed March 15, 2021). · **When and where:** New Mexico and Washington, D.C., 2018–2025.
A descendant of boarding-school students (her grandparents were taken — her own account), she ordered the department that ran the schools to count what it had done, and delivered the count.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="deb-haaland-native-nations" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jessie-little-doe-baird" name="Jessie Little Doe Baird" movie="We Still Live Here: As Nutayunean (2011)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Jessie Little Doe Baird
> **Who:** Mashpee Wampanoag social worker turned linguist who co-founded the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project (1993), earned an MIT linguistics degree, and raised her daughter speaking a language no one had spoken in over 150 years. · **When and where:** Mashpee, Massachusetts, 1993–today; MacArthur Fellowship 2010. · **Movie:** *We Still Live Here: Âs Nutayuneân* (2011, documentary).
The language-revival-teacher target, filled. Her sources included a Bible printed in Wôpanâak in 1663 — the written record of the missionaries, used to undo what came after.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jessie-little-doe-baird" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

---


<a id="chapter-03-land-environment"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="03" slug="land-environment" title="Land and Environment" part="1" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 03: Land and Environment

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-07 — all ten eras verified against `research/research-land-environment.md`; every date/number/name in this outline is sourced there.
**Angle:** The land itself and Americans' changing relationship to it — use, damage, protection. The through-line: a managed continent → land as property and inventory → the great taking → protection as public work → the bill for a century of control (fire, water, warming) → management coming full circle to the first managers.
**Keep out:** mining money (`economy`); the fuels themselves (`energy`); journeys (`exploration`); the Dust Bowl exodus (`migration`); storms/fires as single calamities (`disasters`); farm practice and food (`food-farming`).
**Workspace:** `workspace/land-environment.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-land-environment.md` · **Reference:** `research/research-native-nations.md` (bison, Bison Range, Bears Ears coalition context) · `research/research-migration.md` (Dust Bowl exodus — theirs, not ours)
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="land-environment" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A shaped continent, not an untouched one. Native nations managed land deliberately and at scale — with fire, with planting, and by living alongside two animals that engineered the country: the bison and the beaver. When later Americans called this land "wilderness," they were looking at somebody's managed ground and not recognizing the work.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fire as a tool" -->
Regular low burns, repeated over thousands of years, kept eastern woods open, favored oak and other fire-adapted trees, cleared brush, and fed the game people hunted. Modern research (Penn State, 2019) finds Native burning shaped eastern forest makeup more than climate did. Colonists dismissed the practice; after about 1940 the government put out every fire — and that suppression changed the forests again (the bill arrives in the last era).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Planting and the animal engineers" -->
- The Three Sisters — corn, beans, squash grown together: beans feed the soil, squash shades and holds it, corn carries the beans. Farming that keeps its ground (the food itself is `food-farming`'s story).
- Beaver: estimates before the fur trade run as high as 400 million across the continent (estimates, not counts). Their dams ponded water, slowed floods, and built wet meadows — whole watersheds shaped by an animal.
- Bison: roughly 30 million on the Plains (the early-1800s baseline), grazing and churning the grasslands that grew around them.
- In southwest Florida the Calusa built shell-walled "watercourts" that penned live fish (1300–1400) — engineered water management (`native-nations` leads on the Calusa).
- No named individual survives from this era at story level, and the book does not invent people; the era carries the wide view and the spans.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="land-environment" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The land began changing before most Europeans ever settled on it. Ships brought animals, plants, worms, and disease, and each remade some part of the country on its own. This chapter's telling of the Columbian Exchange is the land's side; `food-farming` leads on what people ate, `health` on the disease.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="New animals, new weeds, new worms" -->
- Hernando de Soto landed near Tampa Bay in May 1539 with a herd of pigs — chronicles say about 13, grown to about 700 by his death in 1542. Escapees went wild; the Southeast's feral hogs descend from Spanish stock. Horses (back on the continent from 1493) and cattle followed.
- The northern forests had no earthworms — glaciers had scraped them away, and the woods that regrew ran on a thick spongy leaf-litter layer. European worms rode in ship-ballast soil and plant roots, then spread west with wagons and plows. Where they invade, they eat the litter layer that native wildflowers and seedlings need. The ground itself, changed by a stowaway.
- One research team (Koch et al., 2019) estimates that after epidemics emptied Native fields across the Americas, about 56 million hectares of farmland regrew into forest — enough regrowth to pull carbon from the air and slightly cool the planet. State as one study's estimate; the starting population is itself disputed.
- Thin era, honestly: big forces, no documented individual from this angle.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="land-environment" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Two ideas of land met on the coast. Native nations used land seasonally — planting grounds, fishing stations, hunting territories — without treating it as a thing one person owned forever. English colonists brought deeds, fences, and livestock: land as permanent, exclusive property. Within one generation the difference showed on the ground itself.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The beaver trade" -->
European hat-makers paid for beaver felt, and the fur trade ran the animal down watershed by watershed, moving inland as each region emptied. From an estimated population as high as 400 million, the long decline began here and ran until about 100,000 were left on the continent by 1900. When beaver vanish, their dams fail — ponds drain, wet meadows dry. The trade's money and routes belong to `economy` and `exploration`; the emptied streams are ours.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fences, hogs, and the first limits" -->
- Colonial cattle and hogs ranged free and rooted through Native planting fields and clam banks — a running cause of conflict the treaties kept circling back to.
- Some colonies noticed the taking: Plymouth barred cutting timber off colony land without consent (1626); William Penn's rules for Pennsylvania (1681) told settlers to leave one acre of trees for every five cleared — widely ignored, but on the books.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="miantonomi" name="Miantonomi" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Miantonomi
> **Who:** Narragansett sachem who put the environmental change of colonization into recorded words a single generation after settlement began. · **When and where:** speech to the Montaukett on Long Island, 1642, as written down by the English soldier Lion Gardener; executed 1643 after capture by the Mohegans.
As Gardener recorded it: our fathers had plenty of deer, skins, and turkeys — but the English cut the grass with scythes and the trees with axes, their cows and horses eat the grass, their hogs spoil the clam banks, "and we shall all be starved." Caveat stated in the telling: the wording is Gardener's, written years later; historians treat the substance as credible, the exact words as filtered through an English pen.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="miantonomi" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="land-environment" label="1700 to 1750" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonial economies settled into taking more from the land than it replaced — trees for the navy, soil for tobacco, whales for lamp oil — and cheap new land westward made the exhaustion a habit instead of a crisis.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The King's pines" -->
The tallest white pines were warship masts, and the Crown claimed them: the Massachusetts charter of 1691 reserved big pines (24 inches through and up), and the White Pine Act of 1722 made cutting any pine over 12 inches without license illegal in New Hampshire. Surveyors marked the King's trees with the Broad Arrow — three hatchet slashes. Colonists cut them anyway; enforcement stayed loose until the 1760s, and what happened when it tightened opens the next era.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Worn-out fields and the first whale ships" -->
- A tobacco field gave three or four good crops, then was left to scrub while the planter cleared new ground. Land around Jamestown wore out early; planting kept moving up the rivers decade after decade.
- New Englanders had taken right whales from shore for decades; by tradition, Nantucket's deep-sea sperm whaling began in 1712 when Christopher Hussey's boat, blown offshore, killed a sperm whale. The story was first written down in 1835 and may be legend; what is certain is that by mid-century Nantucket ran a deep-ocean whale fishery.
- Thin era at story level: no single documented land-story individual found; said plainly rather than padded.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="land-environment" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The era the land was measured. A new country, paying war debts with the one thing it had plenty of, invented a machine for turning land into property: the survey grid. Before most of the interior was even settled by newcomers, it was already squares on paper with prices attached.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The grid" -->
The Land Ordinance of May 20, 1785: public land would be surveyed before sale into townships six miles square, each cut into 36 sections of one square mile — 640 acres — with section 16 in every township reserved to support public schools. The rectangles marched across the continent for the next century, ignoring rivers, hills, and everyone already living there. From an airplane over the Midwest today, the 1785 grid is still the visible shape of the country.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Clearing unleashed" -->
Independence voided the King's tree reservations, and clearing accelerated as settlement crossed the Appalachians into the new survey squares. The settlers' journeys belong to `migration`; the axe-work belongs here.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ebenezer-mudgett" name="Ebenezer Mudgett" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Ebenezer Mudgett
> **Who:** a sawmill owner in Weare, New Hampshire, fined for cutting the King's white pines. · **When and where:** the Pine Tree Riot, Weare, April 14, 1772.
Sheriff Benjamin Whiting rode into South Weare on April 13 with a warrant; Mudgett promised to pay in the morning. At dawn he came back with 20 to 30 men, faces blackened with soot, who beat the sheriff and his deputy with rods and drove them out of town. The rioters got off with small fines, the mast law went unenforced afterward, and some historians credit the riot as a forerunner of the Boston Tea Party a year and a half later — an ordinary mill owner, a tree law, and one of the first open fights over who owns American trees.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ebenezer-mudgett" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="land-environment" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Rivers and forests were put to work at industrial scale — and the first American voices said out loud that something was being lost. Both things are true of this era at once: the East hit its barest, and the argument for keeping some land wild was born.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Dams stop the fish" -->
Mill and factory dams walled off the rivers. The first dam across the Connecticut (Turners Falls, 1798) cut salmon off from their spawning water — by the War of 1812 no salmon entered the river. The Great Stone Dam at Lawrence (1847–48) blocked the Merrimack 30 miles from the sea. Atlantic salmon were gone from southern New England rivers by 1865, and the shad runs that had fed towns every spring collapsed with them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The bare East" -->
By 1850 an estimated 60 to 80 percent of New England was cleared (estimates vary — some put the remaining forest as low as a quarter); one driver with a number was sheep — about 4 million in New England by 1840 eating pastures that had been woods. Eastern forest cover bottomed out around 1872 at roughly half its 1620 extent. Wood was still fuel, fencing, and building material; the forest was being spent like money.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="First voices" -->
The painter George Catlin, watching the bison and the Plains nations from the upper Missouri in 1832, proposed "a nation's park" to keep both — forty years before anyone built one. Audubon painted the birds while they were still uncountable; Thoreau moved to a pond to see what was left of the wild close to home.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-james-audubon" name="John James Audubon" movie="John James Audubon: Drawn from Nature (2007)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John James Audubon
> **Who:** painter and naturalist; *The Birds of America* — 435 life-size bird portraits, published 1827–1838, about 18 years of work. · **When and where:** the American frontier and Atlantic cities, 1785–1851. · **Movie:** *John James Audubon: Drawn from Nature* (PBS American Masters, 2007).
In 1813, riding toward Louisville, he passed under a single passenger-pigeon flock that darkened the sky for three days; his own arithmetic made it more than a billion birds. He painted species that readers of his book would outlive — his pigeon plate is one of the few windows on a bird no one alive has seen.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-james-audubon" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="henry-david-thoreau" name="Henry David Thoreau" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Henry David Thoreau
> **Who:** writer, and a working land surveyor — the man who argued for wild land measured woodlots for a living. · **When and where:** Walden Pond, Concord, Massachusetts, July 4, 1845 to September 6, 1847 — two years, two months, two days in a cabin he built himself.
*Walden* (published 1854) made the case that a life could be measured by something other than what it cleared, built, and earned — and that the wild remnants close to town were worth keeping. Later conservationists from Muir onward read him first.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="henry-david-thoreau" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="land-environment" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The half-century of the biggest taking — the bison brought from tens of millions to hundreds, the passenger pigeon from billions toward zero — and, in the same decades, the invention of protection as public policy: the first national park, the first forest reserves, the first conservation club with lawyers.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The bison slaughter" -->
Roughly 30 million bison in the early 1800s; fewer than 1,000 by 1900 — one 1884 count found 325. The transcontinental railroad (1869) carried hide hunters out and hides back; a good team killed dozens a day for dollar-or-two hides; the Army encouraged it because the herds fed the Plains nations' independence. What the collapse did to those nations is `native-nations`' telling; ours is the animal and the grassland — an ecosystem's keystone shot out from under it in one generation.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The pigeon collapse" -->
Peak population an estimated 3 to 5 billion — possibly four of every ten North American birds. The 1871 Wisconsin nesting held an estimated 136 million breeding birds across 850 square miles. At Petoskey, Michigan in 1878, professional netters worked one of the last great nestings at a reported 50,000 birds a day for months, shipping barrels to city markets by rail while the telegraph told hunters where every new nesting was. By the mid-1890s the wild flocks were effectively gone. The finish arrives in the next era.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Protection invented" -->
- Yosemite Grant, June 30, 1864: Lincoln signed the first federal set-aside of land for preservation and public use (given to California to manage; national park 1890).
- Yellowstone, March 1, 1872: Grant signed the act making it the first national park — kept by the federal government "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people."
- George Perkins Marsh's *Man and Nature* (1864) argued civilizations fall when they destroy their forests and soils; it helped produce the Forest Reserve Act of 1891, the start of the national forests.
- The Sierra Club, founded May 28, 1892, John Muir its first president — citizens organized to defend land in courts and Congress.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-muir" name="John Muir" movie="John Muir in the New World (2011)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John Muir
> **Who:** Scotland-born wanderer, writer, and campaigner; the loudest American voice for keeping wild land wild. · **When and where:** California's Sierra Nevada from 1868; Sierra Club president 1892–1914. · **Movie:** *John Muir in the New World* (PBS American Masters, 2011).
His magazine pieces turned Yosemite's valleys and sequoias into a national cause and helped make Yosemite a national park (1890). He believed wild places had worth beyond board-feet and acre-prices — the position that would lose its biggest fight, at Hetch Hetchy, in the next era.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-muir" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frank-mayer" name="Frank Mayer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Frank Mayer
> **Who:** a buffalo runner — one of the professional hide hunters — from 1872 to 1878. · **When and where:** the southern Plains; died Fairplay, Colorado, 1954, at a reported 104.
His memoir *The Buffalo Harvest* (told at about age 100, published 1958) lays out the trade's arithmetic — rifle, wagons, hired skinners, hides at a dollar or two — and ends in plain regret at what the runners did. Caveats told with the story: a memoir set down in extreme old age, the numbers his own. The other side of the slaughter, in the voice of a man who did it.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frank-mayer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="land-environment" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Conservation became federal work — a president who used it as presidential power, new agencies, a corps of young men planting trees — and the era also delivered two lessons in what failure costs: a bird extinct in a zoo cage, and the southern Plains blowing to the Atlantic.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The conservation presidency" -->
Theodore Roosevelt, 1901–1909: about 230 million acres put under federal protection — 150 national forests, 5 national parks, the first 18 national monuments, 51 federal bird reservations, 4 game preserves (counts vary slightly by source). Pelican Island, Florida (March 14, 1903), the first federal bird refuge. The U.S. Forest Service created in 1905 with Gifford Pinchot as first chief; the Antiquities Act (June 8, 1906) let presidents protect land by proclamation — Devils Tower first, that September.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="theodore-roosevelt-land-environment" name="Theodore Roosevelt" movie="The Roosevelts: An Intimate History (2014)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Theodore Roosevelt
> **Who:** the president who made protecting land a central use of presidential power. · **When and where:** the White House, 1901–1909; Yosemite, May 1903. · **Movie:** *The Roosevelts: An Intimate History* (PBS, Ken Burns, 2014) — a documentary about the family.
In May 1903 he slipped his handlers for three nights of camping with John Muir — under the Grizzly Giant sequoia, in a snowstorm near Sentinel Dome, in a meadow by Bridalveil Fall. A hunter who watched species vanishing, he treated the land as a national inheritance to be defended by law — and used every legal tool he had, sometimes ahead of Congress's wishes.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="theodore-roosevelt-land-environment" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hetch Hetchy — use it or keep it wild" -->
Conservation split into its two lasting camps over one valley. San Francisco, rebuilding after the 1906 earthquake and fire, wanted Hetch Hetchy Valley — inside Yosemite National Park — for a reservoir. Pinchot's camp said conservation means careful use for the greatest good; Muir's said a national park must mean never. Congress sided with the city (Raker Act, signed December 19, 1913); Muir died the next year; the O'Shaughnessy Dam finished in 1923, and the valley is under water today. The National Park Service (Organic Act, August 25, 1916) was created partly in reaction — a bureau whose whole job is the parks.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="gifford-pinchot" name="Gifford Pinchot" movie="Seeking the Greatest Good (2013)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Gifford Pinchot
> **Who:** America's first professionally trained forester; first chief of the Forest Service (1905–1910); later twice governor of Pennsylvania. · **When and where:** Washington and the national forests, 1898–1910. · **Movie:** *Seeking the Greatest Good* (WVIA/PBS, 2013).
His rule for the public lands: "the greatest good to the greatest number for the longest time" — cut, graze, and dam, but carefully, forever. He and Muir were friends until Hetch Hetchy made their two conservations enemies; American land policy has argued their argument ever since.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="gifford-pinchot" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Extinction, witnessed" -->
The passenger pigeon's end had names and dates: the last confirmed wild bird shot in Ohio in 1900, the last of the species dead at the Cincinnati Zoo on September 1, 1914 — the first time Americans watched a species they had numbered in billions go to zero on a known day. Topic documentary: *From Billions to None* (2014).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="press-clay-southworth" name="Press Clay Southworth" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Press Clay Southworth
> **Who:** the 14-year-old Ohio farm boy who shot the last confirmed wild passenger pigeon — and the person through whom the bird's whole ending can be told. · **When and where:** Pike County, Ohio, March 24, 1900; the Cincinnati Zoo to September 1, 1914.
He saw a strange bird eating corn, asked his mother's permission, and used the family 12-gauge; nobody in the family recognized it until a neighbor did. Mounted with button eyes, "Buttons" is held by the Ohio History Connection; Southworth told the story himself decades later. Fourteen years after his shot, Martha — the species' last bird — died in her Cincinnati Zoo cage, about age 29; keeper Sol Stephan had saved her molted feathers in a cigar box (his accounts of where she hatched never stayed consistent — said plainly). Her body went to the Smithsonian frozen in a 300-pound block of ice. A boy with a shotgun, a zookeeper with a cigar box, and the space between them is the extinction.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="press-clay-southworth" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Dust Bowl — the soil itself" -->
War wheat prices and tractors had plowed up tens of millions of acres of native shortgrass; drought came in 1931, and the sod that held the southern Plains was gone. By December 1934 about 35 million acres of farmland were essentially destroyed for crops and 100 million more had lost most of their topsoil; in 1935 alone an estimated 850 million tons blew away. Black Sunday, April 14, 1935: a black wall of soil moving 60 miles an hour. That spring, as soil scientist Hugh Hammond Bennett testified in Washington, Plains dust darkened the sky outside the hearing room — "This, gentlemen, is what I've been talking about" (accounts differ on the exact day). Congress declared soil erosion "a national menace"; the Soil Conservation Service began April 27, 1935 — contour plowing, shelterbelts, grass put back. The exodus west is `migration`'s story; the storms as calamity are `disasters`'; the plowing and the soil are ours. Topic documentary: *The Dust Bowl* (Ken Burns, 2012).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="caroline-henderson" name="Caroline Henderson" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Caroline Henderson
> **Who:** a Mount Holyoke graduate who homesteaded the Oklahoma Panhandle in 1907, farmed it through the dust years — and stayed. · **When and where:** near Eva, Oklahoma; her letters ran 1908–1966.
Her "Letters from the Dust Bowl" in the *Atlantic Monthly* (May 1936 the best known) told the country what the dust actually did — fields drifted like snow, wheat dead, neighbors leaving one by one — from a kitchen table inside the storm. The Secretary of Agriculture wrote to thank her. Where `migration` follows the families who left, she is the documented voice of the ones who stayed with the soil.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="caroline-henderson" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The tree army and the fire rule" -->
- The Civilian Conservation Corps (1933–1942) put about 3 million young men to work; they planted between 2 and 3.5 billion trees (estimates vary; "about 3 billion" is the common figure), fought fires, terraced eroding farmland, and built the parks' trails and shelters.
- After the 1910 "Big Burn" (3 million acres, 78+ dead), the Forest Service set out to kill every fire; the 1935 "10 a.m. policy" ordered each one controlled by the morning after it was spotted, and CCC manpower made that real. Smokey Bear arrived in 1944 ("Only YOU can prevent forest fires," 1947; the living cub rescued from a New Mexico fire, 1950). The policy stood until 1978 — and a century of unburned fuel is part of era 10's megafires.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="aldo-leopold" name="Aldo Leopold" movie="Green Fire: Aldo Leopold and a Land Ethic for Our Time (2011)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Aldo Leopold
> **Who:** Forest Service forester turned professor who gave American conservation its ethics. · **When and where:** the Southwest, then a worn-out Wisconsin sand-county farm; 1887–1948. · **Movie:** *Green Fire: Aldo Leopold and a Land Ethic for Our Time* (2011).
He pushed through the Gila Wilderness in New Mexico (1924) — the world's first designated wilderness area — then bought a spent farm and spent weekends planting it back to life. He wrote about watching the "green fire" die in a wolf's eyes and changing his mind about predators. He died of a heart attack fighting a neighbor's grass fire in April 1948; *A Sand County Almanac* (1949) appeared after his death: people as plain members of the land community, not its conquerors.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="aldo-leopold" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="land-environment" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Pollution became visible — in eagle nests, on a burning river, in a schoolyard over a chemical dump — and then became law. In one decade the country built nearly its whole environmental legal system, and ordinary people, more than experts, forced the building.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The quiet poison" -->
DDT, sprayed everywhere from the mid-1940s, moved up food chains and thinned raptor eggshells until eggs broke under the parents. Bald eagles — the national symbol — were down to 417 nesting pairs in the lower 48 by 1963.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rachel-carson" name="Rachel Carson" movie="Rachel Carson (2017)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Rachel Carson
> **Who:** marine biologist and writer, formerly of the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service; author of *Silent Spring*. · **When and where:** Silver Spring, Maryland; the book September 1962; died April 14, 1964. · **Movie:** *Rachel Carson* (PBS American Experience, 2017).
*Silent Spring* laid out, with citations, what persistent pesticides were doing to birds, soil, water, and people, and asked whether a spring without birdsong was the price of convenience. The chemical industry attacked her as hysterical; she answered on national television (CBS Reports, April 3, 1963) already sick with the cancer that killed her seventeen months later. The DDT ban (1972) and much of the coming decade's law trace to her book.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rachel-carson" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The river that burned" -->
On June 22, 1969, an oil slick on the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland caught fire — about twenty minutes, quickly controlled, and at least the thirteenth fire on that river since 1868 (the 1952 fire did $1.3 million in damage; the 1912 fire killed five men). What changed was the audience: *Time* magazine showed the burning river to the country, and Mayor Carl Stokes — the first Black mayor of a major U.S. city — stood at the riverbank the next day demanding action. The same year, a well blowout blackened Santa Barbara's beaches.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The environmental decade" -->
- Earth Day, April 22, 1970 — an estimated 20 million Americans, one in ten, turned out.
- The laws, in five years: NEPA (Jan 1, 1970) · the EPA opens (Dec 2, 1970) · Clean Air Act (1970) · DDT banned and the Clean Water Act (1972) · Endangered Species Act (Dec 28, 1973).
- The proof came with feathers: bald eagles climbed from 417 pairs (1963) to about 10,000 by 2007, when the bird left the endangered list.
- Wolves came back on purpose: gray wolves from Canada released in Yellowstone starting January 1995 — the first deliberate return of a top predator to reshape land the government had once paid to clear of them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Love Canal and the buried waste" -->
Hooker Chemical buried about 21,000 tons of chemical waste in an abandoned canal in Niagara Falls, New York (1942–1953), then sold the covered site to the school board for one dollar. A school and hundreds of homes went up. By the 1970s chemicals were rising into yards and basements, and the neighborhood counted miscarriages, birth defects, and sick children. State and federal emergencies (1978, 1980) moved about 900 families out; Congress answered with Superfund (December 1980) — polluters pay for toxic cleanups.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="lois-gibbs" name="Lois Gibbs" movie="Lois Gibbs and the Love Canal (1982)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Lois Gibbs
> **Who:** a 27-year-old housewife with no political experience whose son attended the school built on the dump. · **When and where:** Love Canal, Niagara Falls, New York, 1978–1980. · **Movie:** *Lois Gibbs and the Love Canal* (CBS television film, 1982).
Told there was no problem, she went door to door with a health survey, founded the Love Canal Homeowners Association (August 1978), and out-organized the state of New York and the federal government until her neighbors were moved to safety. She then spent the rest of her life teaching other neighborhoods to do the same (Center for Health, Environment & Justice; Goldman Prize, 1990). The era's proof that the person who forces the law can be anyone.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="lois-gibbs" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Who lives next to the dump" -->
Warren County, North Carolina, September 1982: the state trucked PCB-laced soil to a landfill in Afton, in a mostly Black rural county; residents and civil-rights leaders lay down in front of the trucks; about 500 were arrested. The landfill was built anyway — and the fight named a pattern and a movement: environmental justice, the question of whose neighborhood gets the waste. It returns, with a victory, in the last era.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="land-environment" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A warming climate reached into everything this chapter has covered — fire, water, soil, coasts, wildlife. 2024 was the warmest year ever measured, both globally and in the United States (NOAA and NASA agree; the U.S. ran 3.5°F above its 20th-century average). The era's fights are over how the land copes — and its clearest hope is that management has started coming full circle to the continent's first managers. Current through August 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fire comes back bigger" -->
A century of put-out-every-fire left the woods loaded with fuel; heat and drought dried it. The Camp Fire (November 8, 2018) killed 85 people and burned the town of Paradise, California — about 19,000 buildings. The 2020 California season burned about 4.2 million acres, four percent of the state; the August Complex alone passed one million acres — the first "gigafire" of modern record. The reversal followed: agencies that once banned all burning now plan and set fires on purpose.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="margo-robbins" name="Margo Robbins" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Margo Robbins
> **Who:** Yurok tribal member who co-founded the Cultural Fire Management Council to bring traditional burning back to Yurok land. · **When and where:** the Klamath River country, northern California; first community burn 2012, council formed 2013.
She wanted hazel shoots that grow straight after a burn — for weaving the baskets that carry Yurok babies, starting with her own grandchildren. The council's burns brought back hazel and the deer, and its training exchanges now teach cultural burning to government fire crews — the practice this chapter opened with, outlawed and suppressed for a century, taught back to the people who banned it. Native continuity past 1900, on the ground.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="margo-robbins" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The shrinking river" -->
Tree rings say 2000–2021 was the driest 22-year stretch in the Southwest in at least 1,200 years, and a study in *Nature Climate Change* (2022) attributes about 42 percent of its severity to human-caused warming. Lake Mead and Lake Powell — the Colorado River's two great reservoirs, water for some 40 million people — hit record lows in 2021–22, Mead down to about a quarter full. In May 2023 Arizona, California, and Nevada agreed to cut about a tenth of the lower basin's use through 2026. The deals run out as this book is written; the river is not refilling.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Poison, plastic, and justice" -->
- Environmental justice moved from protest to some victories: see Margie Richard, below.
- Plastic is now weather: a *Science* study (2020) measured more than 1,000 tons of microplastic — mostly clothing fibers — falling with rain and dust on western parks and wilderness every year.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="margie-richard" name="Margie Richard" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Margie Richard
> **Who:** a schoolteacher from the Old Diamond neighborhood of Norco, Louisiana — four generations of her family 25 feet from a Shell Chemical fence line. · **When and where:** Louisiana's petrochemical corridor; campaign to 2002; Goldman Environmental Prize, April 2004.
Her neighborhood, wedged between a chemical plant and a refinery, counted cancers, birth defects, and neighbors killed in plant accidents. She led a roughly 13-year campaign — bucket air samples, shareholder meetings, a trip to Shell's headquarters in the Netherlands — until Shell agreed in 2002 to fund the relocation of any Old Diamond family that wanted out, cut emissions 30 percent, and pay $5 million toward community development. First African American winner of the Goldman Prize. The Warren County question — who lives next to the plant — answered once, by one neighborhood that refused to stay put quietly.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="margie-richard" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Comebacks" -->
The recoveries are real and countable: bald eagles at roughly 71,400 nesting pairs; bison at about 420,000 in commercial herds and 20,500 in conservation herds — and the National Bison Range itself returned to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes (2020–2022); wolves at about 500 in the Yellowstone region and 1,600-plus in the northern Rockies, their legal status still fought over.
