<a id="chapter-09-science"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="09" slug="science" title="Science" part="3" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 9: Science

<!-- hb-note -->
**Angle:** Discoveries about how the world works — knowledge and research.
**Keep out:** applied tools (`technology`); medicine (`health`); journeys (`exploration`); element discovery stories (`elements` leads — we take the laboratories lightly).
**Workspace:** `workspace/science.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-science.md` (full bank, researched 2026-08-08; every date sourced there) · **Reference:** `_reference/book-outline-v1.md` §6 Science.
**Date fix kept from v1:** the American Philosophical Society (1743) belongs in **1700–1750**, not 1750–1800.
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="science" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Careful, tested knowledge about the world existed here long before laboratories — held by nations, taught from person to person, and checked against the sky, the plants, and the seasons for thousands of years. No one called it science; it worked the same way: watch, record, test, pass on.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="reading the sky" -->
- Cahokia's Woodhenge (Illinois, about A.D. 900–1100): circles of upright posts marking where the sun rises through the year, including the solstices — sky-watching precise enough to build a calendar from (Cahokia Mounds State Historic Site). The posts as a built thing → `technology`; the sky-knowledge is ours.
- The Sun Dagger on Fajada Butte, Chaco Canyon (New Mexico): three stone slabs channel sunlight into "daggers" that cross two spiral carvings at the solstices and equinoxes; recorded by Anna Sofaer in 1977. Honest status: by 1989 two slabs had shifted — erosion sped up by human visits — and the daggers no longer land as they once did (NPS; Solstice Project). Claims about moon-cycle markings are argued by researchers, not settled.
Shared with: native-nations (the peoples themselves) · technology (Woodhenge as built calendar) · landmarks (Chaco's great houses).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="knowledge of plants and fire" -->
Plant knowledge — which plants feed, which heal, when to harvest — and the use of controlled fire to keep land open and productive were systematic, taught knowledge (the burning's story on the land → `land-environment`; healing practice → `health`). Scientists today call this Traditional Ecological Knowledge and work with it as knowledge, not folklore (Ecological Society of America TEK section).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="robin-wall-kimmerer" name="Robin Wall Kimmerer" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Robin Wall Kimmerer
> **Who:** Citizen Potawatomi Nation botanist; professor at SUNY's College of Environmental Science and Forestry; founded its Center for Native Peoples and the Environment; MacArthur Fellow, 2022. · **When and where:** New York State, present day.
A present-day scientist who works with both kinds of knowledge — laboratory botany and Potawatomi plant teachings — and shows they test and strengthen each other. Her book *Braiding Sweetgrass* (2013) became a national bestseller. The living answer to "was that science?" (ESF; MacArthur Foundation).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="robin-wall-kimmerer" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="science" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A thin era, honestly told: European science barely exists yet — this is still the age of alchemy — and no newcomer is doing sustained study here. What crosses the ocean is collecting and describing, carried back to Europe.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the first field report" -->
Thomas Hariot, an English mathematician on the 1585–86 Roanoke expedition, spent a year recording plants, animals, foods, and the Algonquian people; his *A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia* (1588) was the first book in English about North America written by someone who had been here, printed in 1590 with John White's drawings (Encyclopedia Virginia; UNC).
Shared with: exploration (the voyages, lead) · native-nations (the people being described).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="science" label="The 1600s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
A thin era: a college, an almanac press, a borrowed telescope, and a handful of colonists writing down what they saw. Observation was real; the observers still read the sky as sermon.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="college, almanac, telescope" -->
- Harvard founded 1636, the first college in the English colonies (harvard.edu).
- The colonies' first almanac — *An Almanack for New England for the Year 1639*, calculated by mariner William Pierce — was among the first two things printed in British America; almanacs carried astronomy into ordinary houses for two centuries (Britannica).
- John Winthrop Jr. of Connecticut, elected to the Royal Society in London (1662–63) among its first colonial members, gave Harvard its first scientific instrument about 1672: a 3.5-foot telescope (Linda Hall Library).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the comet argument" -->
When the Great Comet of 1680 blazed over Boston, Thomas Brattle tracked it by telescope and reasoned its two appearances were one body swinging around the sun — measurements that reached Isaac Newton and were cited in his *Principia* (American Antiquarian Society). Increase Mather preached the same comet as God's warning, yet his *Kometographia* (1683) used measurement to show comets were distant bodies, not vapors; his Boston Philosophical Society (1683) lasted about three years (Marco Institute).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-campanius-holm" name="Rev. John Campanius Holm" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Rev. John Campanius Holm
> **Who:** Chaplain to the small Swedish colony on the Delaware; kept the first known systematic weather record in what is now the United States. · **When and where:** Near present-day Wilmington, Delaware, 1644–1645.
Twice a day, with no instruments, he wrote down the weather. The National Weather Service still gives volunteer observers an award named for him (NWS/NOAA).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-campanius-holm" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="science" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonists began doing original work — and organized themselves to share it. By mid-century a Philadelphia printer's electrical experiments were being read in London.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the American Philosophical Society, 1743" -->
The colonies' first lasting scientific society. Botanist John Bartram floated the idea in 1739; Franklin organized it in 1743 with his pamphlet *A Proposal for Promoting Useful Knowledge among the British Plantations in America* — an American answer to London's Royal Society, still operating today (amphilsoc.org). [Kept in this era — the 1743 date controls.]
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="electricity in Philadelphia" -->
From about 1747 Franklin ran electrical experiments and mailed the results to London: positive and negative charge (his words, still used), charge that is never created or destroyed, and the idea that lightning is electricity. The letters were published as *Experiments and Observations on Electricity* (1751); the Royal Society gave him its Copley Medal in 1753 — its top honor, first time to anyone outside Britain (Library of Congress; NMAH).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-franklin-science" name="Benjamin Franklin" movie="Benjamin Franklin (2022)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin Franklin
> **Who:** Printer who became the first American scientist with a world reputation — the theory of electric charge, and the proof that lightning is electricity. · **When and where:** Philadelphia, experiments from about 1747. · **Movie:** Benjamin Franklin (2022)
The scientist Franklin: careful experiments, plain reports, results shared free. His stove and lightning rod → `technology`; his newspaper → `news-communication`. The film is Ken Burns's PBS documentary.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-franklin-science" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-bartram" name="John Bartram" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John Bartram
> **Who:** Quaker farmer-botanist; planted America's oldest surviving botanic garden and proposed the society that became the APS. · **When and where:** Kingsessing, near Philadelphia; garden from 1728; expeditions 1730–1765.
Self-taught; collected from New York to Florida; named the King's Botanist for North America in 1765; he and his sons introduced over 200 American plants to science. Linnaeus reportedly called him the greatest natural botanist in the world — the line is an attribution, not a record (Bartram's Garden).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-bartram" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="science" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
American science earned its first international respect — a lightning experiment copied across Europe, a planet timed across the sun, and a free Black farmer's almanac used against slavery's defenders.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the kite, told honestly" -->
Franklin designed the lightning test; France ran it first — at Marly-la-Ville, May 10, 1752, a tall iron rod drew sparks from a storm cloud, following Franklin's published plan (Founders Archives; APS News). Franklin's own kite flight in Philadelphia is traditionally dated June 1752; he never recorded the day, told it in print only that October, and historians still argue over details. The knowledge held either way: lightning is electricity. The rod on the roof → `technology`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="timing Venus, 1769" -->
The APS organized teams to time Venus crossing the sun on June 3, 1769 — the measurement nations wanted for the distance to the sun. The Norriton team (Rittenhouse, Smith, Lukens, Sellers) filled the first volume of the APS *Transactions*, reprinted by the Royal Society: colonial science treated as equal work for the first time (APS museum; Royal Society).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Jefferson's bones and Buffon's insult" -->
Europe's leading naturalist, Buffon, taught that animals and people grew smaller and weaker in America. Jefferson answered with evidence — *Notes on the State of Virginia*, moose antlers shipped to Paris, and in 1797 the fossil claws he named Megalonyx, presented to the APS: the start of American paleontology (Monticello; American Scientist). Jefferson the founder → `government-politics`; his home → `landmarks`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="david-rittenhouse" name="David Rittenhouse" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### David Rittenhouse
> **Who:** Self-taught instrument maker and astronomer; led the 1769 transit observations at Norriton. · **When and where:** Pennsylvania, 1732–1796.
Built the era's finest American instruments and mechanical models of the solar system; succeeded Franklin as APS president in 1791. His Mint job → `money`.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="david-rittenhouse" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-banneker-science" name="Benjamin Banneker" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin Banneker
> **Who:** Free Black tobacco farmer, self-taught astronomer and mathematician; calculated complete almanacs published 1792–1797. · **When and where:** Baltimore County, Maryland, 1731–1806.
Taught himself astronomy from borrowed books and instruments; correctly predicted the April 14, 1789 solar eclipse against better-known calculators. On August 19, 1791 he mailed Jefferson his manuscript almanac with a letter confronting him on slavery; Jefferson sent the almanac to Paris. Anti-slavery societies printed his almanacs as walking proof against claims of Black inferiority (Britannica; Founders Archives). His survey of the federal district → `city-building` (its story).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-banneker-science" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="science" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Science became a job in America: professors, a journal, government charts — and, from a stranger's gift, a national institution for knowledge.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a professor, a journal, a fallen stone" -->
Benjamin Silliman took Yale's new chemistry chair in 1802; when a meteorite fell on Weston, Connecticut on December 14, 1807, he collected and analyzed it — the first scientifically documented meteorite fall in the New World; in 1818 he founded the American Journal of Science, the country's first lasting scientific journal (Britannica; Connecticut History).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="electricity and honest credit" -->
Joseph Henry, teaching at Albany, built the strongest electromagnets of his day and in 1832 published the discovery of self-induction. On induction itself, Faraday in London published first (1831) and keeps the credit; Henry had seen it and published late. The unit of inductance is named the henry (Smithsonian Archives; Britannica). His magnets made the telegraph possible — the wire → `technology`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="charting sea and sky by crowd" -->
- Navy lieutenant Matthew Fontaine Maury mined thousands of old ships' logs and issued the first Wind and Current Chart of the North Atlantic (1847), then traded charts for captains' standardized logs — crowdsourced ocean science that cut weeks off voyages (Navy history; LOC). He later joined the Confederacy in 1861 — say so.
- From 1849 Smithsonian Secretary Joseph Henry ran about 150 volunteer weather observers reporting by mail and free telegraph — the first national weather maps, and the seed of the National Weather Service (Smithsonian Archives).
Shared with: transportation (what the charts did for shipping) · news-communication (the telegraph carrying weather).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="james-smithson" name="James Smithson" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### James Smithson
> **Who:** English chemist whose will gave the United States — a country he never saw — the money to found the Smithsonian Institution. · **When and where:** Died Genoa, Italy, June 27, 1829; the institution founded in Washington, August 10, 1846.
His will left everything, if his nephew died without heirs, "to the United States of America, to found at Washington... an establishment for the increase & diffusion of knowledge." The nephew died in 1835; more than 100,000 gold sovereigns — over $500,000 — reached the Philadelphia mint in 1838; Congress argued eight years before Polk signed the act. He never explained why. Nobody knows (Smithsonian Institution Archives).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="james-smithson" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="joseph-henry" name="Joseph Henry" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Joseph Henry
> **Who:** Albany schoolteacher turned leading American physicist; electromagnetism, self-induction (1832), and first Secretary of the Smithsonian (December 1846). · **When and where:** Albany, Princeton, and Washington, 1797–1878.
Turned Smithson's gift into a working engine of research — including the volunteer weather network that became the Weather Service (Smithsonian Archives; Princeton).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="joseph-henry" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="maria-mitchell" name="Maria Mitchell" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Maria Mitchell
> **Who:** Nantucket librarian and astronomer; first American to discover a telescopic comet with a standing royal prize — and the first American woman astronomer by profession. · **When and where:** Nantucket, Massachusetts; the comet found October 1, 1847.
From the roof of the Pacific National Bank, sweeping the sky with a small telescope, she found a comet no chart showed. The King of Denmark's gold medal came to her — first woman and first American to win it; in 1848 she was the first woman elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Her Vassar professorship (1865) and the all-women eclipse expedition she led to Denver (1878) belong to the next era — note them forward (Maria Mitchell Association; Smithsonian).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="maria-mitchell" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="science" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
American universities became places where research happened, and American measurements started setting world standards. The era also shows science misused — its most famous professor put its authority behind racism.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Darwin argument in America" -->
Darwin's *On the Origin of Species* (1859) split Harvard: botanist Asa Gray — who arranged Darwin's American publication — defended the evidence; Louis Agassiz, the country's most celebrated scientist, insisted every species was separately created and attacked the book at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences from January 1860. Gray argued the case in print and in debate; working biologists went with the evidence within a generation (AAAS archives; Harvard Magazine).
Shared with: religion (the faith response, and Scopes later) · education (evolution in schools).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what Agassiz also did" -->
Agassiz promoted the doctrine that races were separately created, and in 1850 had enslaved South Carolina people — among them Renty and his daughter Delia — stripped and photographed as "evidence." The daguerreotypes, rediscovered at Harvard in 1976, are the earliest known photographs of enslaved Americans. Science's authority can be misused; this era proves it (Harvard Magazine; Peabody Museum).
Shared with: slavery-freedom (lead — the people photographed and their descendants' fight).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="colleges for everyone, stations in every state" -->
The Morrill Act (1862) built the land-grant colleges → `education` leads. Our slice: they carried science teaching into every state, and the Hatch Act (1887) added an agricultural experiment station to each — research as a public service, not a private hobby (Congress.gov CRS).
Shared with: education (the colleges, lead) · food-farming (what the stations studied).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="women measure the sky" -->
At Harvard Observatory, women hired as "computers" did the measuring and cataloguing. Maria Mitchell, by then a Vassar professor, led an all-women team about 2,000 miles to Denver for the total solar eclipse of July 29, 1878 — a women's scientific expedition with the national press watching (Smithsonian NMAH).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="josiah-willard-gibbs" name="Josiah Willard Gibbs" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Josiah Willard Gibbs
> **Who:** Yale physicist whose 1876–78 paper founded chemical thermodynamics — the rules of energy in chemistry. · **When and where:** New Haven, Connecticut, 1839–1903.
Held America's first engineering doctorate (Yale, 1863); taught nine years unpaid until a Johns Hopkins offer made Yale pay him. He published his masterwork in an obscure Connecticut journal, and Europe understood it before America did — Maxwell built a plaster model of one of Gibbs's surfaces with his own hands and mailed it to New Haven. Copley Medal, 1901 (Britannica; Yale).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="josiah-willard-gibbs" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="albert-michelson" name="Albert Michelson" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Albert Michelson
> **Who:** Immigrant from Prussia, raised in Western mining towns; measured the speed of light with world-record precision. · **When and where:** Annapolis, Maryland (1879) and Cleveland, Ohio (1887).
His 1879 measurement came within about 0.05 percent of today's value. In 1887, with Edward Morley, his light-splitting instrument found no trace of the "ether" light was supposed to travel through — a famous nothing that pointed toward Einstein's relativity. In 1907 he became the first American to win a science Nobel — that prize sits in the next era (USNA; NobelPrize.org).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="albert-michelson" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="williamina-fleming" name="Williamina Fleming" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Williamina Fleming
> **Who:** Scottish immigrant hired as the observatory director's maid; became one of the world's leading star classifiers. · **When and where:** Harvard College Observatory, from about 1879 to 1911.
Classified more than 10,000 stars for the 1890 Draper Catalogue, spotted the Horsehead Nebula on an 1888 photographic plate, and in 1899 became Curator of Astronomical Photographs. Her note in Harvard's 1900 time capsule records $1,500 a year against men's $2,500 for comparable work: "Does he ever think that I have a home to keep and a family to take care of as well as the men?" (Harvard Magazine; Linda Hall Library).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="williamina-fleming" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="science" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Physics moved to the center of American science, refugees from fascist Europe filled American laboratories, and by the era's end the federal government had become science's biggest funder. The universe got bigger; the atom came apart.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="counting and weighing the invisible" -->
Michelson's 1907 Nobel was the first American science Nobel; Robert Millikan's oil-drop experiments (1909–1913) caught the exact electric charge of a single electron (Nobel 1923); Thomas Hunt Morgan's Columbia "fly room," starting from one white-eyed fruit fly in 1910, proved genes sit in line on chromosomes (Nobel 1933 — the first for genetics) (NobelPrize.org; APS).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="measuring the universe" -->
Henrietta Leavitt — a Harvard computer paid 30 cents an hour, deaf since an illness in her twenties — published the law in 1912 that made blinking Cepheid stars into distance markers. Edwin Hubble used it at Mount Wilson's 100-inch telescope: in 1923–25 he proved Andromeda is a separate galaxy, and in 1929 that the farther a galaxy, the faster it runs away — the expanding universe. Honest credit: Belgium's Georges Lemaître published expansion in 1927 in a little-read journal; the law is now the Hubble–Lemaître law. Leavitt died in 1921; a Nobel nomination was started in 1925 by someone who did not know she had died (Harvard Plate Stacks; NASA; APS).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the atom comes apart" -->
Fission was discovered in Berlin (December 1938, Hahn and Strassmann); the explanation came from Lise Meitner — a Jewish refugee excluded from the 1944 Nobel for it — and Otto Frisch (January 1939). In America the response built the wartime laboratory system: the Chicago Metallurgical Lab, Oak Ridge, Los Alamos — and on December 2, 1942, under the stands of a disused Chicago football field, Enrico Fermi's team of 49 ran the first controlled nuclear chain reaction, about half a watt for 28 minutes. Fermi had sailed straight from his 1938 Nobel ceremony to New York because Italy's racial laws targeted his Jewish wife. Berkeley's Radiation Laboratory (independent 1936) had already set the model of the big-machine, big-team lab; Seaborg's actinide concept redrew the periodic table (APS; Atomic Heritage; LBL).
Shared with: war (lead — the bomb and the decision) · elements (plutonium and the discovery run) · city-building (the secret cities).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the transistor's physics, 1947" -->
On December 16, 1947 at Bell Labs, Bardeen and Brattain made a solid crystal amplify a signal — quantum mechanics doing work in a piece of germanium; announced June 30, 1948; Nobel 1956 with Shockley. The physics of surfaces and semiconductors is ours; the device that replaced the vacuum tube → `technology` (Computer History Museum; IEEE Milestone).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frank-chapman-bird-count" name="Frank Chapman and the first Christmas Bird Count" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Frank Chapman and the first Christmas Bird Count
> **Who:** Museum ornithologist who replaced the Christmas "side hunt" — shooting every bird in reach — with a count; 27 volunteers ran 25 counts the first day. · **When and where:** Across North America, December 25, 1900.
The first count tallied about 18,500 birds of 90 species, from Toronto to Pacific Grove, California. It has run every winter since — ordinary people building one of the longest scientific datasets on Earth (Audubon).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frank-chapman-bird-count" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="robert-goddard" name="Robert Goddard" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Robert Goddard
> **Who:** Physics professor who worked out and flew the first liquid-fuel rockets — and was mocked for it by the New York Times. · **When and where:** Worcester and Auburn, Massachusetts; first flight March 16, 1926.
His 1920 Smithsonian paper argued rockets could reach space; a Times editorial (January 13, 1920) jeered that he lacked "the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools." His first liquid-fuel rocket flew 41 feet in 2.5 seconds off a farm in Auburn. On July 17, 1969 — Apollo 11 en route to the Moon — the Times printed a correction: "The Times regrets the error." The knowledge is ours; the rockets that flew to the Moon → `technology` and `exploration` (NASA history).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="robert-goddard" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="edwin-hubble" name="Edwin Hubble" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Edwin Hubble
> **Who:** Astronomer who proved other galaxies exist and that the universe is expanding. · **When and where:** Mount Wilson Observatory, California; 1923–1929.
One marked photographic plate — "VAR!" — recorded the star that put Andromeda far outside the Milky Way; six years later his velocity–distance law changed cosmology. Built on Leavitt's yardstick and Humason's spectra; shares law-credit now with Lemaître (NASA; Carnegie Observatories).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="edwin-hubble" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="albert-einstein-science" name="Albert Einstein" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Albert Einstein
> **Who:** The century's most famous physicist, driven out of Germany; an American from 1933 on. · **When and where:** Princeton, New Jersey, 1933–1955.
Relativity was done in Europe; his American decades are the refugee's story — Institute for Advanced Study from October 1933, citizen October 1, 1940. On August 2, 1939 he signed Szilard's letter warning Roosevelt about German atomic bombs (the bomb → `war`). At Lincoln University in 1946 he called racism "a disease of white people" and said, "I do not intend to be quiet about it" (IAS; Founders-era archives; Harvard Gazette).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="albert-einstein-science" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="barbara-mcclintock" name="Barbara McClintock" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Barbara McClintock
> **Who:** Geneticist who discovered that genes can move — decades before the field could believe it. · **When and where:** Cold Spring Harbor, New York; the key experiments from 1944.
Working alone with corn, she found "controlling elements" that jump between chromosomes and switch other genes on and off; published 1950, presented 1951. Colleagues respected her and mostly set the idea aside until molecular biology confirmed it in the 1960s–70s — tell it as delay, not mockery. Nobel in 1983, unshared — noted in the next era (NLM Profiles in Science; CSHL).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="barbara-mcclintock" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="emilio-segre-science" name="Emilio Segrè" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Emilio Segrè
> **Who:** Italian physicist stranded at Berkeley in 1938 when Mussolini's racial laws erased his job at home. · **When and where:** Berkeley, California, from summer 1938.
Visiting the Radiation Lab when the antisemitic laws passed, he stayed — Lawrence hired him cheap as a research assistant — and became one of America's leading physicists: Nobel 1959 for the antiproton, with Owen Chamberlain. The refugee scientists' story in one life (immigration and language thread). His element discoveries → `elements` (its Segrè story) (OAC Segrè papers; NobelPrize.org).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="emilio-segre-science" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="science" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Federal money, big teams, and the Cold War set what got studied. The era's discoveries redrew the deepest maps: the molecule of heredity, the ocean floor, the inside of the proton, the afterglow of the Big Bang, and the first volcano beyond Earth.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="DNA, 1953 — with honest credit" -->
American James Watson and Briton Francis Crick, in Cambridge, England, published DNA's double helix (Nature, April 25, 1953). They depended on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray work: Wilkins showed Watson her "Photo 51" in early 1953 without her knowledge, and her data reached them in an internal report. Franklin died in 1958 at 37; the 1962 Nobel went to Watson, Crick, and Wilkins — no posthumous prizes. Watson's later racist statements cost him his honorary titles in 2019; say so in a line (Nature; CSHL).
Shared with: health (what the molecule changed in medicine).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the sky hisses, the proton has parts" -->
- 1964–65: Penzias and Wilson at Bell Labs in New Jersey could not silence a faint microwave hiss — they even shoveled pigeon droppings out of the antenna — until Princeton physicists identified it: the cooled afterglow of the Big Bang. Nobel 1978 (APS historic site).
- Gell-Mann named the quark in 1964 (Nobel 1969); the 1968 MIT–SLAC scattering experiments found point-like pieces inside the proton (Nobel 1990) (NobelPrize.org).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the ground moves" -->
Marie Tharp's seafloor maps (with Bruce Heezen, 1957 Atlantic; 1977 world map) revealed the rift valley splitting the mid-ocean ridge; Harry Hess's 1962 seafloor-spreading paper and a decade of evidence made plate tectonics the accepted frame by about 1970 — the continents move (LOC; Lamont-Doherty).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what the space probes taught" -->
The journeys → `exploration`; the learning is ours. Six Apollo crews brought back 382 kilograms of Moon rock — still being studied at NASA Johnson. Viking's 1976 Mars life tests came back mixed and stand unresolved: one experiment looked positive, another found no organics; most scientists credit soil chemistry (NASA; the Viking debate is on the record). Voyager 1 and 2 (launched 1977) remade the outer solar system — Io's volcanoes, Europa's cracked ice, Titan's haze, Uranus, Neptune. Carl Sagan's *Cosmos* (PBS, 1980) carried the results to hundreds of millions (journalism figure — label).
Shared with: exploration (lead — the journeys and craft) · technology (the machines).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="measurement that would not stop climbing" -->
Charles David Keeling (Scripps) began continuous carbon-dioxide measurement on Mauna Loa in March 1958 — about 315 parts per million then, past 430 by 2026. The Keeling Curve is the base measurement under climate science (Scripps; NOAA; ACS landmark).
Shared with: land-environment (lead — the warming and the land) · energy (the fuels).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the lab network, and genetics pays its debts" -->
The national laboratories (Berkeley, Livermore, Argonne, Los Alamos, Oak Ridge) ran Cold War science at industrial scale — the U.S.–Soviet element race included (`elements` tells those discoveries). McClintock's 1983 Nobel — unshared, a first for a woman in that prize — arrived three decades after her experiments. The Human Genome Project launched October 1, 1990: 15 planned years, about $3 billion (genome.gov).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="richard-feynman" name="Richard Feynman" movie="The Fantastic Mr Feynman (2013)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Richard Feynman
> **Who:** Physicist who rebuilt the theory of light and matter, drew the diagrams every physicist now uses, and explained hard things plainly. · **When and where:** Los Alamos in the war; Caltech from the 1950s; died 1988. · **Movie:** The Fantastic Mr Feynman (2013)
Nobel 1965 (with Schwinger and Tomonaga) for quantum electrodynamics. On live television, February 11, 1986, on the Challenger commission, he dropped O-ring rubber into ice water and showed the failure in one minute. The film is a BBC documentary with interviews of Feynman, family, and colleagues (NobelPrize.org; commission record).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="richard-feynman" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="marie-tharp" name="Marie Tharp" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Marie Tharp
> **Who:** Cartographer-geologist who mapped the ocean floor and found the rift valley that helped prove the continents move. · **When and where:** Lamont Geological Observatory, Columbia University, from 1948.
Barred from the research ships as a woman (she first sailed in 1968), she built the maps ashore from soundings. When she pointed out the rift in 1952–53, her partner Bruce Heezen called it "girl talk" — then the data kept agreeing with her. The Library of Congress later named her among the 20th century's great cartographers (LOC; Lamont-Doherty).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="marie-tharp" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="linda-morabito" name="Linda Morabito" movie="The Farthest (2017)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Linda Morabito
> **Who:** JPL navigation engineer who found the first active volcano beyond Earth. · **When and where:** Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, California, March 9, 1979.
Processing a routine Voyager 1 navigation image of Jupiter's moon Io, she noticed a faint 270-kilometer plume off its edge — an erupting volcano, the first ever seen off Earth. A working engineer on the low-priority frames, making one of the mission's biggest discoveries. The film is the Voyager documentary; she appears in it (her arXiv historical review; NASA/JPL).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="linda-morabito" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="darleane-hoffman-science" name="Darleane Hoffman" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Darleane Hoffman
> **Who:** Nuclear chemist who ran chemistry on single atoms of the heaviest elements. · **When and where:** Los Alamos and Berkeley, 1950s–2000s.
Found plutonium-244 occurring in nature (1971) — a "man-made" element that nature made first — and tested where the periodic table's patterns start to bend, one atom at a time. Her element work → `elements` (its Hoffman story) (ACS; Physics Today).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="darleane-hoffman-science" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="science" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Science grew bigger and more international — thousands of people per experiment, machines the size of towns — while public argument about science grew louder. Current through 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the genome, finished twice" -->
The Human Genome Project declared the sequence essentially complete in April 2003 — about 92 percent, timed to the double helix's 50th birthday; the last gaps were truly closed in March 2022. Reading a human genome fell from billions of dollars to hundreds (genome.gov). The medicine → `health`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Higgs, and the machine America cancelled" -->
On July 4, 2012, CERN in Geneva announced the Higgs boson; about 1,700 U.S. scientists worked on the LHC experiments through Fermilab and Brookhaven. The plain truth alongside: Congress cancelled the Superconducting Super Collider in Texas in October 1993 — $2 billion spent, 14 miles of tunnel dug, then abandoned — so the discovery machine was Europe's (CERN; DOE; Physics Today).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="new eyes: JWST" -->
The James Webb Space Telescope launched December 25, 2021; first images July 2022. It has pushed the record for earliest known galaxies into the universe's first few hundred million years and read carbon dioxide in an exoplanet's air (WASP-39b) (NASA; STScI).
Shared with: exploration (the mission as journey) · technology (the machine).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="AI joins the lab" -->
AlphaFold (2020) solved practical protein-structure prediction; free databases now hold over 200 million predicted structures. The 2024 Nobel in Chemistry split between American David Baker (designing new proteins) and DeepMind's Hassabis and Jumper in Britain — say the mix plainly. Wider AI use in labs is still unfolding; recent claims are journalism — label them (NobelPrize.org 2024; EMBL).
Shared with: technology (the AI systems themselves, lead).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the element hunt goes international" -->
Superheavy-element claims are now judged by international working parties; Dubna–Livermore–Oak Ridge collaborations and Berkeley's 2024 result point at an attempted element 120 — a possible new row of the periodic table. The "island of stability" idea is the physics motive (IUPAC; Berkeley Lab). `elements` leads the discoveries.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rainer-weiss" name="Rainer Weiss" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Rainer Weiss
> **Who:** MIT physicist, refugee from Nazi Berlin, who conceived the detector that first heard gravitational waves. · **When and where:** MIT and the LIGO sites in Washington State and Louisiana; detection September 14, 2015.
His family fled Berlin via Prague, reaching New York in January 1939. In 1972 he worked out the laser interferometer idea; four decades later the NSF-funded LIGO detectors caught spacetime ringing from two black holes that collided 1.3 billion light-years away — announced February 11, 2016, a century after Einstein predicted the waves. Nobel 2017 with Barish and Thorne (NobelPrize.org; LIGO/Caltech).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rainer-weiss" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jennifer-doudna" name="Jennifer Doudna" movie="Human Nature (2019)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Jennifer Doudna
> **Who:** Berkeley biochemist; with Emmanuelle Charpentier turned a bacterial defense system into CRISPR, the programmable DNA editor. · **When and where:** UC Berkeley; the key paper June 28, 2012. · **Movie:** Human Nature (2019)
The 2020 Nobel in Chemistry to Doudna and Charpentier was the first science Nobel shared by two women alone. The editing tool is the knowledge; the therapies → `health`. The film is a CRISPR documentary in which she is a central voice (NobelPrize.org; Science).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jennifer-doudna" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="monica-dunford" name="Monica Dunford" movie="Particle Fever (2013)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Monica Dunford
> **Who:** American physicist, then a postdoc on the ATLAS experiment — one of six scientists a film crew followed from the LHC's start-up to the Higgs announcement. · **When and where:** CERN, Geneva, 2008–2012. · **Movie:** Particle Fever (2013)
A documented picture of what working science is now: one young scientist among 3,000 on a single experiment, hauling cables, debugging detectors, and standing in the room on July 4, 2012 (Particle Fever; Symmetry magazine).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="monica-dunford" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

<a id="chapter-10-energy"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="10" slug="energy" title="Energy" part="3" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 10: Energy

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED 2026-08-08 (agent: energy researcher)
**Angle:** What powered American life — muscle, wood, water, coal, oil, electricity, the atom, the sun.
**Keep out:** the machines that used it (`technology`); environmental damage (`land-environment`); element science (`elements`); the miner's job and unions (`work-workers`); oil money (`economy`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/energy.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-energy.md` — every date and number below is sourced there.
**Reference material:** `research/research-technology.md` (Pearl Street and the Tesla deal, parked to us) · `research/research-home-family.md` (REA percentages, parked to us).
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="energy" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Everything ran on muscle, fire, and wood. There were no draft animals north of Mexico — no horse, no ox — so people carried loads themselves, dragged them on frames (dogs pulled the travois on the Plains), and paddled them by canoe. Heat and cooking came from burning wood. Say it plainly: for thousands of years, human strength and fire were the whole energy supply.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fire as a managed tool" -->
Native nations used fire deliberately, on a schedule — regular low burns that cleared underbrush, opened travel routes, and kept land productive for food plants and game (NPS "Indigenous Fire Practices Shape Our Land"; the Karuk, Yurok, and Hupa burning cycles in California are documented examples). Our angle: fire as a controlled energy tool, not an accident.
Shared with: land-environment (what burning did to the landscape) · native-nations (whose knowledge it was, and its suppression later).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="energy" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The first new power source in thousands of years walked ashore: the horse, with Spanish expeditions, along with oxen and mules. For nearly everyone living on this land, nothing changed yet — muscle, fire, and wood still did all the work.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Horsepower arrives, and one water mill" -->
- Spanish expeditions brought horses into the Southeast and Southwest in the 1500s; literal horsepower — riding, hauling, plowing — entered the continent with them.
- In 1598, at the era's very edge, Juan de Oñate's colonists built the first water-powered mills in what is now the United States, in New Mexico — flat-lying "tub wheel" mills, with grindstones hauled up the Camino Real (Santa Fe New Mexican local history — journalism, labeled).
Shared with: native-nations (the horse nations to come) · exploration (whose expeditions carried the animals).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="energy" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Colonial power meant falling water, wind, pulling animals, and wood — enormous amounts of wood. For the first time, machines here ground grain and sawed boards without a human hand driving them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first mills" -->
- Virginia, 1621: the first recorded windmill in English America, built for Sir George Yeardley at Flowerdew Hundred on the James River, and the first recorded gristmill the same year (Encyclopedia sources; Colonial Williamsburg).
- 1634: carpenters sent by John Mason built a water-powered gristmill and sawmill at the falls of Newichawannock (now South Berwick, Maine) — among the first water mills in New England; several towns claim "first," so state the date, not the trophy (Old Berwick Historical Society; Tide Mill Institute).
- By the end of the century, mills stood on usable falls throughout the colonies.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Wood, the ox, and the horse" -->
- Wood was THE fuel. Historians' estimates of what one colonial household burned in a year range from about 15 to as many as 40 cords — a cord is a stack 4 feet by 4 feet by 8 feet — because open fireplaces sent most of their heat up the chimney (estimates vary; state the range). Forests near towns went first.
- Oxen and horses did the plowing and hauling in the colonies. On the Plains, horses were in Native hands earlier than the old story said: a 2023 study found horses ridden and raised in Native communities by the early 1600s, decades before the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 put perhaps 1,500 more Spanish horses into Native hands at once (Science, 2023; Smithsonian NMAI).
- Along Long Island and New England shores, colonists began taking whales near shore; whale oil burned in lamps from about 1690 (NPS New Bedford).
Shared with: land-environment (the shrinking forests) · native-nations (the horse changing Plains life) · food-farming (the plow team).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="william-chadbourne" name="William Chadbourne" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### William Chadbourne
> **Who:** An English carpenter and millwright, one of three men John Mason's Laconia Company sent in 1634 to build a sawmill and a gristmill at Newichawannock. · **When and where:** South Berwick, Maine, 1634.
- July 1634: Chadbourne, James Wall and John Goddard arrived on the ship *Pied Cow*, under contract to build the two mills on the Asbenbedick (Little Newichawannock) River (Old Berwick Historical Society, "Great Works").
- The sawmill stood in the rocky gorge below today's Great Works bridge. The society calls it "thought to be the first" overshot water-powered mill in America. Keep that as the society's claim. An overshot wheel turns under the weight of water falling onto its top.
- Wall's sworn statement of May 21, 1652 says the three men ran a sawmill and a corn mill there for three or four years, and that he and Chadbourne each built a house (OBHS timeline).
- Whose land: Newichawannock is an Abenaki name. Abenaki people lived there. Between 1616 and 1618, European diseases killed about seven in ten of them. No record found shows Mason's men asked anyone's leave to build (OBHS, "South Berwick's First People"). Leave out his birth and death years, which genealogy sites give differently.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="william-chadbourne" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="energy" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Water wheels powered colonial industry, iron furnaces began eating forests as charcoal, and after dark the better-off lit whale oil. The power sources were the same as the century before — there were just far more of them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Charcoal for iron" -->
Iron furnaces ran day and night on charcoal — wood slow-burned for days in earthen mounds by workers called colliers. Feeding one furnace took forestland by the hundreds of acres a year (the documented numbers are at Hopewell Furnace, next era; the practice was already general in this one). `elements` tells the iron at Saugus; `technology` the machinery; the fuel is ours.
- Baltimore Iron Works, Maryland, 1731: five planters founded it (Dr. Charles Carroll, his cousins Charles and Daniel Carroll, Daniel Dulany and Benjamin Tasker). It opened with 89 workers. 42 of them were enslaved. By 1785 the owners advertised "more than 200 Negroes." Enslaved people and convicts shipped from Britain worked 12-hour shifts hauling carts of charcoal, oyster shells and iron ore to the top of the furnace, around the clock, six or seven days a week. The owners did not give them enough food. Some ran away (Mount Clare Museum House).
- The records of these early furnaces name the owners. They do not name the men who made the charcoal.
Shared with: elements (the iron) · technology (the waterwheel-driven works) · land-environment (the cut forests) · slavery-freedom (enslaved labor, their lead).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Light after dark, and a stove that saved wood" -->
- Whale oil was a primary lamp fuel from about 1690 on, and spermaceti — the waxy oil from a sperm whale's head — made the brightest, cleanest candles money could buy (NPS New Bedford; New Bedford Whaling Museum).
- 1741: Benjamin Franklin's "Pennsylvania fireplace" — a cast-iron stove meant to give more heat with less smoke from less wood. It sold poorly until David Rittenhouse improved it. The stove as a machine belongs to `technology`; the wood it saved is ours (Britannica; ushistory.org).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="energy" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Wind, water, wood, and muscle still did nearly all of America's work through the Revolution and after. But in 1755 a machine in New Jersey began pumping water with fire — the first steam engine on the continent.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first steam engine in America" -->
The Schuyler copper mine at what is now North Arlington, New Jersey, kept flooding. John Schuyler ordered a Newcomen-type steam pumping engine from England in 1748; the parts arrived in 1753, and engine-builder Josiah Hornblower had it pumping by 1755 — the first steam engine in America, decades before steam moved a boat or a wheel here (Rutgers University Libraries journal; Engines of Our Ingenuity).
Shared with: technology (the engine as machine — parked there) · elements (copper, the reason the mine mattered).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Charcoal by the acre" -->
Hopewell Furnace, Pennsylvania (founded 1771, now an NPS site), documents an iron furnace's appetite: in blast it burned up to 800 bushels of charcoal a day — about an acre of forest cut for a single day's fuel — and 5,000 to 7,000 cords of wood, more than 200 acres, a year (two NPS pages give 5,000 to 6,000 and 6,000 to 7,000) (NPS Hopewell Furnace).
- How charcoal was made: a collier stacked about 30 cords of wood around a center pole, covered the pile with leaves and dust, and lit it by shovelling hot coals into a chimney left at the center. It smoldered with little air for 10 to 14 days. He watched it day and night and walked on it to find and fill air holes. One pile made about 1,100 bushels, a day and a half of fuel (NPS "Charcoal Making").
- Who did it: in 1780 Hopewell's founder, Mark Bird, enslaved 18 people (10 men, 4 women, 3 boys, 1 girl), the most in Berks County (NPS). At Catoctin Furnace in Maryland, in blast by 1776, at least 271 enslaved people worked as ore miners, colliers, woodcutters and teamsters (Science, 2023). The Johnson family, who owned it, enslaved more than 80 people. One is recorded only as Collier Sam (Catoctin Furnace Historical Society).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Whale oil toward its peak" -->
Whaling grew into one of the young country's biggest businesses; spermaceti candles were the premium light of the era, and the fleet kept growing toward its 1846 peak. The ships belong to `transportation`; the ocean's cost to `land-environment`; the light is ours.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="josiah-hornblower" name="Josiah Hornblower" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Josiah Hornblower
> **Who:** English-born engine-builder who assembled and ran the first steam engine in America at the Schuyler copper mine. · **When and where:** North Arlington, New Jersey; engine at work 1755.
He crossed the Atlantic with the engine parts in 1753, got the machine pumping in 1755, and stayed in New Jersey the rest of his life (Rutgers University Libraries; History of Information).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="josiah-hornblower" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="energy" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Energy started coming out of the ground. Hard Pennsylvania "stone coal" learned to burn in home grates, gas made from coal lit the first city streets, steam engines spread through boats and mills — and the whale fleet reached its peak just before its fall.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Stone coal" -->
- February 11, 1808, Wilkes-Barre: Jesse Fell burned anthracite in an open iron grate at his tavern — proving the hard, hot, nearly smokeless coal could heat a home without bellows. Anthracite needed a draft from below; his grate supplied it (Luzerne County history; explorePAhistory).
- The Lehigh Navigation company (organized 1818) floated anthracite down to Philadelphia in boxy arks; canals then moved it into the cities, and coal stoves and furnaces followed (Lehigh Coal and Navigation records; Hopkin Thomas Project).
Shared with: transportation (the coal canals) · economy (the coal trade) · work-workers (the miners, their lead).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Gaslight" -->
Baltimore, 1816: Rembrandt Peale lit a room of his museum with gas made from coal; investors chartered the Gas Light Company of Baltimore on June 17, 1816 — the first American gas company — and lit the country's first public gas street lamp on February 7, 1817. Street by street, town gas began replacing oil lamps in cities (Maryland Center for History and Culture; American Oil & Gas Historical Society).
Shared with: city-building (lit streets) · news-communication (evening reading, their call).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Whaling's golden age — and who could afford it" -->
The American whaling fleet peaked in 1846 at 735 vessels — most of the world's roughly 900 — with New Bedford the leading port (New Bedford Whaling Museum; Whaling in the United States surveys). Honest framing: whale oil cost roughly $1.30 to $2.50 a gallon, so most ordinary homes actually burned cheaper tallow candles, lard oil, or camphene; the clean bright sperm oil lit the well-off, lighthouses, and public rooms (AOGHS; Nantucket Historical Association).
Shared with: land-environment (what whaling did to the whales) · work-workers (the crew's job) · transportation (the ships).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="nelson-cole-haley" name="Nelson Cole Haley" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Nelson Cole Haley
> **Who:** A New Bedford boy who went to sea at twelve and became a harpooner; his memoir of a four-year whaling voyage survives. · **When and where:** Aboard the ship *Charles W. Morgan*, 1849–1853, Pacific whaling grounds.
Haley (1832–1900) shipped as harpooner on the *Charles W. Morgan* at seventeen; his account, *Whale Hunt*, published by Mystic Seaport, describes the chase, the kill, and the try-works boiling blubber into the oil that lit lamps back home. The *Morgan* itself survives at Mystic Seaport — the last wooden whaleship in existence (Mystic Seaport Museum).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="nelson-cole-haley" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="energy" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Two new kinds of power arrived within a single generation: rock oil pumped from the ground in 1859, and electric current sold from a wire in 1882. Around 1885, coal passed wood as the country's largest energy source for the first time (EIA).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Drake's well, 1859" -->
August 27, 1859, Titusville, Pennsylvania: Edwin Drake's drill struck oil at 69.5 feet — the first well drilled purposely for oil in the United States, and the start of the American oil business. The target product was kerosene, a cheap lamp fuel (Drake Well Museum; AOGHS).
Shared with: economy (the oil business) · big-business (Standard Oil, later).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="edwin-drake" name="Edwin Drake" movie="Born in Freedom: The Story of Colonel Drake (1954)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Edwin Drake
> **Who:** Ex-railroad conductor hired by the Seneca Oil Company to drill for oil; his 1859 well started the industry. · **When and where:** Titusville, Pennsylvania, 1859.
> **Movie:** Born in Freedom: The Story of Colonel Drake (1954)
The honest details: Drake was never a colonel — investor James Townsend invented the title in letters sent ahead to impress Titusville locals. Drake never patented his key drive-pipe idea, lost his money, and lived his last years ill and nearly penniless until Pennsylvania voted him a $1,500-a-year pension in 1873; he died in 1880 (Drake Well Museum; Britannica; AOGHS). The film is a 30-minute industry-sponsored dramatization (American Petroleum Institute) with Vincent Price as Drake — label it as such.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="edwin-drake" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Kerosene takes the lamp" -->
Kerosene won the American lamp in the 1860s — but tell it honestly: whaling had already been shrinking for a decade (the fleet peaked in 1846), whale oil at $1.30–$2.50 a gallon lit mainly the well-off, and the Civil War tax that hit alcohol-based camphene at up to $2.08 a gallon (kerosene's tax: 10 cents) handed the market to petroleum. Kerosene did not so much kill whaling as finish a decline already underway — the "kerosene saved the whales" line oversimplifies (AOGHS; environmental-history critiques of the whale-oil myth, labeled as historians' argument).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pearl Street, 1882" -->
September 4, 1882: from 257 Pearl Street in Manhattan, Edison's crews threw the switch on the first central power station in America — six dynamos, direct current, serving about 85 customers and 400 lamps in a quarter-square-mile district on day one; 513 customers and over 10,000 lamps within a year. Edison stood in banker J.P. Morgan's office when the lights came on (IEEE Milestone / ETHW; IEEE Power & Energy Magazine).
Shared with: technology (the bulb and the machines, their lead on the lamp) · city-building (lit blocks) · big-business (the electric companies).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thomas-edison-energy" name="Thomas Edison" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Thomas Edison
> **Who:** Built the first central power station and the whole system behind it — dynamo, wiring, meter, lamp — and bet it all on direct current. · **When and where:** Pearl Street, Manhattan, September 4, 1882.
Our angle is the current and the grid: DC worked, but it could not travel far from the station — a limit that set up the fight of the next decade. The invention-lab story and the film about Edison live in `technology`.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thomas-edison-energy" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The current war" -->
- Tesla's alternating-current motor patents issued May 1888; Westinghouse licensed them that July for $60,000 plus a $2.50-per-horsepower royalty. AC could be stepped up to high voltage, sent miles, and stepped back down — DC could not (IEEE Spectrum; The Henry Ford).
- The smear campaign is documented and belongs in the telling: engineer Harold P. Brown, quietly backed by Edison's side, electrocuted animals with AC to brand it the killer current, and pushed AC into the first electric chair. William Kemmler's execution on August 6, 1890 was botched and gruesome (Smithsonian Magazine; primary press accounts).
- Westinghouse won anyway: his AC lit the 1893 Chicago World's Fair (a winning bid of $399,000, about 100,000 incandescent lamps), the Adams Plant at Niagara Falls sent its first AC power August 26, 1895, and Buffalo received Niagara power in November 1896. Alternating current became the way electricity travels — and still is (ETHW; standard histories).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="westinghouse-tesla-energy" name="George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla" movie="The Current War (2017)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### George Westinghouse and Nikola Tesla
> **Who:** The manufacturer and the immigrant engineer whose alternating current won the fight over how electricity would travel. · **When and where:** Pittsburgh and New York, 1888–1896.
> **Movie:** The Current War (2017)
Westinghouse licensed Tesla's patents in July 1888 and absorbed the electric-chair smear campaign without answering in kind; Niagara-to-Buffalo transmission in 1896 settled the question. The film is a Hollywood dramatization (Cumberbatch as Edison, Shannon as Westinghouse, Hoult as Tesla) — label it as drama, not documentary. Tesla's motor as a machine is `technology`'s story.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="westinghouse-tesla-energy" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What coal cost the miners" -->
- Avondale, near Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania, September 6, 1869: sparks from the mine's ventilating furnace set fire to the wooden breaker, the building where coal was broken and sorted. The breaker stood right over the mine's only shaft. 110 people died, among them five boys and two men who went in to rescue the miners. The miners suffocated underground (EARTH Magazine, 2018).
- Pennsylvania lawmakers passed the Mine Safety Act of 1870, which required every mine to have more than one exit (EARTH Magazine).
Shared with: work-workers (the miners' job and unions, their lead) · disasters (the fire as event).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Charcoal gives way to coal" -->
Hopewell Furnace burned charcoal from about 1771 until it closed in 1883. The National Park Service gives the reason: charcoal furnaces were replaced by new ironworks that burned hard coal (anthracite). Ironmakers had cut forests for charcoal for more than two hundred years. By the 1880s coal had taken their place (NPS Hopewell Furnace).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="lafayette-houck" name="Lafayette Houck" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Lafayette Houck
> **Who:** A collier (charcoal maker) at Hopewell Furnace, from a family of colliers, and one of the last men who knew how to do the work. · **When and where:** Hopewell Furnace, Berks County, Pennsylvania, later 1800s. Demonstrated the craft in 1936.
- His family's work at Hopewell began with Master Collier Henry Houck in 1818 (NPS "Prominent Families").
- A Hopewell collier lived in a makeshift hut from May to October with one or two helpers, tending eight or nine smoldering piles at once, with no break from lighting until the last load was hauled away (NPS "Charcoal").
- Hopewell closed in 1883. In 1936, after the federal government bought the land, Houck and his son William showed Civilian Conservation Corps men how a collier worked. He taught the Park Service how charcoal was made and gave them a first-hand account of the furnace (NPS).
- Birth year disputed: NPS gives 1846 to 1939 on one page and "82-year-old" in 1936 on another. State both or give no age. The records found do not give his pay or the years he worked.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="lafayette-houck" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1850-1900" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1900-1950" order="08" chapter="energy" label="1900 to 1950" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1900 to 1950
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Oil became the fuel of American movement, electric wires reached city homes and then — by government program — the farms, and dams turned rivers into power plants. By mid-century the United States was fueling a world war largely by itself.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Spindletop, 1901" -->
January 10, 1901, near Beaumont, Texas: the Lucas well blew in at a depth of 1,139 feet, throwing oil over 100 feet high and flowing an estimated 100,000 barrels a day until it was capped nine days later, on January 19. All of Texas had produced 836,000 barrels in 1900 — this one well could beat that in nine days. Cheap, huge Texas oil made gasoline plentiful just as the automobile arrived to drink it (Texas State Historical Association; AOGHS; Lamar University).
Shared with: economy (the oil boom) · big-business (Gulf, Texaco born) · transportation (the car, their lead).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The price of coal in lives" -->
- Coal was still the country's main fuel, and digging it killed thousands of miners every year. In 1907, 3,242 coal miners were killed at work, the worst year on record. From 1900 through 2025, MSHA's yearly counts add up to about 105,000 coal miners killed in accidents (MSHA).
- Monongah, West Virginia, December 6, 1907: explosions in mines No. 6 and No. 8 killed 362 men by the official count. Later estimates run above 500, because boys and helpers who were not on the company's list also went underground. Many of the dead were immigrants from Italy, Poland and Hungary. About 1,000 children lost a father. Sources name the owner as the Fairmont Coal Company (Clio) or the Consolidation Coal Company (West Virginia Mine Wars Museum). Company president C. W. Watson blamed "the careless use of a mining lamp." Experts disagreed on the cause. The disaster pushed Congress to create the federal Bureau of Mines (MSHA).
- Ludlow, Colorado, April 20, 1914: coal miners striking against the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company, whose main owner was John D. Rockefeller, Jr., lived in a tent colony. Governor Elias Ammons had sent the National Guard, paid for by the mine owners. Fighting broke out. Nobody knows who fired first. Guardsmen burned the tents. At least 19 people died, including 13 women and children who suffocated in a pit dug under a tent. Guardsmen shot strike leader Louis Tikas three times in the back (Colorado Encyclopedia). The strike story belongs to work-workers.
Shared with: work-workers (the miners, the strike, their lead) · disasters (Monongah as event).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="samuel-insull" name="Samuel Insull" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Samuel Insull
> **Who:** Edison's onetime secretary who built the modern electric utility — and whose empire's crash helped bring regulation. · **When and where:** Chicago, 1892–1932.
Took over Chicago Edison in 1892 and built Commonwealth Edison and a pyramid of holding companies serving millions; the pyramid collapsed in 1932 in the Depression, wiping out small investors. He fled abroad, was brought back in 1934, tried three times — fraud, bankruptcy violations, embezzlement — and acquitted every time. Candidate Franklin Roosevelt campaigned against "the Ishmael or Insull" in 1932; the crash fed the New Deal's utility laws (ETHW; EBSCO; Britannica). He appears as a character in The Current War (2017), but the film is not about him.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="samuel-insull" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rivers into power: TVA and Hoover Dam" -->
- May 18, 1933: Roosevelt signed the act creating the Tennessee Valley Authority; work on Norris Dam began that October. Before TVA, about 3 in 100 Tennessee Valley families had electricity (Library of Congress; TVA).
- October 1936: Hoover Dam's first generator began sending power 266 miles to Los Angeles (transmission began October 9; the generator reached full operation October 26 — sources give both dates for "first"). The dam as a structure belongs to `landmarks`; the power is ours (HISTORY; EDN).
- Who was moved: from 1933 to 1945 TVA officials bought or took about 1.3 million acres and moved an estimated 82,000 people from their homes to build 16 hydroelectric dams. Norris Dam alone moved more than 3,000 families. TVA lawyer John Snyder described the method: "a price is set and we buy at that price or we condemn." To condemn land is to take it by law and pay a price the government sets (Facing South, 1995).
- Grand Coulee Dam on the Columbia River, built by the Bureau of Reclamation and finished in 1941, had no fish ladders. Its reservoir drowned Kettle Falls, where Native people had fished for salmon for about 9,000 years. In June 1940 the Colville tribes held a three-day Ceremony of Tears there, and 8,000 to 10,000 people came (HistoryLink).
- Oil and Osage land: the Osage Nation kept the oil rights under its Oklahoma land in 1906. In the 1920s oil money made Osage headright holders rich. From about 1920 to 1925 more than 60 of them died in murders and suspicious deaths. Husbands, guardians and others killed them to inherit their shares of the oil money (Osage Nation). Native-nations and crime-justice tell it in full.
Shared with: landmarks (the dam itself) · government-politics (the New Deal) · land-environment (the drowned valleys) · native-nations (Kettle Falls, the Osage).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The night the lights came on" -->
In 1935, fewer than 11 farms in 100 had central-station electricity while most city homes were wired. Roosevelt created the Rural Electrification Administration by executive order May 11, 1935; the Rural Electrification Act of May 20, 1936 funded farmer-owned cooperatives to string the wires the companies would not. About half of farms had power by 1945, 9 in 10 by 1950, roughly 97 in 100 by 1960 (EH.net; Living New Deal; Britannica). A Tennessee farmer's line, recorded in 1930 and famous since: the greatest thing on earth is to have the love of God in your heart, and the next greatest thing is to have electricity in your house (documented in David Nye, *Electrifying America*; it titled the co-ops' own history, *The Next Greatest Thing*, 1984). The REA sent demonstrators like Louisan Mamer town to town — the "electric circus" — teaching farm families what the new power could do (Smithsonian NMAH).
Shared with: home-family (the kitchen and washday after the switch — they ceded the first night itself to us) · government-politics (the New Deal program).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="pearl-yates" name="Pearl Yates" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Pearl Yates
> **Who:** A high school English teacher in rural western North Carolina whose home got electricity in July 1939. She told the story in a 1984 oral history. · **When and where:** Haywood County, North Carolina, 1939.
- Interview D-0044, Southern Oral History Program, UNC, recorded May 29, 1984 by Bonnie Bishop with Pearl and her husband Oral Yates, for the REA's 50th anniversary (UNC catalog).
- Before the power came she cooked on a wood stove and spent whole days washing clothes in a big pot. Carolina Power and Light would not run lines into their rural area, so neighbors formed a cooperative. Many were wary of it at first, and a door-to-door campaign signed them up (UNC catalog abstract).
- When the lights came on she walked from room to room with her small children: "We'd stop and look and they were so pretty and we'd go look at another room and another room" (HISTORY.com, journalism, citing the UNC collection).
- HISTORY.com calls her a farmer's wife. The UNC catalog lists her as a teacher. Use the catalog. Same collection: Lena Boyce and Sam Oswalt (bank era 08).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="pearl-yates" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Oil wins a war" -->
Of the roughly 7 billion barrels of oil the Allies used in World War II, about 6 billion came from the United States (AOGHS). When German submarines sank coastal tankers, the government built the Big Inch and Little Big Inch pipelines from Texas to the East Coast (completed 1943–44); together they moved over 350 million barrels before the war in Europe ended (Texas State Historical Association; NIST). The fighting is `war`'s; the fuel is ours.
Shared with: war (the war itself, their lead) · transportation (tankers and pipelines as systems).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="energy" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The atom joined the fuel supply, and for the first time Americans learned what it feels like when the fuel runs short. By the era's end the country had energy laws, an Energy Department, mileage standards — and a stalled nuclear industry.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Atoms for peace" -->
- December 20, 1951: the EBR-1 test reactor in Idaho generated the first usable electricity ever made from atomic energy — enough for four 200-watt bulbs (Idaho National Laboratory; DOE).
- July 17, 1955: nearby Arco, Idaho (population about 1,200) became the first town anywhere lit entirely by nuclear power — for about an hour, from the BORAX III reactor (Argonne/AEC press record).
- December 8, 1953: Eisenhower's "Atoms for Peace" speech at the UN set the civilian course. Shippingport, Pennsylvania — the first full-scale American nuclear power plant built solely for civilian electricity — sent its first power onto the Duquesne Light grid December 18, 1957 and hit its full 60,000 kilowatts December 23 (DOE; ASME landmark). Say the "first" carefully: first *full-scale, all-civilian* U.S. plant — smaller and dual-use reactors came earlier, and Britain's Calder Hall ran in 1956.
Shared with: elements (uranium and plutonium as elements) · science (the physics) · war (weapons stay there).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Where the uranium came from" -->
From 1944 to 1986 mining companies took nearly 30 million tons of uranium ore from Navajo land (EPA). About 10,000 people worked in uranium, about a quarter of them Navajo. Navajo miners say no one told them about the danger and no one gave them protective gear or fresh air in the mines. Uranium breaks down into radon, a radioactive gas, and breathing it caused lung cancer (Brugge and Goble, 2002). The Atomic Energy Commission bought all the uranium until 1966. After that, uranium also went to power plants. On July 16, 1979, a United Nuclear Corporation dam holding radioactive mill waste broke near Church Rock, New Mexico. About 94 million gallons of radioactive liquid ran down the Rio Puerco past about 1,700 Navajo people. New Mexico Governor Bruce King turned down the Navajo Nation's request for a federal disaster declaration (elements bank, from Richards 2013 and the state's report).
Shared with: elements (uranium, their lead) · native-nations (the nation and its land) · health (the disease).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Dams and the Three Affiliated Tribes" -->
Garrison Dam on the Missouri River was finished in 1953 under the Army Corps of Engineers' Pick-Sloan Plan, for flood control and electric power. Its lake flooded about 152,000 to 155,000 acres (sources differ) of the Fort Berthold Reservation of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara. Farms, homes, schools, a hospital, churches, cemeteries and whole towns went under water, including Elbowoods. More than 300 families had to move, 80 to more than 90 percent of the tribes' people by different counts. At the 1948 signing, tribal chairman George Gillette said the treaty and the tribes' constitution were "being torn to shreds by this contract" (Cultural Survival, 2010. North Dakota Studies).
Shared with: native-nations (lead) · land-environment.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="1973: the fuel runs short" -->
October 1973 – March 1974: Arab oil producers embargoed the United States over its support of Israel in the Yom Kippur War. Oil went from about $2.90 to $11.65 a barrel — roughly quadrupled in six months. Drivers sat in blocks-long gas lines; many states rationed by license plate (odd numbers on odd days); Congress set a national 55 mph speed limit (Federal Reserve History; U.S. State Dept. history; Britannica). The laws followed: the Energy Policy and Conservation Act (December 22, 1975) created the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and the first car-mileage standards (a doubling to 27.5 mpg by 1985), and the Department of Energy opened October 1, 1977 (EBSCO; DOE history).
Shared with: america-world (the embargo's diplomacy, their lead) · economy (the inflation) · transportation (smaller cars).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="david-falconer" name="David Falconer" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### David Falconer
> **Who:** A photographer for the Environmental Protection Agency's DOCUMERICA project who photographed Oregon's gas shortage and wrote a caption for each picture. · **When and where:** Oregon, October 1973 to May 1974.
- His pictures and captions are held by the National Archives (EPA Project DOCUMERICA, 412-DA series).
- October 1973, Interstate 5 at Sutherlin: "By midday gasoline was becoming unavailable along interstate highways." At Lincoln City, stations closed early and on weekends, and "No Gas Today" signs went up.
- December 1973, Portland: a man who had run out of gas stood in line with a gas can.
- February 1974, Portland: drivers with even-numbered license plates lined up on even-numbered days, Monday to Friday. Anyone could try on Saturday. Portland stations closed on Sundays. Falconer's caption says Oregon was the first state to use the odd-even plan. That is his claim, not a checked fact.
- May 1974, after the embargo ended: a downtown Portland station still posted that its day's gas was sold out (Yale Energy History gallery, citing the National Archives). Drivers in the lines are not named in the records found.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="david-falconer" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Three Mile Island, 1979" -->
March 28, 1979: the Unit 2 reactor at Three Mile Island, Pennsylvania, partially melted down — the worst commercial nuclear accident in U.S. history. Governor Thornburgh advised pregnant women and preschool children within five miles to leave; about 140,000 people left on their own amid confused official messages. The radiation released was small; follow-up studies found no detectable health effects, and no deaths are attributed to the accident — but the fear was real and documented, and it mattered: new-plant orders stopped, and no newly built U.S. reactor came online for over four decades (NRC backgrounder; World Nuclear Association; EIA). The accident and response as an event belong to `disasters` (their lead — parked there, incl. the Netflix documentary); the effect on what powered America is ours.
- Who ran the plant, and what failed: General Public Utilities operated Unit 2. A relief valve stuck open and let cooling water out. The operators had no gauge that showed the valve was open, so they cut back the water. At least 45 percent of the core melted.
