Men were forced at gunpoint to gather the dead. Workers loaded bodies on barges, weighted them with rocks and dropped them into the Gulf, but many washed back to shore. After that the dead were burned in fires on the beach, which burned into November. The writer Elizabeth Blasius found that members of the volunteer militia, armed citizens organized as a local guard, forced Black workers at gunpoint to bury the dead. Black people made up about one fifth of the city.

Clara Barton, 78, arrived with Red Cross workers on September 17. A Central Relief Committee led by Mayor Walter C. Jones and the city's bankers and merchants ran the relief and paid for 483 new houses. Afterward, workers built a seawall 17 feet high and pumped sand under the city to raise the ground as much as 17 feet. Workers lifted more than 2,000 buildings on jacks first.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="isaac-cline" name="Isaac Cline" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Isaac Cline
> **Who:** the U.S. Weather Bureau's chief weather forecaster in Galveston, who lost his wife in the 1900 hurricane. · **When and where:** Galveston, Texas, September 8, 1900.
- Isaac Cline ran the Weather Bureau office in Galveston from 1889. His brother Joseph worked with him.
- In 1891 he wrote in the *Galveston Daily News* that the idea of a hurricane doing serious harm to Galveston was "a crazy idea." Some residents had asked for a seawall, and his article helped stop it.
- On September 8, 1900, when the tide rose far above normal, he raised the hurricane warning flags without waiting for approval from Washington.
- In his autobiography he wrote that he rode along the beach warning people. No eyewitness reported seeing him do it. The writer Erik Larson argued that he warned no one before the office's official warning.
- The storm destroyed his house. His wife, Cora, who was pregnant, died. He saved his youngest daughter, Esther, who was 6. Joseph saved his other daughters, Allie May, 12, and Rosemary, 11.
- In 1901 he moved to New Orleans and spent years studying how hurricanes move. He retired in 1935 and died in 1955.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="isaac-cline" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="San Francisco, April 18, 1906" -->
At 5:12 a.m. on April 18, 1906, an earthquake of about magnitude 7.9 on the San Andreas Fault shook San Francisco for about 42 seconds. Broken gas pipes started more than 30 fires. The fires burned for three days. Firefighters and soldiers used dynamite to blow up buildings in the fire's path, and some of the blasts started new fires. Between 80 and 95 percent of the destruction came from the fires. More than 80 percent of the city was destroyed, and between 227,000 and 300,000 people lost their homes.

The first counts of the dead ran from 375 to more than 500. Hundreds of deaths in Chinatown were never recorded. In 2005 the members of the city's Board of Supervisors voted to accept more than 3,000 as the official count, based on the research of the city historian Gladys Hansen. Mayor Eugene Schmitz ordered soldiers and police to "kill any and all persons found engaged in Looting." The records do not say how many people they killed. There were also reports that soldiers themselves looted.

About 15,000 Chinese people lived in Chinatown, and they lost nearly everything. City officials wanted to move Chinatown out of the center of the city. Army officers put the Chinese survivors in separate camps and moved them farther and farther away. The plan to move Chinatown failed, and Chinese residents rebuilt it in the same place.
- Shared with: `immigration` (Chinese exclusion and the records burned in the fire) · `city-building` (the rebuilt city).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="hugh-kwong-liang" name="Hugh Kwong Liang" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Hugh Kwong Liang
> **Who:** a 15-year-old in San Francisco's Chinatown who lived through the 1906 earthquake and fire and was sent to a segregated camp. · **When and where:** San Francisco, April 1906.
- He was 15. He is one of the few Chinese survivors whose own account of the earthquake has survived.
- He woke to see "pieces of plaster falling down like water." As he ran into Washington Street, the building across from his home fell down.
- As the fire spread, city officials directing the survivors told him and his family to go to the open ground of the Presidio, the Army post by the Golden Gate. He remembered: "I turned away from my dear old Chinatown for the last time."
- Army officers moved the Chinese survivors to a cold, windy corner of the Presidio near Fort Point, apart from everyone else.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="hugh-kwong-liang" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Triangle fire, March 25, 1911" -->
Just before quitting time on March 25, 1911, a fire started on the eighth floor of the Triangle Waist Company, a clothing factory on the top three floors of the Asch Building in New York City. Most of the workers were young immigrant women. The fire killed 146 workers. On the ninth floor, the door to the Washington Place stairs was locked. Workers testified that the owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, kept it locked so workers could not leave with stolen blouses. The only fire escape collapsed. Many workers jumped from the windows and died on the sidewalk. Law students at New York University put ladders across to the roof of the building and saved workers who had climbed there from the tenth floor.

Blanck and Harris were tried for manslaughter, the crime of killing a person without meaning to, by carelessness. A jury found them not guilty on December 27, 1911. One juror said he believed the door was locked, but the jury could not be sure the owners knew it. In 1914, 23 families who had sued the building's owner settled for an average of 75 dollars for each life. New York lawmakers created a Factory Investigating Commission and passed new factory safety laws.
- Shared with: `work-workers` (**lead**: the workers, the unions and the safety laws, story `rose-freedman`).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="kate-alterman" name="Kate Alterman" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Kate Alterman
> **Who:** a sewing-machine worker who escaped the Triangle fire and told the jury how her friend Margaret Schwartz died at the locked door. · **When and where:** New York City, March 25, 1911, and the trial in December 1911.
- She had come from Philadelphia, where she lived for nine years, and had worked at the Triangle factory for four months.
- When the fire reached the ninth floor, she and her friend Margaret Schwartz ran to the Washington Place door. The manager's brother tried it and could not open it. Kate pulled the handle "in and out, all ways," and it would not open. Margaret tried next.
- Smoke covered them. Kate saw Margaret kneel at the door, and saw her dress and hair begin to burn. Margaret screamed, "Open the door! Fire! I am lost, there is fire!"
- Kate turned her fur coat inside out, put it over her head, covered her head with dresses and ran out through the Greene Street door, which was burning.
- At the trial, the owners' lawyer, Max Steuer, made her tell her story again and again. Because she used almost the same words each time, he suggested to the jury that she had memorized it. She answered that she told it the same way "because he asked me the very same story over and over."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="kate-alterman" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Ships: the Titanic, 1912, and the Eastland, 1915" -->
The British liner *Titanic* hit an iceberg and sank in the North Atlantic on April 15, 1912, on its way to New York. More than 1,500 people died. The ship did not carry enough lifeboats for everyone on board, though it met British rules. Senator William Alden Smith of Michigan led a U.S. Senate investigation that began in New York on April 19. The senators on his committee blamed the captain's "indifference to danger" and the British officials who wrote the lifeboat rules. They recommended enough lifeboats for everyone on board and radio operators on duty day and night. In March 1915 members of Congress passed the Seamen's Act, which required more lifeboats on American ships.

On July 24, 1915, the Great Lakes passenger ship *Eastland* rolled onto its side while tied to a dock in the Chicago River. It was carrying about 2,500 workers of the Western Electric Company and their families to a company picnic. The ship had long been known to be top-heavy, and its owners had added lifeboats under the new law. The river there was only 20 feet deep, but 844 people died. Many were immigrants from Czech lands, Poland, Norway and other countries. A grand jury charged six officers of the steamship company, the captain and the engineer. A federal judge refused to send them to Illinois for trial, saying there was "barely a scintilla of proof," so they never stood trial there.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Mississippi flood of 1927 and the Okeechobee hurricane of 1928" -->
In the spring of 1927 the Mississippi River broke through its levees, the earth walls along its banks, in at least 145 places. Water covered 27,000 square miles, up to 30 feet deep. About 500 people died, and about 637,000 had to leave their homes. On April 29 a group of New Orleans bankers had 30 tons of dynamite set off at the levee at Caernarvon, Louisiana, to protect their city. The water flooded St. Bernard and Plaquemines parishes. Other levees upstream broke on their own, so the blast was not needed, and the New Orleans businessmen never paid the people whose homes they flooded.

About 325,000 people lived in Red Cross camps, and 69 percent of them were Black. Near Greenville, Mississippi, more than 13,000 people were left for days on top of the levee without food or clean water. Local white leaders ran many of the camps. Supplies and boats went to white people first, and Black people got what was left. Black people got supplies only if they named a white employer, were forced to work and were not allowed to leave. Herbert Hoover, the Secretary of Commerce, led the federal relief. A group of Black leaders headed by Robert Moton reported on the camps, and Hoover kept their reports out of the newspapers. After the flood, members of Congress passed the Flood Control Act of 1928, and Army engineers built the world's longest system of levees.

Early on September 17, 1928, a hurricane that had already killed 312 people in Puerto Rico came ashore near West Palm Beach, Florida. The wind pushed the water of Lake Okeechobee over the low dike at its south end, and floods up to 20 feet deep covered the farm towns of Belle Glade, Pahokee, Chosen and South Bay. At least 2,500 people died in the United States. For many years the official count was the Red Cross's 1,836. About three quarters of the dead were migrant farm workers, most of them Black. Officials saved the few coffins for white victims, who were buried with a service in a grave at Woodlawn Cemetery in West Palm Beach. The bodies of Black victims were burned or thrown into mass graves, and 1,600 were buried in one grave at Port Mayaca. Robert Hazard of West Palm Beach started a group to win recognition for the Black victims. The city got the West Palm Beach grave site back in 2000, and a state marker was put up there in 2003.
- Shared with: `migration` (the Great Migration north after 1927) · `rights-movements`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Dams, gas and dust: 1928 to 1937" -->
Just before midnight on March 12, 1928, the St. Francis Dam in northern Los Angeles County collapsed, two years after it was built. William Mulholland, the city's chief water engineer, had inspected a new leak that morning and judged it safe. The flood killed at least 431 people as it ran 54 miles to the ocean, among them 84 workers of the Southern California Edison company at a construction camp by the river. A coroner's jury found in April 1928 that the collapse came from "an error in engineering judgment" by Mulholland's Bureau of Water Works and Supply. The jurors found no crime and said a great dam should never be left "to the sole judgment of one man." The failure ended Mulholland's career.

On April 14, 1935, a wall of dust from the plowed-up southern Great Plains struck the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles with winds up to 60 miles an hour. For a time the darkness was so complete that people could not see their own hands. The day is called Black Sunday. The next day, an Associated Press reporter, Robert Geiger, used the words "dust bowl" in a news story.

At 3:17 p.m. on March 18, 1937, a school building in New London, Texas, exploded. To save money, the school board had plumbers tap into a pipe of waste gas from a nearby oil company, the Parade Gasoline Company. Natural gas has no smell, and it leaked unnoticed into the space under the building. A spark from an electric sander in a shop class set it off. About 500 students and 40 teachers were in the building. About 298 died by the Texas State Historical Association's count, and other counts run from 294 to more than 400. Most of the dead were children. Courts found no one legally responsible. Texas lawmakers then required gas companies to add a chemical with a strong smell to natural gas, so people can smell a leak.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Hindenburg, 1937, and the Cocoanut Grove, 1942" -->
On May 6, 1937, the German airship *Hindenburg* caught fire as it came in to land at the Naval Air Station at Lakehurst, New Jersey. It was filled with hydrogen, a gas that burns easily. Of the 97 people on board, 35 died, and one man working on the ground, Allen Hagaman, died too. Newsreel cameras filmed the fire, and the radio reporter Herbert Morrison recorded what he saw. The cause of the spark has never been settled. Travel by giant passenger airship ended after the fire.

On November 28, 1942, a fire spread through the Cocoanut Grove nightclub in Boston. More than 1,000 people were inside a club rated for 460. The owner, Barnett Welansky, had locked exit doors and hidden others behind curtains. The main door was a revolving door, and people piled up behind it. Other doors opened inward, and the crowd pressed them shut. Fire officials later said that at least 300 lives could have been saved if the doors had swung outward. The fire killed 492 people. Welansky was convicted of manslaughter and spent nearly four years in prison. New laws banned flammable decorations and locked exits, and required exits other than revolving doors.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Explosions at the docks: Port Chicago, 1944, and Texas City, 1947" -->
On July 17, 1944, two ships being loaded with ammunition blew up at the Port Chicago Naval Magazine in California. The explosion killed 320 men, 202 of them Black sailors, whom Navy officers had assigned to load the ships without proper training.

On the morning of April 16, 1947, a fire broke out in the cargo of the French ship *Grandcamp* at the docks of Texas City, Texas. The ship carried about 2,300 tons of ammonium nitrate, a fertilizer that can explode. The captain ordered his crew not to use water, so the cargo would not be spoiled, and a crowd gathered on the shore to watch the orange smoke. At 9:12 a.m. the ship exploded. The blast set off fires and explosions in chemical plants and oil tanks, and a second ship, the *High Flyer*, exploded early the next morning. At least 581 people died, among them 26 or more of the town's volunteer firefighters. The monument in Texas City lists 576 known dead, 63 of them buried without names. More than 8,000 survivors sued the federal government, under a new law that let people sue it for carelessness. The justices of the Supreme Court ruled against them, 4 to 3, in 1953. In 1955 members of Congress voted to pay the claims, and 1,394 awards were paid.
- Shared with: `war` (**lead** on Port Chicago: the refusal and the mutiny trial) · `rights-movements`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Shared with other chapters" -->
- Mine and work disasters: the Monongah mine explosions in West Virginia (December 6, 1907, 362 dead by the official count, more than 500 by later estimates) and the Hawks Nest tunnel (1930 to 1932, between 109 and about 1,000 dead of silicosis by different counts) are told in `energy` and `work-workers`.
- The Quebec Bridge collapse in Canada (August 29, 1907, 75 or 76 workers killed, 33 of them Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake): `landmarks`.
- The Big Burn wildfire of 1910 in the Northern Rockies: `land-environment`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="disasters" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
From 1950 to 2000, hurricanes, earthquakes, floods and fires killed thousands of Americans, and many deaths came from choices people made. A coal company's waste dam in West Virginia broke and killed 125 people in 1972. A hotel walkway in Kansas City fell and killed 114 in 1981. In 1979 President Jimmy Carter created the Federal Emergency Management Agency, called FEMA, to run the national government's help after disasters. Television crews filmed rescues and ruins as they happened. After the storms and earthquakes, lawmakers and city officials wrote stricter building codes, the rules for how strong a building must be.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hurricanes with names: Audrey, 1957, and Camille, 1969" -->
In 1953 the U.S. Weather Bureau began giving storms human names, and in 1956 it set up a hurricane center in Miami. On June 27, 1957, Hurricane Audrey struck southwestern Louisiana. Its storm surge, the wall of seawater a hurricane pushes onto land, reached about 12 feet and flooded land as far as 25 miles inland. Weather Bureau forecasters issued hurricane warnings about 24 hours before landfall, and about 75,000 people left the coast. The storm sped up as it neared land and arrived sooner than forecasters and residents expected. Audrey killed at least 416 people in the United States, most of them in Cameron Parish, Louisiana. The full count may never be known.

Late on August 17, 1969, Hurricane Camille came ashore near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, with winds of 175 miles an hour. The sea rose 24.6 feet at Pass Christian. Camille killed 172 people in Mississippi. As it moved north, its rain flooded mountain valleys in Virginia and killed more than 153 people there. At least 343 people died in all.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Alaska earthquake, March 27, 1964" -->
At 5:36 p.m. on March 27, 1964, Good Friday, an earthquake of magnitude 9.2 shook southern Alaska for four and a half minutes. It is the strongest earthquake ever recorded in North America. Underwater landslides and the shifting sea floor sent tsunamis, giant waves, into the coast. The U.S. Geological Survey counts 131 dead, 115 in Alaska and 16 in Oregon and California. Other counts reach 139. More than 110 of the dead drowned in the waves. At Valdez, 32 people died when the harbor and docks slid into the sea. The waves crossed the Pacific, and in Crescent City, California, a tsunami killed 10 people.

Chenega was a fishing village of Chugach Alutiiq people on an island in Prince William Sound. About four minutes after the shaking began, a wave 27 feet high destroyed every building but the school and one house. Between 23 and 26 of the roughly 70 people who lived there died, by different counts. The survivors climbed to high ground. Officials of the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs moved them to the village of Tatitlek. Former residents used land they gained under the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act of 1971 to build a new village, Chenega Bay, where people began living in 1984.

President Lyndon Johnson declared all of Alaska a disaster area the day after the earthquake. Army engineers rebuilt roads and laid out new towns, and the people of Valdez moved their town to higher ground. In 1967 federal scientists of the Coast and Geodetic Survey opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska.
- Shared with: `native-nations` (Alaska Native land claims).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Floods of 1972: Buffalo Creek and Rapid City" -->
At about 8 a.m. on February 26, 1972, a dam of coal waste above Buffalo Creek in Logan County, West Virginia, gave way. It was the highest of three dams the Buffalo Mining Company, part of the Pittston Company, had built from mining refuse to hold black waste water from its coal plant. The top dam sat on soft coal sludge, not on rock. About 132 million gallons of black water and sludge rushed down the narrow valley through 16 coal towns. It killed 125 people, among them whole families, and left about 4,000 of the 5,000 people who lived there homeless. A federal mine inspector had called the dam "satisfactory" four days earlier. Pittston officials blamed three days of rain and called the flood "an act of God." The governor's own commission found that Pittston's officials had shown "flagrant disregard" for the people living below the dams. In 1974 Pittston paid $13.5 million to 645 survivors and families who sued, about $13,000 each after the lawyers were paid. Congress and West Virginia lawmakers then passed new laws for building and inspecting such dams.

On June 9 and 10, 1972, about 15 inches of rain fell on the Black Hills of South Dakota. Rapid Creek flooded Rapid City, where houses and businesses stood on the creek's flood plain, the low land a river covers when it floods. The flood killed 238 people. Afterward, city leaders turned the flood plain into parks.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="FEMA and Three Mile Island, 1979" -->
Before 1979, more than 100 separate federal offices could be involved after a single disaster. On April 1, 1979, President Jimmy Carter signed an executive order, a written order from the president, that put much of that work into one new office, the Federal Emergency Management Agency. In July 1979 he moved disaster relief into it with a second order. From 1988 a law called the Stafford Act set the rules for when a president may declare a disaster and send federal money.

At 4 a.m. on March 28, 1979, a chain of equipment failures and mistakes began in the Unit 2 reactor at the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and part of its core melted. It was the worst accident at a commercial nuclear plant in the country's history. The plant's operators, its owner Metropolitan Edison, and state and federal officials gave the public confusing and conflicting reports. On March 30, Governor Richard Thornburgh advised pregnant women and preschool children within five miles to leave. About 140,000 people left on their own. More than a dozen studies since then have found no deaths and no health harm that can be measured from the radiation released.
- Shared with: `energy` (**lead** on what the accident did to nuclear power).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Mount St. Helens, 1980, and the Hyatt Regency walkways, 1981" -->
At 8:32 a.m. on May 18, 1980, an earthquake loosened the north side of Mount St. Helens, a volcano in Washington State, and the whole side slid away. Hot gas and shattered rock blasted north, and hundreds of square miles of forest were destroyed. About 57 people died, most of them choked by hot gas and ash. Among them were Harry R. Truman, who owned a lodge at Spirit Lake below the mountain, and David Johnston, a U.S. Geological Survey volcano scientist on watch at a post about six miles north.

On the evening of July 17, 1981, about 1,600 people were at a Friday tea dance in the lobby of the new Hyatt Regency Hotel in Kansas City, Missouri. Two walkways hung from the ceiling over the lobby, one above the other. Both fell onto the crowd. They killed 114 people and injured 216. The engineer of record, Jack D. Gillum, had signed off on the design, and his engineer Daniel Duncan had approved a change by phone without checking the math. The change doubled the load on the beams of the upper walkway. Investigators found that the walkways would have failed under one-third of the weight they held that night. A Missouri state board found the engineers guilty of gross negligence, meaning a serious failure to take care. The company lost its licenses in Missouri, Kansas and Texas. No one was convicted of a crime.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Air Florida Flight 90, January 13, 1982" -->
On the snowy afternoon of January 13, 1982, Air Florida Flight 90 took off from Washington National Airport with ice on its wings. The captain, Larry Wheaton, 34, and the first officer, Roger Pettit, 31, had not turned on the engines' ice protection. Less than a minute after takeoff, the jet hit the 14th Street Bridge, struck seven cars with people in them, and fell through the ice of the Potomac River. Seventy-four of the 79 people on the plane died, and four drivers on the bridge died. Five people clung to the tail in water of about 34 degrees. The rescuers who reached the bank had no equipment that could reach them.

A U.S. Park Police helicopter pulled the survivors out. One passenger, Arland D. Williams Jr., 46, a bank examiner, twice caught the rescue line and passed it to others. When the helicopter came back for him, the wreck had rolled and he had gone under. He was the only passenger who drowned. When a line was dropped to the passenger Priscilla Tirado, she was too weak to hold it. Lenny Skutnik, a worker at the Congressional Budget Office, took off his coat and boots, swam out and pulled her to shore. Roger Olian, a sheet-metal foreman, had tried first to swim out with a rope. Television crews filmed the rescue live. The National Transportation Safety Board, the federal office that investigates crashes, blamed the pilots' decisions about ice and snow. Its investigators found that the captain did not listen when the first officer said the engine readings looked wrong, and did not stop the takeoff while there was still room on the runway.
- Shared with: `transportation` (the 2025 Potomac collision near the same place).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="melvin-windsor" name="Melvin Windsor" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Melvin Windsor
> **Who:** a U.S. Park Police officer and rescue technician who stood on a helicopter's skid over the frozen Potomac River to pull a survivor out. · **When and where:** Washington, D.C., January 13, 1982.
- Melvin E. "Gene" Windsor, 41, grew up in Rockville, Maryland, and had managed a carpet store before he joined the Park Police in 1971.
- That afternoon he and the chief pilot, Donald W. Usher, 31, were at their hangar waiting out the storm. Usher had already ordered no routine flying because of the weather.
- At 4:09 p.m. a radio call reported a possible plane crash. They took off in their small helicopter at 4:16 and reached the river at 4:20, steering by the highway below through falling snow.
- Six people were holding on to the wreck, in water up to their necks. Windsor, working in the open door without a safety line, dropped ropes and life rings while Usher flew so low that the skids went under the water.
- They carried the survivors to shore one or two at a time. The last was Patricia Felch, too weak to grab a rope after 30 minutes in the river. Windsor unbuckled, stepped out onto the skid, and held her against it with one arm while Usher flew them to the bank.
- They went back for the man who had passed the line to others and could not find him. "In a mass casualty, you'll find people like him, but I've never seen one with that commitment," Windsor told *Time*.
- Windsor, Usher, Skutnik and Olian each received the Carnegie Medal for bravery. Windsor served 22 years with the Park Police and died in 2014, at 74.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="melvin-windsor" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="1989: Hurricane Hugo and the Loma Prieta earthquake" -->
In September 1989 Hurricane Hugo crossed two U.S. territories before it reached the mainland. On St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands, it damaged more than 90 percent of the buildings and killed three people. In Puerto Rico it killed eight people and left nearly 28,000 homeless. On September 22 it struck South Carolina with a storm surge of 20.2 feet near McClellanville, and 13 people died in the state.

At 5:04 p.m. on October 17, 1989, an earthquake of magnitude 6.9 struck near Santa Cruz, California, just before a World Series game in San Francisco. It killed 63 people. In Oakland, 42 of them died when the upper deck of the double-deck Cypress Street Viaduct, part of the Nimitz Freeway, fell onto the cars on the lower deck. A section of the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge also fell, and Anamafi Moala, 23, died there.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hurricane Andrew, 1992" -->
Early on August 24, 1992, Hurricane Andrew struck south Dade County, Florida, with winds of 165 miles an hour. It destroyed more than 63,500 houses and damaged more than 124,000 others. It wrecked 99 percent of the mobile homes in Homestead. Andrew killed 44 people in Florida, 15 of them in the storm itself and 29 from its effects afterward, and 65 people in all in the Bahamas, Florida and Louisiana. Three days after the storm, the county's emergency management director, Kate Hale, went on national television and said: "Where in the hell is the cavalry on this one? They keep saying we're going to get supplies. For God's sake, where are they?" Critics blamed FEMA for its slow start. FEMA officials said they could not act until Governor Lawton Chiles sent a formal request for federal help, and he took five days to send it. Engineers found roofs had torn away where builders had glued tiles to felt paper and stapled shingles the wrong way. Florida lawmakers later wrote one building code for the whole state, which took effect in 2002.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Northridge, 1994, and the Chicago heat wave, 1995" -->
At 4:30 a.m. on January 17, 1994, an earthquake of magnitude 6.7 struck under the San Fernando Valley in Los Angeles. The official count is 57 dead, and other counts run from 60 to 72. Sixteen people died when the Northridge Meadows apartment building fell onto its ground-floor parking.

In mid-July 1995 a heat wave in Chicago killed 739 more people than normally die in a week. Most of the dead were poor and elderly people who lived alone. Many had no air conditioning, or could not pay to run it, and kept their windows shut out of fear of crime. Black residents died at a higher rate than white residents. City officials did not issue a heat emergency warning until the last day, and few people used the city's five cooling centers. The morgue of the Cook County medical examiner, Edmund Donoghue, filled, and refrigerated trucks were brought in to hold the bodies. Mayor Richard M. Daley publicly criticized Donoghue's count. Later studies confirmed hundreds of deaths above normal. In August, 41 victims whose bodies no one claimed were buried together in one grave in Homewood, Illinois.
- Shared with: `health` (heat and health).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Shared with other chapters" -->
- The *Challenger* space shuttle broke apart 73 seconds after launch on January 28, 1986, and all seven people on board died: `exploration` (**lead**).
- The Santa Barbara oil spill of 1969 and the *Exxon Valdez* spill in Alaska on March 24, 1989, which spread about 10 million gallons of oil and reached the shores near Chenega and Tatitlek: `land-environment`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="disasters" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Since 2000, hurricanes, floods, fires, heat and cold have killed thousands of Americans, and after most of them people argued about who should have warned, rescued and paid. Hurricane Katrina killed about 1,400 people in 2005, most of them in New Orleans, where floodwalls built by the Army Corps of Engineers broke. Officials in Puerto Rico counted 64 dead after Hurricane Maria in 2017 and changed the count to 2,975 a year later. Many of the dead were old, sick, poor or disabled, and some waited days for help that came too late. Power lines owned by utility companies started several of the deadliest fires. This section counts deaths and damage through September 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="September 11, 2001, and the illnesses afterward" -->
On September 11, 2001, 19 hijackers flew passenger jets into the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon near Washington, and a field in Pennsylvania. They killed 2,977 people. Among the dead were 343 members of the New York City Fire Department who had gone into the burning towers. Thousands of firefighters, police officers, construction workers and volunteers then spent months digging through the ruins, breathing dust of crushed concrete, glass fibers, asbestos and other poisons from the fires. Many later got cancer or lung disease. By September 2026, 453 more members of the Fire Department had died of illnesses tied to the dust, more than the 343 killed on the day of the attacks. In December 2010 members of Congress passed the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act. President Barack Obama signed it on January 2, 2011. It pays for medical care for sick responders and survivors through the World Trade Center Health Program.
- Shared with: `america-world` (**lead**: the attacks and the wars after them) · `landmarks` (the towers and the memorial) · `health`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hurricane Katrina, August 29, 2005" -->
On August 28, 2005, Mayor Ray Nagin ordered the first mandatory evacuation in New Orleans history. About one million people left the city and its suburbs. Between 100,000 and 150,000 stayed, many of them without cars or money. The city opened the Superdome as a "refuge of last resort." Katrina came ashore on August 29. Its storm surge broke the levees and floodwalls in more than 50 places, and 80 percent of the city flooded, up to more than 10 feet deep in the Lower Ninth Ward, a neighborhood of mostly Black homeowners. Investigators found that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, which Congress had put in charge of the city's flood walls in 1965, had designed and built them with flaws. A federal appeals court ruled that a 1928 law protected the Corps from paying for the damage.

The National Hurricane Center first counted 1,833 dead. In 2023 its scientists lowered the count to 1,392 after new studies. Most of the dead in New Orleans were elderly people who lived near the broken levees. Thousands of people waited for days at the Superdome and the Convention Center with little food, water or medical care. Federal officials did not start helping the people at the Convention Center until September 2. Coast Guard crews rescued more than 33,500 people. Michael Brown, the head of FEMA, was removed from the job and resigned on September 12.

Some police officers turned their guns on survivors. On September 1, police from the city of Gretna and deputies of the Jefferson Parish sheriff blocked the bridge over the Mississippi River and turned back people walking out of New Orleans at gunpoint. On September 4, New Orleans police officers shot six unarmed Black people on the Danziger Bridge. They killed James Brissette, 17, and Ronald Madison, 40, a man with a mental disability whom an officer shot in the back. The officers then made up a story to cover the killings. Five former officers pleaded guilty in 2016 and were sentenced to between 3 and 12 years in prison. At Memorial Medical Center, which flooded and lost power, 45 bodies were found. In July 2006, after an investigation by Louisiana Attorney General Charles Foti, a judge ordered the arrest of a doctor, Anna Pou, and two nurses for murder in the deaths of several patients. In 2007 a grand jury refused to charge Pou, and the state later paid her legal fees.
- Shared with: `migration` (**lead** on the people who left and never came back, and the Gretna bridge, story `kimberly-rivers-roberts`) · `crime-justice`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="herbert-freeman-jr" name="Herbert Freeman Jr." movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Herbert Freeman Jr.
> **Who:** a New Orleans man who took his 91-year-old mother, Ethel Freeman, out of their flooded home in a boat, then watched her die outside the Convention Center while they waited for help. · **When and where:** New Orleans, August 31 to September 4, 2005.
- Ethel Mayo Freeman was 91. She had a pacemaker for her heart and a feeding tube, and she used a wheelchair. She and her son stayed home when Katrina came.
- The floodwater filled their house several feet deep. On August 31, Herbert, 58, borrowed a friend's boat, lifted his mother into it in her wheelchair, and took her to dry ground.
- New Orleans police officers sent them to the Convention Center. Herbert told officers his mother needed a doctor. They told him a bus would come.
- The Convention Center had no food, water, doctors or transportation. "She was calling out for a doctor or a nurse, but there was nothing there," Herbert said. Ethel Freeman died in her wheelchair on September 1.
- Her body stayed outside, covered with a poncho, for days. Photographs of it went around the world. Herbert stayed beside her body for nearly four days, until he was ordered onto a bus on September 4. He put a note with his name and phone number in her pocket. It took him seven weeks to find her body at a morgue in St. Gabriel, Louisiana. She was buried in New Orleans in November 2005.
- He sued the national government. In 2009 federal appeals judges ruled that the Stafford Act protected the government's disaster decisions from such suits, and they dismissed the case.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="herbert-freeman-jr" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, September 20, 2017" -->
Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, and its 3.4 million people are U.S. citizens. Hurricane Maria struck the island on September 20, 2017, two weeks after Hurricane Irma had passed nearby. Maria knocked out power to every home and business on the island. Some customers did not get power back until August 2018, about 11 months later. It was the worst blackout in U.S. history. Most people lost clean water. FEMA officials had sent many of the supplies they kept in Puerto Rico to the U.S. Virgin Islands after Irma, and they later admitted to failures in moving supplies and staff.

The death count became a public fight. Governor Ricardo Rosselló's government counted 64 dead for months. Researchers found that many more people died in the months after the storm, when the sick and elderly could not get dialysis, oxygen or other medical care. A Harvard study in 2018 estimated 4,645 more deaths than normal from September to December 2017, within a range of 793 to 8,498. On August 28, 2018, Rosselló accepted a George Washington University study and raised the official count to 2,975. On September 13, 2018, President Donald Trump said on Twitter that 3,000 people did not die and that Democrats had raised the number to make him look bad. He gave no evidence. On September 29, 2017, a week after the storm, the mayor of San Juan, Carmen Yulín Cruz, had said of the federal relief effort: "We are dying and you are killing us with the inefficiency."
- Shared with: `migration` (about 130,000 people who left for the mainland) · `america-world` (the territories).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jesse-vazquez" name="Jesse Vazquez" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Jesse Vazquez
> **Who:** a retired veteran in Bayamón, Puerto Rico, who lived for months without electricity after Hurricane Maria with his 89-year-old mother, Mercedes Mercado. · **When and where:** Calle Alameda, Bayamón, Puerto Rico, September to December 2017.
- Maria cut the power to their house on September 20, 2017. For weeks the family ran electric fans and charged phones from the battery of Jesse's car.
- A small generator cost about $600 on sale, more than he could afford. In October his son, also named Jesse, and his daughter, Megan, flew from New York and brought a new generator in their luggage. "It's basically cheaper to buy a flight, get a generator and bring it down here," his son said.
- Running it five hours a day took about $80 of gasoline a month. Exhaust from a neighbor's generator blew into their living room, and Megan said they needed a carbon monoxide detector.
- By Christmas the house had been without power for 96 days. Jesse and his mother used the generator for the refrigerator and for fans at night.
- A FEMA inspector told him he was not eligible for help to fix his damaged roof. "It's kind of humiliating," he said. With his son's help he bought four solar panels. He and his mother chose to stay in Puerto Rico.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jesse-vazquez" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Floods and storms: Harvey, 2017, Helene, 2024, and the Texas Hill Country, 2025" -->
Hurricane Harvey stalled over southeast Texas in late August 2017 and dropped as much as 60.58 inches of rain, the most from any storm in U.S. records. Floods covered much of Houston. Rescuers pulled more than 17,000 people from the water. The storm killed 103 people in Texas, 68 of them in the storm itself.

Hurricane Helene came ashore in the Big Bend of Florida on September 26, 2024, and its rain flooded the mountains of North Carolina and Tennessee the next day, with more than 30 inches in one place. The National Hurricane Center counts 250 dead in the United States, 107 of them in North Carolina (report updated February 17, 2026). In Erwin, Tennessee, workers at the Impact Plastics factory were still at work that morning as the Nolichucky River rose. A surviving worker and victims' families said managers did not tell them they could leave until floodwater had covered the road. Five employees and a contractor who cleaned the offices were swept away and died. In 2025 Tennessee's workplace safety agency issued no citations, and after a state police investigation the district attorney, Steven Finney, filed no charges against the company's owner, Gerald O'Connor. The investigators found no evidence that workers were told they would be fired for leaving, and said the workers had a little more than an hour to get out. The family of Johnny Peterson, one of the dead, sued the company.

Early on July 4, 2025, up to 20 inches of rain fell on the Texas Hill Country. The Guadalupe River rose about 26 feet in 45 minutes. The flood killed 136 people, 117 of them in Kerr County. At Camp Mystic, a Christian summer camp for girls with cabins beside the river, 25 campers, two teenage counselors and the camp's owner, Dick Eastland, died. Kerr County had no flood warning system. In 2016 the county sheriff had asked for one with sirens, and County Commissioner H. A. "Buster" Baldwin said, "I think this whole thing is a little extravagant for Kerr County." Camp Mystic's owners had asked federal officials to take several camp buildings off the flood-hazard map. In June 2026 a committee of Texas lawmakers found that the camp had no written emergency plan and did not evacuate in time. In a special session in September 2025, Texas lawmakers passed the Heaven's 27 Camp Safety Act and other laws that set rules for camps in flood zones and require written emergency plans, training and warnings to parents. In July 2026 new sirens in Kerr County warned people during another flood.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fires started by power lines: Paradise, 2018, Lahaina, 2023, and Los Angeles, 2025" -->
On the morning of November 8, 2018, a worn metal hook broke on a transmission tower from the early 1900s owned by Pacific Gas and Electric (PG&E), and the power line sparked a fire. Within hours the Camp Fire burned through the town of Paradise, California. It killed 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 buildings. On June 16, 2020, PG&E pleaded guilty to 84 counts of involuntary manslaughter, the crime of killing people through carelessness.

On August 8, 2023, a wildfire destroyed the town of Lahaina on the island of Maui in Hawaii. It killed 102 people, the most in any U.S. wildfire since 1918. Power lines of Hawaiian Electric, knocked down by high winds, started a fire that morning. Maui firefighters put it out, but embers from it started the fire again that afternoon. Firefighters lost water pressure in the hydrants. Maui County's emergency management chief, Herman Andaya, did not sound the island's outdoor sirens. He said the sirens would have sent people toward the fire, and he resigned the next day. Many people were trapped in traffic and died in their cars, and some jumped into the ocean. Lahaina had been the capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii for 35 years, and many Native Hawaiian families lived in homes they had inherited from earlier generations. Under a settlement of the survivors' lawsuits, Hawaiian Electric, Maui County and others are to pay $4 billion. By late August 2026 no payments had been made, because of court fights over lawyers' fees and insurance.

In January 2025, fires driven by winds of up to 100 miles an hour burned parts of Los Angeles. They killed at least 31 people and destroyed more than 18,000 homes and buildings. The Eaton Fire in Altadena killed 19 people. County and state fire investigators found in August 2026 that it started from sparks on an unused Southern California Edison tower. Seventeen of the 19 died in west Altadena, a historically Black neighborhood, where evacuation orders came hours after the fire turned toward it. Their average age was 77. California's attorney general opened a civil rights investigation into whether race, age or disability affected the warnings. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people. In October 2025 Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, was arrested and charged with setting a fire on January 1 that smoldered underground and flared up again on January 7. His federal trial ended in a mistrial on June 26, 2026, when 10 jurors voted not guilty and 2 voted guilty. Prosecutors said they would try him again. The charges are accusations.
- Shared with: `land-environment` (**lead** on why fires grew larger: fuel, drought and heat) · `energy` (the utilities).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Cold, collapse and FEMA's future: 2021 to 2026" -->
In February 2021 a winter storm froze power plants, gas wells and pipelines across Texas. More than 4.5 million homes and businesses lost power, some for days, in temperatures far below freezing. The state counted 246 deaths, about two-thirds of them from hypothermia, the body cooling until it stops working. Researchers estimated as many as 702. Among the dead was Cristian Pavón Pineda, 11, who died of carbon monoxide poisoning in his family's powerless mobile home in Conroe.

At 1:22 a.m. on June 24, 2021, part of Champlain Towers South, a 12-story condominium in Surfside, Florida, collapsed and killed 98 people. Water had rotted the concrete and steel supports under the pool deck for years. The damage was reported in 2018 and was "much worse" by April 2021. The owners had approved a $15 million repair that had not started.

In 2025 President Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said they wanted to eliminate FEMA and have states handle disasters. Officials fired more than 200 FEMA employees in February 2025. In May 2025 the acting head of FEMA, Cameron Hamilton, told Congress that eliminating it was not in the best interest of the American people, and he was removed the next day. On May 7, 2026, a council the president had created approved a report with ten recommendations to give states the lead. As of September 2026 FEMA still existed, and members of Congress were still debating bills to change it.
- Shared with: `energy` (**lead** on the Texas grid, story `cristian-pavon-pineda`).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Shared with other chapters" -->
- COVID-19 killed 1,245,791 Americans through September 19, 2026, by the CDC's provisional count: `health` (**lead**).
- The *Dali* cargo ship knocked down Baltimore's Francis Scott Key Bridge on March 26, 2024, killing six road workers, and an Army helicopter and a passenger jet collided over the Potomac River on January 29, 2025, killing 67 people: `transportation` (**lead**).
- The Upper Big Branch mine explosion in West Virginia, April 5, 2010: `energy`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

<!-- hb-chapter id="28" slug="drugs-alcohol" title="Drugs and Alcohol" part="7" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 28: Drugs and Alcohol

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** RESEARCHED: all ten eras researched 2026-09-27 (T-266a, T-266r, T-266b, T-266c; bank checks for eras 01 to 05, 06 to 08 and 09 to 10 done). Present-day figures checked 2026-09-27.
**Angle:** Intoxicants over time — alcohol and Prohibition, tobacco, other drugs, their use and control.
**Keep out:** the law itself (`government-politics`); organized crime (`crime-justice`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/drugs-alcohol.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-drugs-alcohol.md`
**Reference material:** `_reference/book-outline-v1.md` §25 Drugs and Alcohol (ten-era seed) · `research/research-health.md` (patent medicines and Radithor as unregulated "cures" — the health effects stay there).
Editor's in-development note — not part of the final book; the parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
People in this land used plants that change how the body and mind feel for thousands of years before 1500. Tobacco is the oldest one found so far. Burned tobacco in a hearth at the Wishbone site, in the desert west, is about 12,300 years old. Most of this use was part of prayer and ceremony. Alcohol was different. Before Europeans came, people brewed beer and wine mainly in the Southwest. Elsewhere only a few scattered nations made it. Nobody here distilled strong liquor.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tobacco for prayer" -->
- Wishbone site, about 12,300 years ago: burned tobacco in a hearth, 9,000 years older than any earlier find. How the people there used it is not known (Duke et al., *Nature Human Behaviour*, 2022).
- A pipe from central Washington State, about 1,430 years old, held traces of a wild native tobacco mixed with sumac leaves (Brownstein et al., 2020).
- Traditional tobacco, mostly the plant *Nicotiana rustica*, was an offering. It was burned in a fire or smoked in a pipe to carry prayers, and the smoke was usually not breathed into the lungs (National Native Network, "Keep It Sacred"). Native health programs today call this traditional tobacco and keep it separate from commercial cigarettes. Practice differed from nation to nation.
- Shared with: `religion` (ceremony as worship) · `food-farming` (tobacco as a crop, from 1612). This chapter's slice is the plant as something taken into the body.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Black Drink, cacao, peyote and datura" -->
- Black Drink: a tea of yaupon or dahoon holly leaves, full of caffeine. Chemists found its traces in beaker cups at Cahokia, in Illinois, from A.D. 1050 to 1250. The holly grows far to the south, so people carried the leaves north. In later centuries, records describe men in the Southeast drinking it in a ceremony to make themselves pure (Crown et al., *PNAS*, 2012).
- Cacao, the bean chocolate is made from: traces in jars at Pueblo Bonito, Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, about A.D. 1000 to 1125. The beans came by trade from Mexico or Central America (Crown and Hurst, *PNAS*, 2009). Caffeine and cacao drinks turn up at 18 sites across the Southwest from about 750 to 1400.
- Peyote: a small cactus whose top contains mescaline, a drug that causes visions. Two dried peyote tops from Shumla Cave on the Rio Grande in Texas are about 5,700 years old and still hold mescaline (El-Seedi et al., 2005).
- Datura: a flowering plant that holds scopolamine and atropine, drugs that cause hallucinations (seeing and hearing things that are not there). People chewed wads of it in Pinwheel Cave, California, under a painting that the researchers read as its flower. Native Californians are recorded using datura to enter a trance. The dates run from late prehistory into Spanish times (Robinson et al., *PNAS*, 2020).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Beer and wine in the Southwest" -->
- Before Europeans arrived, alcohol use in what is now the United States was "primarily confined" to nations in the Southwest, with scattered use elsewhere (Patrick J. Abbott, 1996). The drinks were beer and wine. Most Native nations first met alcohol when Europeans brought it in the 1500s and 1600s.
- The Akimel O'odham and Tohono O'odham (called the Pima and Papago in older books): each late summer the women picked the red fruit of the saguaro cactus. They made most of it into jam and the last of the harvest into wine for the rain ceremony at their New Year. Many Tohono O'odham villages still held the ceremony in the 1990s (Abbott, 1996).
- The Apache made a corn beer called tiswin, learned from peoples of northern Mexico. The Apache reached the Southwest sometime between 1000 and 1550, so the start of tiswin is not firmly dated.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In the 1500s Europeans carried tobacco home from the Americas, and Spanish colonists brought wine to Florida. Tobacco reached the French court in 1560. By 1588 English men and women were taking it too. The Spanish at St. Augustine, founded in 1565, shipped in wine from Spain in clay jars. Few Native nations in this land had met alcohol yet, and no regular trade in it began in this century.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tobacco reaches Europe" -->
- 1560: Jean Nicot, the French ambassador in Portugal, sent tobacco seeds to Queen Catherine de Médicis of France with a letter about its uses as a medicine. In 1561 he showed her how to grind the leaves into a powder to sniff for headaches, and the powder became a fashion at the French court (Britannica, "Jean Nicot").
- The word nicotine, the name of the drug in tobacco, comes from Nicot's name. The Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus named the tobacco plants *Nicotiana* after Nicot in 1753.
- Europeans at first took tobacco as a medicine. Thomas Hariot's report of 1588 says that "men & women of great calling" and "some learned Phisitions" in England were using it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thomas-hariot-drugs-alcohol" name="Thomas Hariot" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Thomas Hariot
> **Who:** English mathematician who learned to smoke tobacco from the Algonquian people and described how they used it. · **When and where:** Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina, 1585 to 1586, and London until 1621.
- Went on the English expedition of 1585 to Roanoke Island, on the land of the Roanoke, Secotan and Croatoan peoples. He learned the Algonquian language from two Algonquian men, Manteo and Wanchese (Encyclopedia Virginia).
- In *A Briefe and True Report* (1588) he described a plant the people called uppowoc and planted in its own plots. They dried the leaves, ground them to powder, and drew the smoke through clay pipes. They believed the smoke kept the body healthy. They also threw the powder on sacred fires and onto the water as an offering, in storms and after escaping danger.
- He wrote that the English "vsed to suck it after their maner" while they were there, and kept smoking after they went home.
- The colony ended in June 1586 after Ralph Lane's men killed the werowance (chief) Wingina, and the English sailed home a week later (NPS, Fort Raleigh).
- An ulcer grew in his nose. Hariot died in London on 2 July 1621 of cancer of the nose, which Encyclopedia Virginia says was "probably caused by heavy tobacco use."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thomas-hariot-drugs-alcohol" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Spanish wine in Florida" -->
- Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and his Spanish colonists founded St. Augustine on 8 September 1565, at the Timucua town of Seloy (Florida Museum of Natural History).
- The Spanish colonists counted wine and olive oil as more important than wheat and beef. Ships brought both from Spain in clay "olive jars" (Florida Museum). The colonists got their corn and cooking pots from Timucua women.
- The historian Peter C. Mancall writes that some Europeans offered alcohol to Native people when they met. The trade in alcohol with Native nations did not begin until about 1650. No record from this century describes the Spanish trading wine to Native nations as a regular business.
- Shared with: `food-farming` (what the colonists ate) · `native-nations` (the Timucua). This chapter's slice is the wine.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
English and Dutch colonists in the 1600s drank beer, cider and wine every day, and the Chesapeake colonies grew rich selling tobacco. Colonists believed alcohol kept the body warm and strong. Some had also fallen sick from bad water. Colony leaders licensed the taverns and punished drunkenness with fines, the stocks and public shame. From about 1650, traders sold rum and brandy to Native nations for furs, and colony leaders passed laws against those sales that traders kept breaking.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Beer, cider and bad water" -->
- The first drinks colonists made were cider and beer, brewed from corn, wheat, oats, persimmons and green cornstalks (Ed Crews, *Colonial Williamsburg Journal*, 2007). Grapevines brought from Europe died of American pests and diseases, so the colonists' wine came by ship.
- Colonists believed alcohol warmed the body, helped digestion and made people strong. Water did make some sick. George Percy wrote that the Jamestown settlers drank river water that was salty at high tide and "full of slime and filth" at low tide, which was "the destruction of many of our men." In Europe people drank alcohol in place of dirty water, and the colonists kept the habit.
- In 1622 the Virginia Company of London wrote to Governor Francis Wyatt that the colonists' drinking was hurting the colony.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Laws about drinking" -->
- Virginia's first General Assembly, 1619: a man found drunk was scolded in private by the minister the first time and in public the second time. The third time he was held for 12 hours in bolts, which are iron shackles, in the provost marshal's house and paid the marshal's fees.
- Massachusetts, laws of 1633 to 1647: only a person licensed by the county court could run a tavern. A tavern keeper could not serve one person more than half a pint of wine at a time, or let anyone sit drinking for more than half an hour or after nine at night. A drunk person was fined 10 shillings. A person who could not pay was put in the stocks, a wooden frame that locked the ankles in public, for up to three hours.
- Prices were set by law. In 1634 a Boston innkeeper could charge sixpence for a meal and one penny for a quart of beer, and paid a 10 shilling fine for charging more (Samuel Adams Drake).
- Shared with: `government-politics` (the assemblies that passed these laws) · `crime-justice` (the courts and punishments). This chapter's slice is the drinking the laws controlled.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="samuel-cole-drugs-alcohol" name="Samuel Cole" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Samuel Cole
> **Who:** a maker of sugar-coated sweets who kept Boston's first licensed tavern. · **When and where:** Boston, Massachusetts Bay Colony, 1634 to 1638.
- Came to Boston with Governor John Winthrop's fleet in 1630 (Samuel Adams Drake, *Old Boston Taverns and Tavern Clubs*).
- Opened his ordinary, the word then for a tavern, on Washington Street in 1634. Drake gives the date as 4 March 1634 and calls it the earliest Boston ordinary known to have had a license. His house had a brew-house for making beer.
- In 1636 Governor Henry Vane made a peace treaty with the Narragansett at Boston. The sachems Miantonomi and two sons of Canonicus ate at the governor's house, and about twenty other Narragansett men ate at Cole's inn.
- The colony court gave him leave to sell the inn in 1638, and he sold it to Robert Sedgwick. He died in 1666.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="samuel-cole-drugs-alcohol" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="robert-coles-drugs-alcohol" name="Robert Coles" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Robert Coles
> **Who:** a farmer the Massachusetts court punished four times for drunkenness, the last time by making him wear a red letter D. · **When and where:** Roxbury and Agawam (now Ipswich), Massachusetts Bay Colony, 1631 to 1634.
- Came from England with the Winthrop Fleet in 1630.
- 1631: fined five marks for being drunk on the ship *Friendship*, which was carrying spiced honey wine, and at Winnisimmet, now Chelsea.
- 1633: fined £10 at Agawam for being drunk, for getting John Shatswell's wife to drink, and for urging her to be unfaithful to her husband. He had to stand in public with a paper on his back that said "drunkard" in large letters.
- 1634: the court ordered him to wear a red cloth D on a white patch around his neck for a year, whenever he was among people, and took away his right to vote. Governor John Winthrop wrote that Coles "having been oft punished for drunkenness, was now ordered to wear a red D about his neck for a year" (Massachusetts court records, through Wikipedia, "Robert Coles (settler)").
- The court gave back his vote about two months later, and no court charged him with drunkenness again. He moved to Providence and in 1640 helped write the Providence Combination, a written plan for governing the town.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="robert-coles-drugs-alcohol" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Selling alcohol to Native nations" -->
- In September 1609, near what is now Albany, Henry Hudson and his mate gave Mahican leaders "so much Wine and Aqua vitae," a strong liquor, that they got drunk. Robert Juet, who kept a journal on the ship, wrote that Hudson and the mate did it to find out whether the leaders were planning "treacherie." One man got drunk and "could not tell how to take it."
- From about 1650, English traders sold rum and French traders sold brandy to Native nations in the fur trade (historian Peter C. Mancall). Young men traded the furs from a season's hunt for liquor and drank it fast, and more families became poor. Native and colonial observers recorded drunken men fighting their families, drowning, falling into fires and killing others.
- In New Netherland (now New York), Director General Willem Kieft and his council banned selling liquor to Native people on 18 June 1643, because "large quantities of strong liquors are daily sold to the Indians." They passed the ban again in 1645. Director General Petrus Stuyvesant passed it a third time in 1647 and raised the fine to 500 guilders.
- Mancall writes that Native people also organized against the trade and complained to colonial officials about traders.
- Shared with: `native-nations` (the fur trade and what it cost the nations) · `exploration` (Hudson's voyage and the killings of October 1609). This chapter's slice is the liquor.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Tobacco and rum" -->
- John Rolfe, a heavy smoker, grew milder Spanish tobacco at Jamestown by July 1612. Virginia shipped 20,000 pounds of it to England in 1617 and grew 29 million pounds in 1709 (Encyclopedia Virginia). Planters took cleared Powhatan land to grow more.
- King James I of England attacked smoking in *A Counterblaste to Tobacco* (1604). He called it "lothsome to the eye, hatefull to the Nose, harmefull to the braine, dangerous to the Lungs," and called Native Americans "barbarous and beastly" for starting it.
- Massachusetts banned smoking within about 330 feet of a house, barn or haystack, because a pipe could start a fire, and in the public rooms of an inn (1638 and 1647).
- Rum is a strong liquor distilled from molasses, the syrup left after sugar is made from sugarcane. A Barbados writer of about 1651 called it "Rumbullion, als Kill-Divill" and "a hott hellish and terrible liquor." New England merchants began trading fish and lumber to the West Indies for molasses and making it into rum in the 1600s ("Rum Trade," *Dictionary of American History*).
- Shared with: `food-farming` (tobacco as a crop, lead) · `economy` and `money` (tobacco as trade and as money) · `slavery-freedom` and `work-workers` (who did the work). This chapter's slice is the smoking and the drinking.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Between 1700 and 1750 rum was the colonists' favorite strong drink, and it was cheap. In Philadelphia in 1740 a gallon of rum made in the colonies cost 1 shilling 8 pence. People drank in taverns, and they also met, heard the news and did public business there. Colony leaders controlled drinking with tavern licenses and election rules. Georgia's leaders banned strong liquor for seven years, from 1735 to 1742. Traders kept selling rum to Native nations, and a Yamacraw leader asked Georgia's founders to stop it. Nobody counted how much colonists drank in these years. The first estimates come from the 1770s.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rum, molasses and tobacco" -->
- Colonial distillers made rum from molasses shipped in from the sugar plantations of the Caribbean. Enslaved Africans did the work on those plantations. Some molasses came in legally and some was smuggled (Ed Crews, *Colonial Williamsburg Journal*, 2007).
- 1740, Philadelphia: a gallon of colonial rum cost 1 shilling 8 pence, and a gallon of better Caribbean rum cost 2 shillings 5 pence.
- 1733: members of the British Parliament passed the Molasses Act, a tax of sixpence a gallon on molasses from the French islands. Large sugar planters in the British islands had pushed for it. Colonial merchants smuggled French molasses anyway. The tax should have brought in 25,000 pounds a year, and British officials collected 259 pounds in 1735 (Mount Vernon, "Rum").
- Slave traders used rum to buy people. Distillers made extra-strong rum for it, so ships could carry more. Captains added water when they reached Africa and traded the rum for captive people (Crews).
- Virginia's planters grew 29 million pounds of tobacco in 1709, the colony's largest crop ever. By 1700 enslaved Africans outnumbered white servants on the tobacco farms (Encyclopedia Virginia).
- Shared with: `economy` (the Molasses Act and the trade) · `slavery-freedom` (the people bought with rum) · `food-farming` (tobacco as a crop). This chapter's slice is the rum and the smoking.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The tavern as the town's meeting place" -->
- In Boston, Francis Holmes kept the Bunch of Grapes from 1712. One traveller called it the best punch house in the town. On 30 July 1733 Henry Price, a Boston tailor, organized a grand lodge of Freemasons there (Samuel Adams Drake, *Old Boston Taverns*, 1886).
- Luke Vardy kept the Royal Exchange tavern. After the town-house burned in the winter of 1747, the members of the colony's legislature finished their meetings at Vardy's.
- In July 1728 two young men quarrelled at Vardy's over cards or wine. They fought with swords on the Common, and one of them killed the other, a man named Woodbridge. Friends put the killer on a ship that sailed at once. Drake does not give the killer's name.
- In 1745, during a war with France, posted notices told sailors to sign on for a raiding ship at the Widow Gray's Crown Tavern. Women kept several Boston taverns, often after a husband died.
- Shared with: `government-politics` (the legislature). This chapter's slice is the drinking place.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Drinks for voters" -->
- In Virginia, only white men who owned land could vote, and each one said his choice out loud in front of the crowd. Voters expected the men running for office to give them liquor and food (Encyclopedia Virginia, "Elections in Colonial Virginia").
- A Virginia law of 1705 limited this. Candidates could give drinks before the sheriff read out the notice of an election and after the voting. The weeks between were meant to be "dry." Some candidates got around the rule by having a friend, a servant or a wife hand out the drinks.
- Shared with: `government-politics` (who could vote). This chapter's slice is the liquor.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Georgia bans rum, 1735 to 1742" -->
- In February 1733 James Oglethorpe's colonists settled on Yamacraw Bluff, now Savannah. Tomochichi, the leader of a Yamacraw town of about 200 Creek and Yamasee people, gave them the land.
- Tomochichi saw more of his people drinking. In 1734 he asked Oglethorpe and the Trustees, the board of men in London who ran Georgia, to ban the sale of rum (Georgia Encyclopedia).
- The Trustees banned rum and brandy in 1735, and King George II and his council approved the law. The law stated that these liquors were "hurtful and pernicious to Man's Body." The Trustees named an officer to enforce it and set fines that grew with each offense. Taverns could sell beer and wine with a license.
- Colonists protested. Merchants said they needed rum to trade for timber and other goods with the British islands in the Caribbean. On 29 September 1742 the Trustees ended the ban. Oglethorpe disagreed with that decision.
- South Carolina traders kept carrying rum up the Savannah River into Native towns while the ban lasted (Wikipedia, "Trustee Georgia").
- Shared with: `native-nations` (Tomochichi and the Creek) · `government-politics` (the Trustees' rule). This chapter's slice is the ban and why it failed.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="alexander-hamilton-physician-drugs-alcohol" name="Dr. Alexander Hamilton" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Dr. Alexander Hamilton
> **Who:** a Scottish-born doctor from Annapolis, Maryland, who kept a diary of the taverns and drinking clubs he saw on a long ride north (not the Alexander Hamilton of the Treasury). · **When and where:** Maryland to York, Maine, and back, 30 May to 27 September 1744.
- Born near Edinburgh in 1712, he came to Maryland in 1738 and worked as a doctor in Annapolis. He was sick in 1743 and rode 1,624 miles to get well (Albert Bushnell Hart, editor of his diary, 1907).
- 31 May 1744, at Tradaway's inn in Maryland: he found "a drunken Club" leaving, the men sitting crooked on their horses.
- 5 June 1744, at an inn near Philadelphia: the landlady did all the work because the landlord was drunk. Hamilton wrote that the liquor had taken away "the use of his tongue," and the man sat without moving in a corner, smoking his pipe.
- 15 June 1744, in New York, he ate with the Hungarian Club at Todd's tavern. The men drank "bumpers," glasses filled to the brim and drunk off at once, at each round. Hamilton drank only three and went home at ten "pretty well flushed." He wrote that some members were "very fond of making a stranger drunk."
- In Boston he drank punch and smoked tobacco with a club of doctors at the Sun Tavern. In 1745 he started his own club in Annapolis, the Tuesday Club. He died on 11 May 1756.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="alexander-hamilton-physician-drugs-alcohol" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="drugs-alcohol" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
By 1770 colonial distillers made about 4.8 million gallons of rum a year, and ship captains carried rum to Africa to buy captive people. After the Revolution, Americans switched from rum to whiskey made from their own corn and rye. In 1791 members of Congress voted a tax on whiskey. In 1794 armed men in western Pennsylvania burned a tax inspector's house, and President George Washington sent nearly 13,000 militiamen against them. In 1785 the Philadelphia doctor Benjamin Rush argued that heavy drinking was a disease. Native leaders asked colonists to stop the liquor trade, and in 1799 the Seneca prophet Handsome Lake stopped drinking and preached against it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="How much people drank" -->
- Nobody measured drinking before the 1770s. One historian estimates that a grown man in the 1770s drank up to three pints of rum a week (Ed Crews, *Colonial Williamsburg Journal*, 2007). Another estimate gives 3.7 gallons of rum a year for each colonist by the time of the Revolution (Mount Vernon, "Rum").
- In 1790, by government figures, the average American over 15 drank 34 gallons of beer and cider, 5 gallons of liquor and 1 gallon of wine in a year (Crews).
- In 2023 Americans aged 14 and older drank an average of 2.48 gallons of pure alcohol each, from all drinks together. That is about 529 drinks a year (National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, Surveillance Report #122).
- People believed alcohol was good for the body. They took whiskey for stomach pain and hot brandy punch for cholera. Women in labor were given a drink of liquor for the pain (Crews).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rum and the slave trade" -->
- By 1764 Rhode Island had about 30 rum distilleries, 22 of them in Newport. Rhode Island merchants traded the rum on the coast of West Africa for captive people. Rhode Islanders made at least 1,000 slaving voyages and carried more than 100,000 Africans into slavery in the century before 1807 (Brown University, *Slavery and Justice*, 2006).
- In 1764 the Brown brothers of Providence sent the ship *Sally* to Africa with 17,274 gallons of rum to trade. Captain Esek Hopkins bought 196 people, and at least 109 of them died.
- In 1764 members of the British Parliament cut the tax on foreign molasses to threepence a gallon in the Sugar Act. Under the act, the navy kept half of any smuggled goods its ships seized (Mount Vernon, "Rum").
- During the Revolution, British warships made molasses hard to get. Scotch-Irish farmers in Pennsylvania, Maryland, western Virginia and western North Carolina made whiskey from rye and corn instead. Before 1800 Kentucky distillers were shipping barrels of whiskey down the rivers to New Orleans (Crews).
- Shared with: `economy` (the *Sally* and the trade, lead) · `slavery-freedom` (the captives). This chapter's slice is the rum.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="George Washington's rum and whiskey" -->
- In 1758 George Washington ran for the Virginia House of Burgesses in Frederick County. He gave voters 28 gallons of rum, 50 gallons of rum punch and 82 gallons of wine, beer and cider, and he won (Mount Vernon, "Rum").
- In June 1779, as commander of the Continental Army, he asked the army's supply officer for "a pretty good stock of rum" for soldiers on work duty. Like many people then, he believed liquor kept tired men awake.
- At Mount Vernon he gave the people he enslaved a ration of liquor for a day's work. He accused his overseer, James Butler, of handing out 36 pints of rum. Butler said he had given "no more than a pint of rum & a pound of Meat to each man."
- In 1797 his farm manager, James Anderson, talked him into building a whiskey distillery. It made 600 gallons that year and almost 11,000 gallons in 1799, one of the largest outputs in the country. John Anderson ran it with an assistant and six enslaved men: Hanson, Peter, Nat, Daniel, James and Timothy (Mount Vernon, "Ten Facts About the Distillery"). Washington died in December 1799.
- Shared with: `slavery-freedom` (the enslaved workers) · `government-politics` (elections). This chapter's slice is the drink.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Native leaders against the liquor trade" -->
- In 1754 Hagler, a leader of the Catawba in the Carolina piedmont, told North Carolina officials, "You Rot Your grain in Tubs, out of which you take and make Strong Spirits." He and other Native leaders asked the colonists to stop the liquor trade, which brought violence to their towns (historian Peter C. Mancall).
- In 1764 Sir William Johnson, the British official in charge of Indian affairs in the northern colonies, wrote to his superiors that "the Trade will never be so extensive" without rum. He wanted the rum trade to go on.
- After the Revolution, traders carried liquor farther west. They added water to it so they had more to sell.
- In 1779 U.S. troops burned Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) villages in New York, and after the war the Haudenosaunee lost most of their land in New York and Pennsylvania. Many drank heavily, including the Seneca leader Handsome Lake. In 1799, sick from years of drinking, he had visions and stopped drinking. He then preached against drunkenness. His teaching became the Longhouse Religion, which Haudenosaunee people still practice (Wikipedia, "Handsome Lake").
- Shared with: `native-nations` (the land and the war) · `religion` (the Longhouse Religion). This chapter's slice is the fight against liquor.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-rush-drugs-alcohol" name="Benjamin Rush" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin Rush
> **Who:** a Philadelphia doctor who signed the Declaration of Independence and wrote that heavy drinking was a disease. · **When and where:** Philadelphia, 1785 to 1790.
- Before Rush, most Americans thought a drunk person simply lacked the will to stop (Crews).
- In 1785 he published *An Inquiry into the Effects of Ardent Spirits Upon the Human Body and Mind*. Ardent spirits meant strong liquor such as rum, gin and whiskey. Some sources date the first printing to 1784.
- He wrote that drinking starts as a free choice and becomes a need: "From habit it takes place from necessity." He said the only cure was to stop drinking completely. His advice was "Taste not, handle not."
- A 1790 edition added a chart he called "A Moral and Physical Thermometer." Water and milk were at the top. Punch led down to "idleness, sickness and debt." Gin, brandy and rum drunk every day led to "murder, madness" and the gallows (Smithsonian, 2015).
- Few people changed their habits at the time. The historian Mark Lender says that today's idea of addiction "can generally be traced back to Benjamin Rush."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-rush-drugs-alcohol" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Whiskey as money, and the Whiskey Rebellion" -->
- The farmers of western Pennsylvania worked land that the Shawnee, Delaware and Mingo had used until Six Nations leaders signed it over to Britain in 1768.
