She married a Pentecostal minister, Robert Semple, and went with him as a missionary to China, where he died. Her first child was born a month later. She married again, to Harold McPherson, and lived in Providence, Rhode Island. In 1916 she left and went preaching across the country.

In 1918 she settled in Los Angeles. By 1923 her preaching had paid for the Angelus Temple on Glendale Boulevard, a church with an auditorium that seats 5,300 people. She put radio towers on the roof and preached to people at home. She used theatre to hold a crowd. Once she rode a motorcycle onto the stage dressed as a policewoman and preached on the subject "Stop! You are breaking God's law!" In 1926 she opened a Bible college; by 1944 it had trained more than three thousand ministers and missionaries.

Her congregation kept a store of food at the Temple, brought in an item at a time. During the Great Depression the Temple gave out more than a million and a half meals.

She held separate meetings for Black people in Florida, because, as she put it, "the dear colored people did not feel free to attend the white meetings." In Oakland, California, she preached to the Ku Klux Klan.

On 18 May 1926 she walked into the sea at Ocean Park, near Santa Monica, and did not come out. Police, lifeguards, lifeboats, motorboats and an aeroplane searched for her, and within two days her friends had given up hope she was alive. Five weeks later, on 23 June, she came out of the desert near Douglas, Arizona, and was carried into a hospital. She said two men and a woman had taken her at the beach and held her in Mexico for half a million dollars in ransom. Posses searched Sonora for the shack she described and found nothing. California charged her over the story, and on 10 January 1927 the district attorney dropped the case. Nobody ever established what happened in those five weeks.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="aimee-semple-mcpherson" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the government was still punishing Native worship" -->
The 1883 rules that made the Sun Dance an offence, and took away a family's food as the penalty, were still being enforced in the 1920s. Agents also found other ways to punish people for worshipping.

At the Kiowa Agency in Oklahoma, Superintendent C. V. Stinchecum held back people's own trust money until they signed a paper promising not to dance. In the autumn of 1916 he withheld payments from about ninety people, and in January 1917 he sent Washington a list of 109 names. Humming Bird, Kiowa Bill, Henry Poolaw, George Mopope, White Horse, Silver Horn, Max Frizzlehead and Kiowa Jim Tongkeamha were among them. In 1921, after a Fourth of July dance where eleven horses were given away, he cited nine Kiowa men for "the reckless giving away of property" and held their money too. By November only three had signed.

Washington backed the agents up. On 26 April 1921 the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, Charles Burke, sent out Circular 1665, which let any superintendent shut down a dance he judged immoral. Burke followed it with a supplement in February 1923 and a message to all Indians the same month.

It changed in 1933, when John Collier became Commissioner. Collier sent every agency a circular titled "Indian Religious Freedom and Indian Culture." It said that "no interference with Indian religious life or ceremonial expression will hereafter be tolerated." That was the first time the federal government had ever written down that Native religion was to be protected. It did not settle it. The 1883 rules stayed legally enforceable until 1978, and a 1940 wildlife law made holding an eagle feather a federal crime.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="nicholas-black-elk" name="Nicholas Black Elk" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Nicholas Black Elk
> **Who:** An Oglala Lakota holy man who was also a Catholic catechist, a teacher of the faith.
> **When and where:** Born December 1863 on the Little Powder River; Pine Ridge, South Dakota; died August 1950.

In his ninth year he had a vision. He met a council of six grandfathers who stood for the four directions and for the earth and the sky, and they gave him the power to heal and a pipe of red pipestone.

He was twelve at the Battle of the Little Bighorn on 25 June 1876. He took his first scalp there, and he gathered guns, ammunition and clothing from dead and dying soldiers.

In 1886 he joined Buffalo Bill's Wild West and performed at Madison Square Garden. The next year the show sailed to England for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee. He got separated from it, travelled around Europe on his own, found Buffalo Bill again and came home.

He was back at Pine Ridge in 1889 and danced the Ghost Dance. In December 1890 he heard cannon and rifle fire from Wounded Knee, rode towards it, helped the survivors and wept for the dead.

His wife Katie War Bonnet died in 1903. In 1904 he was baptised a Catholic and took the name Nicholas. For the rest of his life he worked as a catechist, teaching the Catholic faith and preparing people for baptism, and he remained a holy man among the Lakota. He did not treat the two as a choice.

In 1930 the poet John Neihardt interviewed him, and the book *Black Elk Speaks* came out in 1932. He died in August 1950. Near the end he told his daughter Lucy, "The only thing I really believe is the pipe religion." In 2017 the Catholic diocese of Rapid City asked Rome to make him a saint.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="nicholas-black-elk" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="religion" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
For fifty years about seven Americans in ten told pollsters they belonged to a church, a synagogue or a mosque, and the figure barely moved. Congress put God into the Pledge of Allegiance and made "In God we trust" the national motto. Black congregations in the South housed the civil rights movement, and men bombed their buildings and killed their members for it. Families went to court over what a public school day should contain, and the rulings went both ways. In 1978 Congress passed a law saying that Native Americans were allowed to practise their own religions, which had not been safely true for ninety-five years.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="God in the country's official words" -->
On 14 June 1954 Congress amended the Pledge of Allegiance to the flag. Two words went in, and the pledge became "one Nation under God, indivisible, with liberty and justice for all." On 30 July 1956 Congress passed another joint resolution, three lines long: "That the national motto of the United States is hereby declared to be 'In God we trust.'" The words had been on coins since 1864, which `money` tells. They became the country's official motto in 1956.

The polling company Gallup has asked Americans since 1937 whether they belong to a church, synagogue or mosque. In 1937, 73 per cent said they did. The number stayed near 70 per cent for the next sixty years and was still 70 per cent in 1999. Gallup is a polling company and not a government count, and it asks people what they say they are.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Billy Graham and the crusades" -->
Billy Graham was born in Charlotte, North Carolina in 1918 on a dairy farm, was ordained by the Southern Baptists in 1939, and worked for Youth for Christ from 1944 to 1948 speaking at rallies. In 1949 he held a campaign in Los Angeles that was booked for three weeks and ran for seven. After that he built an organisation around the work: the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, a film company, a weekly radio programme called *Hour of Decision*, and a daily newspaper column. His New York crusade in 1957 ran every night for sixteen weeks in Madison Square Garden.

On 18 July 1957 the man who gave the opening prayer at that crusade was Martin Luther King Jr. Graham had telephoned him, and the evangelist Leighton Ford sent the invitation by telegram on 5 July. King asked in the prayer for help "for a warless world and for a brotherhood that transcends race or color," and then led eighteen thousand people in the Lord's Prayer. Six weeks later King wrote to Graham: "You have courageously brought the Christian gospel to bear on the question of race." The next summer he wrote again to object, because Graham had shared a platform with the governor of Texas, and King called that an "endorsement of racial segregation and discrimination."
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a church that was bombed three times" -->
In June 1956 an Alabama court banned the NAACP from operating anywhere in the state. Ministers in Birmingham answered by founding something a court could not ban. About a thousand people met at Sardis Baptist Church on 5 June 1956 and started the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights. Fred Shuttlesworth, who had been pastor of Bethel Baptist Church since March 1953, said officials could outlaw an organisation but not a movement, and that putting "Christian" in the name gave it a foundation and set it apart from the groups being called Communist. Bethel Baptist Church was the movement's headquarters from 1956 to 1961. Its meetings were on Monday nights, and the National Park Service describes them as "emotional testimony, soul-lifting music, impassioned preaching, and fundraising." By 1958 those weekly meetings were also being held in 55 other working-class churches around the city.

The church was bombed three times. On Christmas night 1956 twelve sticks of dynamite went off in the gap between the church and the parsonage, destroying the parsonage. Shuttlesworth was inside talking to a deacon, his family was watching television, and he came out with a head injury. The bomb was set the night before the movement had said it would ride the segregated buses. Two hundred and fifty people rode them the next day and twenty-two were arrested. A second bomb came on 29 June 1958 and a third in 1962. The 1958 bombing was not solved until 1980, when J. B. Stoner was convicted of it.

After the first bomb the congregation began guarding its own church. `rights-movements` tells the Birmingham campaign, the children's march and the bombing of the 16th Street Baptist Church.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the law that said Native religion was allowed" -->
Congress passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act on 11 August 1978. Its findings say what the country had been doing. "The lack of a clear, comprehensive, and consistent Federal policy has often resulted in the abridgment of religious freedom for traditional American Indians." Such laws "often deny American Indians access to sacred sites required in their religions, including cemeteries," and "at times prohibit the use and possession of sacred objects necessary to the exercise of religious rites and ceremonies." And: "traditional American Indian ceremonies have been intruded upon, interfered with, and in a few instances banned." In the same resolution the members of Congress declared it the policy of the United States to protect "their inherent right of freedom to believe, express, and exercise the traditional religions of the American Indian, Eskimo, Aleut, and Native Hawaiians." That is ninety-five years after the 1883 rules that made the Sun Dance a punishable offence, which this chapter tells in 1850 to 1900.

It was a statement of policy, and it did not decide cases. In 1990, in *Employment Division v. Smith*, the Supreme Court held that Oregon could refuse unemployment pay to two men fired for taking peyote at a ceremony of their Native American Church. Congress answered on 6 October 1994 with an amendment to the 1978 Act. The members wrote into it that 28 states protected the ceremony and 22 did not, and they made the use of peyote by an Indian for traditional ceremonial purposes lawful everywhere in the country. `native-nations` tells what the long ban did to the nations themselves.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="whose Bible was it" -->
For most of American history a public school day opened with a prayer or a Bible reading. In 1962 the Supreme Court stopped official school prayer, in *Engel v. Vitale*. In 1963 it stopped official Bible reading, in *Abington School District v. Schempp*. `education` tells what changed in the school day and `government-politics` tells the rulings as law. The question underneath both was whose religion the school day belonged to.

The parents who brought the 1962 case were not one faith. Ten children's parents sued. The New York court had already found that the school prayer did not fit the beliefs of Jews, Unitarians or the Ethical Culture society, and one of the parents was an agnostic.

The family who brought the 1963 case went to church every week. Edward and Sidney Schempp and their children Roger, Donna and Ellory belonged to the Unitarian church in Germantown, Philadelphia. Pennsylvania law made every school read ten Bible verses each morning, and a child could be excused if a parent wrote in. Edward Schempp would not ask. He testified that teachers and classmates would call his children "odd balls" every day of the school year. He said other children lumped every religious difference together as atheism, and in 1962 atheism meant communist and un-American. He also said that a child excused from the reading had to stand in the corridor outside the homeroom, which looked like a punishment for bad behaviour.

Two scholars testified about the book itself. Solomon Grayzel explained that the Jewish scriptures have no New Testament, that from a Jewish point of view calling Jesus the son of God is close to blasphemy, and that reading those passages to children without explanation had done them harm. Luther Weigle, testifying for the school district, said the Bible was non-sectarian, meaning it belonged to no one denomination. Asked again, he said he meant non-sectarian among Christians.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the day after, and the years after" -->
A congressman filed a constitutional amendment to undo the prayer ruling the day after it came down, and others were being drafted. Representative Taylor of North Carolina was first. The newspapers noted that Billy Graham was one of his constituents. Senator Beall of Maryland had one ready for the Senate. Representative Chelf of Kentucky said that if he could not get an amendment he would try to stop Supreme Court justices serving for life. None of the amendments passed.

Schools worked out other things to do. Some had already been settled. In 1948, in a case brought by a mother named Vashti McCollum, the Court stopped religious teachers coming into public school buildings in Champaign, Illinois, to teach religion for half an hour a week. In 1952 it allowed the opposite arrangement in New York City, where children left the building and went to a church or synagogue for the lesson. The line was physical: religion class inside the school was out, children released to go elsewhere was in.

After 1963 came the moment of silence. Alabama passed a law in 1978 for one minute of silence for meditation. In 1981 it added the words "or voluntary prayer," and in 1982 it let teachers lead willing pupils in a prayer. In 1985 the Court struck down the 1981 law because its purpose was to promote religion, and left the plain silence alone.

In 1992 the Court stopped a school inviting clergy to pray at graduation. Rabbi Leslie Gutterman of Temple Beth El had prayed at Deborah Weisman's middle school graduation in Providence, Rhode Island. The principal had handed him a pamphlet telling him to keep it non-sectarian, and the Court said that made the prayer the school's.

One thing the 1963 ruling did not touch, and said so plainly: teaching *about* religion. Justice Clark wrote that a person's education is not complete without studying the history of religion, and that the Bible is worth studying for its literature and its history, as long as it is taught as a subject and not as a service.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="objecting to the curriculum" -->
Arkansas had made it a crime to teach that people descended from animals, and the law was still there in 1965. That autumn the Little Rock schools handed their biology teachers a new textbook with a chapter on Darwin's theory in it. Susan Epperson, who taught tenth-grade biology at Central High School, sued instead of choosing between the book and the law, and a parent named H. H. Blanchard joined her. On 12 November 1968, in *Epperson v. Arkansas*, the Supreme Court struck the law down and said what it had been for: "fundamentalist sectarian conviction was and is the law's reason for existence." The same ruling said the First Amendment requires neutrality "between religion and religion, and between religion and nonreligion." No justice voted to keep the law, and they did not agree on the reasoning. Justice Black wrote separately that he could not be sure what the voters of 1928 had been thinking.

Louisiana's legislators tried another way. Their law said a school that taught evolution had to teach creation science as well, and a school that taught creation science had to teach evolution as well. The people who sued to stop it were Louisiana parents, Louisiana teachers and religious leaders. Religious organisations filed briefs on both sides: the Catholic League for Religious and Civil Rights and the Christian Legal Society asked the Court to keep the law, the New York Committee for Public Education and Religious Liberty asked it to strike the law down, and separate briefs came from the Rabbinical Alliance of America and from a group headed by the Reverend Bill McLean. On 19 June 1987, by seven votes to two, the Court struck it down in *Edwards v. Aguillard*, holding that "the preeminent purpose of the Louisiana Legislature was clearly to advance the religious viewpoint that a supernatural being created humankind."

The largest fight over books was not in a court. In April 1974 the school board of Kanawha County, West Virginia, which had 46,000 pupils in 124 schools, voted to adopt 325 language-arts textbooks. A board member named Alice Moore, the wife of a minister, said some of them were against religion and against the country. Twenty-seven ministers condemned the books and petitions came in with 12,000 signatures, and in June the board voted three to two to buy most of them anyway. Another minister, Jim Lewis of Charleston, was the books' loudest defender, so there were clergy on both sides in one county. When school opened on 3 September attendance dropped by a fifth, 3,500 coal miners walked out in sympathy with the boycott, and people fired guns, threw firebombs and set off dynamite at schools. Eleven people were arrested and the schools closed for four days from 12 September. The protests ran on into 1977 and drew in the John Birch Society and the Ku Klux Klan, and the Reverend Marvin Horan was tried for plotting to bomb schools. The records of the protest give no count of the injured.

Some families objected to the school itself. In *Wisconsin v. Yoder*, decided 15 May 1972, Old Order Amish and Conservative Amish Mennonite fathers were convicted of keeping their children out of school after the eighth grade, and the Supreme Court ruled that Wisconsin could not make them send them. The belief underneath it was one line from Paul's letter to the Romans, "be not conformed to this world," which the Amish take as a rule for daily life. They did not object to the first eight grades, because a child needs to read the Bible, farm and deal with people outside the community. They objected to the high school as the world. `education` tells what changed in the school day and `government-politics` tells all of these rulings as law. Religious families were also one of the two roots of modern homeschooling, with `home-family` leading on the household side.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="billy-graham" name="Billy Graham" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Billy Graham
> **Who:** A Southern Baptist preacher who held large public meetings, which he called crusades, from 1949 to 2005 · **When and where:** Born Charlotte, North Carolina, 7 November 1918 · died Montreat, North Carolina, 21 February 2018

He grew up on a dairy farm outside Charlotte and decided in 1934, after hearing a travelling preacher there, to give his life to God. He was ordained by the Southern Baptists in 1939, took a theology degree at the Florida Bible Institute in 1940 and a degree at Wheaton College in Illinois in 1943, and married Ruth Bell that August.

From 1944 to 1948 he travelled the country speaking at rallies for Youth for Christ. Then, in 1949, he preached a campaign in Los Angeles that had been booked for three weeks and ran for seven. He built an organisation around the work and kept building it: the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association, a film company, a radio programme, a newspaper column. In 1954 he preached in London for twelve weeks. In 1957 he preached in Madison Square Garden in New York every night for sixteen weeks.

On 18 July 1957 he had Martin Luther King Jr. give the opening prayer at that crusade. King asked for "a warless world and for a brotherhood that transcends race or color" and led eighteen thousand people in the Lord's Prayer. On 31 August King wrote to him, "You have courageously brought the Christian gospel to bear on the question of race." The following July King wrote again to object that Graham had appeared on a platform with the governor of Texas, which King called an "endorsement of racial segregation and discrimination." Graham held integrated crusades in Birmingham, Alabama at Easter 1964.

In 1996 Congress voted Billy and Ruth Graham a gold medal, and it was handed to them in the Capitol Rotunda on 2 May. The law's findings claim his crusades had reached a hundred million people in person and two billion on television. He stepped back from his association in 2000, preached a last crusade in Queens, New York in 2005, and died at ninety-nine. On 28 February 2018 his body lay in honour in the Rotunda of the Capitol, only the fourth private citizen to be given that.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="billy-graham" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="revis-family-bethel" name="The Revis family of Bethel Baptist Church" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### The Revis family of Bethel Baptist Church
> **Who:** A church deacon and his two daughters, whose front porch became the guard post for a congregation that kept being bombed · **When and where:** Collegeville, Birmingham, Alabama, 1956 to the early 1960s

James Revis was a deacon of Bethel Baptist Church and sat on the executive committee of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights. His house stood across the street from the church.

After the bomb of Christmas night 1956 destroyed the pastor's house, members of the church and the movement volunteered to watch the buildings. In 1957 the Revis family closed in their own front porch to make a room for the guards to sit in. His daughter Robbie Revis Smith described it: "with our house sitting on the corner, it gave a very good view several ways that they could see because they had the glass out there and they put a little gas heater out there so they wouldn't be too cold sitting up. They did this year round." Her sister Laverne Revis Martin said their parents made the room "just so the guards would be able to watch."

The volunteers called themselves the Civil Rights Guards. They worked in two shifts, six in the evening to midnight and midnight to six in the morning, and they were armed. Women of the movement took a weekly shift too, among them a florist named Desta Brooks and a schoolteacher named Minnie Eaton.

At about half past one in the morning on Sunday 29 June 1958, Laverne was coming home from work when she saw a bomb smoking beside the church. She told the guards. They carried it into the street, where it went off, blew a hole in the road and broke the church windows without bringing the building down.

Robbie Revis Smith, on what the porch meant to the neighbourhood: "So it was kind of a good feeling coming home because you never came home without a person out there watching you, so you didn't have to worry about that."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="revis-family-bethel" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="jonas-and-frieda-yoder" name="Jonas and Frieda Yoder" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Jonas and Frieda Yoder
> **Who:** An Old Order Amish father who would not send his daughter to high school, and the daughter, who said in court that the decision was her own religion too · **When and where:** Green County, Wisconsin, 1968 to 1972

Wisconsin required every child to be in school until sixteen. Frieda Yoder was fifteen and had finished the eighth grade of the public school, and her father Jonas did not send her on to the high school.

The reason was one line of scripture. Amish belief takes Paul's instruction in his letter to the Romans, "be not conformed to this world," as a rule for ordinary life, and treats the high school as the world. The Amish did not object to the first eight grades. A child needed to read the Bible, farm, and deal with people outside the community.

Jonas Yoder was charged, tried and convicted along with Wallace Miller and Adin Yutzy in the Green County Court. The Supreme Court decided for the three fathers on 15 May 1972.

Frieda was the only child in the case who was called to give evidence. She testified that her own religious beliefs were why she had stopped going to school after the eighth grade. Justice William O. Douglas agreed with the ruling as it applied to her father and disagreed as it applied to the other two men, because nobody had asked Barbara Miller or Vernon Yutzy what they believed. He wrote that the Court had never squarely faced the question of whose religion decides a child's schooling, the parents' or the child's.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="jonas-and-frieda-yoder" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="religion" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Fewer Americans belong to a congregation than at any time since anyone started counting, and the group that has grown fastest is people who say they have no religion at all. The religions practised here are more varied than they have ever been. Two arguments this chapter has followed since the 1600s were still running in these years: what a public school day may contain, and whether a person is safe in the building where they worship. A third became public knowledge. Catholic bishops had known for decades that priests were sexually abusing children, and had moved those priests to new parishes instead of reporting them to the police. Every number in this section carries the year it describes and the year it was published, because a number is no use unless you know which year it belongs to. The newest figures here describe 2022 to 2025 and were published between 2023 and 2026.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="how many people say they have no religion" -->
The Pew Research Center is a polling organisation. Between 17 July 2023 and 4 March 2024 it asked 36,908 American adults about their religion, and published the results on 26 February 2025. Sixty-two per cent said they were Christian, against 71 per cent in a comparable study in 2014 and 78 per cent in 2007. Twenty-nine per cent said they had no religion, against 23 per cent in 2014 and 16 per cent in 2007. Those are the people usually called the "nones," which covers atheists, agnostics and people who answer "nothing in particular." Of the rest, 1.7 per cent were Jewish, 1.2 per cent Muslim, 1.1 per cent Buddhist and 0.9 per cent Hindu. Pew's own headline was that the fall in the Christian share had slowed and might have stopped, because it had been roughly steady for four or five years.

Gallup, another polling company, has asked since 1937 whether people belong to a church, synagogue or mosque. Seventy per cent said yes in 1999. Fifty per cent said yes in 2018. Forty-seven per cent said yes in 2020, the first time the answer had been under half. Gallup published that in March 2021. Broken down by age group over 2018 to 2020, 66 per cent of people born before 1946 belonged to a congregation and 36 per cent of people born between 1981 and 1996 did.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="faith and school now" -->
Maine pays the fees for children who live in towns with no secondary school of their own, and since 1981 it had paid only where the school was nonsectarian, meaning it belonged to no religion. David and Amy Carson of Glenburn sent their daughter to Bangor Christian Schools, founded in 1970 by Bangor Baptist Church, and paid the fees themselves. Troy and Angela Nelson of Palermo sent their son to Temple Academy and could not afford to send their daughter there too. In *Carson v. Makin*, decided 21 June 2022 by six votes to three, the Supreme Court held that Maine could not refuse to pay because a school was religious. The two schools' own descriptions of what they do are in the record. Bangor Christian's stated objectives include "lead[ing] each unsaved student to trust Christ as his/her personal savior," and the school says there is no way to separate its religious teaching from its academic teaching. Temple Academy says the Bible is used in every subject it teaches, including mathematics. `government-politics` tells the four rulings that moved public money towards religious schools as law, and `education` tells vouchers and savings accounts as school choice.

Joseph Kennedy coached football at Bremerton High School in Washington State from 2008. After each game, once the players and coaches had shaken hands, he knelt at the halfway line and prayed for about thirty seconds. Players began asking whether they could join him and he told them, "This is a free country. You can do what you want." Most of the team joined him after some games. Nobody complained for more than seven years. In September 2015 the school district told him to stop, and after he prayed following the games of 16, 23 and 26 October it suspended him on full pay and barred him from the football programme. In *Kennedy v. Bremerton School District*, decided 27 June 2022, the Supreme Court ruled for him by six votes to three. The nine justices read the same record and did not describe the same events. Justice Neil Gorsuch, for the majority, wrote that he had "knelt at midfield after games to offer a quiet personal prayer." Justice Sonia Sotomayor, dissenting, wrote that "to the degree the Court portrays petitioner Joseph Kennedy's prayers as private and quiet, it misconstrues the facts," and that he had led student athletes in prayer at the same place for years.

In 1980, in *Stone v. Graham*, the Supreme Court struck down a Kentucky law requiring the Ten Commandments to be posted in every public classroom. In 2024 Louisiana's legislators passed a law requiring the same thing, on a poster or framed document at least eleven inches by fourteen, with the text as the central focus and printed large, and the law sets out the exact wording that must be used. Parents sued, and the case is named for one of them, the Reverend Darcy Roake. The objections in the record are religious objections. A Jewish parent swore that the law "misappropriates a Jewish text, ripping it from its Jewish context," alters its meaning, and then requires the altered text to be shown to non-Jews, "in violation of core Jewish tenets that oppose proselytizing." Another said Louisiana's version leaves out the deliverance of the Jews from slavery in Egypt, which is a key piece of the Jewish story. A Presbyterian minister who is also a parent objected to the state putting its stamp of approval on one particular version. A federal judge stopped the law, a three-judge appeals panel agreed on 20 June 2025, and then on 20 February 2026 the full Fifth Circuit lifted the order. That court said plainly that it was not deciding whether the law is constitutional, only that the question was not ready to be decided, and three judges dissented. As of September 2026 no court has decided whether Louisiana's law is constitutional. Texas passed a similar law, and a rabbi, Mara Nathan, is one of the parents suing over it. On 21 April 2026 the full Fifth Circuit ruled, by nine votes to eight, that the Texas law does not break the First Amendment. In August 2026 the Texas families asked the Supreme Court to hear their case, and as of September 2026 it had not said whether it would. This is the same argument the Schempp family made in 1963, about whose version of a holy book a school hands to children.

The second school system this chapter describes in 1850 to 1900 was staffed by members of religious orders working for very little, and there are far fewer of them now. The Center for Applied Research in the Apostolate at Georgetown University, which draws its figures from the Catholic Church's own directory, counted 178,740 religious sisters in the United States in 1965 and 33,135 as of 1 January 2025. Catholic elementary schools went from 9,366 to 4,606 over the same sixty years, and Catholic secondary schools from 1,986 to 1,178. `education` tells the enrolment figures.

Some families teach their children at home for religious reasons, and the federal government asks them why. In the 2022–23 school year, 53 per cent of parents homeschooling a child aged 5 to 17 said a desire to provide religious instruction was an important reason and 11 per cent said it was the most important one. More of them named a concern about the environment of other schools, at 83 per cent important and 28 per cent most important. Those figures come from the National Center for Education Statistics and were published in September 2024. `education` tells how many children are homeschooled, and `home-family` tells homeschooling as household life.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what priests did to children, and what bishops did about it" -->
Sexual abuse means an adult using a child's body for sex. In 2002 the Catholic bishops of the United States asked John Jay College of Criminal Justice to find out how much of it their own priests had done, and the college published the answer in February 2004, from surveys covering 98 per cent of the country's diocesan priests. It found allegations against 4,392 priests for the years 1950 to 2002 that had not been withdrawn and were not known to be false, about four per cent of all the priests who had served in those years, and 10,667 people who said they had been abused. Half of them were between eleven and fourteen when it happened. Sixteen per cent were between eight and ten, and nearly six per cent were under seven. Eighty-one per cent were boys. The commonest acts recorded were touching over and under the child's clothes, oral sex performed by the priest, and rape or attempted rape, which was alleged in 22.4 per cent of cases. Most of the priests accused had done more than one of these things to the same child. It happened most often in the priest's own house or the parish house, and next most often inside the church.

Only 384 of those 4,392 priests were ever criminally charged. Fifteen per cent were reported to the police by a victim, and the report says a much smaller number were reported by their own diocese. Before 1993 only a third of the cases were known to church officials at all.

In August 2018 a grand jury in Pennsylvania published what it had found in half a million pages of the internal documents of six Catholic dioceses. It counted credible allegations against more than three hundred priests and more than a thousand children it could identify from the church's own records, and said it believed the real number was in the thousands. Its own summary says that most of the victims were boys but there were girls too, and that some were teenagers and many had not yet reached puberty. Some were raped. "But all of them were brushed aside, in every part of the state, by church leaders who preferred to protect the abusers and their institution above all." The grand jury then set out what it called a playbook for concealing the truth, and its first item was language. Never write "rape" in a diocesan document. Write "inappropriate contact" or "boundary issues" instead. Do not let trained investigators ask the questions. When a priest has to be removed, tell his parish he is on sick leave, or say nothing. Keep paying his housing. If people find out, move him somewhere nobody knows. "Finally and above all, don't tell the police." Because of that concealment, the grand jury wrote, almost every case it found was too old to prosecute.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="killed where they were worshipping" -->
On the morning of Sunday 5 August 2012 a white supremacist with a loaded gun walked into the gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship, at Oak Creek, Wisconsin, and killed six people. Paramjit Kaur was sitting for morning prayers. The others were Sita Singh, Ranjit Singh, Prakash Singh, Suvegh Singh Khattra and Satwant Singh Kaleka, the gurdwara's president, who was killed fighting the gunman. Santokh Singh was shot and lived. Punjab Singh was shot too, and in 2022 a resolution of the United States Senate counted him as the seventh person killed.

On Wednesday 17 June 2015 twelve members of Mother Emanuel in Charleston met in the fellowship hall for their weekly Bible study. It is an African Methodist Episcopal church, part of the denomination Richard Allen founded in Philadelphia in 1816, which this chapter tells in 1750 to 1800. A white man of twenty-one named Dylann Roof came in at about 8.16 in the evening. In the appeals court's words: "The parishioners welcomed Roof, handing him a Bible and a study sheet. For the next 45 minutes, Roof worshipped with the parishioners. They stood and shut their eyes for closing prayer. Roof then took out his gun and started shooting." He fired about seventy-four rounds. Nine people were killed: the Reverend Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, Cynthia Hurd, Susie Jackson, Ethel Lee Lance, the Reverend DePayne Middleton-Doctor, the Reverend Clementa Pinckney, Tywanza Sanders, the Reverend Daniel Simmons Sr. and the Reverend Myra Thompson. He had looked up African American churches in Charleston, visited this one first, and learned from a member which night the Bible study met.

On Saturday morning, 27 October 2018, three Jewish congregations were at prayer in one building in Pittsburgh. Twelve Tree of Life members were in the chapel, part-way through the opening prayers. Audrey Glickman had begun the service. David Rosenthal, who could not read but had memorised every prayer and song, was helping her lead it, and his brother Cecil was one of the greeters at the back. In Dor Hadash's room, a doctor, a hospital chaplain and a third member, Martin Gaynor, were setting out prayer books and copies of the Torah. Downstairs, two members of New Light were in the kitchen making a meal for a men's breakfast the next day. A man came in with three handguns and a rifle and killed eleven of them: Jerry Rabinowitz, David Rosenthal, Cecil Rosenthal, Rose Mallinger, Bernice Simon, Sylvan Simon, Joyce Fienberg, Irving Younger, Richard Gottfried, Daniel Stein and Melvin Wax. The youngest was 54 and the oldest was 97. Two more were badly hurt, and five police officers were injured going in after him. Among the federal charges were eleven counts of obstructing the free exercise of religious beliefs resulting in death.

The FBI counts crimes it classes as motivated by hatred. In its report for 2001 it recorded that incidents aimed at Muslims had gone from being nearly the least reported religious category to the second highest, growing by more than 1,600 per cent over 2000, with 481 incidents and 554 victims. Incidents aimed at Jews were still the highest, at more than half of all religious-bias offences that year. In 2012 the FBI did not count crimes against Sikhs at all.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="congregations dividing, and worship on a screen" -->
The United Methodist Church argued for decades about gay members and gay ministers, and in these years it split. A special conference in 2019 wrote a rule letting a congregation leave the denomination and keep its buildings for reasons of conscience over that argument. The rule ran out on 31 December 2023. By then more than 7,600 congregations in the United States had used it, about a quarter of the denomination's American churches. On 1 May 2024, at the General Conference in Charlotte, North Carolina, the delegates who remained voted 692 to 51 to remove the ban on ordaining ministers described in their rule book since 1984 as "self-avowed practicing homosexuals," and removed the ban on holding same-sex weddings as well.

When buildings closed in 2020, services went onto screens, and many stayed there. Pew asked 11,377 adults about it between 16 and 27 November 2022 and published the answers in June 2023. Sixteen per cent were going to services in person only, ten per cent were watching on a screen only, and seventeen per cent were doing both, which comes to 43 per cent doing one or the other at least monthly and 57 per cent doing neither. Of the people doing both, 76 per cent said they would rather be in the room. The commonest reason given for watching on a screen was that it was convenient.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the churches answer for the boarding schools" -->
This chapter's 1850 to 1900 section gives the federal government's own count: 210 of the 417 federal Indian boarding schools were run by a religious institution. In these years some of those churches said so out loud. On 25 July 2022, in Canada, Pope Francis asked forgiveness "for the ways in which many members of the Church and of religious communities cooperated, not least through their indifference, in projects of cultural destruction and forced assimilation." On 30 March 2023 the Vatican renounced the Doctrine of Discovery, the old teaching used to justify taking land from people who were not Christian. On 14 June 2024 the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops voted 181 to 2 to adopt a document called "Keeping Christ's Sacred Promise," a formal apology for the Catholic Church's part in the schools in this country. The Interior Department, in the report that produced the count, notes that it is unaware of any support by the bishops' conference for a papal apology covering the United States. `native-nations` tells what the schools did to the nations.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="joseph-kennedy-bremerton" name="Joseph Kennedy" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Joseph Kennedy
> **Who:** A high-school football coach who lost his job over a prayer at the halfway line, and won his case in the Supreme Court · **When and where:** Bremerton, Washington, 2008 to 2022

He had spent nearly twenty years in the Marine Corps before he began coaching football at Bremerton High School in 2008. At the end of each game, once the players and coaches had shaken hands, he took a knee at the 50-yard line and prayed for about thirty seconds, giving thanks for what the players had done and for being part of their lives.

At first he prayed alone. Then players asked whether they could join him, and he said, "This is a free country. You can do what you want." After some games most of the team knelt with him, and sometimes players from the other team were asked along. He started adding a short talk to the prayer when other people were there. Nobody complained for more than seven years.

The district superintendent found out in September 2015, when an employee of another school praised the practice to Bremerton's principal. On 17 September the district wrote to him. On 16 October it told him not to do anything that a reasonable onlooker could take as the school endorsing prayer while he was on duty. He prayed after the games of 16, 23 and 26 October. On the 16th, most of his players were singing the school fight song. Players from the other team and people from the crowd came and knelt with him before he finished. On the 23rd nobody joined him. On the 26th other adults gathered round him. After that game the district put him on paid leave and barred him from the football programme.

On 27 June 2022 the Supreme Court ruled for him by six votes to three. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote that the First Amendment protects a person's own religious observance from being punished by the government.

The dissent describes a different scene. Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote that the case was about "whether a public school must permit a school official to kneel, bow his head, and say a prayer at the center of a school event," and that the majority "misconstrues the facts" in calling the prayers private and quiet, because the record showed him inviting others and leading student athletes in prayer in the same place for years.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="joseph-kennedy-bremerton" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="harpreet-singh-saini" name="Harpreet Singh Saini" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Harpreet Singh Saini
> **Who:** An eighteen-year-old whose mother was shot dead at morning prayers, and who asked the United States Senate to start counting people like her · **When and where:** Oak Creek, Wisconsin, and Washington, D.C., August and September 2012

His parents brought him and his brother Kamaljit from India to the United States in 2004, when he was ten, so that the boys could get an education.

On Sunday 5 August 2012 a white supremacist carrying a loaded gun walked into their gurdwara at Oak Creek. He killed Harpreet's mother, Paramjit Kaur, while she sat for morning prayers, and five men, all of whom wore turbans.

Two days later the brothers ate the last rotis their mother had made. She had made them from scratch the night before she died. Harpreet said that with the last bite came the understanding that it was the last food made by her hands they would ever eat.

He had just started his first day of college, and she was not there to see him off.

On 19 September 2012, forty-five days after she was killed, he gave evidence to a subcommittee of the United States Senate. He said: "I want to tell the gunman who took her from me: You may have been full of hate, but my mother was full of love."

He told the senators what his mother's faith required of her. "Like all Sikhs, she was bound to live in Chardi Kala," which he described as "a state of high spirits and optimism." "She was also taught as a Sikh to neither have fear of anyone nor strike fear in anyone."

Then he asked them for one thing. "I came here today to ask the government to give my mother the dignity of being a statistic. The FBI does not track hate crimes against Sikhs. My mother and those shot that day will not even count on a federal form. We cannot solve a problem we refuse to recognize."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="harpreet-singh-saini" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

# Chapter 30: School and Education

<!-- hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="education" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Children learned by watching, doing, and listening. Teaching was a family and community job, not a building. There were no schoolhouses, no grades, no set school year, and no teachers who did only that.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Learning by watching and doing" -->
Stories carried law, history, and geography. Children learned skills by working beside the people who had them, and learning followed the seasons and the work that had to be done.

Nobody north of Mexico wrote anything down, because no writing system was in use there yet. The first one made for a language spoken in this land was the Cherokee syllabary, and that was in 1821, more than three hundred years after 1500. So everything a people needed to keep had to be kept in memory, and people were trained to keep it.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Memory as the storage system: wampum" -->
The Haudenosaunee, five nations in what is now upstate New York, recorded agreements and law in wampum, belts and strings of shell beads. The Onondaga Nation, which still keeps the belts, describes how it works: the speaker puts the words of the agreement into the wampum as the belt is woven, and every speaker after that uses the belt to remember the agreement and what has happened since. The Onondaga call the belts their living history.

A person had to be taught to read a belt and recite what was in it. That was the training, and it was as exact a job as any schoolteacher's.

When the Great Law of Peace that founded the confederacy was agreed is not settled. Haudenosaunee tradition places it between about 1000 and 1400. Scholars working from written records have usually said about 1450. Some argue for the late 1100s. Nobody can prove which is right.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="No names survive" -->
No pupil or teacher in this land before 1500 is known by name, because nobody here kept written records.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="education" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
No schoolhouses stood in this land yet. The only European teaching was religious instruction attached to Spanish missions, and its purpose was to make Catholics, not readers. Native teaching went on as it had.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Mission teaching in Florida" -->
Spanish priests began trying to convert Native people in Florida within a few years of 1565, when Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine. By the 1580s Franciscan friars had missions across Florida. One of the largest, San Juan del Puerto on Fort George Island, was set up sometime in the 1570s. The Park Service can only date it to the decade.

What the friars taught at a mission was Catholic doctrine, European customs, farming, and reading and writing, in Spanish and in Timucua, the local language.

The claim that it worked comes from the man doing the teaching. Father Francisco Pareja wrote that many Timucua men and women had learned to read in less than six months and were writing letters to each other in their own language. That is a friar's report of his own success.

Pareja also wrote the language down in three catechisms, a confession book, and a grammar. Those books were printed in the next century, and they are now the only record of the Timucua language there is. Nobody speaks it. Most Timucua people died of diseases the Spanish brought or were taken in slave raids from Carolina, and Spanish officials shipped the last of them to Cuba in 1763.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="New Mexico, at the very end of the era" -->
Juan de Oñate's expedition reached the upper Rio Grande in 1598. Franciscan missions and their teaching in New Mexico start from that year, with two years of the century left.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="paquiquineo-don-luis" name="Paquiquineo (Don Luís de Velasco)" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Paquiquineo (Don Luís de Velasco)
> **Who:** A young man from the Chesapeake, taught by Spanish priests for nine years and returned home as a missionary's guide · **When and where:** 1561 to 1572, the Chesapeake, Spain, Mexico, and back

He was about seventeen when he left North America on a Spanish ship in late June 1561. Historians still argue over whether he went willingly or was taken. The record does not settle it.

He reached Seville on September 9, 1561, was in Madrid by the end of October, and met King Philip II. He sailed from Cádiz in late May 1562 and reached Mexico on August 10. He fell badly ill there and was baptized in Mexico City that year while, in the words of the record, on the brink of death. He took the name of the viceroy of New Spain: Don Luís de Velasco.

From 1566 to 1570 he studied in Seville with the Jesuits. What he was taught in those four years is not written down anywhere that survives.

In September 1570 he landed on the James River with a party of Jesuits under Father Juan Bautista de Segura, brought along as their guide and interpreter. He went back to his own family instead. On February 4, 1571 he killed three of the priests, then went to the mission and killed Father Segura and the others. One person was left alive: the altar boy, Alonso de Olmos.

In August 1572 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, the Spanish governor of Florida, sent soldiers to the James River. They captured some of Paquiquineo's people in a fight and hanged several of them from the ship's yardarms for the killings. The Powhatan people handed Alonso de Olmos back. Paquiquineo was not found, and no European record mentions him again.

He is the only person in this era whose schooling by Europeans in this land is documented by name. No surviving mission record from the 1500s names an individual pupil.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="paquiquineo-don-luis" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="education" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In New England the men who ran the colony made it a legal duty to teach children to read, and five years later a legal duty for towns to provide a teacher. The reason they wrote into the law was religious: children had to be able to read the Bible for themselves. In the other colonies learning stayed a matter for families and for apprenticeships. Schooling was not free. Under the 1647 law the wages came from the child's parents or from the master a child was bound to.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The two Massachusetts laws" -->
In 1642 the men of the Massachusetts General Court ordered parents and masters to teach their children and apprentices enough to read English and to know the colony's chief laws. They set up no school and hired no teacher. Selectmen came round to check. A household that failed could be fined, and a child or apprentice could be taken away and placed with another master who would do the teaching.

Enough families ignored that law that the same court passed a second one in 1647. People call it the Old Deluder Satan act after its opening line, which says it is one of the chief projects of that old deluder Satan to keep men from the knowledge of the Scriptures. In every town of fifty households the townsmen now had to appoint someone to teach children to read and write, and the parents or masters paid the wages. In every town of a hundred families they had to set up a grammar school to get boys ready for the university, meaning Harvard, founded in 1636. A town that did neither owed five pounds a year to the nearest school. Lawmakers in the other New England colonies passed much the same thing. Rhode Island's did not.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The kinds of school [R7 dame schools and Latin grammar schools]" -->
A small child usually began with a woman teaching in her own kitchen. This was the dame school. She took children of three or four for a few hours a day for a small fee, and she was often paid in eggs, firewood, or a turn at the washing rather than in money. She taught the letters, the catechism, and the Lord's Prayer. A New England town school would not admit a boy until he could stand up and read words of two syllables and keep his place, so someone had to get him that far first, and it was nearly always a woman.

A child's first reading tool was a hornbook. It was not a book. It was a wooden paddle about the shape of a table-tennis bat, with one printed sheet tacked to it and a sheet of transparent animal horn laid over the top so the paper would not wear through. A leather thong through the handle let a child hang it from a belt. The sheet carried a cross, the alphabet in large and small letters, the vowels and their pairings with consonants, and the Lord's Prayer. The Smithsonian holds one made in the 1700s.

Boston Latin School opened on 23 April 1635 and is still open. It is the oldest public school in the country. Collegiate School in New York, started by Dutch colonists, dates itself to 1628, when the minister Jonas Michaelius began teaching in Manhattan, so the two schools disagree about which is oldest of all. Boston stood on the Shawmut peninsula, in the land of the Massachusett nation. Ten days before it opened the townsmen of Boston met and agreed to ask Philemon Pormort to teach. The town record says he "shall be intreated to become scholemaster for the teaching and nourtering of children with us." The first classes met in Pormort's own house. The boys learned Latin and Greek.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The New England Primer" -->
The printer Benjamin Harris made *The New England Primer* for colonial buyers somewhere between 1687 and 1690. That is as close as the American Antiquarian Society will date it, because the only evidence is booksellers' advertisements. The printing records are gone, and no copy printed before 1727 survives anywhere. The book taught reading, spelling, and morals in the same lessons, with a woodcut picture for each letter of the alphabet. Children were told to learn its sentences by heart, and reciting them was the point as much as reading them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Discipline [R7 discipline]" -->
The rod was a real object. Ezekiel Cheever kept a bundle of birch rods beside his desk at the Boston Latin School for thirty-eight years, in a room with poor light and a smoky fireplace.

One of his pupils wrote down what it was like. John Barnard was born in Boston in 1681 and started at Cheever's school at seven, in 1689. Cheever told him in front of the class that because he played too much, he would be beaten whenever a classmate did not know his lesson. Then, in Barnard's words, "our master beat me" each time one boy failed, "and that for several days." Barnard wrote that he was "often beaten for my play." Cheever also beat him for two or three days running because he could not turn Aesop's fables into Latin verse, until Barnard told him he had tried his hardest and Cheever stopped setting it. Barnard does not say what Cheever hit him with. He wrote this down as an old man, in the 1760s.

People usually say "spare the rod and spoil the child" comes from the Bible. Proverbs 13:24 says that whoever spares the rod hates their children, and the words "spoil the child" are not in it. The oldest English version is far older than the King James Bible. Ælfric of Eynsham, an English monk who lived about 950 to 1010, wrote in a homily that "He who spareth his rod hateth his child," and that the one who loves the child "teacheth it soundly." The Wycliffe Bible of 1382 carries the verse in Middle English. John Skelton wrote about sparing the rod of correction around 1529. The wording people use now is Samuel Butler's, from his comic poem *Hudibras*: "Then spare the Rod, and spill the Child," where "spill" later became "spoil." *Hudibras* came out in three parts, and sources give 1662, 1663, and 1664 for the part with that line.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Native children and the first schools built for them" -->
John Eliot and a group of Native leaders founded Natick in 1651, the first of more than a dozen "praying towns" in Massachusetts. Waban and Cutshamekin of the Massachusett and John Speen of the Nipmuc worked on it with him. The town put up a meetinghouse with a school inside it, and a Massachusett man named Monequassun taught there. Eliot printed schoolbooks in the Massachusett language, a catechism in 1653 and an *Indian Primer* in 1669, and every one of them taught Christian doctrine in the same lesson as reading. Reading and conversion were the same lesson here.

In 1675 war broke out between the English colonists and several Native nations led by Metacom, whom the English called King Philip. On 13 October 1675 the men governing the Massachusetts colony ordered the Christian Native people of the praying towns moved to Deer Island in Boston Harbor, starting with Natick. The National Park Service counts about 500 to 1,100 people held there over the winter, most of them women and children, with little food and no proper shelter. More than half of them died, by one historical society's estimate. The colonists let the survivors go in May 1676. An unknown number were taken off the island and sold into slavery in the West Indies or in Tangier, in North Africa. No record reached here says what became of Monequassun, the Natick schoolmaster. Descendants hold a remembrance on Deer Island every year.

The men who wrote Harvard's 1650 charter put into it a promise to pay for "the education of the English and Indian youth of this Country." A building called the Indian College stood in Harvard Yard from 1655. Sources disagree on whether it came down in 1695 or 1698. The printing press kept inside it produced the first Bible published in North America, in the Algonquian language, in 1663. Only a handful of Native students ever went there, and Harvard's own account says what became of them. Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck graduated in 1665. His classmate Joel Iacoomes drowned in a shipwreck days before the ceremony, two more died of disease part-way through, and one left to go to sea.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ezekiel-cheever" name="Ezekiel Cheever" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Ezekiel Cheever
> **Who:** A schoolmaster who taught Latin and Greek for seventy years, the last thirty-eight at the Boston Latin School · **When and where:** Born London 1615, died Boston 21 August 1708. New Haven, Charlestown, and Boston

He taught longer than anyone else in the history of this country: seventy years without a break. He ran the schools at New Haven from 1638, taught at Charlestown from 1661, and on 29 December 1670 the town of Boston asked him to head the Boston Latin School. He was ninety-three and still teaching when he died.

Some sources give his birth year as 1614 rather than 1615, because the English calendar then began the year on 25 March, so the winter months were counted differently.

His classroom is described the same way in every account: bad light, a fireplace that smoked, and a bundle of birch rods beside his desk. Cotton Mather, who had been his pupil, preached at his funeral and said New England had known no better teacher.

His Latin grammar, *A Short Introduction to the Latin Tongue*, was printed in Boston in 1708, the year he died. Schools went on using it for nearly two hundred years, longer than any other Latin textbook printed in this country.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ezekiel-cheever" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="caleb-cheeshahteaumuck" name="Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck
> **Who:** A Wampanoag student from Martha's Vineyard, the first Native American to graduate from Harvard · **When and where:** Graduated 1665, Cambridge, Massachusetts

He came from the Wampanoag community on Martha's Vineyard and took his degree at Harvard in 1665.

One piece of his own writing survives: a short letter in Latin addressed to the English donors who paid for the Indian College, beginning "Honoratissimi benefactores," which means "most honoured benefactors." It is often described as the earliest surviving writing by a Native person on this continent.

He died in 1666, within a year of graduating, of what people then called consumption. Accounts of his death give the cause as tuberculosis, a lung disease. One of them says he died at Watertown. He was about twenty.

He is the only one of the Indian College's students who finished. His classmate Joel Iacoomes drowned days before the ceremony, two others died of disease part-way through, and one left to become a sailor.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="caleb-cheeshahteaumuck" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="education" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Most children in this half-century learned at home or on the job. Apprenticeship was the main training system, and an indenture often required the master to teach the child to read. The schools that existed mostly took boys whose families could pay. The biggest change in these fifty years was a law. In 1740 the men of the South Carolina assembly made it a crime to teach an enslaved person to write.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The law against teaching, 1740" -->
The members of the South Carolina assembly passed "An Act for the Better Ordering and Governing Negroes and Other Slaves in This Province" on 10 May 1740, the year after the Stono Rebellion. Section 45 says that anyone who teaches a slave to write, or has one taught, or uses one as a scribe, "shall, for every such offense, forfeit the sum of one hundred pounds current money."

The wording is exact. Teaching a slave to write was the offence. Teaching a slave to read was not. Historians usually explain it this way: a person who could write could forge a pass and travel with it. The fine fell on the teacher rather than the pupil. This is the first law in these colonies to make teaching someone a crime.

Three years later, in 1743, Commissary Alexander Garden opened a school in Charleston for Black pupils, and put two young Black men named Harry and Andrew in charge of it. The Society for the Propagation of the Gospel had paid to train them as teachers. It ran in the evenings for people who worked in the day, and it lasted until 1763, when one of the two had died and the men who ran the Society judged the other unfit. The historian Carter G. Woodson wrote in 1915 that the Society bought Harry and Andrew as slaves in order to train them as teachers. The schoolhouse opened in 1743 or 1744, depending on the account, with about sixty pupils.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Charity schools and who paid for them" -->
The charity schools were run from London by church societies. King William III gave the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts its charter on 16 June 1701, after Thomas Bray and others pressed for it. Its members subscribed money to send priests and schoolteachers to the colonies, and more than three hundred of them crossed the Atlantic during the 1700s. A separate group, the Associates of Dr. Bray, started in 1724 and set up schools of its own.

These were not free town schools. A society in London paid the teacher, and the men who ran it paid because they wanted pupils who could read the catechism and the Bible.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="How many people could read" -->
Nobody surveyed literacy in the colonies. Historians count signatures on wills and deeds instead: a person who could write signed a name, and a person who could not made a mark. It is the best evidence there is, and it undercounts readers, because many children, girls especially, were taught to read and never taught to write.

By that count, about 60 percent of white men in New England could sign between 1650 and 1670, 85 percent between 1758 and 1762, and 90 percent by the 1790s. Women's figures rose later and faster: 27 percent of those born between 1650 and 1669, 41 percent of those born in the next twenty years, then 76 percent of those born between 1710 and 1729. Literacy ran higher in New England and the middle colonies than in the South, and higher in towns than in the country.

In Virginia, as many as 5 percent of enslaved people may have been able to read by 1775. The check on that figure comes from an ugly source: of about a thousand advertisements placed in the *Virginia Gazette* between 1736 and 1776 by enslavers hunting people who had run away, fifty-five described the person as literate.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The academy is proposed [R7 academies]" -->
Benjamin Franklin published *Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania* in October 1749. He argued for a school that taught in English rather than in Latin and Greek, and that taught geography, natural history, drawing, accounting, and modern languages alongside the old subjects. The school itself opened in 1751.

The first Protestant boarding school for girls in this land had already opened. In May 1742 Countess Benigna von Zinzendorf started classes for twenty-five girls at Germantown, near Philadelphia. The school moved to Bethlehem, Pennsylvania in 1745 and settled there in 1748.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The school day, and what is not known about it [R7 one-room school day]" -->
The familiar picture of the one-room school, with the stove, the slates, the recitation bench and the teacher boarding with each family in turn, is documented for the 1800s. It is not documented for these fifty years. What is documented for 1700 to 1750 is thinner: a town appointed one man to teach, the parents or the master paid his wages, and children of every age sat in the same room because there was only one teacher for them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Indian school at William & Mary" -->
The men who founded the College of William & Mary in Virginia in 1693 wrote into its charter a duty to teach Native boys the Christian religion. Money from the estate of the scientist Robert Boyle paid for it. When Governor Francis Nicholson could not persuade Native families to send their sons, two traders, Robert Hicks and John Evans, bought or otherwise got four captive boys, described as "captives from the Catawba Nation," around 1702, and those four were the first pupils. Their names are not in the published record. The college finished a building for the school, the Brafferton, in 1723, and enslaved workers built it. More than 125 Native students from at least 26 nations lived and studied there between 1723 and 1776. They learned reading, writing, arithmetic and the Church of England's prayers. How many of them died at the school is not recorded in any source found. The college itself bought a tobacco plantation in 1718 and seventeen enslaved people to work it, for £476.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="christopher-dock" name="Christopher Dock" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Christopher Dock
> **Who:** A Mennonite schoolmaster in Pennsylvania who wrote the first book about teaching published in this country · **When and where:** Skippack and Salford, Pennsylvania, about 1718 to 1771

He came to Pennsylvania somewhere between 1710 and 1714 and opened a school at Skippack no later than 1718. He taught for ten years, then farmed for about ten more, then went back to teaching in 1738 and taught for the last thirty-three years of his life, running two schools on alternate days.

On 8 August 1750 he finished a manuscript called *Schul-Ordnung*, which means school management. He did not want it printed while he was alive. Christopher Saur printed it anyway in 1769, with a second edition in 1770. Some sources give 1770 for the first edition. It is the first book about how to teach written in this country, and it was still being reprinted in the 1900s.

What he wrote down is mostly about how he handled children, and he sorted them by what worked on each one. A child who wanted praise got praise. A child who wanted money got a penny for studying hard. A child who wanted sweets got a sugar pretzel for learning a lesson well. The ones who were not moved by a penny or a cake, he threatened with a whipping. He also put a yoke on a boy who swore, and made children sit alone.

He was gentler than most schoolmasters of his time, and he still used the rod and the threat of it.

One evening in the autumn of 1771 he did not come home from school. People went to look for him and found him in his schoolroom, on his knees, dead.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="christopher-dock" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="education" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The men who had just made a new country said it would need citizens who could read. Several of them wrote plans for schools to produce those citizens. Almost none of the plans became law, because the argument was really about who would pay. The schools that did open in these fifty years were private academies and the first chartered schools for girls. One more opened at Williamsburg: a charity school where Black children were taught to read and taught that slavery was God's will.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Jefferson's plan, and who was in it" -->
Thomas Jefferson drafted a Bill for the More General Diffusion of Knowledge and it went to the Virginia House of Delegates on 18 June 1779. He described it himself a few years later. Divide every county into districts five or six miles square, called hundreds, put a school in each one, and let every person send their children three years free and longer if they paid. The district schools would teach reading, writing, and arithmetic. Above them, grammar schools would teach Greek, Latin, geography, and harder arithmetic.

Jefferson also set out how poor boys would be picked out for more schooling. Visitors were to choose "the boy, of best genius in the school, of those whose parents are too poor to give them further education," so that, in his words, "twenty of the best geniusses will be raked from the rubbish annually." Rubbish is his word for the children of poor families.

Girls are not in the plan. Neither are enslaved children. Members put the bill to the legislature again and again and it never passed. A much smaller version became law in 1796, and under it each county's court decided whether to have any schools at all.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Who pays: the Land Ordinance of 1785" -->
The men in Congress passed the Land Ordinance on 20 May 1785. Surveyors were to cut the western land into townships six miles square, each divided into thirty-six numbered sections. Its words: "There shall be reserved the lot N 16, of every township, for the maintenance of public schools, within the said township."

That section was not to be sold to a settler. The rent or sale money from it paid for a school. This is where the first public money for American schools came from, and it is worth being plain about what the land was: land taken from Native nations, sold to settlers, with a share of the proceeds set aside to teach the settlers' children. The first land surveyed under the Ordinance was in eastern Ohio. In January 1785, at Fort McIntosh, US commissioners had signed a treaty with Wyandot, Lenape, Ojibwe and Odawa men that pushed most Ohio nations into a reserve farther west. The Shawnee and other nations refused to accept it. The Ohio historian George Knepper writes that the treaty was made under pressure by minor chiefs who had no authority to speak for their people.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The academies, and the first schools for girls [R7 academies]" -->
Franklin's Academy and Charity School of Philadelphia opened in 1751 and was chartered in 1753. Samuel Phillips founded Phillips Academy at Andover, Massachusetts on 25 April 1778. It opened five days later, and Paul Revere cut its seal. John and Elizabeth Phillips signed the act of incorporation for Phillips Exeter in New Hampshire on 3 April 1781, and that school opened on 1 May 1783 with one teacher and fifty-six students.

John Poor founded the Young Ladies' Academy of Philadelphia on 4 June 1787, and it was chartered on 7 January 1792. Its pupils were taught reading, writing, English grammar, mathematics, geography, rhetoric, composition, chemistry, and natural philosophy.

Sarah Pierce, born in 1767, opened the Litchfield Female Academy in Connecticut in 1792. Over about thirty years more than two thousand girls attended, from seventeen states and territories and from Canada and the West Indies. The local historical society has identified 1,848 of them by name. More than eight in ten came from out of town and boarded with Litchfield families. They studied history, geography, arithmetic, and composition, and later Latin, logic, rhetoric, and natural philosophy, and girls who finished the whole course were given diplomas.

The argument used to justify these schools was about their pupils' future sons. Mothers did the early moral and intellectual training of children, so the reasoning went, and the new country depended on it. Pierce herself thought girls and boys were equally able. She did not argue that women should enter the men's colleges or the professions.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Williamsburg Bray School, 1760 to 1774" -->
The Associates of Dr. Bray, a church charity in London, set up a school in Williamsburg, Virginia in 1760 for Black children, most of them enslaved. Benjamin Franklin recommended it, and the president of William & Mary, Thomas Dawson, backed it. One teacher taught there for the whole fourteen years: a widow named Ann Wager, paid £20 a year, about what a journeyman tradesman earned.

The pupils were three to ten years old, and thirty or more might be in the room on an ordinary day. They learned the true spelling of words and how to read aloud clearly, working up through *The Child's First Book*, the Psalms, the New Testament, the Book of Common Prayer, and the Bible. Lessons opened with reciting the Apostles' Creed, the Lord's Prayer, and the catechism from memory. Girls were also to be taught sewing. Sources disagree on the total: William & Mary says three to four hundred children over fourteen years, and Encyclopedia Virginia says about two hundred. The names of 86 of them survive in the records.

What the school was for is not in dispute, and the institutions that hold it now say so themselves. William & Mary's account states that its faith-based curriculum justified slavery. The lessons were meant to teach enslaved children that their enslavement was God's will and that they should accept it. The same lessons taught them to read. Both things happened in the same room.

The school closed in 1774, when Ann Wager died. A second Bray school at Fredericksburg ran from 1765 to about 1769 with forty or fifty pupils, and closed because enrollment fell and local enslavers objected to it.

The schoolhouse itself still exists. Researchers confirmed in 2020 that a building on the William & Mary campus, later a private home and then student housing, was the school. It was moved to Colonial Williamsburg in February 2023. It is the oldest surviving schoolhouse for Black children in the United States.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Teaching as a job [R7 teaching as a job]" -->
Teaching in this era was not yet a career with a training or a salary scale. Noah Webster's path is the documented example: he left Yale in 1778, taught school at Glastonbury, Hartford, and West Hartford, took another teaching post at Goshen, New York in 1782, and moved on to law and writing.
