While they were held at Poston, the Mendez family was working the Munemitsu farm, and the Westminster school was turning the Mendez children away.

Shared with: `war` and `rights-movements`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The G.I. Bill" -->
The men in Congress voted to pay for a generation to go to college. President Roosevelt signed the Servicemen's Readjustment Act on 22 June 1944, and everyone calls it the G.I. Bill. In 1947, the peak year, veterans made up 49 percent of all college admissions. By the time the original bill ended on 25 July 1956, 7.8 million of the 16 million Second World War veterans had used it for education or training.

The law says nothing about race, and it still did not work the same way for everyone. Local officials handled the applications, and a Black veteran in the South with tuition money in hand still had to find a college that would admit him. The colleges open to him were segregated ones with limited places, and the schools he had come from had been paid for at the rates set out above. Many could not get in.

Black college enrollment rose sharply all the same. Medgar Evers volunteered for the army in 1942 and used the G.I. Bill to enroll at Alcorn A&M in Mississippi, the land-grant college the state had built for Black students under the second Morrill Act.

`economy` carries the middle-class economics. `rights-movements` carries Evers.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-dewey" name="John Dewey" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### John Dewey
> **Who:** Argued that children learn by doing, and ran a school for eight and a half years to test it · **When and where:** Born Burlington, Vermont, 20 October 1859. Died New York City, 1 June 1952

He graduated from the University of Vermont in June 1879 and went straight to work as assistant principal of Oil City High School in Pennsylvania, teaching classics, science and algebra. He was nineteen. He did that for two years before he did any philosophy at all.

He took a doctorate at Johns Hopkins in 1884, taught at the University of Michigan, and accepted a job at the University of Chicago in March 1894. In January 1896 he opened an elementary school in a rented house on 57th Street with sixteen pupils and two adults in charge. It had four homes in eight years. At its largest it held 140 children, 23 teachers and about ten graduate assistants.

It was an experiment and Dewey said so. Two teachers who worked there later wrote its history and called the first six months a trial-and-error period, "chiefly indicative of what not to do." Children cooked, wove, built and grew things, and reading, writing and arithmetic came out of that work rather than before it.

In 1899 he published *The School and Society*, which sold well in its first year. In 1916 he published *Democracy and Education*, where the phrase "learning by doing" appears in his own words.

On 5 April 1904 his wife Alice resigned as principal of the school and he resigned from the University of Chicago the same day. He went to Columbia in 1905, retired in 1930, and died of pneumonia in 1952 at ninety-two.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-dewey" -->

<!-- hb-story:start slug="mamie-garvin-fields" name="Mamie Garvin Fields" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Mamie Garvin Fields
> **Who:** Started teaching in a one-room school at twenty and taught for thirty-five years · **When and where:** Born Charleston, South Carolina, 1888. Died 1987

She went to the Robert Gould Shaw Memorial School in Charleston, then won a church scholarship to the high school department of Claflin College in Orangeburg and stayed on there for college.

In 1908 she took her first job at Pine Wood, a one-room school near Sumter. She was twenty. The schools she taught in over the next few years had one or two teachers between them. They were the schools South Carolina provided for Black children in the countryside.

She came back to Charleston in 1909 as one of the first Black teachers the county hired for its public schools. She taught at Humbert Wood Elementary and at Miller Hill School on Johns Island, where she was principal for two years. After a spell in Boston she went back to teaching in 1926 at the Society Corner School on James Island, and retired in 1943.

Her work was not only with children. She ran adult classes on James and Johns Islands in the early 1920s and started Charleston's first vacation Bible school for migrant workers during the Depression. She led the South Carolina Federation of Colored Women's Clubs from 1958 to 1964.

In 1978, when she was ninety, her granddaughter Karen sat down and recorded her life with her. The book came out in 1983 as *Lemon Swamp and Other Places*. Her papers are at the Avery Research Center in Charleston. She died in 1987, aged ninety-nine.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="mamie-garvin-fields" -->

<!-- hb-story:start slug="sylvia-mendez" name="Sylvia Mendez" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Sylvia Mendez
> **Who:** Turned away from a California school at eight. The case her father brought ended school segregation in the state · **When and where:** Westminster, California, 1944 to 1947

In 1944 her family moved from Santa Ana to a farm in Westminster, California. They leased it from the Munemitsus, a Japanese American family the government had forced into a camp.

Her aunt took Sylvia, her two brothers and her Vidaurri cousins to enroll at the Seventeenth Street School. The staff took the cousins, who had lighter skin and a surname that did not sound Spanish, and turned away the Mendez children. Her aunt's answer was written down: "My kids, they will not go to your school, if those of my brother cannot go, mine will not go!" Sylvia was eight.

The school the Mendez children were sent to instead was Hoover School. Children there were taught embroidery, cooking and farm work in place of mathematics and science. That is what separate meant in Orange County. The Mexican school did not teach the same subjects in a poorer building. It taught different subjects, aimed at different work.

Her father Gonzalo Mendez sued, along with four other fathers: William Guzman, Frank Palomino, Thomas Estrada and Lorenzo Ramirez. Their lawyer, David Marcus, brought the case against four Orange County school districts on behalf of about 5,000 children. After a six-day trial, Judge Paul J. McCormick ruled for the families on 18 February 1946. The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals agreed on 14 April 1947.

Governor Earl Warren then signed a bill that made California the first state to outlaw segregation in all of its public schools. Warren became Chief Justice of the United States in 1953, and in 1954 he wrote the court's opinion in *Brown v. Board of Education*.

Sylvia Mendez received the Presidential Medal of Freedom on 15 February 2011.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="sylvia-mendez" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="education" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Courts and Congress reach into the classroom in this era, and the number of different kinds of school grows.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Brown, and how slowly the schools changed [R7 desegregation]" -->
In 1954 the nine justices of the Supreme Court ruled that separate public schools for Black and white children broke the Constitution. Almost nothing changed in the classrooms for another ten years.

The case was *Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka*, decided on 17 May 1954. All nine justices agreed, and Chief Justice Earl Warren wrote the opinion. Warren had signed California's school desegregation bill seven years before that, when he was governor of the state. On 31 May 1955 the same nine told the states to desegregate "with all deliberate speed." They set no date.

Ten years after the ruling, one study estimated that 99 of every 100 Black children in the South were in schools with no white children in them.

James Coleman and his team made the first national count, surveying schools in 1965-66 under a job the Civil Rights Act of 1964 had given them. Across the country, 65 of every 100 Black pupils were in schools that were more than 90 percent Black. Eighty of every 100 white pupils were in schools more than 90 percent white.

The city figures for elementary schools in the same survey show what that meant in the South. In Mobile, Alabama, 100 percent of Black children were in schools over 90 percent Black. Birmingham was 99, Jackson, Mississippi 99, Atlanta 97, New Orleans 96, Charlotte 96, Memphis 95. Of the twenty-two Southern cities counted, the lowest was Kansas City, Missouri, at 69.

Shared with: `rights-movements` (the campaign that brought the case) and `government-politics` (the ruling as law).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Schools shut rather than mixed [R7 desegregation]" -->
Two places closed their public schools instead of taking Black children, and children lost years of school because of it.

Little Rock, Arkansas came first. On 2 September 1957 Governor Orval Faubus went on television and said he had called out the Arkansas National Guard to keep order at Central High School. Nine Black students tried to go in on 4 September and the soldiers blocked them. Elizabeth Eckford arrived on her own, not knowing the others were being escorted, and walked back through a crowd of more than 300 people to a bus stop. The other eight came with ministers and were turned away.

A federal judge, Ronald Davies, ruled on 20 September that Faubus had used soldiers to stop integration rather than to prevent violence. Faubus pulled the Guard out that evening. On 23 September more than a thousand white people surrounded the school while city police walked the nine in. The crowd attacked four Black reporters, Alex Wilson, James Hicks, Moses J. Newsom and Earl Davy. After three and a half hours the staff took the students out through a side door.

President Eisenhower sent 1,000 soldiers of the 101st Airborne Division. At 9:22 on the morning of 25 September the nine walked in the front doors with more than twenty paratroopers around them, over 350 more soldiers around the building, and an Army helicopter overhead.

The school year inside was the part nobody photographed. White students shoved and insulted them for months. On 3 October about 150 students walked out in protest at their presence. Vice principal Elizabeth Huckaby took 70 names and all 70 were suspended. On 17 December Minnijean Brown dropped chili on two boys who had blocked her way in the cafeteria, and she was suspended for nearly a month. In February some white students wore badges reading "One Down and Eight to Go." On 17 February 1958 the school board expelled her for the rest of the year for calling a student "white trash." She finished school in New York. Ernest Green graduated on 27 May 1958, the first Black student to finish Central High.

The following year Faubus closed the schools. On 15 September 1958 he shut all four Little Rock high schools. Twelve days later the city voted 19,470 to 7,561 against integration, and the high schools stayed shut for the whole year. People in Little Rock call it the Lost Year. White students went to new private schools, to schools in other towns and other states, or took lessons by post from the University of Arkansas. Black students had fewer places to go. Most went to schools in other districts or other states, and some took a course by post run by L. M. Christophe, the principal of the Black high school. The state kept paying the teachers to sit in empty classrooms. Central High's football team kept playing all year. In May 1959 the segregationists on the school board refused to renew the contracts of 44 teachers and administrators. Voters removed three of those board members on 25 May, and the high schools opened again on 12 August 1959.

Prince Edward County, Virginia stayed shut for five years. Its Black high school students had walked out in 1951 over the state of their building, led by sixteen-year-old Barbara Johns, and their case became one of the five decided together as *Brown*. Local men had planned for this since 1954. J. Barrye Wall, who edited the *Farmville Herald*, and Robert Crawford, a laundry owner and former school board chairman, built a group called the Defenders of State Sovereignty and Individual Liberties to fight desegregation. In 1955 the mayor, W. C. Fitzpatrick, had a public meeting vote to set up a private fund to pay white teachers if the public schools closed. Two courts ordered the county to integrate on 1 May 1959. On 26 June the county supervisors voted to stop paying for public schools at all. The schools did not open that September and did not open again until 1964.

Between 1,700 and 2,000 Black children had no school. The two main accounts differ on the number. Some were sent to relatives in other counties or other states. Some were taught in church basements. White children went to Prince Edward Academy, a new private school paid for partly by tuition grants from the state.

Private donors and the Kennedy administration paid for one year of free classes for about 1,500 children, starting on 16 September 1963. On 25 May 1964 the Supreme Court ordered the county to open its schools, and about 1,500 children went back on 8 September 1964.

The state had shown the way. In 1956 the Virginia legislature, under Governor Thomas Stanley, passed a law telling the governor to close any school a federal court ordered to take Black pupils. In September 1958 Governor J. Lindsay Almond used it. He shut nine schools in Front Royal, Charlottesville and Norfolk and locked out about 12,000 to 13,000 children, until two courts struck the closings down on 19 January 1959. In all, four other Virginia places closed schools during the same fight, for months rather than years: Arlington, Charlottesville, Norfolk and Warren County. In 2003 the Virginia legislature passed a resolution of "profound regret" for the closings. It was not an apology, and it was reported at the time that some members would not vote for an apology because they thought it could lead to claims for money. In 2004 the same legislature set up a scholarship fund to pay for schooling for people who had lost those years. It began with $50,000. A donor named John Kluge then gave a million dollars on condition the legislature matched it, and the fund reached $2,050,000.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="A university, 1962" -->
Two men were killed on the night the University of Mississippi took its first Black student.

James Meredith, an Air Force veteran, applied in January 1961 and was turned down after he wrote that he was Black. NAACP lawyers took his case, and on 10 September 1962 Justice Hugo Black ordered the university to admit him. Governor Ross Barnett worked for weeks to stop it.

On the evening of 30 September federal marshals brought Meredith to the campus at Oxford and put him in a dormitory. A crowd of more than 2,500 students and people from outside gathered and attacked the marshals with rocks, bottles, firebombs and guns. Paul Guihard, a French news reporter, was shot in the back. Ray Gunter, a 23-year-old from Oxford, was also killed. Nobody was ever charged with either killing. The counts of the injured run from at least 75 in the first news report to more than 300 in later accounts, many of them marshals. Soldiers took control of the campus by the next morning.

Meredith registered on 1 October 1962 and walked to his first class, an American history lesson, with marshals beside him. Some students walked out of his classes. He graduated in August 1963.

Shared with: `rights-movements` (the campaign).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="What desegregation cost Black teachers, and the bus" -->
Desegregating schools cost thousands of Black teachers their jobs.

The economist Owen Thompson counted teachers in 781 school districts across the eleven states of the old Confederacy. In 1964, 30.6 percent of their teachers were Black. By 1972 it was 24.2 percent. That is a drop of nearly a third in the number of Black teachers in eight years.

The reason was in how districts merged. When two schools became one, school boards let Black teachers go and hired white ones, often with less experience. Districts with the fewest Black pupils cut the hardest. Thompson estimates that about half of the teachers who lost their jobs took lower-skilled work, and the rest left the South to teach somewhere else.

Buses came next. In *Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg*, decided on 20 April 1971, the justices ruled that a judge could order children carried by bus across a district to end segregation. Charlotte-Mecklenburg already had more than 84,000 pupils in 107 schools, about 24,000 of them Black, and it had bused 26,600 children the year before at an average of 15 miles each way and over an hour each trip. Under the desegregation plan the average elementary trip would be about seven miles and "not over 35 minutes at the most." The court said an objection to busing only counts when the trip is long enough to risk a child's health or get in the way of the teaching.

Buses were not new. Districts had been using them for forty years to close small schools. Using them to mix schools was new, and it is what the argument was about.

In Boston the buses began in September 1974 under a federal judge's order. Phyllis Ellison was one of about sixty Black students bused to South Boston High School that year. On the first day people on the corners shouted at the bus and held up bananas at the students inside. In the school, she said, there were ten to fifteen fights on an ordinary day. Black and white students sat on opposite sides of every classroom and the lunchroom. On 11 December 1974 a Black student stabbed a white student, Michael Faith, in a corridor. A crowd gathered at the school gates shouting for the Black students. Police and 125 state troopers held the crowd back while four empty buses pulled up at the front of the school as decoys, and the Black students were taken out of the back and driven home. The school was then closed for a time.

`rights-movements` tells the court case and the attacks on the buses.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Prayer and Bible reading end; the Amish win an exemption" -->
Until 1962 a public school day in much of the country opened with a prayer or a Bible reading. Two rulings ended that as an official school exercise.

In *Engel v. Vitale*, decided on 25 June 1962, the justices struck down a prayer that the New York State Board of Regents had written for schools to say. The school district was Union Free School District No. 9 in New Hyde Park, and it had told each class to say the prayer at the start of every day. The whole prayer is 22 words: "Almighty God, we acknowledge our dependence upon Thee, and we beg Thy blessings upon us, our parents, our teachers and our Country." Justice Hugo Black wrote for the court that "it is no part of the business of government to compose official prayers for any group of the American people to recite as a part of a religious program carried on by government." The vote was six to one.

A year later came *School District of Abington Township v. Schempp*, decided on 17 June 1963. Pennsylvania law said "at least ten verses from the Holy Bible shall be read, without comment, at the opening of each public school on each school day." At Abington the verses and the Lord's Prayer went out over the school intercom. A Baltimore case, *Murray v. Curlett*, was decided with it. A Maryland rule from 1905 required a King James Bible reading and the Lord's Prayer. Justice Tom Clark wrote for eight of the nine justices that government must keep "strict neutrality, neither aiding nor opposing religion." It did not matter that a child could ask to be excused.

The third case ran the other way. In *Wisconsin v. Yoder*, decided on 15 May 1972, the justices let Amish parents stop sending their children to school after eighth grade. Wisconsin required school to age sixteen. Jonas Yoder, Wallace Miller and Adin Yutzy had kept Frieda Yoder and Barbara Miller, both fifteen, and Vernon Yutzy, fourteen, at home, and each father was fined five dollars. Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote that the state could not force them to send the children to high school.

`religion` leads on the faith argument in all three cases. This chapter's part is the school day itself: what a child did at nine in the morning, and how long a child had to keep coming.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Discipline ends, slowly [R7 discipline]" -->
In October 1970 an eighth-grader named James Ingraham was slow to do what his teacher told him at Charles R. Drew Junior High School in Dade County, Florida. He was taken to the principal's office, held down over a table, and hit more than twenty times with a wooden paddle. The blows left a hematoma, a pool of blood under the skin, that needed a doctor and kept him out of school for several days. A ninth-grader at the same school, Roosevelt Andrews, was hit on the arms, and one blow left him unable to use his arm properly for a week.

Hitting children was the ordinary way of keeping order in American schools, and it had rules. Florida law allowed punishment that was not "degrading or unduly severe." Dade County's own policy described the paddle: less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, about half an inch thick. It set the normal punishment at one to five blows. James Ingraham got more than twenty.

The families sued. The case reached the Supreme Court as *Ingraham v. Wright*, and on 19 April 1977 the justices ruled five to four against the children. Justice Lewis Powell wrote that "the Eighth Amendment does not apply to the paddling of children as a means of maintaining discipline in public schools," and that "the Due Process Clause does not require notice and a hearing prior to the imposition of corporal punishment." A school could hit a child without a hearing first. Justice Byron White, dissenting, wrote that the record showed "beatings so severe that if they were inflicted on a hardened criminal for the commission of a serious crime, they might not pass constitutional muster."

The ending came one state at a time instead. New Jersey had banned hitting schoolchildren back in 1867 and stood alone for 104 years. Massachusetts became the second state in 1971. Hawaii followed in 1973, Maine in 1975, Rhode Island and the District of Columbia in 1977. Then the bans came quickly: New Hampshire in 1983, New York and Vermont in 1985, California in 1986, eight states in 1989 alone, four more in 1993, West Virginia in 1994.

It did not end everywhere. Twenty-seven states and the District of Columbia had banned it by 1994, and then no state banned it again for nine years. When the century ended, an adult at school could still lawfully hit a child in twenty-three states. In 1978, four of every hundred American schoolchildren were hit at school. The schools' own reports to the federal government counted about 1.5 million children paddled in 1976, 613,514 in 1990 and 342,038 in 2000. The districts reported those numbers themselves, and nobody checked them, so the real numbers may be higher.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Kinds of school [R7 magnet, charter, private]" -->
Before this era almost every American child went to the public school nearest home, or to a church school. By the end of it there were several other kinds, and most of them were invented because of desegregation.

The magnet school was the first. McCarver Elementary in Tacoma, Washington opened as one in the autumn of 1968. Ninety-one of every hundred of its pupils were Black. Nobody was ordered to go there. School officials in Tacoma set out to make white families want to come: a $200,000 federal grant, the best teachers in the district moved there, team teaching, children working through the lessons at their own speed. Counsellors went to families' houses to ask them to choose it. On opening day about 200 white children enrolled where there had been about 50. By 1970 fewer than half the children at McCarver were Black and there was a waiting list. The second magnet school opened in Boston in 1969. There were about 1,000 of them by 1981 and more than 2,400 by 1991.

The segregation academy was the opposite idea. Historians use that name for a private school started so that white children would not have to sit next to Black children. Mississippi is the clearest case. Before 1954 the state had three private schools that were not run by a church. In 1964 the legislature voted tuition grants of $185 a child to attend a non-religious private school, and more than five hundred children took more than $80,000 in grants that year. One of the new schools was Citizens' Council School No. 1 in Jackson, run by the group that had formed in Indianola in 1954 to keep the schools segregated.

In 1969 the Supreme Court told Mississippi to desegregate its schools by 1970, and the private schools filled. The number in the state went from 121 in 1966 to 236 in 1970, and the number of children in them tripled. In 1970 almost every white child in Canton left the public schools for a private academy, and more than four in ten of Jackson's white children left. The historian Michael Fuquay found the new schools using public school property: books, supplies, sports equipment and buildings handed over, private school teachers kept on the public payroll in Tunica and Clay counties, private school children carried on public school buses in Forrest County. The Mississippi Private School Association had a rule, and its board wrote it into the minutes on 23 January 1971: a school stayed a member "until such a time as they accept a Negro student or faculty member."

Church schools were shrinking while all this happened. Catholic school enrollment peaked in 1964-65 at 5,601,000 children in 13,249 schools. It fell every year after that: 4,363,566 by 1970-71, 3,106,000 by 1980-81, 2,475,439 by 1990-91. In twenty-six years more than half the children were gone and 4,700 schools had closed.

The charter school came last. The Minnesota legislature passed the first charter school law in the country in 1991, as part of a larger education bill, and Governor Arne Carlson signed it. It had been beaten in the state House three years running and it passed by one vote, cut down to let only school districts grant a charter and to allow only eight charter schools in the whole state. The first charter went to Bluffview Montessori in Winona in December 1991. The first charter school in the United States to open its doors was City Academy in St. Paul, in the autumn of 1992. Milo Cutter founded it. Minnesota raised the limit from eight schools to twenty in 1993.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Homeschooling [R7 homeschooling]" -->
Whether a parent was allowed to teach a child at home depended on the state, and in many states the answer was not clear. The attendance laws said a child had to be taught in a school, or by a teacher holding a certificate from the state. Parents who taught their own children were charged with keeping them out of school, and some were convicted. The historian Milton Gaither, who wrote a history of American homeschooling, says the old laws made it "either illegal or dubious," and that the fights between families and governments were sometimes ugly. Six states required a parent to hold a teaching licence.

Two men started the movement. They knew each other, and they came at it for different reasons. John Holt was a school-reform writer who thought ordinary classrooms taught children to obey rather than to think, and told parents to take their children out. He started a newsletter called *Growing Without Schooling* in August 1977, and he made up the word "unschooling." He died in 1985. Raymond Moore was an educational researcher and a Seventh-day Adventist. He and his wife Dorothy argued that school before the age of eight or nine harmed children and that they should be taught at home until then. Their book *Better Late Than Early* came out in 1975 and *Home Grown Kids* in 1981, and for years it was the first book most homeschooling parents read.

In Harrison County, West Virginia, Bobby and Esther Riddle taught their two children, Tim and Jill, at home. They were convicted of breaking the school attendance law and fined ten dollars each. The West Virginia Supreme Court said in its ruling of 11 December 1981 that "the Riddles did an excellent job," possibly a better one than the public schools could do, and upheld the convictions anyway. Larry Delconte moved to North Carolina in 1981 with his wife Michelle and their four children and taught them at home. The state court of appeals ruled that the attendance law did not allow it, and the North Carolina Supreme Court reversed that on 7 May 1985.

Then the states changed their laws, one at a time, through the 1980s. Some wrote detailed homeschooling laws, some added a sentence to the law they already had, and in some the change came from a court rather than a legislature. By 1989 most states had settled with homeschooling families. A few held out into the early 1990s. Michigan still required that a child be taught by a certified teacher, and on 25 May 1993 the Michigan Supreme Court ruled that the state could not apply that rule to a family with a religious objection to it.

(**`home-family` leads on what homeschooling is like as household life.**)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Money from Washington [R7 curriculum and testing]" -->
Before 1958 the federal government paid for almost none of America's schooling. Two laws changed that in seven years.

The first came after the Soviet Union put the first satellite, Sputnik, into orbit in October 1957. President Eisenhower signed the National Defense Education Act on 2 September 1958. It paid for teaching science, mathematics and foreign languages, and it started federal loans for college students. Eisenhower called it "an emergency undertaking to be terminated after four years." Nobody ended it after four years.

The second law was far bigger. President Johnson signed the Elementary and Secondary Education Act on 11 April 1965, on the lawn of the Junction school in Texas, a one-room school he had started at when he was four. His first teacher, Kate Deadrich Loney, sat next to him. He told her, "I started school when I was 4 years old, and they tell me, Miss Kate, that I recited my first lessons while sitting on your lap." He said the law would "bridge the gap between helplessness and hope for more than 5 million educationally deprived children," and that "no law I have signed or will ever sign means more to the future of America." The House voted 263 to 153 and the Senate 73 to 18.

The part of it that mattered most is Title I, which sends federal money to schools with poor children in them. By the end of 1965 the first hundred Title I projects were reaching 347,047 children in twelve states.

Head Start began the same year. Sargent Shriver, who ran the Office of Economic Opportunity, put together the group that designed it, and Johnson announced it on 18 May 1965. It was a summer programme for children too young for school, and it was not only lessons: Johnson described "medical and dental attention that they badly need" and advice for parents. His figures that day were about 530,000 children, 11,000 centres and $112 million. By 31 August he was reporting nearly 560,000 children in 13,400 centres across 2,500 communities, with nearly a million parents and half a million volunteers taking part, including 100,000 teachers, doctors and dentists.

Congress passed Title IX in 1972, and it became law on 23 June. It says that "no person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance."

Shared with: `rights-movements` (Title IX) and `government-politics` (the money as policy).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The children who were not let in at all [R7 who gets schooled]" -->
Until 1975 an American public school could refuse to take a disabled child. No law said it had to let the child in. By the federal government's own reckoning, in 1970 American schools taught only one disabled child in five, and more than a million children with disabilities were shut out of school altogether.

In 1971 the families of seven children in Washington, D.C. sued the school board. George Liddell was eight. His application to Maury Elementary School had been turned down because he needed a special class, and he had never been inside a school. Janice King was thirteen. She had weakness down one side of her body. She had been refused a place from the age the law said she had to be at school, because the schools had no programme for her, and she had never been to school either. Jerome James was twelve and, in the court's words, had been "totally excluded from public school." Duane Blacksheare had been put out of Giddings Elementary School in October 1967, in the third grade, as a "behavior problem," and was still out four years later. Steven Gaston had been out of Taylor Elementary since September 1969. Michael Williams was sixteen. He had epilepsy, which means he had seizures: sudden bursts of activity in the brain that can make a person shake or lose consciousness. He had been out of the Sharpe Health School since October 1969, put out after a stay in hospital because of his health and the days he had missed. The seventh was Peter Mills, and the case carries his name.

The numbers in the case did not agree, and the court printed all of them. The families said about 22,000 children in the District had disabilities and that perhaps 18,000 of them were getting no specialised education at all. The school board said it was teaching at least 3,880. The District's own report for 1971 admitted that an estimated 12,340 disabled children would not be served in the coming school year.

Judge Joseph Waddy decided the case on 1 August 1972. He ruled that the District had to provide a publicly supported education to every child of school age, whatever the child's disability, and that the extra cost was not an excuse. A school also had to give notice and a hearing before it put a child out.

Three years later the same rule was made for the whole country. President Gerald Ford signed the Education for All Handicapped Children Act on 29 November 1975. It gave every disabled child in every state a right to a free education suited to that child.

The counting had already started to change before the law did. Children in special education programmes went from 356,000 in 1947-48, one and a half in every hundred pupils, to 2,677,000 by 1969-70, nearly six in a hundred. All of that happened before the Act. After it: 3,692,000 in 1976-77, and 4,641,000 by 1989-90, more than one child in nine. The Act did not start the change. It made it a right.

The categories changed too. There was no count of children with learning difficulties at all until 1976-77, when 796,000 appeared in the figures. By 1989-90 that group was 2,050,000, nearly half of all children in special education. Meanwhile another group shrank. The government's own word at the time for a child it judged to learn much more slowly than other children was "mentally retarded," and the number counted in that group fell from 830,000 in 1969-70 to 548,000 in 1989-90. Children were being sorted into different groups, as well as counted in greater numbers.

Shared with: `health` (what the conditions were) and `rights-movements` (the parents who organised).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Which language a child could speak at school [R7 curriculum]" -->
In much of the Southwest a child could be punished for speaking Spanish at school, and in 1972 the federal government printed the details.

The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights published *The Excluded Student* in May 1972, part of a study of how Mexican American children were taught in Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. Of about 5,800 schools in the survey area, roughly a third had policies that discouraged children from speaking Spanish in the classroom. About fifteen in every hundred discouraged it in the playground as well.

Texas was the strictest. Two-thirds of the Texas schools surveyed discouraged Spanish in class, and more than a third on the schoolgrounds, at least twice the rate of most other states. California was the loosest, with fewer than a fifth of schools applying it in class. Poor neighbourhoods got it hardest. Five in ten schools serving poor barrios had the rule in the classroom, against about fifteen in a hundred of the schools serving well-off families.

Some districts kept Mexican American children apart by calling it language teaching. In Driscoll, Texas the school made them spend four years getting through the first two grades. Linda Pérez, who spoke only English, was put in the "Mexican" first grade to learn English. In 1957 a federal court called the system "arbitrary and unreasonable" and ordered it stopped.

Teaching in Spanish was a crime in Texas. The Commission wrote that the state "continues to go so far as to make it a crime to speak Spanish in ordinary school activities," and gave a case: in October 1970 a Mexican American teacher in Crystal City was charged for teaching a high school history class in Spanish. The charge was later dropped. That English-only rule had been in Texas law since 1918. Governor Dolph Briscoe signed the bill that ended it on 3 June 1973, fifty-five years later.

The Commission asked schools how they enforced the rule. Forty-eight in a hundred said staff were asked to correct children who spoke Spanish, twelve in a hundred required it, seven in a hundred used other children to do the correcting, and three in a hundred said they punished children who kept speaking it. No principal admitted hitting a child for speaking Spanish. At least three in a hundred admitted punishing children some other way, and witnesses at the Commission's hearing in San Antonio in December 1968 said children were hit. A principal from a Mexican American school in El Paso told that hearing that children caught speaking Spanish were sent to a Spanish detention class for an hour after school. The report prints a copy of the slip a teacher filled in to send a child there.

The clearest account came from the children. In October 1964 a Texas teacher asked a class of seventh-graders to write about their elementary schools, and sent the essays to the Commission. One wrote: "If we speak Spanish we had to pay 5 cents to the teacher or we had to stay after school." Another wrote: "In the first through the fourth grade, if the teacher caught us talking Spanish we would have to stand on the 'black square' for an hour or so." A third was made to "write three pages saying, 'I must not speak Spanish in school'." A fourth described a running tally: "In the sixth grade, they kept a record of which if we spoke Spanish they would take it down and charge us a penny for every Spanish word. If we spoke more than one thousand words our parents would have to come to school and talk with the principal." The report does not give their names, and nobody knows who they were.

One of these schools is now a national park. The Blackwell School in Marfa, Texas taught Mexican American children from September 1909 until 1965, in a building the district had left them when it built a new school for white children in 1892. The Park Service says schools like it ran in more than 120 Texas school districts across 59 counties, and that they aimed to push children into English through a "no Spanish in the classroom" rule. Blackwell closed in 1965 when Marfa built one elementary school for everybody. It became a national historic site in October 2022.

In 1974 the Supreme Court took on the other half of the problem: children sitting in classes taught in a language they could not understand. In San Francisco about 2,856 pupils of Chinese descent spoke no English. About a thousand were getting extra English lessons, which left about 1,800 with none. On 21 January 1974, in *Lau v. Nichols*, Justice William Douglas wrote for the court that this "denies them a meaningful opportunity to participate in the public educational program." The named child in the case was Kinney Kinmon Lau. The ruling did not order schools to teach in Chinese. It said a school cannot sit a child in a class he cannot understand and call it an equal education.

Hawaii had banned teaching in Hawaiian in 1896. In January 1983 a group of Hawaiian-language teachers met to work out how to save the language, and in August 1984 they opened the first Pūnana Leo preschool at Kekaha on Kauaʻi. Pūnana leo means "nest of voices." In 1986 they got the state legislature to lift the ninety-year ban, and in 1987 the first indigenous-language immersion classes in the United States opened at Keaukaha Elementary in Hilo and Waiau Elementary in Pearl City.

Shared with: `immigration` and `native-nations` (the languages themselves).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Indian boarding schools were largest in 1973" -->
The federal Indian boarding schools did not end when the government was told what they were doing. A survey team told the Secretary of the Interior in 1928 that the schools were feeding children on eleven cents a day. Enrolment in them did not peak until about 1973, forty-five years later. The Heard Museum puts that peak at about 60,000 children.

The government's own counts were lower but still large. In 1969 the Bureau of Indian Affairs ran 77 boarding schools with about 35,000 children living in them, and nearly 9,000 of those children were under nine years old. On the Navajo Reservation, 7,476 children aged nine and under lived at 48 boarding schools because there was no day school near their homes. The largest, at Tuba City, housed 1,200 elementary children.

In January 1968 three brothers ran away from the Crownpoint Boarding School in New Mexico, just after the Christmas holiday, to walk about fifty miles home. They were wearing jeans, shorts and light jackets. The temperature that night fell to about ten degrees below zero. Ronald Yazzie, who was nine, and Willie B. Yazzie, who was thirteen, froze to death. Their brother Ray, twelve, lived. A Navajo police officer who searched for them said, "They were lonesome for home and just took off."

In November 1969 a Senate committee published its own report, *Indian Education: A National Tragedy, A National Challenge*. It called the policy behind the schools "coercive assimilation" and said Native nations should run their own schools. It quoted an anthropologist's report of a Navajo boarding school where "children are beaten" and where Navajo girls did the teachers' housework, unpaid, after school.

Some of that then happened. The Navajo Nation opened Navajo Community College in 1968. The college calls itself the first community college in the country run by a tribe. It is now Diné College. In January 1975 Congress passed the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, which let nations sign contracts to run schools themselves. Boarding-school enrolment fell as they did.

Children were also being taken from Native families in another way. Surveys in 1969 and 1974 found that 25 to 35 of every 100 Indian children had been separated from their families and placed in foster homes, adoptive homes or institutions, most of them with non-Indian families. The people who took them were state welfare workers, courts and private adoption agencies, and the Bureau of Indian Affairs through its schools. A 1978 House report said 34,538 children lived in the Bureau's boarding schools and dormitories in 1971 instead of at home. Congress passed the Indian Child Welfare Act, signed on 8 November 1978, to keep Native children with Native families.

`native-nations` leads on what the schools did to the nations. This chapter's part is the schools as schools.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="A Nation at Risk, 1983 [R7 testing]" -->
In 1983 a government commission published a report saying American schools were failing, and the argument it started is still the main argument about American schools.

Secretary of Education T. H. Bell set up the National Commission on Excellence in Education on 26 August 1981 and put David P. Gardner in charge. The commission worked for eighteen months and published *A Nation at Risk* in April 1983.

Its most quoted sentence compares schooling to an attack. "If an unfriendly foreign power had attempted to impose on America the mediocre educational performance that exists today, we might well have viewed it as an act of war. As it stands, we have allowed this to happen to ourselves." The commission also wrote that the foundations of American education were "being eroded by a rising tide of mediocrity."

The report listed what it called indicators of the risk. On nineteen international tests, American students were never first or second, and were last seven times. Some 23 million American adults could not read, write or understand well enough for everyday life. About 13 in every 100 seventeen-year-olds could not either, and the commission said the figure among minority young people might run as high as 40 in 100. Average SAT scores had fallen almost every year from 1963 to 1980, verbal by more than 50 points and mathematics by nearly 40. Nearly 40 in every 100 seventeen-year-olds could not work out what a piece of writing implied, only about one in five could write a persuasive essay, and only about one in three could solve a maths problem that took several steps.

Those are the commission's own numbers, and people argued about them then and have argued since. What the report did is not in doubt. From 1983 on, the argument about American schools was about testing, standards, and comparing one school with another.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="College, and the start of student debt" -->
College went from something a few Americans did to something most families expected, and borrowing to pay for it went from rare to normal in the same fifty years.

In the autumn of 1950, 2,281,298 people were enrolled in American colleges and universities. In 1960 it was 3,639,847. In 1970 it was 8,580,887, more than double in ten years. By 2000 it was 15,312,289, about seven times the 1950 figure.

The government paid for a lot of that. The 1958 National Defense Education Act started federal student loans. President Johnson signed the Higher Education Act on 8 November 1965 at Southwest Texas State College, where he had lived in a room over a garage for three years and swept floors to pay his way. It added grants of up to $1,000 a year based on need, part-time campus jobs worth about $400 a year, and government-backed loans that a student did not have to start repaying until after graduating. Johnson said 140,000 young people would be at college the next year who otherwise would not have gone. He also talked about the year he taught at the Welhausen Mexican School in Cotulla, Texas for $125 a month: "I shall never forget the faces of the boys and the girls in that little Welhausen Mexican School, and I remember even yet the pain of realizing and knowing then that college was closed to practically every one of those children because they were too poor."

Costs rose faster than prices. Measured in the same dollars, a year at a public four-year college, counting tuition, fees, room and board, cost about $7,745 in 1963-64 and about $12,572 in 1999-2000. At private four-year colleges it went from about $15,093 to about $31,509, more than double.

So students borrowed. Of the people who finished a bachelor's degree in 1992-93, 49 in every 100 had borrowed money for it, an average of $12,100. Of those who finished in 1999-2000, 65 in every 100 had borrowed, an average of $19,300. Among students from the richest families the share who borrowed roughly doubled, from 24 to 46 in a hundred.

Shared with: `economy` (the cost) and `work-workers` (what a degree bought).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Teaching [R7 teaching as a job]" -->
Teachers went on strike for the first time in this era, and they got better paid without catching up.

The first teachers' strike in New York City happened on 7 November 1960, and it lasted one day. The new United Federation of Teachers called it on Election Day. The union said it had about a quarter of the city's 39,000 teachers. New York teachers voted for the right to bargain as a group in June 1961 and picked the UFT to do the bargaining that December. It was the first big-city teachers' union in the country to win that.

The first statewide teachers' strike anywhere in the United States began in Florida on 19 February 1968. More than 27,000 teachers and administrators handed in resignation letters and walked out after Governor Claude Kirk refused the Florida Education Association's demands on pay and the school budget. It ended on 8 March, when the state board of education agreed to more money for schools. Thousands of the teachers who had walked out were then refused their jobs back.

Pay went up and down. Measured in the same dollars, the average public school teacher's salary was about $58,700 in 1969-70, fell to about $52,900 by 1979-80, climbed to about $63,500 by 1989-90, and then stopped: it was about $63,500 again in 1999-2000. Ten years of work made no difference to what the job paid.

Against other jobs that need a degree, teaching paid a little less all through these years and then began to fall behind faster. The economist Sylvia Allegretto compares teachers' weekly pay with the weekly pay of other college graduates of the same age and education. Teachers earned about 7 percent less in 1979, about 5 percent less in 1993, and about 6 percent less in 1996. After 1996 the gap widened every few years.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->

<!-- hb-story:start slug="ruby-bridges" name="Ruby Bridges" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Ruby Bridges
> **Who:** Went into a white school in New Orleans at six years old and was the only pupil in it for months · **When and where:** New Orleans, Louisiana, 1960 and 1961

Ruby Bridges was born on 8 September 1954 in Tylertown, Mississippi, the eldest child in her family. She grew up in New Orleans and went to a segregated kindergarten in 1959.

In 1960 a federal judge, J. Skelly Wright, ordered New Orleans to desegregate its public schools one grade at a time, starting with first grade. The school board made Black children sit an entrance test and had their families checked first. White children moving the other way were asked for neither. Six children passed the test, and two of those stayed at their own school.

On the morning of 14 November 1960 four federal marshals walked Ruby Bridges and her mother Lucille into William Frantz Elementary School. She was six. That same morning Leona Tate, Gail Etienne and Tessie Prevost, also six, went into McDonogh No. 19 nearby with marshals of their own. Those four girls were the first Black children in white public schools in Louisiana.

The state government fought the order. Under a law passed that summer, Governor Jimmie Davis took over every decision about desegregation in New Orleans, and the legislature made it a crime, punished by fines and jail, to challenge the state's control of the schools. The White Citizens' Council held a rally of 5,000 people and told white parents to defy the court, and on 16 November a riot broke out in front of the school board building.

A crowd stood outside and screamed at her. A group of white women who called themselves the Cheerleaders came back day after day, shouted at families, damaged property, and tried to get sympathetic parents sacked. One protester threatened to poison her lunch. No record names her.

White parents took their children out of the school. From January to May 1961 Ruby Bridges was the only pupil attending Frantz. Every teacher but one refused to teach her. Barbara Henry, who had come from Boston, taught her alone for the year. Bridges did not miss a day.

Her family paid for it. Her father lost his job. Grocery stores refused to serve her mother. Her grandparents were put off the Mississippi farm they had sharecropped for 25 years. Her parents later separated.

A child psychiatrist named Robert Coles visited her through that year and asked her to draw and to talk about what was happening. Norman Rockwell painted her walk to school in 1964 and called it *The Problem We All Live With*. She saw the painting hanging in the White House on 15 July 2011.

She finished elementary school at Frantz, worked in travel for about fifteen years, and started the Ruby Bridges Foundation in 1999. A bronze statue of her was put up outside the school on 14 November 2015, fifty-five years to the day after she went in.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ruby-bridges" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="peter-mills-education" name="Peter Mills" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Peter Mills
> **Who:** A twelve-year-old put out of his Washington school and kept out, whose name is on the 1972 case that gave disabled children a right to a public school · **When and where:** Washington, D.C., 1971 and 1972

Peter Mills was in the fourth grade at Brent Elementary School in Washington, D.C. On 23 March 1971 the school put him out. The reason it gave was that he was a "behavior problem." Those are the school's words, from the court record.

He was twelve. He was a ward of the District of Columbia, which means the city government was legally responsible for him. Nobody offered him another school. In the court's words, he was "excluded from any publicly-supported education," and he stayed that way.

Later that year lawyers brought a case on behalf of him and six other children who had been shut out of Washington's schools. It was filed as *Mills v. Board of Education of the District of Columbia*. The school board's answer was partly that it did not have the money.

Judge Joseph Waddy decided the case on 1 August 1972. He ruled that the District had to provide a publicly supported education to every school-age child in it, whatever was said to be wrong with the child, and that not having the money was not a defence. Before a school could put a child out or move the child, it had to give notice and a hearing.

Three years later Congress made the same rule for the whole country. When President Ford signed the Education for All Handicapped Children Act on 29 November 1975, the Department of Education named two court cases as the ones that had established that states had to teach disabled children. *Mills* was one of them.

The court record does not say what happened to Peter Mills afterwards.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="peter-mills-education" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="dejonge-family-homeschool" name="Mark and Chris DeJonge" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Mark and Chris DeJonge
> **Who:** Parents in rural Michigan who were convicted of a crime for teaching their own children, and spent nearly ten years appealing · **When and where:** western Michigan, 1984 to 1993

In August 1984 Mark and Chris DeJonge began teaching their children at home in rural western Michigan. They used a course run by a church academy in Illinois. Neither of them held a Michigan teaching certificate.

Chris DeJonge was in her second week when officials from the state Department of Social Services came to the house and told the family the children were truants. Michigan law said a child between six and sixteen had to be taught in a public school, or in an approved private school by a certified teacher. The DeJonges were doing neither.

They were charged and convicted in the Ottawa County District Court in 1985. The trial judge said he had a "very, very favorable report on the education of the children" and was impressed by the help the family had. He convicted them anyway, because the law was about who did the teaching and not about how well it was done. The sentence was two years' probation each, a fine of $200 each, an order to have the children tested, and an order to arrange a certified teacher. The sentence was put on hold while they appealed.

Their argument was religious. They wanted what they called a "Christ centered education," because, as the opinion records it, "the major purpose of education is to show a student how to face God, not just show him how to face the world."

The appeal took the rest of the decade. The Michigan Court of Appeals ruled against them on 8 August 1989. The Michigan Supreme Court sent the case back on 17 October 1990, and the Court of Appeals ruled against them again in 1991.

On 25 May 1993 the Michigan Supreme Court decided for them, four judges to three. Justice Riley wrote that the state does have a strong interest in children being educated, but that Michigan had not shown that requiring a certified teacher was necessary to get it. The certified-teacher rule could not be applied to families with a religious objection to it.

They had been in court nine times over about ten years. Mark DeJonge, asked about it fifteen years later: "We're glad we went through it. We grew as a family and we grew as a couple."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="dejonge-family-homeschool" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="education" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Nearly every American child is in school now, so the arguments in this era are about which school a child goes to and what happens inside it. In the spring of 2020 the school buildings closed. Nearly every state kept them shut for the rest of the year, and children were taught at home over the internet.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Testing and the law [R7 testing]" -->
President George W. Bush signed the No Child Left Behind Act on 8 January 2002, at Hamilton High School in Hamilton, Ohio. The act is named for 2001 because that is the year Congress passed it. Printed at the top of it is what it was for: "to close the achievement gap with accountability, flexibility, and choice, so that no child is left behind."

The law put testing at the centre of American schooling. From the 2005-2006 school year every state had to test every child in reading and mathematics in each of grades 3 through 8. Science had to be tested at least once in grades 3 to 5, once in grades 6 to 9, and once in grades 10 to 12. Schools had to publish the scores broken out by race, by poverty, by disability, and by whether a child was still learning English. At the signing Bush said: "The fundamental principle of this bill is that every child can learn, we expect every child to learn, and you must show us whether or not every child is learning."

A deadline was written into the act. Twelve years after the end of the 2001-2002 school year, which is the school year 2013-2014, "all students in each group" were to "meet or exceed the State's proficient level of academic achievement." Every child in the country was to be good enough at reading and mathematics by 2014.

That did not happen, and Congress wrote a new law instead. The Department of Education's own account says No Child Left Behind's "prescriptive requirements became increasingly unworkable for schools and educators." President Obama signed the Every Student Succeeds Act on 10 December 2015. It kept the yearly tests, which the Department describes as "annual statewide assessments that measure students' progress toward those high standards," and gave the states back most of the decisions about what to do with the scores.

Both laws are the same 1965 law rewritten. No Child Left Behind and the Every Student Succeeds Act are new versions of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act that President Johnson signed at his old one-room school in Texas.

The Council of the Great City Schools counted what all of that meant for one child. It went through the testing calendars of 66 big-city school districts for the 2014-15 school year. It found 401 different tests in use, and worked out that a child in those districts was required to take an average of 112.3 of them between pre-kindergarten and grade 12, about eight a year. Eighth grade was the heaviest year: 20 to 25 hours of required testing, which the report put at 4.22 school days, or 2.34 percent of the year. That count leaves out practice tests, optional tests, and the time a teacher spends getting a class ready to sit one.

Shared with: `government-politics` (the law as policy).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Choice [R7 charter, magnet, private, parochial]" -->
A charter school is a public school run outside the usual school district rules, under a written agreement called a charter. In the 2022-23 school year there were 7,998 of them teaching 3,717,857 children, which is 7.6 percent of all American public school pupils. Ten years earlier, in 2012-13, it was 4.6 percent. Those figures come from the federal count of every public school in the country, and the table was prepared in February 2024. It is the newest year the federal count covers.

A magnet school is a public school that specialises in something, such as science or the arts or a language, and takes pupils from across a district instead of only from the streets around it. The first ones opened in 1968, to get white families to choose a mostly Black school without a court ordering them to, and districts still run them.

Private schools teach about one American child in eleven. In the autumn of 2021 there were 4.7 million children in private schools from kindergarten through grade 12, 9 percent of all schoolchildren. Catholic schools had 1.7 million of them, other religious schools 2.0 million, and schools with no church behind them 1.1 million. Ten years earlier the total was almost the same, 4.5 million, but the mix was different: Catholic schools lost about 200,000 children over those ten years while other religious schools gained about 300,000. Those figures were published in May 2024 and describe the autumn of 2021. The next full federal count of private schools was still being collected in 2026.

Catholic schools have been shrinking for sixty years. They had 5,601,000 children in 1964-65. In the autumn of 2021 they had 1.7 million, under a third of the number at the peak.

Vouchers and education savings accounts are the newest kind of choice, and they spend public money on private schooling. A voucher is a payment from the state that a family can put towards a private school's fees instead of sending the child to the local public school. An education savings account, usually called an ESA, is a pot of state money set aside for one child that the family can spend on several things: private school fees, a tutor, books, an online course. A tax-credit scholarship works a third way. A person or a company gives money to a scholarship fund and the state takes the same amount off their tax bill.

EdChoice, an organisation that supports these programmes and keeps the count of them, listed 69 across the country for the 2024-25 school year: 488,736 children in education savings accounts, 349,923 using vouchers, 217,194 on tax-credit scholarships, and 106,442 on tax-credit ESAs in Florida. That comes to about 1,162,000 children.

Shared with: `government-politics` (public money paying for private schools) and `religion` (the church schools).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Homeschooling [R7 homeschooling]" -->
Homeschooling roughly doubled in this era, and most of the growth came in one year. The federal survey that counts it found 1.7 percent of children aged 5 to 17 homeschooled in 1999 and 3.4 percent in 2012. In 2019 it was 2.8 percent, about 1.5 million children. Another 1.2 percent were in full-time online school. Counting both, 3.7 percent of American children were being taught at home.

Then the buildings closed. The Census Bureau put the same question to households twice in 2020. In the survey run from 23 April to 5 May, 5.4 percent of households with school-age children said they were homeschooling. In the survey run from 30 September to 12 October it was 11.1 percent. Among Black households the figure went from 3.3 percent to 16.1 percent, five times as many. The Census Bureau published that in March 2021 and was careful to say it meant real homeschooling and not a public school teaching over a screen.

Most of it stayed. Two researchers, Genevieve Smith and Angela R. Watson, went through the Census Bureau's weekly surveys from September 2022 to August 2023 and found 5.82 percent of school-age children reported as homeschooled for the 2022-23 school year, against 10.06 percent in private schools and 84.12 percent in public schools. Week by week the homeschooling figure moved between 5.14 and 6.66 percent. They point out that people had expected it to drop back once the schools reopened and it did not. It is about twice what it was before 2020.

The figure is not the same everywhere. In that same survey Alaska was highest at 12.6 percent, then Tennessee at 9 percent and West Virginia at 8.9 percent. Rhode Island was lowest at 2.9 percent, then Massachusetts at 3.1 and New York at 3.2.

Whether anyone checks on a homeschooled child depends entirely on the state, and the difference between states is enormous. These counts are kept by the Coalition for Responsible Home Education, a group that argues for more oversight, and were updated in March 2026. Twelve states do not require a family to tell anyone that they are homeschooling. Twenty-nine states do not require a homeschooled child to be assessed for progress at any point in the whole of their schooling, and only three require it of every homeschooled child. Only 31 states require a home educator to teach core subjects such as English and mathematics. Twenty-two states do not require a family to keep any academic records at all.

Texas sits at one end. A family there does not have to tell the state it is homeschooling, does not have to have the child assessed, and does not have to keep records. New York sits at the other. A parent must send the local superintendent a written notice of intent by 1 July each year, then send in an individualised home instruction plan, then file a report every quarter giving the hours of instruction and what was covered in each subject, then file an annual assessment along with the fourth quarterly report.

(**`home-family` leads on what homeschooling is like as household life.**)
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The school day now [R7 school day, school year]" -->
The American school year is 180 days almost everywhere. Of the 38 states that set a minimum number of days, 27 of them and Washington D.C. require exactly 180. Seven require fewer, and Colorado is lowest at 160. Four require more, and Kansas is highest at 186 days for kindergarten through grade 11. Those figures were checked against state law and published in September 2023.

Districts have tried changing the shape of the year. Year-round school keeps about the same number of days but spreads them across twelve months with shorter breaks. It grew and then shrank: 4.4 percent of public schools had all their pupils on a year-round cycle in 2007-08, 3.2 percent in 2011-12, and 2.5 percent in 2017-18.

The four-day week went the other way. It is mostly used by small rural districts, to save money and to hold on to teachers. Paul Thompson, an economist at Oregon State University who tracks it, counted about 2,100 schools in almost 900 districts across 26 states in September 2023. He said that was about double the number ten years earlier and almost 40 percent more than in 2019. Missouri shows how fast it moved there: 105 districts in 2020, and 128 by 2022, a quarter of the districts in the state.

The other argument about the clock is what time school starts. The American Academy of Pediatrics said in a policy statement in 2014 that middle and high schools should not start before 8:30 in the morning, because teenagers who start earlier do not get enough sleep. In the 2020-21 school year the average American public high school started at 8:07. Of those schools 8.8 percent started before 7:30, 27.5 percent between 7:30 and 7:59, 35.5 percent between 8:00 and 8:29, and 28.2 percent at 8:30 or later. About seven in ten still started before the time the doctors recommend.

Two states wrote a start time into law and then went opposite ways. California's Senate Bill 328, signed on 13 October 2019, says the school day "for middle schools ... shall begin no earlier than 8:00 a.m." and "for high schools ... shall begin no earlier than 8:30 a.m." Schools had until 1 July 2022 to comply, and rural districts were left out of it. Florida passed a similar law in 2023, to start in 2026, and then repealed it before it took effect. The Florida Senate voted for the repeal, Senate Bill 296, on 27 March 2025, after districts said they did not have the buses or the drivers to do it.

Almost every school now hands a child a computer. In the spring of 2020, 45 percent of public school principals said their school gave pupils a computer or other digital device to use at home. By September 2021, 96 percent of public schools said they were giving digital devices such as tablets to pupils who needed them, 70 percent were supplying home internet access, and 49 percent were providing internet somewhere else.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Discipline [R7 discipline]" -->
It is still lawful for an adult at school to hit a child in some American states. In 2026 the laws of 15 states allowed it, and 30 states and Washington D.C. had banned it outright. The remaining five neither allow it nor ban it in plain words. Some have other laws that courts have read as bans, and some have no law about it at all. Different organisations give different counts for that reason, and they say so themselves. At the end of the 1990s it was lawful in twenty-three states.

The federal government counts the children. In the 2021-22 school year about 24,500 public school pupils were hit at school. That is the newest national count anyone has published. The count comes out about every two years. Officials posted the data for 2023-24 in September 2026, about eight months late, as raw files without a national summary. Not every district reports it. Almost all the reported cases came from eight states, most of them in the South, and Mississippi and Arkansas had the highest rates in the country.

The same count shows which children were hit. White boys were 23 percent of all public school pupils and 47 percent of the children who received corporal punishment. Black boys were 8 percent of pupils and 20 percent of those hit. American Indian and Alaska Native boys were under 1 percent of pupils and 2 percent of those hit. Girls of every group were hit less often than their share of the school population.

Suspension is the ordinary punishment now, and it is not handed out evenly. In the 2021-22 school year about 2.3 million children, 5 percent of all public school pupils, got at least one in-school suspension, and about 2.4 million got at least one out-of-school suspension.

Black boys were 8 in every 100 public school pupils. They were 18 in every 100 of the children given an in-school suspension, 22 in every 100 of those sent home on suspension, and 21 in every 100 of those expelled. The federal report's own sentence is that "Black boys were disciplined at higher rates, compared to boys of other races." Black girls were 7 in every 100 pupils, 13 in every 100 of those sent home, and 13 in every 100 of those expelled. Every other group of girls was suspended and expelled less often than its share of the school population. White boys were 23 in every 100 pupils, 27 in every 100 of the in-school suspensions and 24 in every 100 of the expulsions.

Children with disabilities were 17 in every 100 pupils, 29 in every 100 of the children sent home on suspension, and 24 in every 100 of those expelled.

Schools also call the police. In that year districts referred about 220,000 children to law enforcement, and about 17 in every 100 of those referrals ended in an arrest at school. Black children were 15 in every 100 public school pupils, 28 in every 100 of the children referred to the police, and 33 in every 100 of the children arrested at school.

The youngest children are suspended and expelled too. In 2021-22 about 2,700 children in public preschool were suspended out of school and about 370 were expelled, out of 1.4 million children in public preschool. Black preschool children were 18 in every 100 of those enrolled and 38 in every 100 of those suspended. Preschool children with disabilities were 23 in every 100 of those enrolled and 74 in every 100 of those expelled.

Shared with: `rights-movements` (the campaigns against school discipline gaps) and `crime-justice` (police in schools).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Shootings at school" -->
Children and teachers have been shot dead inside American schools in this era. Statisticians at the National Center for Education Statistics count every time someone fires or shows a gun on school grounds, whether or not anyone is hit. In the 2021-22 school year they counted 327 shootings. Eighty-one people were killed in them and 269 were hurt, the highest numbers in the 22 years the count covers. That is the newest year of the federal count.

On 14 December 2012 Adam Lanza, who was 20, shot his way into Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut, with a rifle. He had already shot his mother dead at their home. In the school he killed the principal and the school psychologist, then went into two first-grade classrooms. He killed 20 first graders and 4 more adults there, and then shot himself. Stephen Sedensky, the state prosecutor who investigated, found that fewer than 11 minutes passed between 9:30 a.m., when the school doors were locked, and the moment Lanza killed himself.

On 14 February 2018 Nikolas Cruz, a 19-year-old former student, shot 14 students and 3 staff members dead at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, and wounded 17 more. The state commission that investigated found that Scot Peterson, the sheriff's deputy assigned to the school, "fled to a position of personal safety while Cruz shot and killed" students and staff. A jury found Peterson not guilty of child neglect on 29 June 2023.

On 24 May 2022 an 18-year-old gunman went into Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, at 11:33 a.m. with a rifle and killed 19 children and 2 teachers in two joined classrooms. Eleven police officers were inside the school within three minutes. They were shot at, pulled back, and then waited. The school district's police chief, Pete Arredondo, told officers to hold off while they looked for keys and tried to talk to the gunman. About 380 officers from 24 agencies came to the school in all. A team of Border Patrol agents and sheriff's deputies finally went in and killed the gunman at about 12:50 p.m., 77 minutes after the first officers entered the building. The Justice Department's review, published on 18 January 2024, named the officers' "most significant failure": they treated the gunman as a man shut in a room who was no longer attacking, when he was an active shooter, someone still trying to kill. Arredondo and one school officer, Adrian Gonzales, were charged with endangering and abandoning children. A jury found Gonzales not guilty on 21 January 2026. Arredondo's trial had not taken place by September 2026.

Shared with: `crime-justice` (the trials).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Remote schooling and cost" -->
School buildings across the United States closed in the spring of 2020 because of the coronavirus pandemic. Education Week tracked the closures from 6 March to 15 May 2020, first school by school and then state by state. At their peak the closures reached at least 55.1 million children in 124,000 public and private schools, and nearly every state either ordered or advised that schools stay shut for the rest of the 2019-20 school year.

School moved onto screens, and the screens were not evenly spread. In the spring of 2020, 45 percent of public school principals said their school provided a computer or digital device for pupils to use at home. In September 2020, 59 percent of adults with a child in school said the school or district had provided the computer.

National test scores are lower than they were before 2020. The National Assessment of Educational Progress is the same test given to a sample of American children decade after decade. It was given from January to March 2022, the first time since the closures. Average mathematics scores had fallen 5 points in fourth grade and 8 points in eighth grade since 2019, the largest drops since the test began in 1990. It was given again from January to March 2024. The average fourth-grade reading score was 2 points lower than in 2022 and 5 points lower than in 2019. Thirty-one percent of fourth graders reached the level the test calls Proficient, 4 percentage points fewer than in 2019. Fourth-grade mathematics was 3 points below 2019, and twelfth-grade reading and mathematics were each 3 points below 2019. The twelfth-grade results came out on 9 September 2025. Both were the lowest ever reported on those tests. Forty-five percent of high school seniors scored below the lowest level the test names, called Basic, in mathematics, and 32 percent in reading. The test does not say why scores fell, and reading scores had already started to drop between 2017 and 2019.

Schools have trouble finding teachers. In August 2024 the National Center for Education Statistics asked 1,392 public schools in every state how their hiring was going for the year ahead. Seventy-four percent said they had had difficulty filling at least one vacant teaching post. Those schools reported an average of six teaching vacancies each, and had filled 79 percent of them with fully certified teachers. The reason given most often was a lack of qualified candidates, at 64 percent, and the next was too few candidates applying, at 62 percent.

Pay is part of it. The average salary of an American public school teacher was $74,495 in the 2024-25 school year, 3.5 percent more than the $71,985 of the year before. A new teacher started on $48,112 on average. The National Education Association, the teachers' union that keeps these figures, works out that once the rise in prices is counted, teachers were earning about 5 percent less than teachers had ten years earlier.

College is the part of education that families pay for themselves. In the 2022-23 academic year the average total cost of a year at a four-year college, for a first-time full-time student living on campus, was $27,100 at a public college, $33,600 at a private for-profit college, and $58,600 at a private non-profit college. Thirty-eight percent of first-time full-time undergraduates were awarded a loan in 2020-21, down from 50 percent ten years before. Students who finished a bachelor's degree in 2015-16 with federal loans owed an average of $45,300 by 2020.
