In June 2026, 42.3 million people owed more than $1.7 trillion in federal student loans, and more than 9.3 million of them were in default, meaning they had stopped paying for long enough that the loan was counted as unpaid.

The figures in this era do not all come from the same year, because the federal counts behind them come out at different times. The school discipline figures describe the 2021-22 school year and were published in January 2025. The private school figures describe the autumn of 2021. The charter school figures describe 2022-23. The teacher pay figures describe 2024-25, and the student loan figures describe June 2026. Each was the newest published in September 2026.

Shared with: `work-workers` (teaching as a job and teacher pay) and `money` (student debt).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The boarding schools counted" -->
In this era federal officials investigated the government's own Indian boarding schools and counted the children who died at them. Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland, who is Laguna Pueblo, ordered the investigation on 22 June 2021. The announcement stated that she acted after a First Nation in Canada reported 215 unmarked graves at a former residential school in Kamloops. The final report, issued in July 2024 under Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs Bryan Newland, lists the results. Investigators found 417 federal boarding schools in 37 states or territories between 1819 and 1969, and at least 973 children who died at them. They also found burial sites at 65 of the schools, and wrote that the real number of deaths is higher.

The first report, in May 2022, listed what staff at the schools did to children: solitary confinement, withholding food, whipping, slapping, cuffing, which means hitting with the hand, and flogging, which means beating with a whip or rod. Staff also made older children punish younger ones.

On 25 October 2024 President Joe Biden spoke at the Gila Crossing Community School in the Gila River Indian Community in Arizona. "I formally apologize today as President of the United States of America for what we did," he said. He said the government had never formally apologized before. On 9 December 2024 he made the 24.5 acres of the old Carlisle Indian Industrial School grounds in Pennsylvania a national monument. The Bureau of Indian Education lists four federal off-reservation boarding schools open today: Chemawa in Oregon, Flandreau in South Dakota, Riverside in Oklahoma and Sherman in California.

Shared with: `native-nations` (leads on what the schools did to the nations).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Books and what teachers may teach" -->
School boards and state officials took thousands of books out of school libraries in this era. Lawmakers and officials in 18 states also limited what teachers may say about race and sex. PEN America, a writers' group that defends free speech, counts a school book ban as any removal or restriction of a book because of what is in it, after a complaint or an order from officials. It counted 10,046 bans in the 2023-24 school year and 6,870 in 2024-25. Florida had the most in 2024-25, at 2,304, then Texas at 1,781 and Tennessee at 1,622. In July 2025 Defense Department officials removed nearly 600 titles from the schools the Defense Department runs for children on military bases.

The American Library Association, the national group for librarians, counts school, public and college libraries together. For 2025 it recorded 4,235 different titles that people tried to have removed. Pressure groups, government officials and other decision makers started 92 percent of those attempts.

Education Week counted those 18 states, out of 44 whose lawmakers or officials had considered such limits between 2021 and March 2024. In Florida, Governor Ron DeSantis signed the Parental Rights in Education law on 28 March 2022. It limits classroom teaching about sexual orientation and gender identity in some grades.

On 27 June 2025, in *Mahmoud v. Taylor*, six Supreme Court justices ruled that parents in Montgomery County, Maryland, were entitled, while their lawsuit went on, to have their children excused from lessons using five storybooks with LGBTQ characters, which the parents objected to on religious grounds.

Shared with: `art` (the books themselves), `religion` (the court case) and `government-politics` (the laws).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Education Department, 2025 and 2026" -->
The staff of the federal Department of Education send federal money to schools and enforce the laws against discrimination in them. On 11 March 2025 Secretary of Education Linda McMahon announced layoffs that cut the staff from 4,133 people to 2,183. On 20 March President Donald Trump signed an order telling her to "take all necessary steps to facilitate the closure of the Department of Education." A federal judge in Massachusetts blocked the layoffs in May 2025. On 14 July 2025 a majority of the Supreme Court let them go ahead while the case continued. Justices Sotomayor, Kagan and Jackson disagreed in writing.

Officials then began moving the Department's work to other departments. In June 2026 they announced that special education would move to the Department of Health and Human Services, and the Office for Civil Rights, which investigates discrimination in schools, to the Justice Department. Only a law passed by Congress can close a cabinet department. By June 2026 members of Congress had voted for no such law.

Shared with: `government-politics` (the order and the court case).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="tabatha-rosproy-2020-teaching" name="Tabatha Rosproy" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Tabatha Rosproy
> **Who:** A preschool teacher who was named National Teacher of the Year in the weeks after every school building in her state closed · **When and where:** Winfield, Kansas, 2020

Tabatha Rosproy taught preschool at the Winfield Early Learning Center in Winfield, Kansas. Her classroom was not in a school building. It was inside Cumbernauld Village, a retirement community and nursing home in the town, and the programme was called Little Vikes. Her class had children with disabilities and children without them in it together, and the residents took part with the children every day. In May 2020 she was named National Teacher of the Year, the first early childhood teacher to win it.

She won it while her classroom was shut. On 17 March 2020 Governor Laura Kelly ordered every K-12 school building in Kansas closed for the rest of the school year, which made Kansas the first state in the country to do that. Rosproy was one of the co-chairs of the state task force that wrote the guidance telling Kansas teachers what to do next.

With her classroom shut, she recorded her lessons and put them on an app called Seesaw, then video-called each child once a week, one at a time. When a family could not get online she rang them, texted them, or took the materials to their home. For the families of her pupils with disabilities she prepared materials showing the parents how to do at home what she would have done in the room. She posted each child a bin of the sensory toys they liked best from the classroom, and she went round and put pinwheels in their front yards.

She was asked about it in an interview published on 22 May 2020. "Nothing will replace what we are able to do in person," she said. "But we are surviving through this and we are looking for the small victories when we have them."

She had been worried about winning in that particular year. "At first, I was nervous to be named National Teacher of the Year during this pandemic," she said, "because I wondered if I was able to make a difference."
<!-- hb-story:end slug="tabatha-rosproy-2020-teaching" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

---


<a id="chapter-31-news-communication"></a>

<!-- hb-chapter id="31" slug="news-communication" title="News and Communication" part="8" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 31: News and Communication

<!-- hb-note -->
**Angle:** How Americans learned what was happening: messengers, the post, the press, radio, TV, the feed.
**Keep out:** the inventions themselves (`technology`)
**Workspace:** `workspace/news-communication.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-news-communication.md` · **Reference:** `control/RESTRUCTURE-PLAN.md` §4 (ten-era seed, transcribed below) · `research/research-technology.md` (the machines themselves stay there). New chapter.
Editor's in-development note. Not part of the final book. The parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="news-communication" label="Before 1500" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Before 1500, news in this land moved only as fast as a person could walk, run or paddle a canoe. People carried messages along foot trails and rivers between towns. Most of what is known about how they did it comes from later accounts by Native nations and by Europeans, and from objects that archaeologists have dug up.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="runners and wampum" -->
Among the Haudenosaunee (the Six Nations, also called the Iroquois) of what is now New York, runners called the nations to council, carried news from one nation to another, and warned of danger. A runner carried a string of wampum to show that his message was official. Wampum is small beads cut from the white and purple parts of a clam shell.
The Onondaga Nation, which keeps the Confederacy's wampum, describes how a council was called. A string of wampum told each nation what the meeting was about. A wooden stick tied to the string told them when. Each day, someone cut a notch off the stick.
Shell beads found in the Northeast are about 4,500 years old. Beads drilled with stone drill bits were larger than later wampum and less common, because stone made drilling slow. After Europeans arrived, Native bead makers used iron awls and nails as drill bits.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="hand signs and trade" -->
Many different languages were spoken in this land. Near the Gulf coast and in what is now Texas, nations that could not understand each other's speech talked with their hands. Spanish travellers reported this sign language from 1527 on, and language scholars think it was in use long before they came.
Trade goods moved hundreds of miles. Copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf of Mexico turned up far from where they came from. No record survives of what news the traders passed along with the goods.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="news-communication" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In the 1500s, Spanish, French and English newcomers could send news home only by ship. Commanders wrote reports to their kings. Survivors and explorers wrote books, and printers in Europe sold them. Native nations went on sending messages by runner and by hand sign, as they had before.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a letter to a king and a book by a survivor, 1565 and 1566" -->
In September 1565 the Spanish commander Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and his soldiers killed French Protestants at Fort Caroline, in Florida, in the homeland of Timucua-speaking peoples. They then killed more of the French at an inlet to the south. On 15 October 1565 Menéndez wrote to King Philip II of Spain. By his own count his men cut the throats of 132 men at the fort and 10 more the next day. At the inlet, he wrote, the Frenchmen gave up their weapons, and "I had their hands tied behind them and put them to the knife."
The French side of the story reached Europe in print. Nicolas Le Challeux, a carpenter who escaped from Fort Caroline, wrote an account of the killings. A printer in Dieppe, France, published it in 1566. Its title called the killings the cruelty of the Spaniards against the French king's subjects.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="hand signs on the plains, 1541" -->
In 1541 the Spanish army of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado met a buffalo-hunting people on the plains of what is now the Texas Panhandle. The Spaniards called them Querechos. Pedro de Castañeda, a soldier who later wrote the army's history, recorded that "although they conversed by means of signs they made themselves understood so well that there was no need of an interpreter."
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a message carved in a post, Roanoke, 1587 to 1590" -->
In 1587 John White left 117 English colonists on Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina, and sailed to England for supplies. His granddaughter Virginia Dare, born on the island that August, was one of the colonists. The island and the coast around it were the land of Algonquian-speaking peoples, the Roanoke, Secotan and Croatoan among them. Before he left, White and the colonists agreed on a signal. If they moved, they would carve the name of the new place on a tree or a doorpost. If they left because they were in danger, they would carve a cross above the name.
War between England and Spain kept White from sailing back until 1590. On 18 August 1590 he found the houses gone and a fence of posts around the empty site. One post had CROATOAN carved on it "in fayre Capitall letters," and a tree had the letters CRO. There was no cross. White wrote that Croatoan was the place where Manteo was born. Manteo was an Algonquian man who sailed to England in 1584, learned English on the voyage and in London, and came back in 1585 as an interpreter for the English. White called the people of Croatoan "our friends." A storm drove White's ship out to sea before he could search there. No record shows that anyone from England ever found the colonists.
Readers in Europe learned about this coast from printed books. Thomas Harriot, who had been there in 1585 and 1586, published *A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia* in 1588. In 1590 the engraver Theodor de Bry printed it again in four languages, with engravings copied from John White's paintings.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="manteo-news-communication" name="Manteo" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Manteo
> **Who:** An Algonquian man, born on Croatoan by John White's account, who learned English and interpreted for the English · **When and where:** the Outer Banks of North Carolina and London, 1584 to 1590

In 1584 the English captains Philip Amadas and Arthur Barlowe spent six weeks on the Outer Banks. When they sailed home, Wingina, a leader of the Algonquian people there, chose two men to go with them: Manteo and Wanchese. The ship reached England in mid-September. Both men began to learn English from the sailors during the voyage. In London they met Sir Walter Raleigh, who sent the voyages.

By the end of 1584 Manteo could speak enough English to interpret. He sailed home on 9 April 1585 on the *Tyger*, the lead ship of Raleigh's fleet.

In 1587 he helped the new colonists set up a village near the old English fort on Roanoke Island. On 13 August 1587 the English baptized Manteo into their church and named him Lord of "Dasamongueponke." White wrote in 1590 that the colonists had gone to Croatoan, "the place where Manteo was borne." When White came back, he found neither the colonists nor Manteo. No record says what happened to him.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="manteo-news-communication" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="news-communication" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In the 1600s the English colonies got their first mail services and their first newspaper. The men who governed the colonies decided who could print news. In 1690 the governor and council of Massachusetts shut down the first newspaper four days after it appeared. In Virginia the governor and council stopped all printing in 1683. In New Mexico, Pueblo runners carried the plan for a revolt against Spanish rule from town to town.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="letters by ship, by tavern and by planter" -->
Most letters in the early colonies went across the ocean to England and back. In 1639 the General Court of Massachusetts named Richard Fairbanks's tavern in Boston as the place to leave and collect letters sent "beyond the seas." Inside the colonies, people sent letters with friends, merchants and Native messengers.
In Virginia, around the middle of the 1600s, officials marked government letters "for public service." Each planter had to send them on to the next plantation. A planter who failed to do it lost a hogshead (a large barrel) of tobacco. On the big Southern plantations, the messengers were usually enslaved people, according to the Postal Service's own history.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the first post rider, 1673, and the first postal system, 1692" -->
On 22 January 1673 the first post rider left New York for Boston, about 250 miles, on a monthly mail route between the two colonies. Governor Francis Lovelace of New York set it up with John Winthrop Jr. of Connecticut. The rider was to go once a month and took about two weeks each way. The service did not last long, but his route became the Boston Post Road. William Penn set up Pennsylvania's first post office in 1683.
In 1692 the English Crown gave Thomas Neale the right to run a mail service for all the colonies for 21 years. Neale never came to America. Andrew Hamilton, governor of New Jersey, ran it as his deputy.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Virginia: no printing allowed, 1671 to 1730" -->
In 1671 Governor William Berkeley of Virginia wrote to the king's officials in London: "I thank God, there are no free schools nor printing, and I hope we shall not have these hundred years." He gave his reason: printing spread new religious groups, disobedience and attacks on the government.
In 1682 a merchant named John Buckner brought a printer, William Nuthead, to Virginia. By February 1683 Nuthead had printed the colony's new laws. Governor Thomas Culpeper and his council ordered both men to stop printing. The next governor, Francis Howard, arrived in 1684 with orders from King Charles II that barred printing in Virginia. Virginia had no printer again until William Parks arrived about 1730.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the first newspaper, 1690, closed after one issue" -->
From 1667 on, printers in Massachusetts printed single sheets of news, called broadsides, each about one event. On 25 September 1690 Benjamin Harris printed *Publick Occurrences, Both Forreign and Domestick*. He marked it "Numb. 1" and planned to print it once a month. It was three printed pages and a blank fourth page. Harris's notice suggested that readers could write more news on the blank page and pass the paper on.
Four days later, on 29 September, Governor Simon Bradstreet and the Massachusetts council ordered it "Suppressed and called in." They said Harris had printed it without their permission. They also objected to what it said. It accused Native allies of the English of "barbarous" cruelty to French prisoners, and it complained that colonial officials told the Mohawks too much about English war plans. It also printed a rumour about the private life of King Louis XIV of France. The council ordered that no one could print news in the colony without a licence from the government. There was never a second issue. One copy is known to survive, in London.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-harris-news-communication" name="Benjamin Harris" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin Harris
> **Who:** The London printer who printed the first newspaper in the English colonies · **When and where:** London, then Boston, 1679 to 1695

Benjamin Harris was born about 1647. In London in the 1670s and 1680s he printed pamphlets for Protestants who had broken away from the Church of England. He was a Baptist and spoke out against King Charles II. In 1679 he printed a newspaper without a licence, *The Domestick Intelligence*. English officials jailed him twice. After a third arrest in 1685 he fled to the Netherlands. A year later he sailed to Boston and opened a print shop.

On 25 September 1690 he printed *Publick Occurrences*. His opening notice said he wanted to stop the "many False Reports, maliciously made, and spread among us." The paper reported a fire that burned about 20 houses and smallpox spreading through Boston. On 29 September the governor and council ordered every copy called in and forbade him to print any newspaper again.

Harris obeyed. In 1692 he became the colony's official printer. He went back to England in 1695 and started a London paper, the *London Post*, in 1699. He died in 1720.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-harris-news-communication" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="knotted cords and the Pueblo Revolt, 1680" -->
In 1680 the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico planned to drive out the Spanish. Spanish soldiers and settlers had come in 1598 under Juan de Oñate and had taken Pueblo land, labour and food. In 1675 the Spanish governor Juan Francisco Treviño ordered the arrest of 47 Pueblo religious leaders. Four were sentenced to hang. Three were hanged, and one killed himself. Spanish officials whipped the others in public and put them in prison. One of the men released was Po'pay, a Tewa leader from Ohkay Owingeh.
Po'pay planned the revolt with towns that spoke at least five different languages. To make them all rise on the same day, he sent runners with knotted cords. Each town untied one knot a day. When the last knot was untied, the revolt would begin. Sources differ on the day planned: 11 August or 13 August.
The Spanish learned of the plan when they caught two of the runners on 9 August. The revolt began a day early, on 10 August 1680. Pueblo fighters killed about 400 people, including 21 of the 33 Spanish priests in New Mexico. On 21 August Governor Antonio de Otermín led about 2,000 Spanish settlers out of Santa Fe, south to El Paso. The Spanish did not return until 1692.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="catua-and-omtua" name="Nicolás Catua and Pedro Omtua" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Nicolás Catua and Pedro Omtua
> **Who:** Two young runners from Tesuque Pueblo who carried the knotted cords of the Pueblo Revolt · **When and where:** New Mexico, 8 and 9 August 1680

On the morning of 8 August 1680, Pedro Omtua and Nicolás Catua set out from Tesuque Pueblo with knotted cords for the Tano towns to the south. Tesuque is Tewa for "village of the narrow place of the cottonwood trees." The first town they reached was Pecos.

After they left Pecos, Christian Pueblo people told the Franciscan missionary Fernando de Velasco that two Tewa messengers had visited the war chief's house. Two Pueblo leaders from the Galisteo Basin who sided with the Spanish also sent word of the revolt to Governor Antonio de Otermín. On 9 August Otermín ordered the messengers arrested. Spanish officials tortured Catua and Omtua to make them explain the knotted cord, and then hanged them. The surviving accounts do not name the men who tortured and hanged them.

When Po'pay heard that the runners had been caught, he ordered the revolt to start a day early. It began on 10 August.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="catua-and-omtua" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="news-communication" label="1700 to 1750" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Between 1704 and 1750, weekly newspapers started in Boston, Philadelphia, New York, Charleston and Williamsburg. Most were run by printers, and several printers were also postmasters. Colonial governors and assemblies still jailed printers who offended them. The papers made money from advertisements, and many of the advertisements offered enslaved people for sale or offered rewards for people who had escaped from slavery.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Boston News-Letter, 1704" -->
On 24 April 1704 John Campbell, the postmaster of Boston, printed the first issue of the *Boston News-Letter*. It was one small sheet printed on both sides, once a week. The words "Published by Authority" appeared in its title from the first issue until 1720, which told readers that Campbell printed it with the government's approval. Most of the first issue was copied from London newspapers of mid-December, more than four months old. Local news filled one column.
The *News-Letter* came out every week until February 1776, the first newspaper in the colonies to keep going. It had no rival in Boston until the *Boston Gazette* began on 21 December 1719. The *American Weekly Mercury* started in Philadelphia the next day.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Courant: a paper the government did not approve, 1721 to 1723" -->
James Franklin started the *New-England Courant* in Boston in August 1721, during a smallpox epidemic. The minister Cotton Mather and the doctor Zabdiel Boylston urged inoculation. In inoculation, a doctor put a little pus from a sick person into a cut in the skin of a healthy person, to give a milder case. Mather had learned of the method from Onesimus, an African man he held in slavery, and from other enslaved Africans. Almost all Boston doctors except Boylston opposed it. The *Courant* printed attacks on the people who supported it. On 14 November 1721 someone threw a homemade bomb through a window of Mather's house, with a note that read "Cotton Mather, You Dog, Dam You: I'll inoculate you with this, with a Pox to you." The thrower was never identified. About 6,000 people in Boston caught smallpox that year, and 844 died. Of the 248 people Boylston inoculated, 98 out of 100 survived. Among people who caught smallpox the ordinary way, 85 out of 100 survived.
In June 1722 the *Courant* printed a short item hinting that the Massachusetts government was slow to send a ship after pirates. The General Court, the colony's assembly, had James Franklin jailed for a month. His younger brother Benjamin, then 16, ran the paper while he was locked up. James was let out on 2 July 1722. Early in 1723 the General Court forbade James Franklin to print the *Courant* unless officials checked it first. The paper then came out under Benjamin's name instead, until it closed in 1726.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Weekly Journal and the Zenger trial, 1733 to 1736" -->
In New York the only newspaper, the *New-York Gazette*, printed Governor William Cosby's side. In 1733 Cosby removed the chief judge, Lewis Morris, after Morris ruled against him. Morris and his friends started the *New-York Weekly Journal* on 5 November 1733 to attack the governor, with the German-born printer John Peter Zenger as its printer. Cosby had copies of the paper burned in public by the hangman.
Officials arrested Zenger on 17 November 1734 for seditious libel. Seditious libel then meant printing anything that lowered people's opinion of the government, whether or not it was true. He could not pay his bail of £400 and stayed in jail for more than eight months. His wife Anna kept the *Journal* coming out. On 4 August 1735 a jury found him not guilty. The verdict changed no law, but in 1736 Zenger printed an account of the trial, *A Brief Narrative of the Case and Tryal of John Peter Zenger*, and printers reprinted it many times.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="anna-zenger-news-communication" name="Anna Catharina Zenger" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Anna Catharina Zenger
> **Who:** The printer's wife who kept the *New-York Weekly Journal* coming out while her husband was in jail, and ran the print shop after he died · **When and where:** New York City, 1734 to 1748

Anna Catharina Maulin married John Peter Zenger on 11 September 1722. When officials jailed him on 17 November 1734, she took charge of the shop and kept the *Journal* coming out every week. Zenger later wrote that he gave her his instructions "through the hole of the door of the prison."

After the trial Zenger became New York's official printer in 1737. He died on 28 July 1746. Anna Zenger ran the family print shop for more than two years, until their eldest son, John, took over in December 1748.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="anna-zenger-news-communication" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="printers who were postmasters, and papers in German" -->
Many printers were also postmasters, because the post office brought them letters and news from other towns first. A postmaster could also refuse to let the post riders carry a rival's newspaper. Andrew Bradford, printer of the *American Weekly Mercury*, did that to Benjamin Franklin's paper while Bradford kept Philadelphia's post office. Franklin wrote that he got his papers carried only by bribing the riders to take them in secret. In 1737 Alexander Spotswood, the deputy postmaster general for the colonies, took the post office away from Bradford and gave it to Franklin, who was 31.
Franklin also set up partners as printers in other towns. In November 1733 he set up Lewis Timothy as printer of the *South-Carolina Gazette* in Charleston. Virginia got its first newspaper, the *Virginia Gazette*, on 6 August 1736, printed by William Parks.
Franklin tried a German-language paper, the *Philadelphische Zeitung*, in May and June 1732, and it failed. On 20 August 1739 Christopher Sauer, a German printer in Germantown, started a German-language paper. His family printed it, under changing names, until 1777. Sauer took his news of Europe from sixteen European newspapers that reached him each month.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="elizabeth-timothy" name="Elizabeth Timothy" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Elizabeth Timothy
> **Who:** A Dutch-born widow who ran the *South-Carolina Gazette* and became the first woman in the colonies to own and publish a newspaper · **When and where:** Charleston, South Carolina, 1738 to 1746

Elizabeth Timothy's husband, Lewis Timothy, printed the *South-Carolina Gazette* in Charleston under a six-year partnership with Benjamin Franklin. He died in December 1738 after what the paper called "an unhappy Accident." He left her with six small children and a seventh about to be born.

The partnership said that their eldest son, Peter, would carry on the business. Peter was too young, so she ran the shop herself. She printed the next issue on 4 January 1739 and promised to make the paper "as entertaining and correct as may be reasonably expected." By the end of 1739 she had bought out Franklin's share. The *South Carolina Encyclopedia* calls her the first woman in the American colonies to own and publish a newspaper. Franklin praised how exactly she kept her accounts.

She handed the shop to Peter when he came of age in 1746 and opened a bookstore next to it. She died in 1757. Her will left her children eight enslaved people, along with her other property.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="elizabeth-timothy" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="advertisements for people as property" -->
Newspaper owners made much of their money from advertisements. Franklin's *Pennsylvania Gazette* printed advertisements from slave owners and slave traders. Some offered enslaved men, women and children for sale. Others offered rewards for people who had escaped. By the 1750s these made up nearly a quarter of the paper's advertisements. Franklin was paid for printing them.
Franklin's own household held enslaved people from about 1735 until 1790. Records show he bought at least seven people: Joseph, Jemima, Peter, King, Othello, George and Bob.
In 1740 lawmakers in South Carolina made it a crime to teach an enslaved person to write.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="benjamin-franklin-news-communication" name="Benjamin Franklin" movie="Benjamin Franklin (2022)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Benjamin Franklin
> **Who:** A Boston printer's apprentice who became Philadelphia's leading newspaper owner and its postmaster · **When and where:** Boston, 1718 to 1723, and Philadelphia, 1723 to 1753
> **Movie:** Benjamin Franklin (2022), a documentary by Ken Burns about his life

Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706. In 1718 he was apprenticed to his brother James, a printer. He carried copies of the *New-England Courant* through the streets to the people who paid for it. In 1722, at 16, he wrote letters to the paper under the name "Silence Dogood." He later wrote that his brother "had often beaten me." When James was jailed in 1722, Benjamin ran the paper. In 1723, at 17, he broke his apprenticeship and ran away to Philadelphia.

On 2 October 1729 he bought the *Pennsylvania Gazette* from the printer Samuel Keimer. Advertising became its main source of money, and he grew it from two pages to four partly to hold more advertisements. In 1732 he began *Poor Richard's Almanack*, which he wrote under the name Richard Saunders. He wrote that he sold "near ten thousand" copies a year, and that people "bought scarcely any other books."

In 1737 he became postmaster of Philadelphia. He wrote that the post office "facilitated the correspondence that improv'd my newspaper" and brought more readers and more advertisements. In 1753 the Crown made him one of two deputy postmasters general for all the colonies.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="benjamin-franklin-news-communication" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="news-communication" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
From 1765 to 1800, printers, letter writers and post riders spread the arguments and the news that led to the American Revolution. Supporters of independence wrecked the press of a New York printer who took Britain's side. In 1791 the new country wrote freedom of the press into the First Amendment. In 1798 the Federalist majority in Congress passed the Sedition Act, and federal officials jailed newspaper editors who criticized President John Adams.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Stamp Act and the printers, 1765" -->
Parliament in London passed the Stamp Act in March 1765, and it took effect on 1 November 1765. It taxed newspapers, pamphlets, almanacs and legal papers in the colonies. Each newspaper printed on half a sheet of paper owed a halfpenny, and a paper on a whole sheet owed a penny. Every advertisement in a newspaper owed two shillings. The tax had to be paid on stamped paper made in London.
On 31 October 1765, the day before the tax began, William Bradford of Philadelphia printed his *Pennsylvania Journal* with black borders, like a tombstone. In place of the official stamp he printed a skull and crossbones. His front page said the paper was "EXPIRING: In Hopes of a Resurrection to LIFE again." Bradford never actually stopped. He printed the next issue on 7 November. John Hughes, the man appointed to hand out the stamps in Philadelphia, had promised not to enforce the act after opponents of the tax threatened him with violence and with destroying his property. Parliament repealed the tax in 1766.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="committees of correspondence, 1772 to 1774" -->
On 2 November 1772 Boston's town leaders voted to set up a Committee of Correspondence of 21 men, with Samuel Adams among them. The committee wrote a report on the colonists' rights and on how Parliament had broken them. Printed as the Boston Pamphlet, it went to every town in Massachusetts. On 12 March 1773 Virginia's House of Burgesses, the colony's elected assembly, set up an 11-man committee, including Patrick Henry and Thomas Jefferson, to write to the other colonies' assemblies. The Virginia committee asked the other assemblies to share news of laws from London and of what each colony planned to do about them. Within a year, eleven colonial assemblies had their own committees. Only North Carolina and Pennsylvania did not.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the news of Lexington, April 1775" -->
On the morning of 19 April 1775 British soldiers fired on the militia at Lexington, Massachusetts. At about 10 o'clock that morning, in Watertown, Joseph Palmer of the Massachusetts Committee of Safety wrote a letter "To all the Friends of American liberty." It said the soldiers had killed six men and wounded four. He gave it to a rider, Isaac Bissell, to carry toward Connecticut. At each town, the local committee copied the letter, added a line saying the copy was true, and sent riders on with copies.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="isaac-bissell" name="Isaac Bissell" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Isaac Bissell
> **Who:** A 26-year-old blacksmith from Suffield, Connecticut, who carried a written report of the Lexington shooting from Massachusetts to Connecticut · **When and where:** Watertown, Massachusetts, to Connecticut, 19 and 20 April 1775

Isaac Bissell was a blacksmith from Suffield, a town on Connecticut's northern border. On 19 April 1775 he was in Watertown, Massachusetts. At about 10 in the morning Joseph Palmer handed him the letter about the killings at Lexington. The letter said that "the Bearer Mr. Isaac Bissell" was "charged to alarm the country quite to Connecticutt," and it asked people along the way to give him fresh horses.

Bissell reached Worcester in the early afternoon. The town clerk, Nathan Baldwin, copied the letter and signed the copy. At Springfield another copy was made. On the morning of 20 April the letter reached Connecticut's leaders. In Wethersfield, the politician Silas Deane wrote in his journal that the news "was discredited, from the suddeness of its arrival." Governor Jonathan Trumbull believed it and called Connecticut's assembly together to raise soldiers.

Bissell then marched to the siege of Boston as a private in the Suffield militia. In July 1775 the Massachusetts committee approved his bill as a post rider for two pounds and one shilling, but he had trouble getting paid.

Many books call the rider "Israel Bissell" and say he rode all the way to Philadelphia. The historian J. L. Bell found that his name was Isaac and that other riders carried copies of the letter beyond Connecticut.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="isaac-bissell" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Common Sense and the Declaration in print, 1776" -->
On 10 January 1776 the Philadelphia printer Robert Bell published *Common Sense*, a pamphlet by Thomas Paine that argued for independence from Britain. Twenty-five printings are known, sixteen of them in Philadelphia. Paine claimed that 120,000 copies sold in the first three months, and later claimed 150,000. A biographer in 1892 guessed half a million. No sales records survive. The historian Trish Loughran counted the known printings and put the highest possible number at 75,000, and she thinks the real number was much lower.
Congress approved the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776. That night the Philadelphia printer John Dunlap printed about 200 copies, called broadsides, to send to the states and to the army. On 9 July George Washington's soldiers in New York City heard it read aloud. Twenty-six of Dunlap's copies are known to survive.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="thomas-paine" name="Thomas Paine" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Thomas Paine
> **Who:** An English-born writer whose pamphlet *Common Sense* argued that the colonies should declare independence · **When and where:** Philadelphia, 1774 to 1776, and with the army, 1776

Thomas Paine was born in Thetford, England, on 29 January 1737. He met Benjamin Franklin in London, and Franklin gave him letters of introduction. He arrived in Philadelphia on 30 November 1774. He helped edit the *Pennsylvania Magazine* and wrote articles under false names, including one called "African Slavery in America" that attacked the slave trade.

*Common Sense* came out on 10 January 1776 without his name on it. Paine was paid nothing for it. He fell out with its first printer, Robert Bell, and other printers printed it without asking him. Paine later wrote that he gave the right to print it to every state.

On 19 December 1776, when Washington's army was close to breaking apart, Paine published *The American Crisis*. It began, "These are the times that try men's souls." Washington ordered it read to his troops. Paine died in New York City on 8 June 1809.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="thomas-paine" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a Loyalist printer's press wrecked, 1775" -->
Supporters of independence also attacked printers who took Britain's side. James Rivington printed the *New-York Gazetteer*, one of the most widely read newspapers in the colonies, which took the British government's side. In November 1775 Isaac Sears led a band of armed Sons of Liberty from New Haven, Connecticut, to Rivington's shop in New York City. They wrecked his press and his type, the metal letters a printer sets by hand. Rivington left for England a few weeks later. After the British army took New York in 1776, he came back with the title of King's Printer and printed his paper again on the British side until the British left in November 1783.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="a postal service for the new country, 1775 to 1792" -->
In 1774 British officials dismissed Benjamin Franklin as deputy postmaster general for being, in the Postal Service history's words, "too much of an American." The printer William Goddard set up a rival mail service, which he called the Constitutional Post. He warned that the British post let officials open letters and read them as proof of treason. On 26 July 1775 the Continental Congress made Franklin its postmaster general. Goddard's network of post offices became the base of the new American postal system.
The Constitution, approved in 1788, gave Congress the power "To establish Post Offices and post Roads." In 1789 the country had 75 post offices and about 2,400 miles of post roads for almost four million people. The Post Office Act of 20 February 1792 let newspapers travel by mail at very low rates and made it a crime for postal officials to open letters.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="mary-katharine-goddard" name="Mary Katharine Goddard" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Mary Katharine Goddard
> **Who:** A printer and newspaper publisher who ran Baltimore's post office for 14 years and printed the first copy of the Declaration that listed the signers · **When and where:** Baltimore, Maryland, 1774 to 1789

Mary Katharine Goddard was born on 16 June 1738 in Connecticut, in a family of printers and postmasters. She learned printing in the 1760s in her brother William's shop in Providence, Rhode Island. In 1774 she moved to Baltimore to run his print shop and his newspaper, the *Maryland Journal*, while he travelled to promote his Constitutional Post. She reprinted *Common Sense* in the *Journal*.

In 1775 she became postmaster of Baltimore, the first woman known to be a postmaster under the new American government. Postmasters then earned a share of the postage, not a salary, and prices rose fast during the war. When Congress did not pay her, she paid the post riders and the rent herself. In 1778 she let readers pay for the paper in beeswax, flour, lard, butter, beef or pork.

In January 1777 the Continental Congress, then meeting in Baltimore, ordered new copies of the Declaration of Independence. Goddard printed them on 18 January 1777. They were the first printed copies to show the signers' names. At the bottom she printed "Baltimore, in Maryland: Printed by Mary Katharine Goddard." Nine are known to survive.

In January 1784 her brother pushed her out of the *Maryland Journal*. In October 1789 the new postmaster general, Samuel Osgood, replaced her with a man. His assistant, John Burrell, said the job might need "more travelling ... than a woman could undertake." More than 200 people in Baltimore signed a letter asking that she keep the job. She wrote to President George Washington and to the Senate. Neither helped her. She ran a bookshop in Baltimore until about 1810 and died there on 12 August 1816.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="mary-katharine-goddard" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the First Amendment and the party papers, 1789 to 1793" -->
The First Amendment took effect on 15 December 1791. It says that "Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press."
Newspapers took sides at once. From 1789 John Fenno's *Gazette of the United States* supported Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton. Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson and Congressman James Madison wanted a paper on their side. Jefferson gave the poet Philip Freneau a part-time State Department job as a translating clerk, paid $250 a year, and Freneau started the *National Gazette* on 31 October 1791. It attacked President George Washington's government and had about 1,700 subscribers before Freneau closed it on 26 October 1793. Benjamin Franklin's grandson, Benjamin Franklin Bache, attacked Washington and later John Adams in his Philadelphia paper, the *Aurora*.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Sedition Act, 1798 to 1801" -->
In 1798 the United States was close to war with France. President John Adams's party, the Federalists, held a majority in Congress. The Federalist majority passed the Sedition Act, and Adams signed it on 14 July 1798. It made it a crime to write or print "any false, scandalous and malicious writing" against the federal government, Congress or the President. The punishment was a fine of up to $2,000 and up to two years in prison. Unlike the old law in the Zenger trial, the act let a defendant prove that his words were true, and it let the jury decide the law as well as the facts.
Federal judges and prosecutors used it mostly against editors of newspapers that supported Jefferson's party, the Democratic-Republicans. Historians have long counted 17 indictments and 10 convictions. The legal historian Wendell Bird found 11 more prosecutions of 16 more people. Among those charged were Congressman Matthew Lyon of Vermont, William Duane of the *Aurora*, Ann Greenleaf of New York's *Argus*, and Anthony Haswell of the *Vermont Gazette*. Luther Baldwin and Brown Clark of Newark, New Jersey, were charged for words against President Adams spoken in a tavern.
Federalist supporters assaulted Benjamin Franklin Bache in Philadelphia, and he was barred from attending the House of Representatives. Officials arrested him in 1798 for libelling President Adams. He kept printing the *Aurora* through a yellow fever epidemic and died of the fever on 10 September 1798, at 29, a month before his trial date. His widow kept the paper going, with William Duane as editor. The act ended on 3 March 1801.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="matthew-lyon" name="Matthew Lyon" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Matthew Lyon
> **Who:** An Irish-born congressman and newspaper owner, the first person tried under the Sedition Act · **When and where:** Vermont, 1798 to 1799

Matthew Lyon came to America from Ireland, fought in the Revolutionary War, and in 1797 went to Congress for Vermont. He owned a newspaper. In a letter that a newspaper printed, he wrote of seeing the public good "swallowed up in a continual grasp for power, in an unbounded thirst for ridiculous pomp, foolish adulation, or selfish avarice." He also read aloud at campaign rallies a letter by the poet Joel Barlow that said Adams should be sent to a "madhouse."

On 5 October 1798 a federal grand jury in Vermont charged him on three counts under the Sedition Act. A deputy marshal arrested him the next day. He was the first person tried under the act. At his trial in Rutland on 9 October he defended himself and argued that the act broke the Constitution. Justice William Paterson of the Supreme Court told the jury that its job had "nothing whatever to do with the constitutionality or unconstitutionality of the sedition law." The jury, drawn from towns that supported Adams's party, found him guilty within an hour. Paterson sentenced him to four months in jail and a $1,000 fine.

He was held in the jail at Vergennes. He ran for Congress again from his cell, and the voters of his district re-elected him. He was let out on 9 February 1799.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="matthew-lyon" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="news-communication" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
By the 1830s the United States had about 900 newspapers, and the 1850 census counted 2,526. Together they printed about half a billion copies a year for a population of about 23 million. From 1833 a New York printer sold a daily paper for one cent, when most daily papers cost six. From 1844 the telegraph carried news along a wire in minutes. Free Black New Yorkers started the first Black-owned newspaper in 1827, and the Cherokee Nation started the first Native American newspaper in 1828. People who defended slavery or wanted Cherokee land attacked these editors. Georgia's militia seized the Cherokee press, the Postmaster General let Southern postmasters hold back antislavery papers, and mobs wrecked presses and killed an editor.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the last Sedition Act trials, 1800" -->
The Sedition Act of 1798 was still the law in 1800. On 24 May 1800 a federal grand jury in Richmond, Virginia, charged the writer James Callender for a pamphlet called *The Prospect Before Us*, which attacked President John Adams. The jury found him guilty on 3 June, the same day the trial began. Justice Samuel Chase sentenced him to nine months in prison and a fine. The Federal Judicial Center's history gives the fine as $400 in one place and $200 in another. In Philadelphia the same year, Chase sentenced the writer Thomas Cooper to six months and a $400 fine. The act ended on 3 March 1801. Thomas After Thomas Jefferson became president in 1801, he pardoned Callender.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="newspapers by mail, and who could carry it" -->
Newspapers travelled through the post office. Under the Post Office Act of 1792, newspapers went by mail at very low rates, and editors mailed papers to each other for free. Small papers used these free copies as their source of news from far away. Indiana had one newspaper in 1810 and 73 by 1840. By 1831 the post office employed 76 percent of all the people who worked for the federal government. Postmasters outnumbered soldiers, 8,764 to 6,332.
Letters cost much more than newspapers. From 1799 to 1815 a letter of one sheet cost 8 cents to send 40 miles and 25 cents to send more than 500 miles. A second sheet doubled the price. In 1845 postal officials began charging by weight, and in 1847 they introduced postage stamps.
From 1802 to 1865, federal postal law required mail carriers to be "free white persons." Mail contractors who broke the rule were fined. For 63 years no Black American, free or enslaved, could legally carry the mail.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Freedom's Journal, the first Black-owned newspaper, 1827" -->
In March 1827 a group of free Black New Yorkers met to start a newspaper. They chose Samuel Cornish, a Presbyterian minister, and John Brown Russwurm, one of the first Black Americans to graduate from a college in the United States, as editors. *Freedom's Journal* came out on 16 March 1827 from 5 Varick Street in Manhattan. It was the first newspaper owned and run by Black Americans. The first issue said, "We wish to plead our own cause. Too long have others spoken for us." The editors answered the attacks on Black people printed in other New York papers and wrote against slavery. The paper cost $3 a year and reached readers in 11 states, Washington, D.C., Canada, Europe and Haiti. David Walker, who in 1829 wrote a pamphlet urging enslaved people to fight for their freedom, sold subscriptions for it. Cornish quit in September 1827 because Russwurm supported sending free Black Americans to Africa, a plan called colonization, and Cornish opposed it. The last issue came out on 28 March 1829.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Cherokee Phoenix, 1828 to 1835" -->
In 1825 the Cherokee Nation's council set aside $1,500 for a printing press and type. With help from the missionary Samuel Worcester, the Cherokee set up a print shop at New Echota, their capital, in land the state of Georgia claimed. The iron press came by ship from Boston. Workers cast type for the Cherokee syllabary, the writing system Sequoyah made, in which each symbol stands for a syllable. Sources count 85 or 86 symbols. The *Cherokee Phoenix* came out on 21 February 1828, with columns in Cherokee beside columns in English. It was the first newspaper printed by a Native American nation. It printed the Cherokee Nation's laws and news, and it argued against the plan to force the Cherokee to move west.
Georgia and federal officials made the paper hard to keep going. Colonel Charles Nelson, commander of the Georgia Guard, a state militia sent to police Cherokee land, threatened to shut the paper down and to beat its editor. President Andrew Jackson ordered the Cherokee Nation's yearly payment from the federal government paid to individuals, which cut off the paper's money. Georgia officials ordered the paper's white printer to leave, and a local sheriff sued the editor, Elijah Hicks, for libel. The last issue came out in May 1834. In 1835 Principal Chief John Ross planned to start the paper again. Men of the Georgia Guard went to New Echota, took the press and threw out the type. Two accounts say they also burned the building, and that Stand Watie, a Cherokee who supported removal, helped them. The records do not name the officer who led them.
Shared with: `native-nations` (the Cherokee Nation, removal and the Trail of Tears) · `education` (Sequoyah's writing system and Cherokee reading).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="elias-boudinot" name="Elias Boudinot" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Elias Boudinot
> **Who:** A Cherokee writer who edited the *Cherokee Phoenix*, the first Native American newspaper, and later signed the treaty that gave up the Cherokee homeland · **When and where:** New Echota, Cherokee Nation (in present-day Georgia), 1826 to 1835, and Park Hill, Indian Territory, 1837 to 1839

Elias Boudinot was born in the Cherokee Nation, in what is now northwest Georgia, about 1804. Sources give years from 1802 to 1804. His Cherokee name was Gallegina, which means "the Buck." He studied at a missionary school in Cornwall, Connecticut, and took the name of Elias Boudinot, a white supporter of the school. When he became engaged to Harriet Gold, a white woman from Cornwall, opponents of the marriage burned the couple in effigy, meaning they set fire to dummies made to look like them. They married in 1826.

In 1826 Boudinot went on a speaking tour, including Philadelphia, giving a speech called "An Address to the Whites" and collecting money for a Cherokee press. He became editor of the *Cherokee Phoenix* when it began in 1828. He printed reports of how the Georgia Guard treated missionaries in the Cherokee Nation, and the Guard's commander threatened to beat him.

By 1832 Boudinot had decided that the Cherokee could not stop the United States from forcing them west. He wanted to argue for a removal treaty in the paper. Principal Chief John Ross and the council opposed removal, and Boudinot resigned in August 1832. In December 1835 he and a small group of Cherokee signed the Treaty of New Echota, which gave up all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi River. Most Cherokee opposed removal.

Boudinot moved west to Park Hill, in Indian Territory, in 1837. On 22 June 1839 a group of Cherokee who supported John Ross and opposed the treaty stabbed him to death. On the same day other men killed his uncle Major Ridge and his cousin John Ridge, who had also signed. The killers were never identified or tried.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="elias-boudinot" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="newspapers against slavery, and the mobs that attacked them, 1831 to 1835" -->
On 1 January 1831 William Lloyd Garrison, a white abolitionist, began *The Liberator* in Boston. It called for ending slavery at once. It had about 3,000 paying readers. Its masthead showed an enslaved man being whipped and children being sold away from their parents in Washington, D.C. Garrison wrote that "slavery and freedom of the press cannot exist together." By 1835 the American Anti-Slavery Society was printing more than a million papers and pamphlets a year.
In the summer of 1835 the society mailed its papers to people in the South. On the night of 29 July 1835 a group of men in Charleston, South Carolina, broke into the post office, took the bags of antislavery papers and burned them. Federal law protected the mail. Postmaster General Amos Kendall, a close ally of President Andrew Jackson, gave Southern postmasters permission to refuse to deliver antislavery papers.
On 21 October 1835 a crowd gathered outside *The Liberator*'s office in Boston, where the Boston Female Anti-Slavery Society was meeting. A local paper put the crowd at 5,000. The men forced the women out, seized Garrison, tied a rope around his waist and dragged him through the streets. They nearly tarred and feathered him. The mayor had him held in the city jail overnight for his safety. Garrison later wrote that "every mail" brought letters telling him he had "only so many days to live."
Shared with: `rights-movements` (the abolitionist campaign) · `slavery-freedom`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the penny press, 1833" -->
In 1833 Benjamin Day, a New York printer, started *The Sun* to bring work to his print shop. Most daily papers cost six cents. Day sold *The Sun* for one cent a copy, and boys sold it on the street. He printed crime stories and short reports from the police court. In 1835 he printed a made-up report that living creatures had been discovered on the Moon. Sales rose, and Day was criticized when readers learned it was false. By 1839 *The Sun* sold 50,000 copies a day. Day paid for the paper mostly by selling advertisements. By 1842 New York City had nine daily papers that cost one or two cents.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="elijah-lovejoy" name="Elijah Lovejoy" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Elijah Lovejoy
> **Who:** A white Presbyterian minister and newspaper editor who wrote against slavery and was shot dead by a mob while defending his press · **When and where:** St. Louis, Missouri, 1833 to 1836, and Alton, Illinois, 1836 to 1837

Elijah Lovejoy was born in Albion, Maine, on 9 November 1802. In 1833 he became editor of the *St. Louis Observer*, a Presbyterian weekly in St. Louis, Missouri, a state where slavery was legal. He wrote against slavery. In 1835 a group of leading men in St. Louis signed a letter asking him to tone down what he wrote. He printed a reply saying he had the right to publish his views.

On 28 April 1836 a white mob in St. Louis took Francis McIntosh, a free Black steamboat worker, out of the jail, chained him to a tree and burned him alive. Judge Luke Lawless refused to convict anyone and blamed abolitionists for stirring up McIntosh. Lovejoy attacked the judge in the *Observer*. In May 1836 he was driven out of St. Louis.

He moved his paper across the Mississippi River to Alton, Illinois, a free state. Men in Alton who supported slavery destroyed his press three times. They threw one press out of a second-floor window. On 6 November 1837 a fourth press arrived by steamboat. Lovejoy and his supporters stored it in a stone warehouse owned by Benjamin Godfrey and Winthrop Gilman.

On the night of 7 November 1837 a mob surrounded the warehouse. They said they would burn it and kill every man inside unless the press was handed over. About twenty men inside had guns. One of them shot and killed a man in the mob named Bishop. A man in the mob climbed a ladder to set the roof on fire. When Lovejoy stepped outside, men in the mob shot him five times, and he died moments later. He was 34. The mob destroyed the press and threw it into the river.

In January 1838 the city of Alton charged 12 of the men who had defended the press with riot. A jury found Winthrop Gilman not guilty, and the city attorney dropped the charges against the other eleven. On 19 January 1838 several men from the mob were tried for breaking into the warehouse and destroying the press. The jury found them not guilty. No one was ever charged with killing Lovejoy.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="elijah-lovejoy" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the telegraph, 1844, and who owned it" -->
In 1843 members of Congress voted Samuel Morse $30,000 to build a test telegraph line from Washington to Baltimore. On 24 May 1844 Morse sent the first message over it, "What hath God wrought," from the U.S. Capitol. Morse and his partners then tried to sell the patent to the federal government and to businessmen, and no one bought it. Morse hired Amos Kendall, the former Postmaster General, to run the business. Kendall sold the right to use Morse's patent to separate companies, one region at a time. By 1851 the census counted 75 telegraph companies with 21,147 miles of wire. Private companies owned the lines, not the government.
In 1846 the United States went to war with Mexico. Getting fast news of the war cost more than any one paper wanted to pay. Moses Yale Beach, the owner of *The Sun*, got the leading New York papers, six counting his own, to share the cost. That group grew into the New York Associated Press.
Shared with: `technology` (the telegraph as a machine, and Samuel Morse's story).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="frederick-douglass-publisher" name="Frederick Douglass" movie="Becoming Frederick Douglass (2022)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Frederick Douglass
> **Who:** A man who escaped slavery in Maryland and started his own newspaper so that Black Americans could speak for themselves · **When and where:** Rochester, New York, from 1847
> **Movie:** Becoming Frederick Douglass (2022), a PBS documentary directed by Stanley Nelson about his life

Frederick Douglass was born enslaved in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818. He escaped on 3 September 1838 and began speaking against slavery alongside William Lloyd Garrison. In 1845 he published the story of his life. He then gave speeches across Britain and Ireland, and the money from that tour paid to start his newspaper.

Douglass split with Garrison over how to end slavery. Garrison relied on persuading people that slavery was wrong. Douglass came to believe that political action, such as voting and passing laws, could also attack slavery. He believed Black Americans had to lead the fight for their own freedom. On 3 December 1847 he published the first issue of the *North Star* in Rochester, New York. Its motto was "Right is of no sex, Truth is of no color, God is the Father of us all, and we are brethren." The paper was four pages long and came out every week. It had more than 4,000 subscribers in the United States, Europe and the West Indies.

On the front page Douglass said the paper would "attack SLAVERY in all its forms and aspects." It also printed news for free Black families in the North. Its first printer and publisher was William Cooper Nell, a Black writer from Boston.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="frederick-douglass-publisher" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1800-1850" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1850-1900" order="07" chapter="news-communication" label="1850 to 1900" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1850 to 1900
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
From 1861 a telegraph wire crossed the continent, and by 1866 one company, Western Union, owned nearly all the telegraph lines in the country. During the Civil War, Northern papers sent dozens of reporters to the battlefields, and Union generals and cabinet members closed newspapers and arrested editors without trials. From 1863 the post office hired its first Black workers. White men in Memphis in 1892 and Wilmington, North Carolina, in 1898 drove Black editors out of town, and the Wilmington mob burned a Black-owned newspaper. In New York, Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst competed for readers with large headlines and some stories that were false. In 1896 the post office began carrying mail to farm families at their homes.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Pony Express and the wire across the continent, 1860 to 1861" -->
On 3 April 1860 William H. Russell and his partners started the Pony Express, which carried mail on horseback about 2,000 miles from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California. Riders changed horses every 10 to 15 miles and covered 75 to 100 miles a day. The first run took ten days. In March 1861 riders carried President Abraham Lincoln's first inaugural address across in 7 days and 17 hours. The company charged up to $5 for half an ounce of mail, when ordinary postage was ten cents or less, and it still lost money. On 24 October 1861 workers finished the first telegraph line across the continent. Two days later the Pony Express shut down.
Shared with: `transportation` (the route and the riders) · `native-nations` (the land the route crossed).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="news of the Civil War, 1861 to 1865" -->
Newspapers in the North and the South were very unequal in 1861. In 1860 the South had fewer than 10 percent of the country's print shops. It had 70 of the country's 387 daily papers, and they sold only about 10 percent of all daily copies. On the day after Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in April 1861, the *New York Herald* printed 135,000 copies, about as many as all the South's daily papers together. The South had few paper mills and no factory that made printing presses, and only about 20 Southern daily papers were still printing when the war ended.
The *New York Herald* alone kept more than 40 reporters with the armies. Reporters sent short reports by telegraph and wrote longer ones on trains. After the Battle of Antietam in September 1862, George W. Smalley of the *New York Tribune* wrote his story on a train to New York, and the *Tribune* had it on the streets two mornings after the battle. The Associated Press, a group of New York papers that shared news, served only the North, so Southern publishers started their own Press Association in 1862.
Cameras of the time could not capture action, and photographs could not be copied quickly. Weekly papers such as *Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper* and *Harper's Weekly* sent artists to draw the battles. Engravers carved the drawings into blocks of wood for printing, and readers saw the pictures within about a week.
Shared with: `war` (the battles and the dead) · `art` (the photographers and the artists).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="editors arrested and papers closed, 1861 to 1864" -->
The First Amendment says Congress shall make no law "abridging the freedom ... of the press." During the Civil War, Union officers and Lincoln's cabinet shut papers down anyway, mostly without any court. From April 1861 Lincoln's officials censored reporters' telegraph messages to and from Washington, which means they read them and cut out what they did not want printed. Soldiers arrested editors and closed their presses, and military courts sent some editors south into the Confederacy.
Secretary of State William Seward had an editor of the *Freeman's Journal* arrested for what he printed. The editor was held for 11 weeks and let go without a trial. Secretary of War Edwin Stanton let a military governor destroy the office of the *Sunday Chronicle* in Washington. In Canton, Ohio, a mob wrecked the office of the *Stark County Democrat* after its editor, Archibald McGregor, printed words that his opponents called treason, and a year later soldiers arrested him without saying what the charge was. In 1863 General Ambrose Burnside closed the *Chicago Times*, a Democratic paper. Lincoln overturned Burnside's order. He said he was "embarrassed" that his general had not weighed the needs of the Union against "the Liberty of the Press."
In May 1864 two New York reporters printed a fake proclamation, signed with Lincoln's name, calling for a much larger draft of soldiers. They did it to change the price of gold. Lincoln ordered General John A. Dix to arrest the editors of the *New York World*, which had printed it, and to seize the paper's offices. He withdrew the order once it was clear the two reporters had forged the proclamation.
Shared with: `government-politics` (Lincoln and wartime power) · `war`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the first Black postal workers, 1863 to 1869" -->
From 1802 to 1865 federal law barred anyone but "free white persons" from carrying the mail. In early 1863 John Palfrey, the postmaster of Boston, hired William Cooper Nell as a clerk. He was the first Black American known to hold a job in the federal government. The rule for mail carriers ended in 1865. In June 1869 James Christian began delivering mail in Richmond, Virginia, the first Black letter carrier on record in the United States. He was hired by Richmond's postmaster, Elizabeth Van Lew, who had spied for the Union during the war.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="william-cooper-nell" name="William Cooper Nell" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### William Cooper Nell
> **Who:** A Black writer and printer from Boston who printed Frederick Douglass's first newspaper and became the first Black American known to work for the federal government · **When and where:** Boston and Rochester, New York, 1840s to 1874

William Cooper Nell grew up in Boston. In the 1840s he went to Rochester, New York, and worked for nearly two years with Frederick Douglass. He was the first printer and publisher of Douglass's newspaper, the *North Star*.

In 1844 Nell and other Black Bostonians asked the Boston School Committee to let Black children attend the city's public schools with white children. Nell kept sending petitions and holding meetings for 11 years. In 1855 the governor of Massachusetts signed a law that banned schools from turning children away because of race. The same year, Nell published a 396-page book, *The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution*, about Black Americans who had fought for independence.

In early 1863, during the Civil War, Boston's postmaster, John Palfrey, hired Nell as a clerk in the Boston Post Office. Palfrey had also worked against slavery and worked for newspapers. Nell was the first Black American known to hold a job in the federal government. At that time federal law still said that only white people could carry the mail. Nell worked at the post office until he died in 1874.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="william-cooper-nell" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="one company owns the telegraph, 1866 to 1900" -->
In the 1850s dozens of companies ran telegraph lines, and they merged into a few large ones. In 1866 Western Union bought its last two big rivals and ended up with more than 90 percent of the country's telegraph business. The economic historian Tomas Nonnenmacher calls it the country's first nationwide industrial monopoly. Members of Congress brought bills to regulate it or to have the government buy the lines in almost every session, and Western Union's lobbyists blocked nearly all of them. From 1867 to 1900 the number of telegrams it carried rose from 5.8 million a year to 63.2 million, and the average price of a telegram fell from $1.09 to 30 cents. For every dollar customers paid, about 30 to 40 cents was profit.
By the late 1800s the New York Associated Press, run by a few New York papers, held what the American Antiquarian Society calls a news monopoly. Newspaper owners in Chicago and other Western cities formed a rival group, and in 1892 they started a new national Associated Press.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the telephone, 1876 to 1900" -->
Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876. He offered the patent to Western Union for $100,000, and the company turned it down. In 1900 the United States had about 1.36 million telephones, about 18 for every 1,000 people. That means fewer than 2 Americans in 100 had one. Nearly all calls, 97 out of every 100, were local calls within one town.
Shared with: `technology` (the telephone as a machine).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="newspapers in Chinese, 1854 and 1855" -->
Before the Civil War there were already American newspapers in German, French, Spanish, Polish, Swedish, Norwegian, Hawaiian and other languages. Chinese was harder to print, because it has thousands of characters instead of an alphabet. The first Chinese-language paper in the country, *Golden Hill's News*, came out in San Francisco in 1854 and lasted a few months. The second, *The Oriental*, began there on 4 January 1855, edited by William Speer, a Presbyterian minister. Its printers drew the characters on stone with a grease pencil and printed from the stone. It closed in 1857, and no other Chinese paper was tried until the 1870s.
Shared with: `immigration`.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="nellie-bly" name="Nellie Bly" movie="Escaping the Madhouse: The Nellie Bly Story (2019)" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Nellie Bly
> **Who:** A newspaper reporter who pretended to be mentally ill so she could report from inside New York City's asylum for women · **When and where:** Pittsburgh, 1885 to 1887, and New York City, 1887 to 1895
> **Movie:** Escaping the Madhouse: The Nellie Bly Story (2019), a Lifetime television film that its makers describe as a fictionalized account

Nellie Bly was the pen name of Elizabeth Cochran, born in Cochran's Mills, Pennsylvania, on 5 May 1864. In 1885 the *Pittsburgh Dispatch* printed an article called "What Girls Are Good For," which said they were not good for much. She wrote an angry letter to the editor, and he hired her. She wrote about working girls and poor neighbourhoods in Pittsburgh.

In 1887 she went to work for Joseph Pulitzer's *New York World*. For her first big story she acted as if she were insane until doctors sent her to the city asylum for women on Blackwell's Island. She stayed ten days. When she arrived, nurses undressed her in front of other patients. A patient scrubbed her with soft soap, and then three buckets of ice-cold water were poured over her head. She saw 52 women tied together by leather belts locked around their waists and fixed to one long rope. She watched a nurse named Grady and other nurses slap a patient named Urena Little-Page, bang her head and choke her. The finger marks stayed on the woman's throat all day. Other patients told Bly that the nurses beat them if they complained.

Bly's reports ran in the *World* and then as a book, *Ten Days in a Mad-House*. A grand jury investigated the asylum. Bly wrote that New York City then set aside $1,000,000 a year more than before to care for people in its asylums.

In November 1889 the *World* sent Bly to go around the world faster than the hero of the novel *Around the World in Eighty Days*. She did it in 72 days, 6 hours, 11 minutes and 14 seconds. The *World*'s contest to guess her time drew nearly a million entries. She died in New York on 27 January 1922.
<!-- hb-story:end slug="nellie-bly" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="ida-b-wells-news-communication" name="Ida B. Wells" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Ida B. Wells
> **Who:** A Black newspaper editor in Memphis who counted lynchings, printed what she found and was driven from her city for it · **When and where:** Memphis, Tennessee, 1889 to 1892, and New York City, 1892

Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Holly Springs, Mississippi, on 16 July 1862. By 1892 she was an editor and part owner of the *Free Speech*, a Black newspaper in Memphis, Tennessee.

On 9 March 1892 a white mob took three Black men, Thomas Moss, Calvin McDowell and a third man named in different sources as Will Stewart or Henry Steward, out of the Memphis jail and killed them. The three ran the People's Grocery, a store that took business from a white-owned store nearby. No one was ever charged. Wells wrote in the *Free Speech* that Black people should leave Memphis. Thousands did, and those who stayed stopped riding the streetcars.

Wells began to study lynchings, the killing of people by mobs without any trial. She used the lists the *Chicago Tribune* printed each year. In 1892 she wrote that mobs had killed 728 Black people in the previous eight years. Only one-third of them had even been accused of raping a white woman, which was the reason usually given for lynching. Her list included "the boy Will Lewis," hanged in Tullahoma, Tennessee, "for being drunk and 'sassy' to white folks," and a fifteen-year-old girl hanged in Louisiana.

On 21 May 1892 the *Free Speech* printed her editorial saying that white Southerners' claim that Black men raped white women was a lie. Wells was in New York. White men in Memphis held a meeting at the Cotton Exchange and sent a group to find the paper's editors, and Wells later wrote that they would have lynched them if they had found them. The business manager, J. L. Fleming, fled the city. Letters and telegrams warned Wells she would be hurt if she came home. Creditors, people the paper owed money to, took over the office and sold the press and type. Two major reference pages say a mob burned or smashed the office. Wells's own account says creditors sold it.

Wells stayed in the North. On 25 June 1892 the *New York Age*, a Black newspaper in New York, printed most of her account under the name "Exiled." Black women in New York and Brooklyn held a meeting at Lyric Hall on 5 October 1892 and raised the money to print it as a pamphlet, *Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases*. In 1895 she published *A Red Record*, 100 pages of lynching counts and the reasons mobs gave.
Shared with: `rights-movements` (her campaign against lynching, story `ida-b-wells-rights-movements`) · `crime-justice` (lynching).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="ida-b-wells-news-communication" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Rural Free Delivery, 1896" -->
From 1863 people in cities had their mail brought to their homes for free. Farm families still had to travel to a post office to get letters and newspapers. In 1890 about 41 million Americans, 65 percent of the population, lived in the country. Postmaster General John Wanamaker argued that rural people needed the information in newspapers. After members of Congress set aside $40,000 for a test, postal officials began Rural Free Delivery on 1 October 1896 at Charles Town, Halltown and Uvilla in West Virginia. Within a year 44 routes ran in 29 states. Rural families sent more than 10,000 petitions asking for routes. Rural delivery became permanent on 1 July 1902, with about 8,500 rural carriers.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
