Crowds of white young men carrying baseball bats and bricks beat Black people as they left the pool. About 12 people were hurt, and police arrested 7 or 8 people. The sources read do not name the attackers. The city then separated the pools by race again (Wikipedia. Encyclopedia MDPI, search summary).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="radio, comic books and the movies" -->
- In 1931 the radio show *Little Orphan Annie* went national. Children mailed seals from the sponsor's drink, Ovaltine, to get a badge for decoding a secret message at the end of each show. *The Lone Ranger* began on a Detroit radio station in 1933 (search summaries).
- On Saturdays many children spent the afternoon at the movies. In Muncie, Indiana, at least half the children at Saturday matinees stayed five or six hours. In a working-class part of New Haven, Connecticut, more than half the children went twice a week or more. Researchers in the 1930s found children choosing movies over outdoor games (Richard Butsch, 2001). From 1929 to 1933 researchers paid by a private foundation, the Payne Fund, ran 13 studies of what movies did to children (Wikipedia).
- Superman first appeared in a comic book in 1938. A publishers' survey in 1944 found that 95 of every 100 boys and 91 of every 100 girls aged 6 to 11 read comic books, about 12 a month. A comic book cost 10 cents (Toronto Metropolitan University Library exhibit).
- In 1940 Sterling North, a newspaper book editor in Chicago, wrote that comic books were "badly drawn, badly written and badly printed" and a strain on children's eyes and nerves. People in some towns burned comic books in the 1940s (Comic Book Legal Defense Fund).
- In 1935 Parker Brothers began selling the board game Monopoly. It grew out of *The Landlord's Game*, which Lizzie Magie patented in 1904 (British Library, search summary).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1900-1950" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1950-2000" order="09" chapter="sports-play" label="1950 to 2000" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1950 to 2000
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In 1969 almost half of American children in kindergarten through eighth grade walked or biked to school. In 1995 about 45 percent went by car, and time-diary studies found children spending more time in organized sports and lessons and less in free play. Little League kept girls out from 1951 until a court case in 1974. After Title IX became law in 1972, the number of girls playing high-school sports rose from about 294,000 to about 2.7 million by 1999. Television networks paid to show football, and the first Super Bowl in 1967 drew about 51 million viewers. Boxing officials took Muhammad Ali's title after he refused the draft in 1967, and US Olympic officials sent Tommie Smith and John Carlos home from the 1968 Games after they protested on the medal stand. From 1972 children could play video games for a quarter in arcades, and from 1977 on home consoles.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="kathryn-johnston" name="Kathryn Johnston" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Kathryn "Tubby" Johnston
> **Who:** A girl who played a season of Little League baseball dressed as a boy, which led Little League officials to ban girls · **When and where:** Corning, New York, 1950
- In the spring of 1950 Kathryn Johnston played baseball with boys on a sandlot near her home in Corning, New York. She wanted to play on a Little League team, and Little League teams took only boys (Little League. StoryCorps).
- She tucked her hair under a cap and went to the tryouts with her brother. In her own words: "I ran into my brother's room, got a pair of his slacks, put on a baseball cap and signed up as Tubby Johnston." She took the name from a comic strip, *Little Lulu* (StoryCorps, 2018. Little League).
- She made the King's Dairy team and played first base. Then she told the coach she was a girl. He said she was good enough to make the team, so she could stay. More people came to the games once word got out (Little League).
- In 1951 Little League officials made a rule that no girls could play. Johnston said, "It's known as the Tubby Rule because I was the reason why they put that rule in" (StoryCorps).
- In 1974, after the ban ended, she wrote to Little League's headquarters. The officials checked her story and wrote back that she was the first girl to play in Little League (Little League).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="kathryn-johnston" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="who could play Little League" -->
- In 1955 the Cannon Street YMCA in Charleston, South Carolina, entered its all-star team of 14 Black boys in the city Little League tournament. The 61 other teams, all white, withdrew rather than play them. Cannon Street won the city and state titles because no one would play them. At the regional tournament, officials ruled that a team that had not won on the field could not go on, and Little League's president upheld the ruling. The white leagues' managers left Little League and started their own segregated league. Little League officials invited the Cannon Street boys to watch the Little League World Series. The crowd chanted "Let them play," and the boys watched from the stands (Bruce Markusen, National Baseball Hall of Fame).
- One of the players, John Rivers, said in 2023: "So we didn't talk about it. So it tells me how painful it was." His father was serving in the Army in Korea at the time (Markusen).
- In 1972 Maria Pepe, 12, pitched three games for a Little League team in Hoboken, New Jersey. Little League officials told the Hoboken league to drop her or lose its right to be part of Little League, and the league dropped her. The National Organization for Women took her case to New Jersey's civil rights office. On 7 November 1973 Sylvia Pressler, the officer hearing the case, ruled that keeping girls out broke the state's law (Little League. Wikipedia).
- Little League officials lost their appeal. In December 1974 President Gerald Ford signed a law changing Little League's federal charter to let girls play. That year nearly 30,000 girls signed up for Little League's new softball program (Little League. Wikipedia).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="who could swim" -->
- In 1963 officials in Jackson, Mississippi, closed four public swimming pools and gave up a fifth, which the YMCA then ran for white people only, rather than let Black residents swim in them. On 14 June 1971 five Supreme Court justices ruled that closing the pools to everyone was lawful. Four justices disagreed (Wikipedia, *Palmer v. Thompson*).
- On 18 June 1964 Black and white protesters jumped into the pool of the Monson Motor Lodge in St. Augustine, Florida. The manager, James Brock, poured acid into the water while they were in it. A photograph of him doing it ran in newspapers across the country (Wikipedia).
- The historian Jeff Wiltse found that when Black Americans won the right to use city pools, many white swimmers left them for private pools, and cities spent less on public pools (Wiltse, 2018 interview).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="television and the Super Bowl" -->
- On 15 January 1967 the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles in the first championship game between the two pro football leagues. Tickets cost $6 to $12. Two TV networks, CBS and NBC, showed the game to about 51 million viewers, and a 30-second advertisement cost $42,000. From the third game, in 1969, the official name was the Super Bowl. Lamar Hunt, who founded one of the leagues, took the name from his children's toy, a Super Ball (Wikipedia).
- In November 1990 Arizona's voters refused to make Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday a state holiday. NFL owners then moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Tempe, Arizona, to Pasadena, California (Pima County Public Library, via `holidays`).
- On 22 February 1980 the US Olympic hockey team, college players with an average age of 21, beat the Soviet Union 4 to 3 at Lake Placid, New York. Two days later they won the gold medal (Wikipedia).
- In December 1969 Curt Flood, a St. Louis Cardinals outfielder, refused to be traded. He wrote to baseball's commissioner: "I do not feel that I am a piece of property to be bought and sold irrespective of my wishes." He lost in the Supreme Court in 1972. In 1975 an arbitrator, Peter Seitz, ruled that players whose contracts ran out could sign with any team (The Henry Ford. Wikipedia, search summaries).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="muhammad-ali" name="Muhammad Ali" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Muhammad Ali
> **Who:** The heavyweight boxing champion whose title was taken from him when he refused to be drafted · **When and where:** Louisville, Rome, Atlanta and Zaire, 1942 to 2016
- Cassius Clay was born in Louisville, Kentucky, on 17 January 1942. When he was 12, someone stole his bicycle. A police officer, Joe Martin, taught boxing, and he started Clay in the sport (Wikipedia).
- He won an Olympic gold medal in Rome in 1960. On 25 February 1964, at 22, he beat Sonny Liston for the heavyweight title. He then joined the Nation of Islam and took the name Muhammad Ali (Wikipedia).
- In April 1967 he refused to be drafted into the Army during the Vietnam War. The New York State Athletic Commission and the World Boxing Association, which ran boxing, took away his title. He could not box for more than three years (Wikipedia). Shared with: `war` (the draft case and the Supreme Court).
- He fought again on 26 October 1970. On 28 June 1971 the Supreme Court overturned his conviction. On 30 October 1974 he beat George Foreman in Zaire, in Africa, and won the title back (Wikipedia).
- He retired in 1981. In 1984 he said he had Parkinson's syndrome, a disease of the brain that makes the body shake and move slowly. He died on 3 June 2016 (Wikipedia).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="muhammad-ali" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the 1968 Olympic protest" -->
- On 16 October 1968 Tommie Smith won the 200 meters at the Olympic Games in Mexico City in a world-record 19.83 seconds. John Carlos came third. During the US national anthem both men raised a fist in a black glove. They stood in black socks without shoes to stand for poor people. Peter Norman of Australia, who came second, wore their protest group's badge (Wikipedia).
- Smith said they were protesting "the lack of black assistant coaches," the taking of Muhammad Ali's title, and the "lack of access to good housing" (Wikipedia).
- Avery Brundage, the head of the International Olympic Committee, said he would ban the whole US track team unless the two men were punished. US Olympic officials suspended them and sent them out of the Olympic Village. Writers at *Time* magazine and the sports commentator Brent Musburger criticized them. At home they and their families got death threats (Wikipedia. History.com).
- Both men later played pro football. Smith became a college track coach and teacher. Australian officials left Norman off their 1972 Olympic team although his times qualified him. Australia's parliament apologized to him in 2012, six years after he died (History.com).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="girls' sports after Title IX" -->
- Title IX became law on 23 June 1972. In the 1971-72 school year 294,015 girls and 3,666,917 boys played high-school sports. Girls were about 7 of every 100 players. By 1977-78 about 2.1 million girls played. In 1999-2000 2,675,874 girls and 3,861,749 boys played, and girls were about 41 of every 100 (National Federation of State High School Associations). Shared with: `education` and `rights-movements` (the law itself).
- In 1979 Yale University had 13 women's varsity teams. Yale's own archivists found that they got only a small part of the money and equipment that the men's teams got (Yale Library, 2022).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="chris-ernst" name="Chris Ernst" movie="A Hero for Daisy (1999, documentary about her)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Chris Ernst
> **Who:** The captain of Yale's women's rowing team, who led a protest that won the team a locker room · **When and where:** Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, 1972 to 1977
- Chris Ernst grew up in Scituate, Massachusetts. In high school she beat boys at arm wrestling to win time on the gymnastics equipment (Wikipedia).
- She began rowing at Yale in her second year and was captain of the women's team by her last year. The showers at the boathouse were for the men's team only. After practice the women waited on a bus in wet clothes while the men showered. Then they rode back to campus to wash (Wikipedia. Yale Library).
- In March 1976 the 19 women on the team wrote "Title IX" on their bodies and went into the office of Joni Barnett, the director of women's sports. They took off their clothes, and Ernst read a statement that began, "These are the bodies Yale is exploiting" (Wikipedia).
- A *New York Times* reporter called the university that day. Yale officials set up a trailer with running water and planned a $250,000 addition to the boathouse. By 1977 the women had a locker room (Yale Library. Wikipedia).
- Ernst later won a world rowing title in 1986. In 1980 she became the first woman in the plumbers' union in New Haven (Wikipedia).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="chris-ernst" -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="billie-jean-king" name="Billie Jean King" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### Billie Jean King
> **Who:** A tennis champion who started the Women's Tennis Association and beat Bobby Riggs in the "Battle of the Sexes" · **When and where:** Long Beach, California, and Houston, Texas, 1943 to 1973 and after
- Billie Jean King was born in Long Beach, California, on 22 November 1943. At 11 she switched from softball to tennis after her parents suggested a more "ladylike" sport. She saved $8 to buy her first racket and took free lessons on the city's public courts (Wikipedia).
- As a young player she was kept out of a group photograph because she wore shorts her mother had sewn instead of a tennis dress (Wikipedia).
- In June 1973 she founded the Women's Tennis Association, a group that speaks for women players (Wikipedia).
- On 20 September 1973 she beat Bobby Riggs, a 55-year-old former champion, 6-4, 6-3, 6-3, at the Houston Astrodome. About 30,000 people watched in the stadium, and about 50 million watched on television in the United States. She won $100,000 (Wikipedia).
- She won 39 Grand Slam titles in singles and doubles. In 2009 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom (Wikipedia).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="billie-jean-king" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="arcades and home consoles" -->
- In August 1972 Nolan Bushnell and Allan Alcorn of Atari put a test machine of their game *Pong* in a bar in Sunnyvale, California. The owner soon called them because the machine had stopped. Its coin box was jammed full of quarters. Atari sold *Pong* from 29 November 1972, at 25 cents a game, and sold more than 8,000 machines by the end of 1974. Sears sold a home version for $98.95 at Christmas 1975 (Wikipedia).
- The Atari home console came out in 1977 for $199. Atari sold about 30 million by 1992. In 1980 the arcade game *Pac-Man* came to North America. Its designer, Toru Iwatani, wanted "a nonviolent, cheerful game" that women would play, and by 1981 its machines had taken in more than $1 billion in quarters (Wikipedia).
- By 1982 there were about 30 million game consoles in the country, and about 35 million households had children aged 6 to 16. Then sales fell from about $3.2 billion in 1983 to about $100 million in 1985. Atari's managers buried about 728,000 unsold game cartridges in a landfill in New Mexico. Sales rose again after Nintendo began selling its console in the United States in 1985. Nintendo's Game Boy, which could be carried anywhere, came out in 1989 for $89.95 (Wikipedia).
- In 1971 three student teachers from Carleton College, Don Rawitsch, Bill Heinemann and Paul Dillenberger, made *The Oregon Trail* for a Minneapolis junior high class. Later versions were played in schools across the country (Wikipedia). Shared with: `migration` (the trail itself) · `storytelling-evolution` (games as story).
- In December 1993 and March 1994 Senators Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl held hearings on violent video games such as *Mortal Kombat*. The game companies then set up the Entertainment Software Rating Board, which from September 1994 put age ratings on games (Wikipedia).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what a child's afternoon looked like" -->
- In 1969, 47.7 percent of children in kindergarten through eighth grade usually walked or biked to school, and 12.2 percent were driven. In 1995, on the day of a national survey, 44.9 percent went by car and about 14 percent walked or biked (Noreen McDonald and others, *American Journal of Preventive Medicine*, 2011, using US Department of Transportation surveys).
- Researchers Sandra Hofferth and John Sandberg compared diaries of how children spent their time in 1981 and 1997. Children spent more time in school, day care, sports and art lessons, and less time in free play, housework and watching television (Hofferth, 2009).
- More mothers worked for pay. In 1975, 47 of every 100 mothers with children under 18 were in the labor force. By 2000 it was 73 of every 100 (US Bureau of Labor Statistics).
- In the fall of 1995 about 6.9 million children aged 5 to 14, 18 of every 100, regularly looked after themselves for part of the week, about six hours a week on average. About 15 million children that age took part in sports, lessons or clubs (US Census Bureau).
- In a survey of adults, about 4 of every 100 born in the 1950s had played on a private club or travel team as children. For those born in the 1990s it was 13 of every 100 (Chris Knoester and Chris Bjork, reported by Ohio State University, 2025).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Iroquois Nationals" -->
- In 1983 Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) people formed a national lacrosse team, and the Grand Council of the Haudenosaunee approved it. The International Lacrosse Federation turned the team down for 1986 and accepted it as a member nation in 1988. In 1990 the team played in the world championship in Perth, Australia (Wikipedia).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1950-2000" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="2000-today" order="10" chapter="sports-play" label="2000 to Today" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 2000 to Today
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In 2014-15, 73 of every 100 American teenagers had a smartphone. By 2022 it was 95 of every 100, and by 2025 four in ten teenagers said they were online "almost constantly." Children played games such as Minecraft, Fortnite and Roblox online, often with people they had never met. Fewer walked to school or played outdoors, and organized sport cost families hundreds of dollars a season. Researchers measured these changes and disagreed about what they did to children. In sport, doctors found a brain disease in football players. A team doctor who had sexually abused more than 500 girls and women was sentenced to prison for the rest of his life. College athletes won the right to be paid, and the United States hosted the 2026 World Cup.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="phones and social media" -->
- The Pew Research Center surveys American teenagers aged 13 to 17. In 2014-15, 24 of every 100 said they were online "almost constantly." In 2022 it was 46, and in 2025 it was 40. In 2025 about 90 of every 100 teenagers used YouTube, and about 60 used TikTok (Pew Research Center, 2022 and 2025).
- In a 2021 survey by Common Sense Media, children aged 8 to 12 spent an average of 5 hours 33 minutes a day on screens for fun, not counting schoolwork. Teenagers aged 13 to 18 spent 8 hours 39 minutes. That was 49 minutes more a day for the younger group than in 2019, and 1 hour 17 minutes more for the older group. Children often used two screens at once, so two hours of screen time could fit into one hour of the day (Common Sense Media, 2021).
- On 23 May 2023 the US Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, the country's top public health doctor, warned about social media. He wrote that "we do not yet have enough evidence to determine if social media is sufficiently safe for children and adolescents." He cited a study of 6,595 children aged 12 to 15. Those who spent more than 3 hours a day on social media had double the risk of symptoms of depression and anxiety. He asked lawmakers to set safety rules and age limits (Surgeon General's Advisory, 2023).
- In 2023 Florida lawmakers passed a law banning students' phone use during class time. By January 2026, 26 states banned phones for the whole school day, from the first bell to the last (Ballotpedia, reported by *Newsweek*). By July 2026 at least 39 states and Washington, DC, required schools to ban or limit phones (*Education Week*). Shared with: `technology` (the phone itself) · `education` (the school day) · `news-communication` (the feed).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="games played online, and with strangers" -->
- *Minecraft*, a game of building and digging in a world of blocks, came out in 2011. By 2023 it had sold more than 300 million copies, more than any other video game. *Fortnite* came out in 2017. In its best-known version, up to 100 players land on an island and fight until one is left. *Roblox* opened in 2006. Its players build games and play each other's. Company officials say half of all American children under 16 play it each month (Wikipedia).
- All three games cost little or nothing to start. The companies sell game money, V-Bucks in Fortnite and Robux in Roblox, which players buy with real money to spend on costumes and other items (Wikipedia).
- In December 2022 officials of the Federal Trade Commission, the federal agency that enforces laws protecting buyers, charged Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite. They said Fortnite collected information on children under 13 without their parents' permission. They said the game's settings turned on live voice and text chat for children, and the game matched "children and teens with strangers." Children had been "bullied, threatened, harassed," some of them sexually. Epic employees had asked for the chat to be turned off for children as early as 2017. Under the settlement Epic Games paid $520 million (FTC, 19 December 2022).
- In January 2026 Roblox's managers began requiring every player to prove their age, with an ID or a video scan, before chatting. They made the change after lawsuits accused the company of letting adults use the game to sexually exploit children (Wikipedia).
- Esports are video game competitions played for prize money. The first Fortnite World Cup, in July 2019 in New York City, paid $30 million in prizes. About 40 million players tried to qualify (Wikipedia). Shared with: `storytelling-evolution` (games as story) · `marketplace` (what is sold inside games) · `technology` (the machines).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="kyle-giersdorf" name="Kyle Giersdorf" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Kyle "Bugha" Giersdorf
> **Who:** A 16-year-old who won the first Fortnite World Cup and $3 million · **When and where:** Arthur Ashe Stadium, New York City, 28 July 2019
- Kyle Giersdorf was born on 30 December 2002. His father, who also played video games, got him started on Fortnite. He played under the name "Bugha," a nickname from his grandfather (Wikipedia).
- In March 2019 he joined an esports team called Sentinels. That summer he qualified for the first Fortnite World Cup, out of about 40 million players who tried (Wikipedia).
- On 28 July 2019 he played six games against 99 other finalists in Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York City. He scored 59 points. The second-place player scored 33. He won $3 million, more than any other Fortnite player has won in all their games put together (Wikipedia).
- Hours after he won, someone broke into his Twitter and Twitch accounts and posted in his name (Wikipedia).
- He later became a streamer on Twitch, a website where players show their games live to viewers (Wikipedia).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="kyle-giersdorf" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what is measured" -->
- In 1969, 47.7 of every 100 children in kindergarten through eighth grade walked or biked to school. In 2009 it was 12.7 (Noreen McDonald and others, 2011, US Department of Transportation surveys). In 2017, 9.6 of every 100 students aged 5 to 17 usually walked and 1.1 biked (Kontou and others, 2020, from the 2017 survey).
- Sandra Hofferth, a researcher at the University of Maryland, compared time diaries of children aged 6 to 12. Their free time fell from about 57 hours a week in 1981 to about 48 in 2003. From 1997 to 2003 the share who played a sport on the diary days fell from 76 to 60 of every 100. The share who spent time outdoors fell from 16 to 10 (Hofferth, 2009).
- In 2023, 55 of every 100 children aged 6 to 17 played on a sports team or took sports lessons (National Survey of Children's Health, reported by the Aspen Institute). Children from richer homes played more. In 2024 the gap between children from homes earning under $25,000 a year and homes earning $100,000 or more was 20 percentage points (Sports and Fitness Industry Association).
- In 2022 the average parent spent $883 in a season on one child's main sport. Soccer averaged $1,188 and basketball $1,002. Travel to games cost more than any other part. The richest families spent about four times as much as the poorest (Aspen Institute and Utah State University survey).
- In 2012, 15 of the 50 states had rules that recommended or required a daily recess (Bridging the Gap, 2013).
- Doctors measure obesity with a child's weight against height. From 1971 to 1974, 5 of every 100 children aged 2 to 19 had obesity. From 2017 to 2020 it was about 20 of every 100, about 14.7 million children (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention). Shared with: `health` (obesity as illness).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="what researchers disagree about" -->
- ADHD stands for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Doctors diagnose it when a child has trouble paying attention, or is overactive and acts without thinking, badly enough to cause problems at home and at school. In national surveys of parents, 7.8 of every 100 children aged 4 to 17 had been diagnosed with ADHD in 2003 and 11 of every 100 in 2011 (Visser and others, 2014). In 2022 it was 11.4 of every 100 children aged 3 to 17, about 7.1 million (Danielson and others, 2024, for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention).
- The rules for diagnosing ADHD changed during these years. In 2013 the American Psychiatric Association's manual allowed a diagnosis when symptoms began by age 12 instead of age 7 (Wikipedia). The researchers who counted the diagnoses wrote that the rise "could also reflect better detection" and more awareness, not only more children with ADHD (Visser, 2014. Danielson, 2024).
- In 2018 researchers at the University of Southern California, led by Chaelin Ra and Adam Leventhal, followed 2,587 high-school students in Los Angeles County for two years. Students who used more kinds of digital media many times a day reported more ADHD symptoms later. Among students who used none that often, 4.6 of every 100 reported the symptoms. Among students who used 7 kinds, 9.5 of every 100 did. The researchers called the link "modest" and wrote that more research was needed "to determine whether this association is causal" (*JAMA*, 2018).
- In 2019 the researchers Orben and Przybylski studied surveys of 355,358 teenagers in the United States and Britain. They found that technology use explained "at most 0.4%" of the differences in teenagers' well-being (*Nature Human Behaviour*, 2019).
- In 2024 the psychologist Jonathan Haidt wrote in *The Anxious Generation* that phone and social media companies had "rewired childhood" by taking the place of play and time with friends. The psychologist Candice Odgers answered in the journal *Nature* that his claim "is not supported by science." She wrote that studies had found "a mix of no, small and mixed associations" (*Nature*, 29 March 2024).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="football and the brain" -->
- Mike Webster played center for the Pittsburgh Steelers for 15 seasons and won four Super Bowls. After he retired he had memory loss and depression, and at times he lived in his pickup truck. He died on 24 September 2002, aged 50 (Wikipedia).
- Bennet Omalu, a doctor in Pittsburgh who examines bodies to find out why people died, studied Webster's brain. In 2005 he and other doctors described a brain disease they called chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. Repeated blows to the head cause it. It damages memory, mood and behavior and can lead to dementia, the loss of the ability to think and remember. Doctors can find it only by examining the brain after death (Wikipedia).
- Members of the NFL's own brain injury committee wrote in 2006 asking the journal to take back Omalu's paper. From 2003 the committee had published papers saying concussions caused no lasting harm in NFL players. A league official later told members of Congress that "there is a link between football-related head trauma and chronic traumatic encephalopathy" (Wikipedia).
- More than 4,500 former players sued the NFL, saying the league had hidden the dangers. In April 2015 Judge Anita Brody approved a settlement to pay retired players with brain illness. It had no cap and was expected to cost more than $1 billion over 65 years. Until 2021 the tests used to judge players' claims assumed Black players started with lower thinking skills, which made it harder for them to be paid. League officials ended that practice in June 2021 (Wikipedia).
- By 2023 researchers at Boston University had found CTE in 345 of the 376 former NFL players whose brains they studied. The researchers warned that families who suspected the disease were the ones who gave the brains, so the figure does not mean that 92 of every 100 players have CTE (Boston University). Enrollment in Pop Warner youth football fell 9.5 percent from 2010 to 2012 (Wikipedia).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the team doctor who abused gymnasts" -->
- Larry Nassar was the doctor for the US women's gymnastics team from 1996 to 2014 and for athletes at Michigan State University from 1997 to 2016. During appointments he said were treatment, he put his ungloved finger into girls' vaginas and called it therapy for pain. Sometimes a parent was in the room and could not see what he was doing. More than 500 girls and women were abused (Wikipedia, USA Gymnastics sex abuse scandal).
- Athletes said they told Michigan State employees about him as early as 1997. The gymnastics coach Kathie Klages was accused of pressuring gymnasts to stay quiet. Michigan State officials looked into a complaint in 2014 and let him keep treating patients. In June 2015 a coach, Sarah Jantzi, reported him to USA Gymnastics. Its president, Steve Penny, told FBI agents in Indianapolis. They did not open a formal investigation. In July 2021 the Justice Department's inspector general reported that the agent, W. Jay Abbott, failed to act and later lied about it. At least 70 more girls and women were abused after the FBI was told (Wikipedia, citing the inspector general's report).
- In September 2016 reporters at the *Indianapolis Star* published the story. Nassar pleaded guilty to federal child pornography crimes and to sexually assaulting girls in two Michigan counties. Judges sentenced him to 60 years in federal prison and to 40 to 175 years and 40 to 125 years in Michigan. Before he was sentenced, more than 200 women and girls spoke about his abuse in court over nine days (Wikipedia).
- The heads of USA Gymnastics, Michigan State and the US Olympic Committee resigned. His dean at Michigan State, William Strampel, was convicted of neglect of duty. Michigan State paid $500 million to 332 victims in 2018. USA Gymnastics and the US Olympic and Paralympic Committee paid $380 million in 2021. The Justice Department paid $138.7 million in 2024 to victims who sued over the FBI's failure (Wikipedia).
- On 15 September 2021 the Olympic gymnasts Simone Biles, McKayla Maroney, Maggie Nichols and Aly Raisman told senators how FBI agents had handled their reports. Raisman said it "was like serving innocent children up to a pedophile on a silver platter" (Wikipedia).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="rachael-denhollander" name="Rachael Denhollander" movie="Athlete A (2020, documentary about the scandal)" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Rachael Denhollander
> **Who:** A former gymnast who was the first woman to accuse Larry Nassar in public · **When and where:** Kalamazoo and Lansing, Michigan, 2000 to 2018
- Rachael Denhollander was born in Kalamazoo, Michigan, on 8 December 1984. She was a club gymnast. In 2000, when she was 15, she saw Larry Nassar for back pain. He sexually abused her on five visits (Wikipedia).
- At least seven other girls and women had told someone about Nassar over twenty years before she spoke. Her complaint was the first that led to action (Wikipedia).
- By 2016 she was a lawyer. In August 2016 she reported Nassar to the Michigan State University police and filed a complaint with the university. On 20 September 2016 the *Indianapolis Star* printed her accusation, and hundreds of other women came forward (Wikipedia).
- She spoke last at both of his sentencing hearings in January and February 2018. She asked the judge, "How much is a little girl worth?" She answered that "everything is what these survivors are worth" and asked for the longest sentence the law allowed. Judge Rosemarie Aquilina called her "the bravest person I have ever had in my courtroom" (Wikipedia).
- *Time* magazine named her one of its 100 most influential people of 2018. In 2019 she published a book about the case, *What Is a Girl Worth?* (Wikipedia).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="rachael-denhollander" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="college athletes paid" -->
- Until 2021, rules written by NCAA officials let college athletes receive only scholarships and school costs. In September 2019 California's governor, Gavin Newsom, signed the first state law letting college athletes be paid for their name, image and likeness. That means payment for ads and appearances that use who they are (Wikipedia).
- On 21 June 2021 all nine Supreme Court justices ruled against NCAA limits on education benefits in *NCAA v. Alston*. Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that antitrust law, which forbids businesses from agreeing to hold down pay, "should not be a cover for exploitation of the student athletes." From 1 July 2021 NCAA officials let athletes be paid for their name, image and likeness (Wikipedia).
- In 2020 Grant House, a swimmer at Arizona State, and Sedona Prince, a basketball player, sued the NCAA. On 6 June 2025 Judge Claudia Wilken approved a settlement. Athletes who played from 2016 to 2024 will share about $2.8 billion over ten years. From the 2025-26 school year each college may pay its athletes directly, up to about $20.5 million a year. Eight women athletes appealed, saying most of the money would go to men who played football and basketball (WilmerHale, 2025).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="betting on games" -->
- A 1992 federal law barred states from allowing betting on sports, except in Nevada and three other states. On 14 May 2018 the Supreme Court struck it down in *Murphy v. NCAA*, a case New Jersey brought. By September 2023, 38 states and Washington, DC, allowed sports betting. Americans bet $121 billion with licensed sportsbooks in 2023 (Wikipedia, citing the American Gaming Association).
- On 17 April 2024 NBA Commissioner Adam Silver banned Jontay Porter, a Toronto Raptors player, for life. League investigators found that Porter told a bettor about his health before a game, then left that game after three minutes saying he felt ill. An associate had bet $80,000 that Porter would play poorly. Porter had also placed at least 13 bets on NBA games (NBA).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="transgender athletes" -->
- In March 2020 Idaho's governor, Brad Little, signed the first state law keeping transgender girls and women off girls' and women's teams. A transgender girl is a girl who was counted as a boy at birth. By June 2026, 27 states had passed such laws (Wikipedia. Supreme Court).
- On 5 February 2025 President Donald Trump signed an order titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports." The next day NCAA officials limited women's college events to athletes counted as female at birth (Wikipedia).
- On 30 June 2026, in *West Virginia v. B.P.J.* and *Little v. Hecox*, six Supreme Court justices ruled that Title IX lets schools keep separate teams "defined by biological sex." Three justices disagreed in part. B.P.J., named in court only by her initials, had wanted to run on the girls' cross-country and track teams at her school (Supreme Court). Shared with: `rights-movements` (the rights fight and the other rulings).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="protest and equal pay" -->
- In 2016 the San Francisco 49ers quarterback Colin Kaepernick knelt during the national anthem before games to protest police brutality, meaning violence by police officers, and racial inequality. After the season no team signed him. He accused NFL owners of agreeing among themselves to keep him out and settled with the league in February 2019 (Wikipedia).
- In April 2016 five players on the US women's soccer team, Hope Solo, Carli Lloyd, Alex Morgan, Megan Rapinoe and Becky Sauerbrunn, filed a complaint that they were paid less than the men. The women won the World Cup in 2019. In February 2022 US Soccer officials settled for $24 million. In May 2022 they signed contracts that pay the women and the men equally (Wikipedia).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the Haudenosaunee Nationals" -->
- The Haudenosaunee have issued their own passports since 1927. In 2010 British officials refused to accept them for the world lacrosse championship in England and told the players to travel on US or Canadian passports. The players refused and did not play (Wikipedia).
- The team won third place at the world championships of 2014, 2018 and 2023. After Olympic officials added lacrosse to the 2028 Los Angeles Games, they said only countries with a national Olympic committee could enter. In January 2025 President Joe Biden and Canada's prime minister, Justin Trudeau, asked them to let the Haudenosaunee play under their own flag (Wikipedia). Shared with: `native-nations` (sovereignty and the passports).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="the 2026 World Cup" -->
- The United States, Canada and Mexico hosted the men's soccer World Cup from 11 June to 19 July 2026. It was the first with 48 teams. The United States hosted 78 of the 104 games in 11 cities. About 6.8 million people went to the games, more than at any World Cup before. Spain beat Argentina 1 to 0 in the final at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey. The US team lost to Belgium 4 to 1 in the round of 16 (Wikipedia).
- Tickets for the final started at $6,730. For the first time, FIFA officials raised prices as demand grew (Wikipedia).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="2000-today" -->

<!-- hb-chapter id="37" slug="holidays" title="Holidays" part="9" mode="outline" -->

# Chapter 35: Holidays

<!-- hb-note -->
**Status:** eras 1 to 5 RESEARCHED 2026-09-27 (T-273a). Eras 6 to 8 RESEARCHED 2026-09-28 (T-273b). Eras 9 and 10 RESEARCHED 2026-09-28 (T-273c), facts current to that date.
**Angle:** American holidays and celebrations: how the country marks its days and how that changed.
**Keep out:** sports (`sports-play`). Religion itself (`religion`).
**Workspace:** `workspace/holidays.md` (shared events, famous-names checklist, verify-queue, thin eras, open questions)
**Research bank:** `research/research-holidays.md`. The Thanksgiving myth is also the `how-we-know` Afterword's subject. Coordinate rather than duplicate.
Editor's in-development note, not part of the final book. The parser strips it.
<!-- /hb-note -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="before-1500" order="01" chapter="holidays" label="Before 1500" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## Before 1500
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
The nations here marked the year with ceremonies. Each one fell at a set point in the year: when a star rose, when the sun reached the end of its path along the horizon, when the corn ripened, or when the salmon came back up the river. Many of them gave thanks for food as it came in: the maple sap, the strawberries, the first ripe corn, the first salmon. Nobody here wrote in an alphabet before 1500, so the written descriptions come from later. Outsiders wrote some of them in the 1700s. The nations wrote others themselves, and many of the ceremonies are still held.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Giving thanks through the year in the Northeast" -->
- The Onondaga Nation, one of the Haudenosaunee nations of what is now New York, lists seven ceremonies in its year: Midwinter, Maple Sap, Planting, Bean, Strawberry, Green Corn and Harvest (Onondaga Nation website).
- Men and women called Faith Keepers decide when each ceremony happens. They go by the seasons and the moon, so the dates move from year to year. Midwinter lasts 21 days, with thanks given for different things on each day (Onondaga Nation).
- Haudenosaunee people open and close their gatherings with the Thanksgiving Address, which they call the Words That Come Before All Else. The speaker thanks the people, the earth, the waters, the fish, the plants, the food plants, the medicine plants and more, one by one. Each part ends with the words "Now our minds are one" (Mohawk version, English translation published 1993, Six Nations Indian Museum and the Tracking Project, via NMAI).
- Nancy Eldredge, a Nauset Wampanoag writer, wrote in 1998 that Wampanoag people held thanksgiving ceremonies in early spring for a good growing season and in the fall for the harvest. They also gave thanks for the strawberries and the cranberries as they ripened, through the thirteen moons of the year (Plimoth Patuxet Museums).
- The Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah), on Martha's Vineyard, still holds Cranberry Day each October. The day opens with a greeting at sunrise, and people pick the cranberries, share a meal and set aside a portion for the elders (Aquinnah Wampanoag tribal website).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The Green Corn Ceremony in the Southeast" -->
- The Muscogee (Creek) and other nations of the Southeast held the Green Corn Ceremony in midsummer, when the first corn was ripe. It lasted four or eight days. Men fasted for about a day and a half to two days (Eric Bowne, Encyclopedia of Alabama).
- People put out every fire in the town and lit a new one in the town square. Each household then relit its own fire from it. The towns forgave every crime except murder (Encyclopedia of Alabama). `crime-justice` tells the forgiveness as law.
- English traders called the ceremony the busk, from the Creek word *puskita*, which means a fast (Britannica) (unconfirmed: search summary only).
- William Bartram, a naturalist from Philadelphia, traveled through Creek towns in the 1770s and published his account in 1791. He wrote that the Creek had a feast for almost every month of the year, and that the busk, in August, was the main one. Each town held its own busk when its own corn was ripe (Bartram, *Travels*, pages 509 to 510, Documenting the American South).
- Bartram wrote that families first made new clothes, pots and pans. They swept their houses and the whole town, piled up worn-out clothes and the old grain, and burned the pile. After three days of fasting, on the fourth morning, the high priest made a new fire by rubbing dry wood together, and every house took its fire from it. The women then brought in the new corn, and the town danced in the square at night (Bartram).
- The written accounts come from the 1700s: James Adair, William Bartram and Benjamin Hawkins (Encyclopedia of Alabama). Creek and Yuchi towns in Oklahoma still hold the ceremony at their stomp grounds (Encyclopedia of Alabama).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Watching the sun in the Southwest" -->
- In the Pueblo towns of the Southwest, a Sun-priest watches where the sun comes up on the horizon each morning. His sightings set the planting calendar and the dates of the ceremonies (High Altitude Observatory, National Center for Atmospheric Research).
- Among the Hopi of northern Arizona, the ceremonial year opens with the Soyal ceremony at the winter solstice in December, the shortest day of the year. A ceremony follows in each village about once a month until the Niman, or Home Dance, in late July (High Altitude Observatory).
- `religion` tells the buildings lined up with the sun, at Chaco Canyon and Cahokia. This chapter tells the calendar.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The First Salmon Feast on the Columbia River" -->
- The Yakama, Umatilla, Warm Springs and Nez Perce peoples of the Columbia River hold a First Salmon Feast each spring before the fishing season opens (Columbia River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission).
- Their tradition says that when the Creator was about to bring people onto the earth, Salmon offered his body to feed them. At the feast people bless and drink water first, then eat the salmon and the other foods (CRITFC).
- The feast at the Celilo Longhouse in Oregon is held on the second weekend of April (CRITFC).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Makahiki in Hawaii" -->
- In Hawaii, which became part of the United States much later, the new year began when the Pleiades, a small group of stars the Hawaiians call Makaliʻi, rose at sunset in late October or early November (Kamehameha Schools, Kaʻiwakīloumoku).
- The Hawaiian historian David Malo, born about 1793, wrote that four months were set aside for the Makahiki season (Malo, *Hawaiian Antiquities*, quoted by Images of Old Hawaiʻi).
- Priests carried an image of the god Lono around each island. At the edge of each land division, the local chief handed over the taxes for the king: pigs, taro, sweet potatoes, feathers, kapa cloth and mats (Malo). Chiefs were forbidden to make war during the season (Kamehameha Schools).
- People held races, boxing and wrestling matches, and games of skill during Makahiki (Kamehameha Schools).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="before-1500" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1500s" order="02" chapter="holidays" label="The 1500s" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## The 1500s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Spanish and French colonists brought the Christian church year to a few places on the coast of Florida and along the Rio Grande. That year was built around Sundays, Easter, Christmas and the feast days of saints. The colonists named places after those days, and they held church services of thanks when they landed. Several towns today call one of those services the "first Thanksgiving." None of them became a yearly holiday. Across almost all the rest of the land, the Native nations kept their own ceremonies, and Europeans saw very few of them.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Places named for holy days" -->
- Juan Ponce de León reached the coast of what is now Florida in early April 1513, during the Easter season. He named the land *la Florida* after *Pascua Florida*, the Spanish name for the Easter feast (Wikipedia and University of South Florida FCIT) (unconfirmed: search summary only).
- Pedro Menéndez de Avilés sighted the Florida coast on 28 August 1565, the feast day of Saint Augustine. He named his town St. Augustine after the saint (Florida Museum of Natural History timeline).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Services of thanks on the Florida coast, 1564 and 1565" -->
- French Protestants, called Huguenots, built Fort Caroline near what is now Jacksonville in June 1564. Their leader, René de Laudonnière, wrote that on 30 June 1564 he had them gather on the beach and sing and pray to thank God for their safe arrival (Laudonnière, published 1586, quoted by the National Huguenot Society via Heidelblog). Timucua people lived on that land.
- On 8 September 1565, Menéndez and about 800 Spanish settlers came ashore at Seloy, a Timucua town. Father Francisco López de Mendoza Grajales said a Mass of thanksgiving. Afterward, the priest wrote, Menéndez "had the Indians fed and dined himself" (National Park Service, Castillo de San Marcos, and Jacksonville History Center).
- The Park Service calls this Mass and meal "the first community act of religion and thanksgiving in the first permanent European settlement," 56 years before Plymouth. It also says the day "did not become the origin of a national annual tradition" (NPS, quoting historian Michael Gannon).
- Two weeks later, on 20 September 1565, Menéndez's soldiers captured Fort Caroline and killed most of the men there. At an inlet south of St. Augustine they then killed French survivors who had surrendered: 111 in late September and 134 in October, by the Park Service's count. The Spanish named the inlet Matanzas, which means "slaughters" (NPS, Fort Matanzas). In a letter of 15 October 1565, Menéndez told King Philip II that he killed them because they "spread the Lutheran sect," meaning the Protestant faith, and because they had settled "without permission of Your Majesty" (Menéndez, letter, Early Visions of Florida). `war` tells the killings in full.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="A thanksgiving on the Rio Grande, 1598" -->
- Juan de Oñate led about 500 colonists, with about 7,000 cattle and other animals, north across the Chihuahuan Desert to colonize New Mexico. The crossing took about 50 days. They reached the Rio Grande near what is now San Elizario, Texas (Texas Almanac, adapted by Mike Kingston).
- On 30 April 1598, Oñate ordered a day of thanksgiving. Franciscan friars said Mass. The colonists ate game they had hunted and fish that local Native people brought them. Oñate then read out a claim to all the land along the river for King Philip II of Spain (Texas Almanac). `storytelling-evolution` tells the play performed that day.
- Some Texans claim this day as the first Thanksgiving. Others made the same claim for a feast held by Francisco Vázquez de Coronado's men in Palo Duro Canyon in 1541, and historians later questioned that one (Texas Almanac).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="A harvest dance at Secotan, 1585" -->
- In July 1585 the English artist John White visited Secotan, an Algonquian town in what is now North Carolina, and painted a large ceremony there. Men and women from other towns danced around a ring of carved wooden posts. Thomas Hariot, who traveled with White, wrote that each visitor had marks on his back to show which town he came from (Encyclopedia Virginia, "A Festive Dance," British Museum painting).
- Encyclopedia Virginia states that the ceremony was "perhaps connected to the corn harvest." The surviving records do not say what the ceremony was called or what it meant to the people of Secotan.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1500s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1600s" order="03" chapter="holidays" label="The 1600s" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## The 1600s
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
English colonists in the 1600s did not agree about holidays. In Virginia they kept Christmas as people did in England. In New England the Puritan leaders kept Sundays and nothing else on a fixed date. They called fast days for prayer in times of drought or war, and days of thanksgiving, spent in church, after rain, a harvest or a victory. In 1659 the men of the Massachusetts Bay General Court made keeping Christmas a crime. The Plymouth harvest meal of 1621, which Americans now call the first Thanksgiving, was a three-day feast with about ninety Wampanoag men. Nobody called it the first Thanksgiving until 1841.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Christmas and thanksgiving in Virginia" -->
- In the winter of 1608 to 1609, bad weather kept John Smith and his men at Kecoughtan, a Powhatan town where Hampton, Virginia, is now, for six or seven days over Christmas. Smith wrote that they "were never more merry," and that the people of Kecoughtan fed them oysters, fish, meat, wild birds and bread (Smith, *Generall Historie*, 1624, Book 3).
- On 4 December 1619 the ship *Margaret* landed 35 settlers and Captain John Woodlief at Berkeley Hundred on the James River. The land belonged to the Weyanock people, part of the Powhatan alliance (Wikipedia, "Weyanoke people") (unconfirmed: search summary only). The London investors who sent the settlers had ordered that the day of arrival "shall be yearly and perpetually kept holy as a day of Thanksgiving to Almighty God" (Berkeley Plantation). The settlers held the service.
- On 22 March 1622, Powhatan men attacked the English settlements along the James River. They killed eleven people at Berkeley (Berkeley Plantation). Virginians began holding the Berkeley thanksgiving again in 1958 (Berkeley Plantation).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The harvest meal at Plymouth, 1621" -->
- The Plymouth colonists built their town in 1620 on the site of Patuxet, a Wampanoag town. Most of the Patuxet people had died in an epidemic between 1616 and 1619 (Marr and Cathey, via `health` bank). Of the 102 people who came on the *Mayflower*, 53 were alive by the fall of 1621: 24 men, 5 women and 24 children and teenagers (Plimoth Patuxet Museums).
- Two people who were there wrote about the harvest that fall. Edward Winslow wrote a letter in December 1621, printed in London in 1622 in a book now called *Mourt's Relation*. William Bradford, the governor, wrote a history of the colony years later (Pilgrim Hall Museum).
- Winslow wrote that after the harvest, Governor Bradford sent four men hunting birds "so we might after a special manner rejoice together." Massasoit, the leader the English called the Wampanoag's "greatest king," came "with some ninety men." The English "entertained and feasted" them for three days. The Wampanoag men went out, killed five deer, and gave them to the governor and other leaders (Winslow, in *Mourt's Relation*, 1622, Pilgrim Hall Museum).
- Massasoit's name was Ousamequin. Plimoth Patuxet Museums states that the Wampanoag understood an alliance as a spoken agreement sealed by giving gifts, and that the three days may have been a show of strength and a renewal of the alliance the two sides had made that year.
- Neither Winslow nor Bradford called the meal a thanksgiving. To the colonists, a thanksgiving was a day of prayer in church. In 1841 a Boston minister, Alexander Young, printed Winslow's letter with a note: "This was the first Thanksgiving, the harvest festival of New England." Plimoth Patuxet Museums names that note as the first time anyone called the 1621 meal the first Thanksgiving. New Englanders had already credited the Pilgrims with starting their yearly thanksgiving. The *Salem Gazette* of 28 November 1816 called it the festival that "our Pilgrim forefathers" began (Jane Hampton Cook, GenealogyBank, 2020). `how-we-know` tells how the story grew after 1841.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="william-bradford-holidays" name="William Bradford" movie="" kind="famous" status="verified" -->
### William Bradford
> **Who:** Governor of Plymouth Colony, who wrote the colony's history, *Of Plimoth Plantation*. · **When and where:** Plymouth, in what is now Massachusetts, 1621 to 1623.
- In the fall of 1621 Bradford, as governor, sent four men to hunt birds for the harvest meal. The Wampanoag men who came with Massasoit gave him and other leaders five deer (Winslow, in *Mourt's Relation*, Pilgrim Hall Museum).
- On Christmas Day 1621, Bradford called the men of Plymouth out to work. Most of the men who had just arrived on the ship *Fortune* said that working on Christmas went against their consciences, and Bradford let them stay behind (Bradford, *Of Plimoth Plantation*).
- At noon he found them playing games in the street. Some were throwing a heavy bar, and some were playing stool-ball, a bat-and-ball game. Bradford took their equipment away. He told them they could keep the day by praying at home, but that nobody would play in the streets while others worked (Bradford).
- In the summer of 1623 a drought was killing Plymouth's corn. Bradford wrote that the colonists held a day of humiliation, which meant fasting and praying. When rain came and the harvest was good, they held a day of thanksgiving (Bradford).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="william-bradford-holidays" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Fast days and thanksgiving days in New England" -->
- The Puritan leaders of New England called a fast or a thanksgiving when something happened, and each was a day of church services. At Plymouth in 1623, the colonists fasted during a drought and held a thanksgiving after the rain came (Bradford).
- In Massachusetts Bay, the General Court and the church elders set these days. In September 1638 the Court asked the elders of each church to keep a day of thanksgiving on the last Thursday of the eighth month (October, because their year began in March) for the ships that had arrived safely and for the harvest (*Records of the Massachusetts Bay*, vol. 1).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Thanksgiving days after the Pequot War, 1637" -->
- On 26 May 1637, Connecticut colonists under Captain John Mason, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, set fire to the fortified Pequot town at Mystic and shot the people who tried to escape. Between 400 and 700 Pequot were killed, most of them old men, women and children, by the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation's own history (`war` bank). `war` and `native-nations` tell the war.
- In early June 1637, the Massachusetts Bay Court set 15 June as a day of thanksgiving in the churches (*Records*, vol. 1). John Winthrop, the governor, wrote in his journal that a day of thanksgiving was kept in all the churches "for the victory obtained against the Pequods" (Winthrop's journal, quoted in search summaries) (unconfirmed: search summary only).
- In August 1637 the Court asked the magistrates to work out a day of thanksgiving with the church elders for the soldiers' return, with the soldiers to be feasted by their towns. It then ordered that 12 October 1637 be kept as a day of thanksgiving to God for "subdewing the Pecoits, bringing the soldiers in safety," for the end of a church meeting, and for good news from Germany (*Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay*, vol. 1, 1853).
- Some writers say the 1637 thanksgiving was the first official Thanksgiving Day and the start of the modern holiday. William B. Newell, a Penobscot man and a former head of anthropology at the University of Connecticut, said the first Thanksgiving Day was proclaimed in 1637 to mark the killing of 700 Pequot men, women and children who had gathered for their Green Corn ceremony (quoted on many websites) (unconfirmed: search summary only). The records of the attack do not mention a ceremony. The historian Jeremy Bangs disputes Newell's claim (History News Network, 2005). The court records show that Massachusetts Bay held thanksgiving days for the victory over the Pequot. They also show that the colonists held many other thanksgiving days, before 1637 and after it, for ships, harvests and rain.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Christmas made a crime, 1659 to 1681" -->
- On 11 May 1659 the General Court of Massachusetts Bay passed a law that anyone found "observing any such day as Christmas or the like, either by forbearing of labor, feasting, or any other way" would pay a fine of five shillings (Mass Moments, Mass Humanities).
- The Puritans said nothing in the Bible told Christians to keep Christmas. The minister Increase Mather called Christmas "a profane and superstitious custom" (Mass Moments).
- King Charles II's officials in London pressed Massachusetts to bring its laws in line with England's. In 1681 the Court repealed the Christmas law (*Records of the Massachusetts Bay*, vol. 5, 1681 entries, page 339). Most people in Massachusetts still did not celebrate Christmas for many years after that (Mass Moments).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Ceremonies banned in New Mexico" -->
- From 1656 to 1665, the Franciscan leader in New Mexico, Alonso de Posada, forbade the Pueblo people's own ceremonies. He ordered the friars to go into the kivas, the Pueblos' underground rooms for worship, and to burn the masks and destroy the sacred objects there (Dennis Zotigh, NMAI, via `religion` bank).
- In 1675 Governor Juan Francisco Treviño had 47 Pueblo religious leaders arrested for "sorcery." Three were hanged. A fourth killed himself. The rest were whipped in public and put in prison, until Pueblo men came to Santa Fe and forced Treviño to free them. One of the men freed was Po'pay, who led the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 (Zotigh, Newberry Library, via `religion` bank). `religion` and `native-nations` tell the revolt.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1600s" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1700-1750" order="04" chapter="holidays" label="1700 to 1750" state="thin" progress="researched" -->
## 1700 to 1750
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
From 1700 to 1750 the colonies still had no holiday in common. Each colony kept its own days, and many of them came from Britain. New England governors printed orders for days of thanksgiving and days of fasting, and nobody was allowed to work on those days. Boys and young men in Boston marched through the streets on Pope's Night every 5 November. In New York, enslaved and free Black people gathered for Pinkster, a spring holiday brought by the Dutch. In New England, Black communities began choosing their own governors and kings.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Thanksgiving and fast days by the governor's order" -->
- A New England governor, with the advice of his council, named each thanksgiving and each fast day. Printers published his order as a large sheet called a broadside, and the order called on people to go to worship (Library of Congress, Printed Ephemera Collection).
- On 14 October 1721, Governor Gurdon Saltonstall of Connecticut set Wednesday, 8 November, as a thanksgiving. His order named the colony's escape from the smallpox then spreading in Boston, the peace, and that year's harvest (Library of Congress, Saltonstall proclamation, 1721).
- Governor William Shirley of Massachusetts ordered a thanksgiving for Thursday, 14 August 1746, because the Duke of Cumberland's army had defeated a rebellion in Scotland. The order ended: "all servile Labour is prohibited on said Day" (Library of Congress, Shirley proclamation, 1746). Servile labor meant ordinary work.
- Massachusetts governors also ordered fast days, such as the public fasts proclaimed by Jonathan Belcher in 1734 and by Spencer Phips in 1745 (Library of Congress).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pope's Night in Boston" -->
- In the early hours of 5 November 1605, guards in London found Guy Fawkes under the Parliament building with fuses and matches. He and a group of other English Catholics had planned to kill King James I when Parliament opened. Parliament then passed a law for a public thanksgiving every year on 5 November (Royal Museums Greenwich). In New England the day became Pope's Night, and crowds burned figures of the Pope (Old North Church).
- In Boston, young men and older boys built wagons with moving figures of the Pope, the Devil and other enemies of the king. They dressed up, paraded through town, and asked homeowners for money. The night ended with a meal outdoors and a bonfire (J. L. Bell, *Boston 1775*).
- Boston had two gangs, from the North End and the South End. Each built its own Pope wagon and tried to capture the other's. The winners burned the captured figures on Copp's Hill or on the Common (J. L. Bell). The fights between the gangs began in the 1740s (Wikipedia, "Pope Night") (unconfirmed: search summary only).
- The printer Isaiah Thomas, born in 1749, remembered the crowds blowing on conch shells, beating on the sides of houses with clubs, and shouting "North end forever" or "South end forever." As a boy he got too close to a wagon and was knocked out by a brick (Isaiah Thomas, *History of Printing in America*, second edition, quoted by J. L. Bell).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pinkster in New York" -->
- Pinkster is the Dutch name for Pentecost, a Christian feast held seven weeks after Easter. Dutch settlers brought it to New Netherland in the 1620s (Historic Hudson Valley).
- The oldest known written account of Pinkster, in the *New-York Weekly Journal* of March 1737, describes a gathering in the fields outside New York City and African-style musical instruments (Historic Hudson Valley).
- Enslavers gave enslaved men and women several days off at Pinkster. Many walked from farms into the city to see family members who lived apart from them. They sold berries, herbs, sassafras bark, drinks and oysters, and spent the money at the celebration (Historic Hudson Valley).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Black governors and kings in New England" -->
- Black communities in New England held their own elections for a governor or a king. In Connecticut and Rhode Island, where white men elected their governor, Black men elected a Black governor. In Massachusetts and New Hampshire, where the king of England appointed the governor, Black men elected a king (New England Historical Society).
- The first known name comes from New London, Connecticut, in 1749. A man named Hercules served as governor there, and he is known from his wife Florio's gravestone (Connecticut State Library). Black election days in Massachusetts may have begun earlier, in 1741 (Wikipedia, "Negro Election Day") (unconfirmed: search summary only).
- In Connecticut the Black election came the day after the white men's election, and the celebration went on for a week. People dressed in their best clothes, some borrowed from the people who enslaved them. The enslaver of the man elected was expected to pay for food, decorations and liquor (Connecticut State Library).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1700-1750" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1750-1800" order="05" chapter="holidays" label="1750 to 1800" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1750 to 1800
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
Americans began celebrating their independence on its first anniversary, 4 July 1777, and within a few years they also celebrated George Washington's birthday. Neither was a national holiday yet. In 1781 Massachusetts became the first state to make the Fourth of July an official holiday. Congress, and then President Washington, asked Americans to keep days of thanksgiving on dates they chose, but nobody set a yearly date. Older customs changed too. Boston's leaders turned Pope's Night into a protest against British taxes, and General Washington banned it in his army. In the South, enslaved people got a few days off at Christmas, while those who worked in the house served their enslavers' guests.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Pope's Night, 1764 to 1775" -->
- On Pope's Night, 5 November 1764, one of the Pope wagons in Boston ran over and killed a boy named Brown. Sources give his age as five to nine. The surviving records do not give his first name or say who was driving. The death happened early in the day, and the parades and the fight between the gangs went on that night (J. L. Bell, *Boston 1775*).
- In August 1765, crowds in Boston protesting the Stamp Act, a British tax on printed paper, used the Pope's Night customs: figures hanged and burned, marches and bonfires. They broke into three or four large houses and smashed the furniture. Ebenezer Mackintosh, a shoemaker and captain of the South End gang, led crowds at the protests (J. L. Bell).
- On 5 November 1765, Mackintosh and Henry Swift, captain of the North End gang, agreed to march together instead of fighting. Wealthy merchants paid for a dinner for them (J. L. Bell).
- On 5 November 1775, General George Washington ordered his soldiers not to keep "that ridiculous and childish Custom of burning the Effigy of the pope." He wrote that the Americans were asking Catholic Canadians to join them, and that insulting their religion at such a time was wrong (Washington, General Orders, 5 November 1775, Founders Online). Pope's Night ended in Boston during the Revolution (Old North Church).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="The first Fourth of July, 1777" -->
- On 2 July 1776, the Continental Congress voted for independence. The next day John Adams wrote to his wife Abigail that the day "ought to be solemnized with Pomp and Parade, with Shews, Games, Sports, Guns, Bells, Bonfires and Illuminations from one End of this Continent to the other." Congress formally adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July, and Americans celebrate that date (Massachusetts Historical Society. National Park Service).
- In July 1776, crowds greeted the public readings of the Declaration with parades, bonfires and gunfire. The first planned Fourth of July celebrations came a year later, in Philadelphia and in Boston (Mount Vernon).
- In Philadelphia on 4 July 1777, the armed ships in the Delaware River were decorated with flags. At one o'clock each ship fired thirteen cannon, one for each state. That night bells rang, fireworks went up on the city's common, and people lit their windows (*Pennsylvania Evening Post*, 5 July 1777, quoted by Mount Vernon).
- In 1781 Massachusetts became the first state to make the Fourth of July an official state holiday (Mount Vernon).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="henry-wight-holidays" name="Henry Wight" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### Henry Wight
> **Who:** A Congregational minister and Revolutionary War veteran who started a Fourth of July celebration that has been held every year since. · **When and where:** Bristol, Rhode Island, 1785 to the 1820s.
- Henry Wight was born in Medfield, Massachusetts, on 26 May 1752. He left his studies at Harvard to serve in the Revolutionary War. One account says he served as a soldier, and another says he served as a surgeon (New England Historical Society. Rev War Bristol).
- In January 1785 the First Congregational Church of Bristol, Rhode Island, which had 36 members, hired him as its minister (New England Historical Society).
- Bristol stands on Mount Hope, Montaup in the Pokanoket language, where the Pokanoket Wampanoag lived and where Metacom had his base in King Philip's War. Metacom was killed there on 12 August 1676, in an ambush led by the English captain Benjamin Church. After the war four Boston merchants bought the land, as part of Plymouth Colony, and started the town (Wikipedia, "Bristol, Rhode Island"). `native-nations` tells the war.
- Bristol people had already fired cannon on the Fourth. In 1777 they fired 13 cannon at dawn, one for each state (New England Historical Society).
- In 1785, his first year in Bristol, Wight led the town's first Patriotic Exercises on the Fourth of July. He gave a speech that honored the veterans and celebrated the new country's freedoms (New England Historical Society. Bristol Fourth of July Committee).
- He was Bristol's minister for 43 years and spoke at the Fourth of July for about 40 of them (search summaries) (unconfirmed: search summary only). He died in 1837 (Rev War Bristol).
- Bristol has held the celebration every year since 1785. The town calls it the oldest continuous Fourth of July celebration in the United States. Its parade probably grew out of the walk to the Patriotic Exercises in the early 1800s (Bristol Fourth of July Committee. Town of Bristol).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="henry-wight-holidays" -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Thanksgiving days for the new country" -->
- After the American army forced a British army to surrender at Saratoga, New York, in October 1777, the Continental Congress set 18 December 1777 as a day of thanksgiving for the whole country. Samuel Adams, Richard Henry Lee and Daniel Roberdeau wrote the order (search summaries) (unconfirmed: search summary only). The date is from US House of Representatives History, Art and Archives.
- Congress also named days of fasting in 1775, 1776, 1778, 1779, 1780, 1781 and 1782, and days of thanksgiving in 1777, 1778, 1781 and 1783 (US House History).
- In 1789 Elias Boudinot, a member of the House of Representatives from New Jersey, asked Congress to request a day of thanksgiving for the new Constitution. Both houses agreed. On 3 October 1789, President George Washington named Thursday, 26 November 1789, as a day of thanksgiving (Mount Vernon).
- Washington sent his order to the state governors and asked them to announce it. On the day, he went to church at St. Paul's Chapel in New York City and sent beer and food to the men held in the city jail for their debts (Mount Vernon). Washington named another day of thanksgiving in 1795, to give thanks that the Whiskey Rebellion in western Pennsylvania was over (Mount Vernon). `drugs-alcohol` tells the rebellion and the army Washington sent against it. None of these became a yearly holiday.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Washington's birthday" -->
- On 22 February 1778, at the army's winter camp at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, soldiers gathered to wish Washington a happy birthday (Mount Vernon). Musicians from Proctor's artillery regiment played for him outside his quarters (National Park Service, via search summary) (unconfirmed: search summary only). In 1779 people in Milton, Massachusetts, held a public celebration of the day (Mount Vernon).
- Washington was born on 11 February 1731 by the old calendar. In 1752 Britain and its colonies changed to the calendar used today, and his birthday became 22 February 1732 (search summary of Mount Vernon and National Park Service pages) (unconfirmed: search summary only).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Christmas on the plantations" -->
- At Mount Vernon, George Washington's plantation in Virginia, most enslaved workers had four days off at Christmas. They used the days to rest and to visit family on Mount Vernon and on nearby plantations. Enslaved cooks, housemaids and waiters had more work than usual over Christmas, because the Washingtons had extra guests (Mary V. Thompson, Mount Vernon).
- Philip Vickers Fithian, a young tutor from New Jersey, spent Christmas 1773 at Nomini Hall, the Virginia plantation of Robert Carter. He wrote that guns fired all around the house woke him that morning (Fithian's journal, 25 December 1773).
- Before he was dressed, several enslaved men and boys came to his room to wish him a merry Christmas and to ask for a "Christmas Box," a small gift of money. They were Nelson, a boy who made his fire and blacked his shoes, a man who lit the schoolroom fire, Tom the coachman, and Dennis, a boy who waited at table. Fithian gave them five bits in all, about three shillings (Fithian).
- `slavery-freedom` tells what the Christmas days off meant for enslaved people in the 1800s. `drugs-alcohol` tells how enslavers used whiskey at Christmas.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Black governors in wartime Hartford, 1776" -->
- Black governors kept being elected in Connecticut through these years. In Hartford, London was governor in 1755 and was enslaved by Thomas Seymour. Quaw was governor in 1760 and was enslaved by George Wyllys, the secretary of the colony. Cuff was governor from 1766 to 1776 (Connecticut State Library).
- The governors had little power of their own. A Black governor had no power to punish a white person who wronged a Black person (Andy Piascik, Connecticut History).
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-story:start slug="john-anderson-black-governor" name="John Anderson" movie="" kind="ordinary" status="verified" -->
### John Anderson
> **Who:** An enslaved man who became Hartford's Black governor in 1776, in a dispute that white officials investigated as a possible plot. · **When and where:** Hartford, Connecticut, 1776 to 1780.
- In May 1776, white men in Connecticut elected Jonathan Trumbull governor again. Soon after, Cuff, the Black governor of Hartford, resigned and named John Anderson as governor in his place, without an election. A journal entry by a Hartford man, Major French, dated 11 May 1776, records it (Chris Menapace, Digital Farmington).
- Anderson was enslaved by Philip Skene, who had been a major in the British army. Skene was being held as a prisoner because the Americans suspected he was loyal to Britain (Menapace. Andy Piascik, Connecticut History).
- White people in Hartford feared that Skene planned to use Anderson to bring Black people over to the British side. A committee of the Connecticut government investigated (Menapace. Piascik).
- The two sources disagree on what the committee found. One says Skene had tried to pay voters, and that many Black people refused to back a Loyalist's slave. Skene told the committee it was done for amusement (Menapace). The other says the committee cleared Anderson but found that he had paid some Black people to support him, and that the government approved his four-year term (Piascik).
- Anderson served as governor until 1780 (Piascik).
<!-- hb-story:end slug="john-anderson-black-governor" -->
<!-- hb-time:end id="1750-1800" -->

<!-- hb-time:start id="1800-1850" order="06" chapter="holidays" label="1800 to 1850" state="full" progress="researched" -->
## 1800 to 1850
<!-- hb-zoom level="era" -->
In these years Christmas changed from a noisy street holiday into a day for families and children, and a poem printed in 1823 gave Americans their picture of St. Nicholas. Thanksgiving was still a New England day that each governor set. Sarah Josepha Hale, a magazine editor, began asking governors and presidents to make it one national day. Enslaved people in the South got a few days off at Christmas, and on New Year's Day many were hired out or sold away from their families. Free Black Americans made their own days of celebration: 1 January 1808, when bringing enslaved people from Africa became illegal, 5 July 1827 in New York, and 1 August after 1834. In 1811 Albany's city council banned Pinkster, the spring holiday of the Black people of the Hudson Valley.
<!-- /hb-zoom -->
<!-- hb-zoom level="span" label="Christmas becomes a children's day" -->
- In the early 1800s, Christmas in American towns still meant heavy drinking, begging from door to door and rowdy parades. Wealthier families and newspaper editors worked to turn it into a quiet family day centred on children (Mass Moments).
- On 23 December 1823 the *Troy Sentinel*, a newspaper in Troy, New York, printed a poem with no author's name, "Account of a Visit from St. Nicholas." It begins "'Twas the night before Christmas" and describes stockings hung by the chimney for St. Nicholas to fill (the newspaper page, Wikisource).
- Clement Clarke Moore, a New York professor, was named as the author in 1837 and put the poem in his own book in 1844. The family of Henry Livingston Jr., a New York farmer and poet, says he wrote it as early as 1808. The question has never been settled (St. Nicholas Center).
